be6b39a58e4fdfab.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Svalbard

A Norwegian archipelago governed under the Svalbard Treaty. Shown with the entry for Norway, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Under section 18 of the Norwegian Penal Code (2005), an otherwise punishable act is lawful when it is done to avert an unlawful attack, goes no further than necessary, and does not 'obviously' go beyond what is justifiable given how dangerous the attack is, what interest it violates and the attacker's guilt. The statute does not mention retreat, but because force must be 'necessary', a lawyer answering for the state youth-information service ung.no wrote in 2023 that if there were other ways to avert the attack, 'such as calling for help or running away', a killing cannot be claimed as self-defence; the Supreme Court's appeals committee has also upheld a conviction where the defendant had 'several alternative courses of action' and had partly provoked the fight (HR-2022-1377-U). Someone who goes too far can still be acquitted where 'special reasons' justify it, and the sentence can in any case be reduced (sections 80 and 81, as described by the national encyclopedia). Lawful self-defence is not just unpunished but lawful, so the Supreme Court held in 2018 (HR-2018-2427-A) that the defender cannot be ordered to pay damages when the attack was real.

At home

No separate home-defence rule was found; section 18 applies to attacks on persons and on property alike.

What the law says
Straffeloven (Penal Code 2005), § 18 første ledd (as quoted by the Supreme Court in HR-2022-1377-U)
En handling som ellers ville være straffbar, er lovlig når den a. blir foretatt for å avverge et ulovlig angrep, b. ikke går lenger enn nødvendig, og c. ikke går åpenbart ut over hva som er forsvarlig under hensyn til hvor farlig angrepet er, hva slags interesse som angrepet krenker, og angriperens skyld.

ae1d208fd1268805.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Finland

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Chapter 4, section 4 of the Finnish Criminal Code allows an act necessary to defend against an ongoing or imminent unlawful attack, unless it 'manifestly exceeds' what is justifiable when the nature and strength of the attack, the people involved and other circumstances are weighed as a whole. According to a 2022 peer-reviewed article citing the government bill (HE 44/2002) and Supreme Court case law, the mere fact that the defender could have escaped does not by itself make the defence unlawful, especially when the attacker is not a child or mentally ill person. The same article reports, however, that the courts of appeal often stress the defender's chance to flee or leave when judging whether the defence was justifiable. If the defence goes beyond the limits (excessive self-defence), the person is still exempt from liability when they could not reasonably have been expected to act otherwise, given the danger and suddenness of the attack.

At home

No separate home-defence rule in the Criminal Code; the general self-defence section applies.

What the law says
Criminal Code (Rikoslaki 39/1889), chapter 4, section 4 (515/2003) (unofficial English translation)
An act that is necessary to defend against an ongoing or imminent unlawful attack is permissible as self-defence, unless the act manifestly exceeds what is to be deemed justifiable when assessed as a whole, taking into consideration the nature and strength of the attack, the personal characteristics of the defender and the attacker, and the other circumstances. If the defence exceeds the limits of self-defence (excessive self-defence), the perpetrator is, nonetheless, exempt from criminal liability if the circumstances were such that the perpetrator could not have reasonably been expected to act otherwise, taking into consideration the dangerousness and unexpected nature of the attack and the situation also in other respects.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

0997adfdd927cab7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

France

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 122-5 of the Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. The defence must be simultaneous with the attack; a blow struck after the attacker has left is treated as ordinary violence. Neither art. 122-5 nor art. 122-6 mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Judges decide whether the defence was disproportionate; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes that an excessive response may lead to mitigating circumstances or a conviction for a lesser offence rather than full exoneration.

At home

Art. 122-6 of the Penal Code presumes self-defence for a person who acts "to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place", and against perpetrators of violent theft or looting. The presumption is rebuttable and does not cover daytime intrusions, which fall under the general rule of art. 122-5.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

b3bd2bc06d65c229.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Venezuela

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 65(3) of Venezuela's Penal Code, a person who acts in defence of their own person or rights is not punishable if there was an unlawful attack by the person harmed, the means used were necessary to prevent or repel it, and the defender did not sufficiently provoke it. Article 66 says that someone who exceeds the defence, or the means used, 'doing more than necessary', is punished with the normal penalty reduced by one to two thirds. The code does not mention retreat or contain a home-defence rule in the text found, and no Venezuelan court decision on retreat was found. The text used is the version published in Gaceta Oficial No. 5494 Extraordinario of 20 October 2000 (WIPO Lex copy); later reforms were not checked.

What the law says
Código Penal (Gaceta Oficial N° 5494 Extraordinario, 20 Oct. 2000), art. 65(3)
No es punible: [...] 3. El que obra en defensa de su propia persona o derecho, siempre que concurran las circunstancias siguientes: a Agresión ilegítima por parte del que resulta ofendido por el hecho. b. Necesidad del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla. c. Falta de provocación, suficiente de parte del que pretenda haber obrado en defensa propia
Código Penal (2000), art. 66
El que traspasare los límites impuestos por la Ley en el caso del número 1º del artículo anterior, y por la autoridad que dio la orden en el caso del número 2º del mismo, y el que se excediere en la defensa, o en los medios empleados para salvarse del peligro grave e inminente, haciendo más de lo necesario, será castigado con la pena correspondiente, disminuida desde uno a dos tercios. La pena pecuniaria se aplicará con disminución de la mitad.

bc644bcb6e716759.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Italy

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Article 52 of the Italian Penal Code exempts from punishment a person forced to act by the need to defend their own or another's right against a present danger of an unjust offence, 'provided that the defence is proportionate to the offence'. The code does not mention retreat, but the annotated code commentary on Brocardi.it reports that prevailing legal doctrine allows self-defence by someone who could have fled only where flight would itself expose them or others to harm equal to or greater than the harm caused by defending, so a safe escape is expected (the Latin maxim cited is 'commodus discessus', a convenient withdrawal). Inside a home or workplace, statutory presumptions introduced in 2006 and strengthened in 2019 (Law 26 April 2019 no. 36) treat the defence as proportionate and an intrusion with violence or threats as always justifying defence. If a person negligently exceeds the limits of self-defence, they are punished under the rules for negligent crimes (Article 55); since 2019 there is no punishment for excess in the home cases when the person acted in grave disturbance caused by the danger.

At home

Article 52(2)-(4) of the Penal Code (added 2006, amended 2019): when someone lawfully present in a home (or a shop, office or other workplace) uses a lawfully held weapon or other suitable means to defend their own or another's safety, or property where there is no withdrawal by the intruder and a danger of aggression, the defence is always deemed proportionate; and a person who repels an intrusion carried out with violence or threat of weapons or other physical coercion 'always' acts in legitimate defence. Article 55(2) excludes punishment for excess in these home cases when the person acted in 'grave disturbance' caused by the danger.

What the law says
Codice penale, art. 52 (Difesa legittima)
Non è punibile chi ha commesso il fatto per esservi stato costretto dalla necessità di difendere un diritto proprio od altrui contro il pericolo attuale di un'offesa ingiusta, sempre che la difesa sia proporzionata all'offesa. Nei casi previsti dall'articolo 614, primo e secondo comma, sussiste sempre il rapporto di proporzione di cui al primo comma del presente articolo se taluno legittimamente presente in uno dei luoghi ivi indicati usa un'arma legittimamente detenuta o altro mezzo idoneo al fine di difendere: a) la propria o la altrui incolumità; b) i beni propri o altrui, quando non vi è desistenza e vi è pericolo d'aggressione. Le disposizioni di cui al secondo e al quarto comma si applicano anche nel caso in cui il fatto sia avvenuto all'interno di ogni altro luogo ove venga esercitata un'attività commerciale, professionale o imprenditoriale. Nei casi di cui al secondo e al terzo comma agisce sempre in stato di legittima difesa colui che compie un atto per respingere l'intrusione posta in essere, con violenza o minaccia di uso di armi o di altri mezzi di coazione fisica, da parte di una o più persone.
Codice penale, art. 55 (Eccesso colposo)
Quando, nel commettere alcuno dei fatti preveduti dagli articoli 51, 52, 53 e 54, si eccedono colposamente i limiti stabiliti dalla legge o dall'ordine dell'Autorità ovvero imposti dalla necessità, si applicano le disposizioni concernenti i delitti colposi, se il fatto è preveduto dalla legge come delitto colposo. Nei casi di cui ai commi secondo, terzo e quarto dell'articolo 52, la punibilità è esclusa se chi ha commesso il fatto per la salvaguardia della propria o altrui incolumità ha agito nelle condizioni di cui all'articolo 61, primo comma, n. 5) ovvero in stato di grave turbamento, derivante dalla situazione di pericolo in atto.

58e6e0509d1be7fd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Maldives

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The Maldives Penal Code of 2014 (chapter 40, Justification Defenses; the English text published by CJAD is headed 'Law No 6/2014', the mvlaw.gov.mv listing calls it Law 9/2014) justifies force in defence of person if it is 'necessary to defend against an unjustified use or threat of force by an aggressor' and 'not disproportionate to the harm threatened' (s. 45(a)); force risking death or serious bodily injury is justified only against a threat of death, serious bodily injury or forcible intercourse (s. 45(b)). The code does not use the word retreat, but it defines 'necessary' (s. 41(b), applied to self-defence by s. 47(f)): force is necessary only if it 'could not have as effectively avoided the threatened harm' at a later time and 'less harmful or wrongful conduct could not have as effectively avoided the threatened harm or wrong'. That statutory 'no less harmful way to avoid' test is why the entry is placed in the avoidance category; the code was drafted on the Model Penal Code pattern but does not reproduce the MPC's express retreat clause, and no Maldivian court decision applying s. 41(b) to escape was found. A person who caused the justifying circumstances keeps the defence but may be liable for culpably causing them (s. 40(c)-(d)); an offender who believed a justification applied or came close to its conditions gets a one- or two-level sentence reduction (s. 1108).

At home

Deadly force is never justified in defence of property alone (s. 46(b)); no separate dwelling rule was found in chapter 40.

What the law says
Penal Code 2014, s. 45 Defense of Person (English text)
(a) Subject to Subsection (b), a person's use of force is justified if: (1) it is necessary to defend against an unjustified use or threat of force by an aggressor against: (A) his own person, or (B) the person of another; and (2) the amount of force used is not disproportionate to the harm threatened. (b) Use of Force Risking Death or Serious Bodily Injury. A person's use of force that creates a substantial risk of causing death or serious bodily injury is justified under Subsection (a) only if such force is necessary to defend against a threat of death, serious bodily injury, or forcible intercourse.
Penal Code 2014, s. 41(b) Definition of 'necessary' (applied to s. 45 by s. 47(f))
(b) Definition. Conduct or the use of force is "necessary" if: (1) the conduct could not have as effectively avoided the threatened harm or wrong if it was performed at a later time, and (2) less harmful or wrongful conduct could not have as effectively avoided the threatened harm or wrong.
Penal Code 2014, s. 47(f)
(f) "Necessary" has the meaning given in Section 41(b).
Penal Code 2014, s. 46(b) Defense of Property
(b) Use of Force Risking Death or Serious Bodily Injury. A person's use of force that creates a substantial risk of causing death or serious bodily injury is not justified in the defense of property alone.
Penal Code 2014, s. 40(c) General Provisions Governing Justification Defenses
(c) Causing the Justifying Circumstances No Bar to a Justification Defense. The fact that a person has caused the circumstances giving rise to a justification defense under this Chapter does not prevent his conduct from being justified. However, he nonetheless may be liable under Subsection (d).
Penal Code (Law No. 9/2014), s 45(a)–(b) (Dhivehi) — carried over
(ހ) މި މާއްދާގެ (ށ) ގައި ބަޔާންކޮށްފައިވާ އުސޫލުތަކަށް އުނިކަން ނާންނާނެ ގޮތުގެމަތިން، މީހަކު ބާރުގެ ބޭނުންކުރުން ހުއްދަވެގެންވަނީ އަންނަނިވި ޙާލަތްތަކުގައި އަންނަނިވި ސަބަބުތަކަށްޓަކައެވެ: (1) އަންނަނިވި ފަރާތްތަކާ ދެކޮޅަށް އެހެން މީހަކު ހުއްދަނޫން ގޮތެއްގައި ބާރުގެބޭނުން ކުރާ ހިނދުގައި ނުވަތަ ބާރުގެ ބޭނުންކޮށްފާނެ ކަމަށް ބެލެވޭ ހިނދުގައި ބޭނުންކުރަންޖެހޭ ބާރަކަށްވުން؛ (i) ތިމާގެ އަމިއްލަ ނަފުސު؛ ނުވަތަ (ii) އެހެން މީހެއްގެ ނަފުސު؛ އަދި (2) ބޭނުންކުރާ ބާރަކީ ކުރިމަތިވާނެކަމަށް ބެލެވޭ ގެއްލުމާ އަޅައިބަލާއިރު ނިސްބަތުން އިތުރަށް ބޭނުންކުރެވުނު ބާރަކަށް ނުވުން.

0fea061d481f99cb.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Iceland

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 12 of Iceland's General Penal Code (no. 19/1940) makes an act done in self-defence (neyðarvörn) unpunishable if it was necessary to prevent or avert an unlawful attack that has begun or is imminent, provided no defence was used that is clearly more dangerous than the attack and the harm it threatened; excess caused by fright or confusion that prevented full self-control is also unpunished. The code does not mention retreat or the home. Supreme Court judgments opened for this entry (case 129/2013 of 19 September 2013; case 51/2000 of 30 March 2000; a Reykjavík district judgment on a fight in Skógarsel) decide self-defence on whether the defence was 'clearly more dangerous than the impending attack' or whether the attack was still ongoing (in the Skógarsel case the victim was already fleeing and unarmed), and none states whether a defender who could safely withdraw must do so. Nothing settles the retreat question.

What the law says
Almenn hegningarlög nr. 19/1940, 12. gr. (unofficial English translation via CJAD)
This work is unpunished by emergency response, insofar as it has been necessary to prevent or avert an unlawful attack that is initiated or imminent, provided that no defenses have been used that are clearly more dangerous than the attack and damage what could be expected of her gave reason.
Hæstiréttur, mál nr. 129/2013, 19 September 2013 (reasoning on 12. gr.)
Samkvæmt því ákvæði er það skilyrði neyðarvarnar að ekki hafi verið beitt vörnum sem séu augsýnilega hættulegri en sú árás sem vofir yfir. Þótt ákærði hafi mátt óttast það að á hann yrði ráðist, var sú háttsemi hans að kasta glasinu á þann veg sem lýst hefur verið stórhættuleg og í ljósi atvika hættulegri en yfirvofandi árás og tjón, sem af henni mátti vænta, gaf ástæðu til. Verður því ekki fallist á að verknaðurinn hafi verið unninn í neyðarvörn. [Our rendering: Under that provision it is a condition of self-defence that no defence was used that is clearly more dangerous than the impending attack. Although the accused may have feared being attacked, throwing the glass in the way described was highly dangerous and, in the circumstances, more dangerous than the impending attack and the harm to be expected from it warranted. It is therefore not accepted that the act was done in self-defence.]

ae7b80ff0bb07a99.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Korea

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 21 of the Criminal Act says an act to prevent an impending and unjust attack on one's own or another's legal interests is not punishable 'if there are reasonable grounds'. The Act does not mention retreat. According to a Seoul law-firm explainer, courts read 'reasonable grounds' to require a means adequate to stop the attack and, where several means exist, the one causing the least harm, and judge this more strictly for minor attacks. If the defence goes beyond normal limits ('excessive self-defence'), the punishment may be reduced or waived, and it is not punishable at all if done at night or in other alarming conditions out of fear, surprise, excitement or confusion. In decision 2021Hunma994 (31 August 2023), discussed by the firm D&A LLC on Mondaq, the Constitutional Court treated force used 'solely to defend oneself and to escape' from an assault as socially acceptable.

At home

No separate home-defence rule in the Criminal Act. In the Wonju 'braindead burglar' case, a homeowner was convicted (with probation) because the court saw his second round of blows against an intruder as 'more offensive than defensive in nature'; the Supreme Court affirmed on 12 May 2016 (reported by K Law Guru).

What the law says
Criminal Act, art. 21 (Korean)
제21조(정당방위) ①자기 또는 타인의 법익에 대한 현재의 부당한 침해를 방위하기 위한 행위는 상당한 이유가 있는 때에는 벌하지 아니한다. ②방위행위가 그 정도를 초과한 때에는 정황에 의하여 그 형을 감경 또는 면제할 수 있다. ③전항의 경우에 그 행위가 야간 기타 불안스러운 상태하에서 공포, 경악, 흥분 또는 당황으로 인한 때에는 벌하지 아니한다.
Criminal Act, art. 21 (KLRI English translation, unofficial)
(1) An act which is performed in order to prevent impending and unjust infringement of one's own or another person's legal interest shall not be punishable if there are reasonable grounds for that act. (2) When a preventive act has exceeded normal limits, the punishment may be mitigated or remitted according to the extenuating circumstances. (3) In the case of the preceding paragraph, an act performed through fear, surprise, excitement, or confusion in the night or under other extraordinary circumstances shall not be punishable.

6104e0ed2a2b1be0.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Thailand

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Section 68 of the Criminal Code says a person who must act to protect his own or another's rights from an imminent, unlawful attack acts in lawful defence and commits no offence if the act was reasonable under the circumstances ('พอสมควรแก่เหตุ'). The code does not mention retreat. The Secretary-General of the Lawyers Council, quoted by Daily News, explains that the defender should use the least harmful means available and keep the response in proportion to the danger, and that a person who started the trouble or freely joined a fight cannot claim defence (Supreme Court decisions 2154/2519, 1961/2528, 6630/2562). Under section 69, if the defence went beyond what was reasonable or necessary, the court may impose less than the normal punishment, or none at all if the act came from excitement, fright or fear.

At home

No separate home-defence rule. A Payap University journal article cites Supreme Court Decision 1923/2519 (1976), where a man whose storehouse had been burgled before strung an electrified wire that killed an intruding thief; the court held this was lawful defence of property, proportionate to the circumstances.

What the law says
Criminal Code, s. 68 (Thai)
ผู้ใดจำต้องกระทำการใดเพื่อป้องกันสิทธิของตนหรือผู้อื่นให้พ้นอันตรายซึ่งเกิดจากการประทุษร้ายอันละเมิดต่อกฎหมาย และเป็นภยันตรายที่ใกล้จะถึง ถ้าได้กระทำพอสมควรแก่เหตุ การกระทำนั้นเป็นการป้องกันโดยชอบด้วยกฎหมาย ผู้นั้นไม่มีความผิด
Criminal Code, ss. 68-69 (unofficial English translation)
Section 68 Any person is to commit any act for defending his own right or other person's right in order to except from a danger arising out of violence tortuous to the law and such danger to be imminent, if reasonably having committed under the circumstance, such act is a lawful defense, and such person shall not have a quilt. Section 69 In the cases as provided in Sections 67 and 68, if the act committed is in excess of what is reasonable under the circumstances or in excess of what is necessary, or in excess of what is necessary for the defense, the Court may inflict less punishment to any extent than that provided by the law for such offence. But, if such act occurs out of excitement, fright or fear, the Court may not inflict any punishment at all.

a64f2cca292fcadb.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Colombia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 32.6 of the Penal Code (Ley 599 of 2000) removes criminal liability for a person who acts out of the need to defend their own or another's right against an unjust, current or imminent aggression. Before 2022 the text required that the defence be "proportionate to the aggression"; the 2022 amendment (Ley 2197) left the sentence ending "siempre que la defensa sea:" and added a presumption for home and vehicle intrusions. The Supreme Court, as cited in a 2023 law-review study, describes the necessity requirement as an aggression "not rationally avertable by another route", so the chance to avoid the attack is weighed, though no code text expressly requires retreat. A person who exceeds the limits of self-defence is not acquitted but receives a reduced penalty: no less than one sixth of the minimum and no more than half of the maximum for the offence.

At home

Since 2022 (Ley 2197) art. 32.6.1 presumes self-defence ("legítima defensa privilegiada") against a stranger who uses tricks or violence to enter or remain without right in a dwelling, its immediate outbuildings, or an occupied vehicle, and states that lethal force may be used "exceptionally". A paragraph adds that in these cases the defence is still assessed under a standard of proportionality.

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley 599 de 2000), art. 32 num. 6 (as amended by Ley 2197 de 2022)
6. Se obre por la necesidad de defender un derecho propio o ajeno contra injusta agresión actual o inminente, siempre que la defensa sea: 6.1. Legítima defensa privilegiada. Se presume también como legítima la defensa que se ejerza para rechazar al extraño que usando maniobras o mediante violencia penetre o permanezca arbitrariamente en habitación o dependencias inmediatas, o vehículo ocupado. La fuerza letal se podrá ejercer de forma excepcional para repeler la agresión al derecho propio o ajeno. PARÁGRAFO. En los casos del ejercicio de la legítima defensa privilegiada, la valoración de la defensa se deberá aplicar un estándar de proporcionalidad en el elemento de racionalidad de la conducta.
Código Penal, art. 32 (excess)
El que exceda los límites propios de las causales consagradas en los numerales 3, 4, 5, 6 y 7 precedentes, incurrirá en una pena no menor de la sexta parte del mínimo ni mayor de la mitad del máximo de la señalada para la respectiva conducta punible.

3876bd4a46bb23cd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Turkey

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Turkey's Penal Code (Law 5237 of 2004), article 25(1), excuses acts done out of the necessity to repel, at that moment and in proportion to the attack, an unjust attack on one's own or another's rights that is happening, about to happen, or certain to be repeated. The article on self-defence has no 'no other way out' wording; that wording appears only in the separate necessity rule in article 25(2). A law-firm guide (Harbiye Hukuk) says Turkish law does not impose a duty to flee and that the Court of Cassation's General Criminal Assembly has stressed that 'in no case can a duty to flee be imposed on the accused'; the defence must still be necessary and proportionate. A Court of Cassation General Assembly ruling of 18 September 2018 (E.2015/1-424, K.2018/399), as summarised on Hukuki Haber, held that a woman who killed her abusive husband while he lay asleep from drink was not acting under necessity because she could have left or taken other measures. If the limits of a defence are exceeded without intent, the penalty for the negligent offence is reduced by one sixth to one third (art. 27(1)); if excess in self-defence came from excusable excitement, fear or panic, there is no punishment at all (art. 27(2)).

What the law says
Türk Ceza Kanunu (Law 5237), art. 25(1) – Meşru savunma
Gerek kendisine ve gerek başkasına ait bir hakka yönelmiş, gerçekleşen, gerçekleşmesi veya tekrarı muhakkak olan haksız bir saldırıyı o anda hal ve koşullara göre saldırı ile orantılı biçimde defetmek zorunluluğu ile işlenen fiillerden dolayı faile ceza verilmez.
Turkish Criminal Code, art. 25(1) (English translation)
No punishment is given to an offender who acts with immediate necessity, according to the prevailing conditions, to repulse or eliminate an unjust assault against his or another person's rights, of which the recurrence is highly expected.
Türk Ceza Kanunu, art. 27 – Sınırın aşılması
(1) Ceza sorumluluğunu kaldıran nedenlerde sınırın kast olmaksızın aşılması halinde, fiil taksirle işlendiğinde de cezalandırılıyorsa, taksirli suç için kanunda yazılı cezanın altıda birinden üçte birine kadarı indirilerek hükmolunur. (2) Meşru savunmada sınırın aşılması mazur görülebilecek bir heyecan, korku veya telaştan ileri gelmiş ise faile ceza verilmez.
Law-firm explainer citing Yargıtay Ceza Genel Kurulu
hukuk sistemimiz saldırıya uğrayan kişiye kaçma yükümlülüğü yüklememiştir. Saldırı altındaki kimse, kaçma imkanı olsa bile kaçmak zorunda değildir – direnip kendini savunabilir. Yargıtay Ceza Genel Kurulu da "hiçbir halde sanığa kaçma mükellefiyeti yüklenemeyeceğini" vurgulamıştır.

1cde7bd1c6728ef2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Germany

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Under section 32 of the Criminal Code, a person may use whatever defensive force is necessary to stop a present unlawful attack on themselves or someone else, and such an act is lawful. The statute does not mention retreat, and German courts and commentary read it as imposing no general duty to flee: running away is not treated as a 'milder means' the defender must choose. There is also no strict proportionality test in the statute; instead, courts use the word 'called for' (geboten) to limit self-defence in a few recognised situations, such as a gross imbalance between what is attacked and the harm done, attacks by children or people plainly not responsible, close personal relationships, and cases where the defender provoked the attack; in those situations the defender may be expected to avoid the attack. If a person goes beyond the limits of self-defence out of confusion, fear or fright, section 33 says they incur no penalty.

At home

No separate home-defence rule; defence of the home is covered by the general self-defence provision (s. 32 StGB), which protects any legal interest, including property and the home.

What the law says
Strafgesetzbuch (Criminal Code), section 32 (official English translation)
(1) Whoever commits an act in self-defence does not act unlawfully. (2) 'Self-defence' means any defensive action which is necessary to avert a present unlawful attack on oneself or another.
Strafgesetzbuch (Criminal Code), section 33 (official English translation)
Whoever exceeds the limits of self-defence due to confusion, fear or fright incurs no penalty.
Who makes criminal law here

Under the Basic Law, art. 74(1) no. 1, criminal law is a matter of concurrent legislation, and under art. 72(1) the Länder may legislate on it only 'so long as and to the extent that the Federation has not exercised its legislative power by enacting a law.' The Federation has enacted the Criminal Code (StGB), which applies throughout Germany.

Basic Law (Grundgesetz), art. 74(1) no. 1
(1) Concurrent legislative power shall extend to the following matters: 1. civil law, criminal law, court organisation and procedure (except for the law governing pre-trial detention), the legal profession, notaries and the provision of legal advice;
Basic Law, art. 72(1)
(1) On matters within the concurrent legislative power, the Länder shall have power to legislate so long as and to the extent that the Federation has not exercised its legislative power by enacting a law.

b1951973e6fa963a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Spain

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Spanish law excuses a person who acts in defence of themselves or others if three conditions are met: an unlawful aggression, rational necessity of the means used to stop or repel it, and no sufficient provocation by the defender (Penal Code art. 20.4). The code says nothing about retreat. The Supreme Court has held that a person attacked is not required to flee: STS 399/2003 rejected the idea that the victim must take an available escape because that would mean 'the triumph of the aggressor', and STS 544/2007 said flight is not required, as summarised in a University of Zaragoza thesis. Whether escape was possible can still be weighed when judging whether the means used were rationally necessary. If not all conditions are met (for example the force was more than necessary), the defence becomes a mitigating circumstance (art. 21.1) and the court must lower the penalty by one or two degrees (art. 68), often called 'incomplete self-defence' (eximente incompleta).

At home

Article 20.4 of the Penal Code says that, when defending a dwelling or its outbuildings, unlawful entry into them counts as an 'unlawful aggression'. The means used must still be rationally necessary; there is no automatic right to use deadly force against an intruder.

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley Orgánica 10/1995), art. 20.4
Están exentos de responsabilidad criminal: ... 4.º El que obre en defensa de la persona o derechos propios o ajenos, siempre que concurran los requisitos siguientes: Primero. Agresión ilegítima. En caso de defensa de los bienes se reputará agresión ilegítima el ataque a los mismos que constituya delito y los ponga en grave peligro de deterioro o pérdida inminentes. En caso de defensa de la morada o sus dependencias, se reputará agresión ilegítima la entrada indebida en aquélla o éstas. Segundo. Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla. Tercero. Falta de provocación suficiente por parte del defensor.
Código Penal, art. 21.1
Son circunstancias atenuantes: 1.ª Las causas expresadas en el capítulo anterior, cuando no concurrieren todos los requisitos necesarios para eximir de responsabilidad en sus respectivos casos.
Código Penal, art. 68
En los casos previstos en la circunstancia primera del artículo 21, los jueces o tribunales impondrán la pena inferior en uno o dos grados a la señalada por la ley, atendidos el número y la entidad de los requisitos que falten o concurran, y las circunstancias personales de su autor...
Tribunal Supremo, STS 399/2003 (13 March 2003), as quoted in Univ. of Zaragoza TFG 2016-1024
[considera tesis no aceptable] la consistente en afirmar que siendo posible la huida, a ella debe acogerse el agredido porque, de hacerlo, significaría el éxito de la sinrazón y el triunfo del agresor, lo que vendría a constituir un factor criminógeno
Tribunal Supremo, STS 544/2007 (21 June 2007), as quoted in the same thesis
la fuga no es exigible, refiriéndose esta Sala Segunda a que fuese posible por inexistencia de riesgo y no vergonzante
Who makes criminal law here

Under the Spanish Constitution, art. 149.1.6ª, the State has exclusive competence over criminal legislation ('legislación ... penal'), so criminal law is made nationally (the Criminal Code).

Constitución Española, art. 149.1.6ª (original)
1. El Estado tiene competencia exclusiva sobre las siguientes materias: ... 6.ª Legislación mercantil, penal y penitenciaria; legislación procesal, sin perjuicio de las necesarias especialidades que en este orden se deriven de las particularidades del derecho sustantivo de las Comunidades Autónomas.
Art. 149.1.6ª (English rendering, not an official translation)
[My English rendering:] 1. The State has exclusive competence over the following matters: ... 6. Commercial, criminal and penitentiary legislation; procedural legislation, without prejudice to the necessary special features in this field deriving from the particularities of the substantive law of the Autonomous Communities.

fcf7637c4afdf42b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cuba

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Cuba's former Penal Code (Ley 62 of 1987, art. 21) exempted from liability a person who prevents or repels an unlawful, imminent or current and unprovoked aggression, if the defence was objectively necessary and proportionate, judged "with reasonable criteria, according to the circumstances of persons, means, time and place". It did not mention retreat. If the defender exceeded the limits, especially by using disproportionate means, the court could cut the sentence by up to two thirds of its minimum, and could impose no sanction at all if the excess was caused by excitement or violent emotion provoked by the attack. That code was replaced by a new Penal Code, Ley 151 of 2022; a 2026 Cuban explainer cites its article 23 as exempting a person who acts "in defence of themselves, another person or legal interests" subject to necessity, reasonableness and no sufficient provocation, but the full current text could not be opened. The 1987 code also allowed defence of the "public peace" and state interests.

What the law says
Código Penal, Ley No. 62 de 1987 (repealed), art. 21
1. Está exento de responsabilidad penal el que obra en legítima defensa de su persona o derechos. 2. Obra en legítima defensa el que impide o repele una agresión ilegítima, inminente o actual y no provocada, si concurren, además, los requisitos siguientes: a) necesidad objetiva de la defensa; b) proporcionalidad entre la agresión y la defensa, determinada en cada caso con criterios razonables, según las circunstancias de personas, medios, tiempo y lugar. ... 5. Si el que repele la agresión se excede en los límites de la legítima defensa, y, especialmente, si usa un medio de defensa desproporcionado en relación con el peligro suscitado por el ataque, el tribunal puede rebajar la sanción hasta en dos tercios de su límite mínimo, y si se ha cometido este exceso a causa de la excitación o la emoción violenta provocada por la agresión, puede aún prescindir de imponerle sanción alguna.
Código Penal, Ley No. 151 de 2022, art. 23 (as quoted in a secondary source)
No es responsable penal quien actúe en defensa de sí mismo, de otra persona o de bienes jurídicos

81ba1b9618f3361e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ukraine

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 36 of Ukraine's Criminal Code allows 'necessary defence' of one's own or another's rights, or public or state interests, by causing the harm that is necessary and sufficient to avert or stop an attack. The code states that every person has this right 'notwithstanding any possibility to avoid' the attack or to ask others or the authorities for help, so there is no duty to retreat. Excess of necessary defence means intentionally causing grave harm that is not adequate to the danger, and it is punishable only under two specific lighter offences (Articles 118 and 124, killing or grave injury in excess of defence); there is no liability if high excitement prevented the person judging proportionality. Using weapons against an armed attacker, a group, or a violent intrusion into a home is never treated as excess. The English text quoted is the 2010 version held in a university database; the official Ukrainian site could not be reached to check later amendments.

At home

Article 36(5): using weapons or other means to avert an unlawful violent intrusion into a dwelling or other premises is not treated as excess of necessary defence and carries no criminal liability, whatever the harm caused to the intruder.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Ukraine, Article 36 (English translation, 2010 version)
1. The necessary defense shall mean actions taken to defend the legally protected rights and interests of the defending person or another person, and also public interests and interests of the state, against a socially dangerous trespass, by inflicting such harm upon the trespasser as is necessary and sufficient in a given situation to immediately avert or stop the trespass, provided the limits of the necessary defense are not exceeded. 2. Every person shall have the right to necessary defense notwithstanding any possibility to avoid a socially dangerous trespass or request assistance of other persons or authorities. 3. The excess of necessary defense shall mean an intended causing of a grievous harm to the trespasser, which is not adequate to the danger of the trespass or circumstances of the defense. The excess of necessary defense shall entail criminal liability only in cases specifically prescribed in Articles 118 and 124 of this Code. 4. A person shall not be subject to criminal liability where that person was not able, due to high excitement, to evaluate if the harm caused by that person was proportionate to the danger of the trespass or circumstances of defense. 5. The use of weapons or other means or things for protection against an attack of an armed person or an attack of a group of persons, and also to avert an unlawful violent intrusion upon a dwelling place or other premises, shall not be treated as the excess of necessary defense and shall not entail criminal liability irrespective of the gravity of harm caused to the trespasser.

85a0f2785bf01437.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Malaysia

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Malaysia's Penal Code (Act 574) says nothing done in the exercise of the right of private defence is an offence (s. 96) and gives every person a right to defend their own or another's body and property (s. 97). There is no right where there is time to have recourse to the public authorities, and the right never extends to more harm than is necessary (s. 99(3)-(4)); death may be caused against the assaults listed in s. 100 (fear of death or grievous hurt, rape, unnatural lust, kidnapping or abduction, certain wrongful confinement). The code does not mention retreat. According to Prof. Stanley Yeo (NUJS Law Review, 2011), Malaysian and Singaporean courts hold that private defence imposes no duty to retreat, citing Musa bin Yusof v Public Prosecutor [1953] MLJ 70 and Public Prosecutor v Balwant Singh (No. 2) [2003] 3 MLJ 395; those two judgments were not opened.

What the law says
Penal Code (Act 574, reprint as at 1 January 2015), s. 96
96. Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.
Penal Code (Act 574), s. 99(3)-(4)
(3) There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. (4) The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.
Penal Code (Act 574), s. 100
100. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in the last preceding, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the assailant, if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right is of any of the following descriptions: (a) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; (b) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; (c) an assault with the intention of committing rape; (d) an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; (e) an assault with the intention of kidnapping or abducting; (f) an assault with the intention of wrongfully confining a person, under circumstances which may reasonably cause him to apprehend that he will be unable to have recourse to the public authorities for his release.

As for references to non-Indian case authorities, the Court could have usefully referred to judicial decisions from jurisdictions like Malaysia and Singapore which have adopted the IPC ... The Court in Darshan Singh could also have referred to cases from these jurisdictions possessing the IPC to further support its ruling that our law of private defence does not impose a duty to retreat. 0a497230918f508e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Iran

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Iran's Islamic Penal Code of 2013 (art. 156, IHRDC English translation) exempts from punishment conduct committed in defence of one's own or another's life, honour, chastity, property or physical freedom against actual or imminent aggression, if four conditions are met: (a) the conduct is necessary to counter the aggression or danger; (b) the defence is based on reasonable circumstances or rational fear; (c) the danger was not the result of the defender's own voluntary action or aggression; (d) resorting to governmental forces is not practicable in a reasonable time. Note 2 puts on the aggressor the burden of proving the conditions were not met once the defence is basically established; Note 3 says no diya is payable for lawful defence except against an insane person (then paid from the public treasury). The article does not say in words whether a safe chance to escape defeats the defence; the only avoidance-type condition is that government help be impracticable, like Yemen's art. 27. An Iranian comparative study (Islamic Azad University, 'A Comparative Study of Duty to Retreat ... in Common Law and Imamiyah Jurisprudence') says that in Imamiyah (Shia) jurisprudence, once the conditions of defence are met, 'his failure to escape has not a legal effect', but the abstract does not state the rule of Iranian statute law or cite art. 156, so the retreat question is left unsettled.

At home

Art. 156 covers defence of property and 'physical freedom' as well as life, honour and chastity; no separate home-defence rule was read.

What the law says
Islamic Penal Code 2013, art. 156, opening words (IHRDC English translation)
If anyone commits a conduct that is considered as an offense by law in defense of his/her, or someone else's, life
Islamic Penal Code 2013, art. 156(a)
The conduct committed is necessary to counter the aggression or danger.
Islamic Penal Code 2013, art. 156(b)
The defense is based on reasonable circumstances or rational fear.
Islamic Penal Code 2013, art. 156(c)
The danger and aggression are not results of the person's voluntary action or his/her aggression
Islamic Penal Code 2013, art. 156(d)
Resorting to governmental forces is not practicable in a reasonable time
Islamic Penal Code 2013, art. 156, Note 2 (excerpt)
it is up to the aggressor to prove that the conditions for defense are not met
'A Comparative Study of Duty to Retreat from the Position of Self-defense in Common Law and Imamiyah Jurisprudence', abstract (excerpt on Imamiyah jurisprudence)
his failure to escape has not a legal effect
What was tried

iranhrdc.org by direct download returned a bot-check block (403); the web reader succeeded. The IHRDC page has no mention of escape or flight in art. 156. The Tehran comparative study's abstract compares common law, German law and Imamiyah jurisprudence; it does not state the Iranian statutory rule. The Persian original (rc.majlis.ir / dotic.ir) was not retried on 18 October. searching stopped early (search limit reached).

20625e1cbbff248d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Democratic Republic of the Congo

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

No article defining legitimate defence was found in the DRC Penal Code (decree of 30 January 1940, as amended to 30 November 2004 in the copy checked). Two undergraduate theses describe the Congolese rule through doctrine: a 2015 thesis from the Université Officielle de Bukavu and a 2018 thesis from the Université Libre de Kinshasa. Both say the attack must be current or imminent and unjust, force must be the only means of protection, and the response must be proportionate. The 2018 thesis says that, in principle, a person who could have escaped by fleeing is still justified, quoting the French writer Garçon that 'flight, often shameful, cannot be a legal obligation'; it gives exceptions (a son attacked by his father, a person attacked by someone insane), where flight is expected. The 2015 thesis also cites article 66 ter of the Penal Code (Ordinance-Law 78-015 of 4 July 1978) as making it a duty to defend others when this involves no risk to oneself or third parties. Because these points come from student theses relying on French doctrine, with no Congolese ruling cited, the retreat question is marked unclear.

What the law says
Chris Yoka-Mwana Ngalula, 'Analyse et critique des causes de justification de la responsabilité pénale en droit pénal congolais: cas de la légitime défense' (graduate thesis, Université Libre de Kinshasa, 2018), part 3 (commentary, not law)
Mais, il se pose la question de savoir si l'agent cesse d'être justifié s'il pouvait échapper à l'agression par la fuite. En principe, la réponse est négative : « le Droit, écrivait GARCON, n'est pas tenu de céder devant l'injustice ; et la fuite, souvent honteuse, ne peut être une obligation légale ». Mais ce principe n'est pas absolu puisque certaines situations concrètes appellent une solution contraire : un fils qui frapperait son père ou qui le tuerait ; un agent qui frapperait ou qui tuerait un fou ne serait pas justifié s'ils pouvaient se soustraire à l'agression par la fuite qui, en ces circonstances précises n'a pas un caractère honteux. [English rendering, not an official translation: But the question arises whether the person ceases to be justified if they could have escaped the attack by fleeing. In principle the answer is no: 'the law,' wrote Garçon, 'is not bound to yield before injustice; and flight, often shameful, cannot be a legal obligation'. But this principle is not absolute, since some concrete situations call for the opposite solution: a son who struck or killed his father, or a person who struck or killed an insane person, would not be justified if they could have escaped the attack by fleeing, which in those precise circumstances is not shameful.] (Footnote 34 cites Garçon, Traité élémentaire de droit criminel et de législation pénale comparés, 3rd ed., 1947, no. 47.)
What was tried

Earlier pass: no Congolese LII reachable. on 18 October: web search 'RDC "légitime défense" jurisprudence "fuite" OR "fuir" agression Kinshasa "droit pénal congolais" Nyabirungu' found the 2018 ULK thesis (opened, parts 0-3). web search '"République du Congo" code pénal pdf "commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense"' found the LAGA copy of the DRC Penal Code (the web reader: text returned only to art. 154, no légitime défense) and leganet.cd JO 30.11.2004 (direct download: self-signed certificate, not opened). Juricaf searches returned no DRC decision on légitime défense. No Congolese court ruling on flight was found.

95775e189ea46fee.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mozambique

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Mozambique's Penal Code (Law 24/2019, published in the Boletim da República on 24 December 2019) lists self-defence of oneself or another as a ground that makes an act lawful (art. 51(1)(b)). Article 53 allows it only when all of these are present: an unlawful attack that is under way or about to happen and was not caused by the defender's own provocation or crime; it is impossible to call on the police or other public force; and the means used are rationally necessary to prevent or stop the attack. Excess caused by excusable confusion or fear is not punished. The Code does not mention retreat or flight, and no court decision or commentary on whether the defender must escape was found, so the retreat question is not settled by the sources found.

At home

Article 185 says self-defence covers homicide or bodily harm committed in repelling someone climbing into or breaking into an inhabited house or its outbuildings that give access to it, and in defending oneself against people committing violent robbery or destruction. Exceeding the article 53 limits in these cases is punished with up to 2 years' prison and a fine, or the person may be released from punishment and owe only civil compensation.

What the law says
Código Penal (Lei n.º 24/2019), art. 51(1)(b) (Exclusão da ilicitude e da culpa)
1. Constituem causas de exclusão da ilicitude, justificando o facto: a) o estado de necessidade; b) a legítima defesa própria ou alheia; [English rendering, not an official translation: 1. The following are grounds that exclude unlawfulness, justifying the act: a) state of necessity; b) self-defence of oneself or of another;]
Código Penal (Lei n.º 24/2019), art. 53 (Legítima defesa)
1. Só pode verificar-se a justificação do facto, nos termos da alínea b), do número 1 do artigo 51, quando concorrerem os seguintes requisitos: a) agressão ilegal em execução ou iminente, que não seja motivada por provocação, ofensa ou qualquer crime actual praticado pelo que defende; b) impossibilidade de recorrer à força pública; c) necessidade racional do meio empregado para prevenir ou suspender a agressão. 2. Não é punível o excesso de legítima defesa devido a perturbação ou medo desculpável do agente. [English rendering, not an official translation: 1. The act can be justified under article 51(1)(b) only when the following requirements are all present: a) an unlawful attack under way or imminent, not prompted by provocation, offence or any current crime committed by the person defending; b) impossibility of resorting to the public force; c) rational necessity of the means used to prevent or stop the attack. 2. Excess in self-defence caused by the agent's excusable confusion or fear is not punishable.]
Código Penal (Lei n.º 24/2019), art. 185 (Legítima defesa — homicide and bodily harm)
1. A regra estabelecida na alínea b) do número 1 do artigo 51, compreende os casos em que o homicídio ou ofensas corporais forem cometidos: a) repelindo o escalamento ou arrombamento de uma casa habitada ou de suas dependências, que podem dar acesso à entrada na mesma casa; b) defendendo-se contra os autores de roubos ou destruições executadas com violências. 2. Se, no caso da alínea b) do número 1 do artigo 51, qualquer pessoa exceder os limites fixados no artigo 53, é, segundo a qualidade e circunstâncias do excesso, ou punido com pena de prisão até 2 anos e multa, ou absolvido da pena, ficando somente sujeito à reparação civil pela sua falta. [English rendering, not an official translation: 1. The rule in article 51(1)(b) includes cases where homicide or bodily harm is committed: a) repelling the climbing into or breaking into an inhabited house or its outbuildings that can give access to the house; b) defending oneself against the perpetrators of robberies or destruction carried out with violence. 2. If, in a case under article 51(1)(b), anyone exceeds the limits set in article 53, they are, according to the nature and circumstances of the excess, either punished with up to 2 years' prison and a fine, or released from punishment, remaining liable only for civil compensation.]
What was tried

No Mozambican court decision or commentary on fleeing or retreat was searched beyond this, owing to the shared search budget.

021ff940a5ab1e1b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bangladesh

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Bangladesh still uses the Penal Code of 1860 (ss 96–106, 'right of private defence'). Deadly force in defence of the body is allowed against an assault that reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt, and against assaults intended to rape, abduct, kidnap or wrongfully confine (s 100). The Code does not require retreat, but there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities' (s 99). No Bangladeshi court decision on retreat was found in the sources opened.

At home

s 103: the right of private defence of property extends to causing death against robbery, house-breaking by night, arson of a building used as a dwelling, and theft, mischief or house-trespass that reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt.

What the law says
Penal Code, 1860 (Act XLV of 1860), s 99
There is no right of private defence against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or of grievous hurt, if done, or attempted to be done by a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, though that act may not be strictly justifiable by law. ... There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code, 1860, s 100
The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in the last preceding section, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the assailant, if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right be of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:- Firstly.-Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Secondly.-Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Thirdly.-An assault with the intention of committing rape; ...
Penal Code, 1860, s 103
The right of private defence of property extends, under the restrictions mentioned in section 99, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the wrong-doer, if the offence ... be an offence of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:- Firstly.-Robbery; Secondly.-House-breaking by night; Thirdly.-Mischief by fire committed on any building, tent or vessel, which building, tent or vessel is used as a human dwelling ...; Fourthly.-Theft, mischief or house-trespass, under such circumstances as may reasonably cause apprehension that death or grievous hurt will be the consequence, if such right of private defence is not exercised;

ed9646a8e31b7154.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Peru

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 20(3) of the Penal Code exempts from criminal liability a person who defends their own or another's legal interests, and since a 2024 amendment (Law 32026, promulgated by the President of Congress on 15 May 2024) the text expressly says this may include the use of lethal force. The defence must be against a current, unlawful and real attack, the means must be rationally necessary, and the defender must not have sufficiently provoked it. The code expressly excludes a 'proportionality of means' test and instead weighs the intensity and danger of the attack, how the attacker acted and the means available for defence. The 2024 law also bars pre-trial detention where self-defence clearly applies, unless there is firm evidence of a crime. Article 21 ('responsabilidad restringida') covers cases where not all requirements are met; its full text was not opened. No source was found that addresses whether a person must retreat, and there is no special home-defence rule in the text found.

What the law says
Código Penal (D. Leg. 635), art. 20(3), as amended in 2024 (text quoted by the Congress of Peru)
El que obra en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o de terceros, con uso de la fuerza, incluido el uso de la fuerza letal, siempre que concurran las circunstancias siguientes: [...] Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla. Se excluye para la valoración de este requisito el criterio de proporcionalidad de medios, considerándose en su lugar, entre otras circunstancias, la intensidad y peligrosidad de la agresión, la forma de proceder del agresor y los medios de que se disponga para la defensa. Falta de provocación suficiente de quien hace la defensa.
Código Procesal Penal (D. Leg. 957), art. 268(d), added 2024
No precede la prisión preventiva en los casos de inminente aplicación de la legitima defensa propia o de tercero conforme a ley; salvo la presencia de antecedentes y/o pruebas fehacientes que justifiquen la existencia del delito o que recaiga sobre la persona sentencia firme condenatoria

2d1d4a2dd8939467.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Denmark

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Section 13 of the Danish Criminal Code makes acts of self-defence unpunishable if they were necessary to resist or avert a begun or imminent unlawful attack and do not 'obviously go beyond' what is justifiable given the danger of the attack, the attacker and the importance of what is attacked. Danish legal commentary (the national encyclopedia, written by law professors) states that killing can be lawful self-defence against someone who is himself trying to kill, but only 'unless the attack can be averted by flight, calling the police or the like', so escape is expected before lethal force where it is possible. If a person exceeds the limits of self-defence, they are still not punished when the excess is reasonably explained by fright or agitation caused by the attack (section 13(2)). Under civil (damages) law, an act that does not obviously exceed what is justifiable generally gives no liability for the harm caused. The wording of section 13 is the same in the 2022, 2024 and November 2025 consolidated texts.

At home

No separate home-defence rule in the Criminal Code; section 13 covers attacks on 'life, body, property etc.' generally.

What the law says
Straffeloven (Criminal Code), § 13, stk. 1
Handlinger foretagne i nødværge er straffri, for så vidt de har været nødvendige for at modstå eller afværge et påbegyndt eller overhængende uretmæssigt angreb og ikke åbenbart går ud over, hvad der under hensyn til angrebets farlighed, angriberens person og det angrebne retsgodes betydning er forsvarligt.
Straffeloven (Criminal Code), § 13, stk. 2
Overskrider nogen grænserne for lovligt nødværge, bliver han dog straffri, hvis overskridelsen er rimeligt begrundet i den ved angrebet fremkaldte skræk eller ophidselse.

c7a2127e2a154d9e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ireland

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Outside the home, Ireland's Non-Fatal Offences against the Person Act 1997 allows reasonable force in self-defence, and section 20(4) says the fact that a person had an opportunity to retreat 'shall be taken into account, in conjunction with other relevant evidence' when deciding whether the force was reasonable, so retreat is a factor rather than an absolute duty. Inside one's own dwelling, the 2011 Defence and the Dwelling Act removes any retreat requirement: force that is reasonable in the circumstances as the occupier believes them to be is not an offence, the force may include lethal force, and the chance to retreat is immaterial. The 2011 Act also gives the occupier immunity from civil (tort) claims for force it permits. The common-law rules on lethal self-defence outside the home were not covered by a source opened here.

At home

Criminal Law (Defence and the Dwelling) Act 2011: a person in their dwelling may use reasonable force, which can include force causing death, against someone they believe entered as a trespasser to commit a criminal act; it is 'immaterial' whether they had a safe and practicable chance to retreat, nothing in the Act requires them to retreat from their dwelling, and a person using force permitted by the Act is not liable in tort for resulting injury, loss or damage.

What the law says
Non-Fatal Offences against the Person Act 1997, s. 20(4)
The fact that a person had an opportunity to retreat before using force shall be taken into account, in conjunction with other relevant evidence, in determining whether the use of force was reasonable.
Criminal Law (Defence and the Dwelling) Act 2011, s. 2(5), 2(7), 3 and 5
2(5) It is immaterial whether the person using the force had a safe and practicable opportunity to retreat from the dwelling before using the force concerned. ... 2(7) The use of force shall not exclude the use of force causing death. ... 3.— Nothing in this Act shall operate to require— (a) a person to retreat from his or her dwelling, or (b) a lawful occupant in a dwelling to retreat from the dwelling. ... 5.— Notwithstanding the generality of any other enactment or rule of law concerning the civil liability of persons in relation to trespassers, a person who uses such force as is permitted by section 2 in the circumstances referred to in that section shall not be liable in tort in respect of any injury, loss or damage arising from the use of such force.

0f16e6dabad01d4d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Pakistan

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The Pakistan Penal Code (1860) says nothing done in the exercise of the right of private defence is an offence (s. 96); the right does not exist where there is time to have recourse to the public authorities and never extends to more harm than necessary (s. 99); deadly force is allowed against the assaults listed in s. 100. The code does not use the word 'retreat'. The Supreme Court of Pakistan, in Ghulam Farid v. The State, 2009 SCMR 929 (Jillani J., 28 January 2009), set out as one of four things an accused must show to claim self-defence 'that no reasonable course was available to accused to escape or avoid the necessity'. In Sultan Muhammad v. The Crown, 1970 SCMR 242, the Supreme Court rejected self-defence because the accused could escape through the door 'without obstruction', so 'there was no necessity for him to fire'. These rulings treat an available safe escape as defeating the defence, so the entry is placed under retreat; no Pakistani ruling saying one need not run away was opened.

At home

Section 103 of the Pakistan Penal Code allows causing death in defence of property against, among other things, robbery, 'house-breaking by night', and arson of a building used as a human dwelling, subject to the limits in section 99.

What the law says
Pakistan Penal Code (Act XLV of 1860), s. 96
Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.
Pakistan Penal Code, s. 99 (extract)
There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. Extent to which the right may be exercised: The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.
Pakistan Penal Code, s. 100
The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in the last preceding section, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the assailant, if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right be of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:-- First: Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Secondly: Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Thirdly: An assault with the intention of committing rape; Fourthly: An assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust. Fifthly: An assault with the intention of kidnapping or abduction. Sixthly: An assault with the intention of wrongfully confining a person, under circumstances which may reasonably cause him to apprehend that he will be unable to have recourse to the public authorities for his release.
Pakistan Penal Code, s. 103 (extract)
The right of private defence of property extends, under the restrictions mentioned in Section 99, to the voluntary Causing of death or of any other harm to the wrong-doer, if the offence ... be an offence of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:- First: Robbery; Secondly: House-breaking by night; Thirdly: Mischief by fire committed on any building, tent or vessel, which building, tent or vessel is used as a human dwelling or as a place for the custody of property; Fourthly: Theft, mischief or house-trespass, under such circumstances as may reasonably cause apprehension that death or grievous hurt will be the consequence...
Ghulam Farid v. The State, 2009 SCMR 929 (Supreme Court of Pakistan, Criminal Appeal No. 110 of 2006, decided 28 January 2009)
(2) Private defence of body.--- Accused would be within his right to defend his own body and that of any other person against any offence affecting human body. ... In order to avail of the exception of self defence, it is essential to show:--- (i) that the occurrence was not due to the fault or act of accused; (ii) that there was an immediate danger to life, in honest belief of accused; (iii) that no reasonable course was available to accused to escape or avoid the necessity; and (iv) that there was no intention to cause more harm than necessary for the purpose.
Sultan Muhammad v. The Crown, 1970 SCMR 242 (Supreme Court of Pakistan)
In those circumstances having by far the more effective weapon with the longer reach, and being able to escape out of the room through the door without obstruction, there was no necessity for him to fire at Khuban at all.
Who makes criminal law here

Since the Eighteenth Amendment (2010), Parliament and the provincial assemblies both have power to make criminal law; where a provincial Act conflicts with an Act of Parliament, Parliament's Act prevails. Whether any province has made its own self-defence rule was not checked.

Constitution of Pakistan, art. 142(b)
Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament) and a Provincial Assembly shall have power to make laws with respect to criminal law, criminal procedure and evidence;
Constitution of Pakistan, art. 143
If any provision of an Act of a Provincial Assembly is repugnant to any provision of an Act of Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament) which Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament) is competent to enact, then the Act of Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament), whether passed before or after the Act of the Provincial Assembly, shall prevail and the Act of the Provincial Assembly shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void.

25351eacbcf9261a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Solomon Islands

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Solomon Islands' Penal Code (s 17) does not spell out self-defence; it says criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property is decided 'according to the principles of English common law', and the Constitution (s 4(2)(a)) permits force 'reasonably justifiable' to defend a person from violence. The courts apply the Privy Council's test in Palmer v R: force must be reasonably necessary in the circumstances, and retaliation wholly out of proportion, or force used after the danger has passed, is not self-defence. There is no duty to retreat: in R v Mona (2014) the High Court called a duty to retreat 'a restrictive approach, which has now being abandoned', saying the real question is whether the accused acted reasonably in using force rather than retreating. If self-defence is fully accepted the accused is acquitted, but where force became excessive after the danger passed the courts have convicted of manslaughter instead of murder (Ofea v R, 2019, as described by the Court of Appeal in R v Sapa, 2022). No special rule for the home was found.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 26), s 17 Defence of person or property
Subject to any express provisions in this Code or any other law in operation in Solomon Islands, criminal responsibility for the use of force in the defence of person or property shall be determined according to the principles of English common law.
Regina v Mona [2014] SBHC 19 (High Court, Faukona J, 9 April 2014), para 11
The phrase "taking some simple avoiding action" may well be interpreted as one meaning of duty to retreat. ... This is a restrictive approach, which has now being abandoned. ... What is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his actions that he does not want to fight ... If possible to retreat then use of force is unnecessary ... but the real question is whether the accused acted reasonably in using force rather than retreating.
R v Sapa [2022] SBCA 21 (Court of Appeal, 4 November 2022), quoting Palmer v R [1971] AC 814
It is both good law and good sense that a man who is attacked may defend himself.

73a5f48882ea2877.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Croatia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 21 of the Criminal Code (2011) says an act done in necessary defence is not unlawful, and defines necessary defence as the defence that is 'strictly necessary' (prijeko potrebna) to repel a simultaneous or directly imminent unlawful attack on oneself or another. The code does not mention retreat; by contrast, the necessity defence in article 22 applies only to a danger that 'could not be removed in another way'. No court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits of necessary defence may receive a lighter sentence, and is not guilty at all if the excess came from excusable severe fright caused by the attack; this fright rule was introduced by the 2011 code, according to a commentary in Informator, because courts had tended to impose high sentences for excess regardless of the defender's state of mind.

What the law says
Kazneni zakon (NN 125/11 and amendments), čl. 21
(1) Isključena je protupravnost djela počinjenog u nužnoj obrani. (2) Nužna je ona obrana koja je prijeko potrebna da se od sebe ili drugoga odbije istodobni ili izravno predstojeći protupravni napad. (3) Počinitelj koji prekorači granice nužne obrane može se blaže kazniti. (4) Nije kriv tko prekorači granice nužne obrane zbog ispričive jake prepasti prouzročene napadom.
Kazneni zakon, čl. 22(1) (necessity, for contrast)
Isključena je protupravnost djela počinjenog radi toga da se od sebe ili drugoga otkloni istodobna opasnost koja se na drugi način nije mogla otkloniti ako je učinjeno zlo manje od onoga koje je prijetilo.
Supreme Court of Croatia, I Kž-210/2019 (24 Apr 2019), as summarised in the court's 2019 bulletin
Kazneno djelo u prekoračenju nužne obrane može se počiniti i sa izravnom i sa neizravnom namjerom.

e4d41b868083c03d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

French Polynesia

Part of France, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

French Polynesia applies the French Penal Code: art. 711-1 makes Books I to V applicable there, subject to the adaptations in that title, so self-defence is governed by arts. 122-5 and 122-6 (necessity, simultaneity, no disproportion; presumption for repelling night-time entry into an inhabited place and violent theft). Neither article mentions retreat. In the one Cour de cassation decision found that discusses flight (Crim., 28 February 2006, no. 05-87400), the defendant argued that 'la fuite n'est pas une obligation légale' (flight is not a legal obligation) after the investigating chamber found later shots disproportionate partly because the pharmacist 'pouvait alors se mettre à l'abri à l'arrière de l'officine' (could then have taken shelter at the back of the shop), when the robbers were already fleeing; the Cour de cassation rejected the appeal on the ground that the investigating chamber's assessment of the facts was sovereign, without ruling on whether flight is required. The retreat question therefore remains unsettled by the sources opened.

At home

Art. 122-6 presumes self-defence for a person who repels, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, or defends against violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal (France), art. 711-1
Sous réserve des adaptations prévues au présent titre, les livres Ier à V du présent code sont applicables, dans leur rédaction résultant de la loi n° 2026-813 du 24 août 2026 ..., en Nouvelle-Calédonie, en Polynésie française et dans les îles Wallis et Futuna.
Code pénal (France), art. 122-5, first paragraph
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte.
Cass. crim., 28 février 2006, n° 05-87400 (appellant's ground, not the Court's holding)
4 / alors que si l'existence d'un choix autre que la violence exclut la légitime défense, la fuite n'est pas une obligation légale ; qu'en affirmant que la riposte était disproportionnée dès lors que le commerçant pouvait fuir pour se mettre à l'abri à l'arrière de l'officine, la chambre de l'instruction a violé les textes susvisés [English rendering, mine: 4. whereas, although the existence of a choice other than violence excludes self-defence, flight is not a legal obligation; by holding that the response was disproportionate because the shopkeeper could flee to shelter at the back of the pharmacy, the investigating chamber breached the above provisions]
Cass. crim., 28 février 2006, n° 05-87400 (Court's answer)
Qu'en effet, les juridictions d'instruction apprécient souverainement si les faits retenus à la charge de la personne mise en examen sont constitutifs d'une infraction, la Cour de cassation n'ayant d'autre pouvoir que de vérifier si, à supposer ces faits établis, la qualification justifie la saisine de la juridiction de jugement ; Que, dès lors, les moyens ne peuvent qu'être écartés ; [English rendering, mine: Investigating courts assess sovereignly whether the facts charged constitute an offence, the Cour de cassation having no power other than to check whether, assuming those facts proven, the legal characterisation justifies sending the case to trial; the grounds must therefore be dismissed.]
What was tried

Juricaf (France) searches: '"obligation de fuir"' (only administrative/immigration decisions), '"tenu de fuir"' (none), '"légitime défense" "pouvait fuir"' (Cass. crim. 28 Feb 2006, opened, above), '"légitime défense" "possibilité de fuir"' (none), '"légitime défense" fuir' (Cass. crim. 16 Feb 2021 no. 20-86552, 6 Oct 2021 no. 21-84295, 21 Jun 2022 no. 21-85174, and Cass. civ. 2e 16 Jun 2022 no. 20-18.837, opened: they concern police shooting at fleeing persons or a defender who fled by car; none states whether a defender must flee). No doctrine stating 'il n'est pas exigé de fuir' was opened.

19e19ee65f75cd73.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

The Bahamas

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The Bahamas Penal Code (Ch. 84) grades the force allowed by the crime being resisted; killing is justified only 'in the case of extreme necessity' against listed grave crimes (s. 107(4)), and force beyond what is reasonably necessary is never justified (s. 99). The Code's self-defence sections do not mention retreat; the word appears only in the definition of assault, which says an assault can be made although the victim could avoid it by retreating. The Court of Appeal in Doyle Mackey v DPP (2021) required an honest-belief direction, and the Privy Council in James Miller v The King (2023) was opened; neither addresses retreat. Retreat is not settled by the sources found.

What the law says
Penal Code (Ch. 84), definition of assault, para. (c) (not a self-defence rule)
(c) an assault can be made on a person, within the meaning of this section, although he can avoid actual assault and battery by retreating, or by consenting to do, or to abstain from doing, any act.
Doyle Amaro Mackey v DPP, Court of Appeal of The Bahamas, SCCrApp No. 187 of 2019, 1 Jul 2021 (held)
The trial judge should make it clear to the jury that the test for self defence is whether the defendant had an honest belief
What was tried

Privy Council judgments on caselaw.nationalarchives.gov.uk (atom feed search 'self-defence' court=ukpc, 17 results; 'retreat', 1 unrelated result): opened Kirk Gordon v The Queen (Belize) [2010] UKPC 18, Francis Eiley v The Queen (Belize) [2009] UKPC 40, James Miller v The King (Bahamas) [2023] UKPC 10, The Queen v Vasyli (Bermuda) [2020] UKPC 8 and five others in full XML — none mentions retreat.
