741fe569f8363b02.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

United Kingdom

No duty to retreat, written in the law

In England and Wales, self-defence is a common-law defence, and section 76 of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 says force is judged on the circumstances as the defender honestly believed them to be, and is not reasonable if it was disproportionate (or 'grossly disproportionate' in a householder case). Since 2013, section 76(6A) has stated that the possibility of retreat is only a factor to weigh, 'rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat'; that subsection and the householder rule apply in England and Wales only, while the rest of section 76 also covers Northern Ireland. Self-defence is a complete defence: there is no partial 'excessive self-defence' verdict in these provisions, though the jury must consider that a person under attack cannot 'weigh to a nicety' the exact force needed. In civil law, an offender convicted of an imprisonable offence on the same occasion needs the court's permission to sue the defender for trespass to the person, and the defender has a defence unless their act was grossly disproportionate (Criminal Justice Act 2003, s. 329, England and Wales). Scotland has separate common-law rules that were not covered by the sources opened here.

At home

England and Wales: in a 'householder case' (force used by a non-trespasser inside a dwelling against someone believed to be a trespasser), force is unreasonable only if it was 'grossly disproportionate' in the circumstances as the defender believed them to be, instead of merely 'disproportionate' (s. 76(5A), inserted 2013). This householder rule does not apply in Northern Ireland or Scotland.

What the law says
Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s. 76(5A), (6), (6A), (7)
(5A) In a householder case, the degree of force used by D is not to be regarded as having been reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them to be if it was grossly disproportionate in those circumstances. (6) In a case other than a householder case, the degree of force used by D is not to be regarded as having been reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them to be if it was disproportionate in those circumstances. (6A) In deciding the question mentioned in subsection (3), a possibility that D could have retreated is to be considered (so far as relevant) as a factor to be taken into account, rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat. (7) In deciding the question mentioned in subsection (3) the following considerations are to be taken into account (so far as relevant in the circumstances of the case)— (a) that a person acting for a legitimate purpose may not be able to weigh to a nicety the exact measure of any necessary action; and (b) that evidence of a person's having only done what the person honestly and instinctively thought was necessary for a legitimate purpose constitutes strong evidence that only reasonable action was taken by that person for that purpose.
Criminal Justice Act 2003, s. 329(3)-(4)
(3) The court may give permission for the proceedings to be brought only if there is evidence that either— (a) the condition in subsection (5) is not met, or (b) in all the circumstances, the defendant's act was grossly disproportionate. (4) If the court gives permission and the proceedings are brought, it is a defence for the defendant to prove both— (a) that the condition in subsection (5) is met, and (b) that, in all the circumstances, his act was not grossly disproportionate.

3fb85e74fe96124a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Saudi Arabia

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Saudi Arabia has no written penal code provision on self-defence; courts apply Islamic law on repelling an attacker (daf' al-sa'il, called 'al-siyala'). A 2026 guide by a Saudi law firm (Numas Law Firm) says that if self-defence is proven, both retaliation (qisas) and blood money (diya) fall away, that the burden of proof is on the person claiming it, and that the judge must be satisfied killing was the only means of repelling the attack: the judge asks whether the defender could have fled, and if the defender could have escaped safely or repelled the attack with less lethal means, the defence may not be fully accepted. This rests on a law-firm guide, not a published court ruling or academic study; the guide cites judicial principles (dated 97/6/20 and 24/4/1400 AH) only for its point on proving who started the attack.

What the law says
Numas Law Firm, 'عقوبة القتل دفاعا عن النفس (الصيالة) بالسعودية 1447هـ', section 2 'إثبات شرط الضرورة (عدم وجود خيار آخر)'
يجب إثبات أن القتل كان هو الوسيلة الوحيدة لدفع الاعتداء، وأن المدافع لم يكن لديه أي خيار آخر. هل كان بإمكانه الهرب؟ هل كان بإمكانه استخدام قوة أقل لصد المعتدي؟ هل كان الاعتداء وشيكًا وحقيقيًا لدرجة تبرر القتل؟ إذا تبين للقاضي أن المدافع كان بإمكانه الفرار بأمان أو صد العدوان بوسيلة أقل فتكًا ولكنه اختار القتل، فقد لا تُقبل حجة الدفاع عن النفس بالكامل. [English rendering, not an official translation: It must be proven that killing was the only means of repelling the attack and that the defender had no other option. Could he have fled? Could he have used less force to repel the attacker? Was the attack imminent and real enough to justify killing? If the judge finds that the defender could have escaped safely or repelled the aggression by less lethal means but chose to kill, the self-defence argument may not be fully accepted.]
Same guide, on the result of proven self-defence
إذا ثبت للقاضي أن القتل كان دفاعًا شرعيًا عن النفس (صيالة)، فإن النتيجة هي سقوط كل من القصاص والدية. [English rendering, not an official translation: If the judge finds the killing was legitimate self-defence (siyala), the result is that both retaliation and blood money fall away.]

fefb1f54c9e43d26.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Panama

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 32 of Panama's Penal Code (Law 14 of 2007), there is no crime when a person acts in legitimate defence of themselves, their rights, or another person or their property, if the circumstances require it. Three conditions must be met: an unjust, current or imminent attack; use of a rational means to prevent or repel it; and no sufficient provocation by the defender. A person who reasonably repels someone who entered their home without consent is presumed to act in self-defence. The code does not mention retreat, and no Panamanian court decision on retreat or rule on excessive self-defence was found. The text used is the 2007 code as amended in 2008 (WIPO Lex copy); later amendments were not checked.

At home

Penal Code art. 32 presumes legitimate defence for anyone who reasonably repels a person who has entered their residence, dwelling, house or room without consent.

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley N° 14 de 18 de mayo de 2007, con modificaciones de la Ley N° 26 de 2008), art. 32
No comete delito quien actúe en legítima defensa de su persona, de sus derechos o de un tercero o sus bienes, siempre que las circunstancias así lo requieran. La defensa es legítima cuando concurran las siguientes condiciones: Existencia de una agresión injusta, actual o inminente de la que resulte o pudiera resultar afectado por el hecho; Utilización de un medio racional para impedir o repeler la agresión; y Falta de provocación suficiente por parte de quien se defiende o es defendido. Se presume que actúa en legítima defensa quien razonablemente repele al que, sin su consentimiento, ha ingresado a su residencia, morada, casa o habitación.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Código Penal de la República de Panamá (Ley N° 14 de 2007, con modificaciones de la Ley N° 26 de 2008) (WIPO Lex (World Intellectual Property Organization))
  • WIPO Lex record for the Panama Penal Code (WIPO Lex)

0a436f6c03f2ad61.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nigeria

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states; ss. 286-287) and the Penal Code (northern states and FCT; ss. 59-67). The Criminal Code allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where he believes on reasonable grounds he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself; s. 287 requires a provoker to have 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable'. The Penal Code gives no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities' (s. 63) and limits killing to grave attacks (s. 65). What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), was not re-opened in this round.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287 (second paragraph)
This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Egheghe v The State (SC, 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal

9302c3238ee3ec33.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Africa

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

South Africa has no criminal code on self-defence; 'private defence' is a common-law defence. The Supreme Court of Appeal in Steyn v S [2009] ZASCA 152; 2010 (1) SACR 411 (SCA) (Leach AJA, Mthiyane JA and Wallis AJA concurring, 27 November 2009) described private defence as allowing a person to use such force as may be necessary to repel unlawful attacks that have commenced or are imminent. On fleeing it said: 'Whether a person is obliged to flee from an unlawful attack rather than entitled to offer forceful resistance, is a somewhat vexed question', found it unnecessary to decide, and held that the appellant could not be expected to gamble with her life by turning her back on an attacker with a knife, so she could not be faulted for resisting rather than fleeing; it also held she was entitled to move about her own home without first telephoning for help. Earlier, R v Zikalala 1953 (2) SA 568 (A) (seen only as summarised on Wikipedia) endorsed the view that a person who can save himself by flight should flee, but need not if flight is not a safe way of escape. Snyman, whom Steyn cites, argues there is no absolute duty to retreat. Because the highest court that addressed it left the general question open, it is marked unclear.

At home

In Steyn v S (SCA 2009, para 23) the court held the appellant 'was entitled to leave her bedroom, in her own home, and go to the kitchen' and that 'it cannot have been expected of her to telephone for assistance every time she needed to do something in her own home'. No statute on defending the home was found.

What the law says
Steyn v S [2009] ZASCA 152; 2010 (1) SACR 411 (SCA), para 16
[16] I therefore turn to consider whether the court quo was correct in concluding that, on her own evidence, the appellant had acted unlawfully. In denying her guilt, the appellant relied on a plea of so-called 'private defence' (commonly referred to in circumstances such as the present as 'self-defence') which goes to negative unlawfulness and recognises that persons may lawfully use such force as may be necessary to repel unlawful attacks upon them which have either commenced or are imminent and which threaten their lives or bodily integrity.
Steyn v S (SCA 2009), para 21 (footnotes 7 and 8: 'See eg Snyman op cit at 107-109'; 'In this regard I endorse the view of Snyman op cit at 108')
[21] Whether a person is obliged to flee from an unlawful attack rather than entitled to offer forceful resistance, is a somewhat vexed question. But in the light of the facts in this case, it is unnecessary to consider the issue in any detail. It could not have been expected of the appellant to gamble with her life by turning her back on the deceased, who was extremely close to her and about to attack her with a knife, in the hope that he would not stab her in the back. She would have had to turn around in order to return to her bedroom, by which time the deceased would have been upon her and flight would have been futile. The appellant testified that the deceased would probably have caught her before she reached her room, and that appears to be a reasonable assumption. That being so, the appellant cannot be faulted for offering resistance to the deceased rather than attempting to flee from him.
R v Zikalala 1953 (2) SA 568 (A), endorsing Gardiner and Lansdown (as summarised on Wikipedia, pointer only)
Where a man can save himself by flight, he should flee rather than kill his assailant [...]. But no one can be expected to take to flight to avoid an attack, if flight does not afford him a safe way of escape. A man is not bound to expose himself to the risk of a stab in the back, when by killing his assailant he can secure his own safety
Commentary: Goosen, PER 2013, quoting Snyman
Snyman argues that there is no duty upon the attacked person to flee, because "this is a negation of the whole essence of private defence [which deals] … with the upholding of justice … not a capitulation to injustice". However, he submits that "there is no absolute duty to retreat and that the approach of our law ought to be that the question of whether or not the battered woman could or should have retreated is merely one of the issues to be taken into account"
Grigor v S (SCA, 607/11, 1 June 2012), Tshiqi JA, as quoted by Sherika Maharaj
[t]he facts of this matter, even on the appellants version, show that he had several other harmless means he could have adopted to avoid a physical confrontation. He could have driven off and ignored the complainant

97e337c652521f4a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mongolia

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Mongolia's Criminal Code of 2015 (art. 4.1, 'necessary defence') provides that an act having the features of a crime done against an unlawful and imminent attack on one's own or another person's life or health is not a crime (wording amended on 10 January 2020). Part 2 states that anyone has the right of necessary defence regardless of profession, special training or official position, and regardless of whether it was possible to avoid the dangerous attack or to ask others for help — so there is no duty to retreat. Defence may be used once an unlawful attack has started or is clearly about to start, but not after the attack has ended. The current text of art. 4.1 contains no separate clause on excessive defence; other consequences of excess were not examined. English summary is an unofficial translation.

At home

No separate home-defence rule found in art. 4.1.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Mongolia (2015), art. 4.1(1)–(3) (Mongolian, as displayed on the official portal)
4.1 ДҮГЭЭР ЗҮЙЛ.АРГАГҮЙ ХАМГААЛАЛТ 1.ӨӨРИЙН, ЭСХҮЛ БУСДЫН АМЬ НАС, ЭРҮҮЛ МЭНДИЙН ЭСРЭГ ХУУЛЬ БУС БА ТУЛГАРСАН ДОВТОЛГООНЫ ЭСРЭГ ХИЙСЭН ГЭМТ ХЭРГИЙН ШИНЖТЭЙ ҮЙЛДЛИЙГ ГЭМТ ХЭРЭГТ ТООЦОХГҮЙ. /ЭНЭ ХЭСЭГТ 2020 ОНЫ 01 ДҮГЭЭР САРЫН 10-НЫ ӨДРИЙН ХУУЛИАР ӨӨРЧЛӨЛТ ОРУУЛСАН./ 2.АЛИВАА ХҮН МЭРГЭЖИЛ, ТУСГАЙ БЭЛТГЭЛ, АЛБАН АЖЛЫН БАЙДАЛ, АЮУЛТАЙ ДОВТОЛГООНООС ЗАЙЛСХИЙХ, БУСДААС ТУСЛАМЖ АВАХААР ХАНДАХ БОЛОМЖТОЙ БАЙСАН ЭСЭХЭЭС ҮЛ ХАМААРАН АРГАГҮЙ ХАМГААЛАЛТ ХИЙХ ЭРХТЭЙ. 3.АРГАГҮЙ ХАМГААЛАЛТЫГ БУСДЫН ХУУЛЬ БУС ХАЛДЛАГА ЭХЭЛСЭН, ЭХЛЭХ ГЭЖ БАЙГАА НЬ ТОДОРХОЙ БОЛСОН ҮЕД ХИЙНЭ. 7ad5c6aaa95fe2db.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Turkmenistan

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 34 of the Turkmen Criminal Code says defending oneself, another person, society or the state by causing any harm to the attacker is lawful when the attack involved violence dangerous to life or an immediate threat of such violence. Against attacks not dangerous to life, defence is lawful only if the limits of necessary defence were not exceeded, meaning no deliberate acts clearly out of line with the nature and danger of the attack. The article states that the right of defence exists regardless of any possibility of avoiding the attack or turning to others or the authorities for help, so there is no duty to retreat. The text used is the Criminal Code of 12 June 1997 No. 222-I as amended to 12 April 2025, published on a Kazakh legal database (prg.kz); the penalty for excessive defence was not checked.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Turkmenistan, art. 34
1. Не является преступлением и признаётся правомерной защита личности, прав и законных интересов обороняющегося, другого лица, общества и государства путём причинения любого вреда посягающему, если нападение было совершено с насилием, опасным для жизни обороняющегося или другого лица, либо с непосредственной угрозой применения такого насилия. 2. Защита от нападения, не сопряжённого с насилием, опасным для жизни обороняющегося или другого лица, либо с угрозой применения такого насилия, является правомерной, если при этом не было допущено превышение пределов необходимой обороны, то есть умышленных действий, явно не соответствующих характеру и опасности посягательства. 3. Право на необходимую оборону принадлежит лицу независимо от возможности избежать посягательства либо обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или органам власти.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Уголовный кодекс Туркменистана от 12 июня 1997 года № 222-I (по состоянию на 12.04.2025) (Paragraph (prg.kz) legal database)

4faa2d8da68318cb.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

North Korea

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

In an unofficial English translation of North Korea's Criminal Law as amended in 2009, Article 15 (Self-Defence) says an act defined as an offence is not punished if committed to prevent an offence against the interests of the state, the public, other persons or oneself, and if it is 'a reasonable defensive measure'. Articles 281 and 285 punish killing or grave injury that goes 'beyond a measure of justifiable self-defence' with short terms of labour. The text does not mention retreat, and no North Korean commentary or decision was found. Later versions of the law (2015 and after) were not opened.

What the law says
Criminal Law of the DPRK (as amended 2009), Article 15 (Self-Defence) — unofficial English translation
Should an act that is defined as an offence under this law be committed in order to prevent an offence against the interests of the state, against the public interests, or against the legitimate interests of other persons or oneself, and should the offence be considered a reasonable defensive measure, it shall not be punished.
Same, Article 281 (Homicide beyond Justifiable Self-Defence)
A person who kills another by an act that goes beyond a measure of justifiable self-defence or beyond the measure necessary for the performance of his or her duty or responsibility shall be punished by reform through labour for less than three years.
Same, Article 285 (Infliction of Grave Injury beyond Justifiable Self-Defence)
A person who causes grave injury to another by an act that goes beyond a measure of justifiable self-defence or beyond the measure necessary for the performance of his or her duty shall be punished by short-term labour for less than two years.
What was tried

a89d366de8068799.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Madagascar

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Madagascar's Penal Code (text consolidated to 31 March 2005 in the copy found) follows the old French model: there is no crime when homicide, wounds or blows were 'commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence of oneself or another' (art. 328). Article 329, as amended in 1978 and 1996, lists four situations automatically counted as self-defence, including repelling night-time break-ins of homes and many other buildings, repelling violent, armed or gang robbery by day, and killing or wounding criminals during or while pursuing them, by members of the Fokonolona (local community) or the security forces, in cases of violent or armed banditry or tomb violation. The code says nothing about retreat, and no court decisions on retreat or on the proportionality test were found. The 2010 Constitution (art. 8) says death is not a violation of the right to life when it results from force 'absolutely necessary' to defend any person against illegal violence.

At home

Article 329(1) counts as 'current necessity of legitimate defence' any blows, wounds or homicide committed while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or the entrance of a house or flat or their outbuildings, and also of shops, warehouses, religious buildings, schools, hospitals, offices, factories, banks, cattle pens, stables, pigsties and poultry yards, or while preventing theft of harvested crops in the fields.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 328
Il n’y a ni crime ni délit, lorsque l’homicide, les blessures et les coups étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d’autrui.
Code pénal, art. 329 (Loi n°78-039 du 13.07.78; Loi n°96-001 du 06.02.96), extract
Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de légitime défense, les quatre cas suivants : 1° Si les coups ont été portés, si les blessures ont été faites, si l’homicide a été commis en repoussant pendant la nuit l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d’une maison ou d’un appartement ou de leurs dépendances ... 2° Si les coups ont été portés, si les blessures ont été faites, si l’homicide a été commis en repoussant pendant le jour tout vol avec effraction, tout vol avec violence, toute attaque ou vol en bande ou tout vol avec port d’armes apparentes par nature ; 3° si les coups ont été portés, si les blessures ont été faites, si l’homicide a été commis sur les malfaiteurs au moment des faits ou au cours de leur poursuite par les membres du Fokonolona ou des agents de la force publique, en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillage ou de tout autre acte de banditisme, exécutés avec violence, ou en bande ou avec port d’armes apparentes ou cachées ...
Constitution 2010, art. 8 (English translation)
Death is not considered as inflicted in violation of this Article in the cases where it would result from recourse to the force rendered absolutely necessary, in view of assuring the defense of all persons against illegal violence.

cbc8d85f1a560cd6.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

United Republic of Tanzania

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Tanzania's Penal Code (sections 18 to 18C, added in 1980) gives every person the right to defend themselves, another person, or property, but only with "such reasonable force as may be necessary for that defence". Deadly force or grievous harm is allowed where the defender acts in good faith with an honest belief, on reasonable grounds, that it is needed to preserve life or limb, including against acts reasonably feared to cause death or grievous harm, rape, kidnapping, burglary, robbery or arson. The Code does not mention retreat, and the sources opened here did not settle whether a chance to escape counts against the defender. A person who uses excessive force is criminally liable, and causing death through excessive defensive force is manslaughter rather than murder.

What the law says
Penal Code [Cap. 16], ss. 18B and 18C(1)
18B. (1) In exercising the right of self defence or in defence of another or in defence of property, a person shall be entitled to use only such reasonable force as may be necessary for that defence. (2) A person shall be criminally liable for any offence resulting from excessive force used in self defence or in defence of another or in defence of property. (3) Any person who causes the death of another as the result of excessive force used in defence, commits an offence of manslaughter. 18C. (1) The right of self defence or the defence of another or defence of property shall extend to a person who, in exercising that right, causes death or grievous harm to another and the person so acting, acts in good faith and with an honest belief based on reasonable grounds that his act is necessary for the preservation of his own life or limb or the life or limb of another or of property, in the circumstances where— (a) the lawful act is of such a nature as may reasonably cause the apprehension that his own death or the death of another person could be the consequence of that act; ... (c) the unlawful act is with the intention of committing rape or defilement or an unnatural offence; (d) the unlawful act is with the intention of kidnapping or abducting; or (e) the unlawful act is burglary or robbery or arson or any offence which endangers life or property.

eb96e3af07eff8a4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Fiji

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Fiji's Crimes Act 2009, which repealed the old Penal Code, defines self-defence in s 42 on the same model as the Australian Commonwealth Criminal Code: conduct is self-defence only if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or another (or for listed property and trespass purposes) and it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceive them. The section does not mention retreat and no duty to retreat is stated; no Fijian court decision on retreat was opened. Deadly force solely to protect property or deal with trespassers is excluded.

At home

No home-specific rule; force intentionally inflicting death or grievous harm may not be used only to protect property or to prevent or remove a criminal trespasser (s 42(3)).

What the law says
Crimes Act 2009, s 42 Self defence
(1) A person is not criminally responsible for an offence if he or she carries out the conduct constituting the offence in self defence. (2) A person carries out conduct in self defence if and only if he or she believes the conduct is necessary— (a) to defend himself or herself or another person; or (b) to prevent or terminate the unlawful imprisonment of himself or herself or another person; or (c) to protect property from unlawful appropriation, destruction, damage or interference; or (d) to prevent criminal trespass to any land or premises; or (e) to remove from any land or premises a person who is committing criminal trespass, and the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as he or she perceives them. (3) This section does not apply if the person uses force that involves the intentional infliction of death or grievous harm— (a) to protect property; or (b) to prevent criminal trespass; or (c) to remove a person who is committing criminal trespass.

670b04f9d1859b54.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Laos

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Laos's Penal Code (promulgated by Presidential Decree No. 118/PO of 26 June 2017) defines legitimate defence as acts taken to protect the interests of the State or society, or one's own or another person's life, health or legitimate rights and interests, against aggression that is a public danger, provided the aggression truly exists and is dangerous and the defence is 'proportionate with the acts of aggression' (art. 36). The code does not mention retreat or flight, and no Lao court decision on the point was found; the test in the text is real danger and proportion. Exceeding the limits of legitimate defence is a separate, lighter offence: causing death this way is punished by one to three years' imprisonment or re-education without deprivation of liberty plus a fine (art. 192), and causing injuries by re-education and a fine, with higher penalties for more serious harm (art. 196). Excessive legitimate defence is also listed as a circumstance reducing criminal liability (art. 64). The English texts opened are unofficial translations.

At home

No separate home-defence rule was found in the articles opened.

What the law says
Penal Code 2017, art. 36 Legitimate Defense (unofficial draft English translation)
Acts of legitimate defense are acts taken by an individual to safeguard the interests of the State or society, to safeguard his/her own or another individual's life, health, or legitimate rights and interests against acts of aggression regarded as public danger; provided that the acts of aggression truly exist and are dangerous, and the acts of legitimate defense against act of aggression must be proportionate with the acts of aggression.
Penal Code 2017, art. 192 Excessive Self-Defense resulting in Death (English text as published by CJAD)
Any person causing the death of another in circumstances which exceed the limits of legitimate self-defense shall be sentenced to imprisonment for a term ranging from one year to three years or by re-education without deprivation of liberty and a fine shall be imposed ranging from 5,000,000 kip to 15,000,000 kip.
Penal Code 2017, art. 64(3) (unofficial draft English translation)
Circumstances conducive to the reduction of penal liabilities are: [...] 3. An excessive legitimate defense;

a4d0ed3958dd65dd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Egypt

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Egypt's Penal Code (Law 58 of 1937, as amended) exempts from punishment a person who kills or injures while lawfully defending their own or another's life or property, using the force 'necessary' to ward off a criminal act (arts. 245–246). The right does not exist when it is possible to rely in good time on the protection of the public authorities (art. 247); the code says nothing explicit about retreating. Intentional killing in self-defence is allowed only against an act feared on plausible grounds to cause death or serious wounds, rape or indecent assault by force, or kidnapping (art. 249). Someone who in good faith exceeds the limits of defence, without intending more harm than needed, is not fully exempt, but a judge may treat the act as excusable and impose detention instead of the normal felony penalty (art. 251).

At home

Article 250 allows intentional killing in defence of property when warding off, among other things, 'entering at night into a tenanted house or one of its appurtenances'.

What the law says
Penal Code (Law 58/1937), arts. 246–247 (English translation)
Article 246: The right of lawful self-defense allows a person, in other than the exceptional cases defined hereinafter, to use the power necessary to obviate any act considered as a crime on one's life prescribed as prescribed in this law. ... Article 247: Such right shall have no existence once it is possible to rely in due course on seeking the protection of the public authority men.
Penal Code, arts. 249–250
Article 249: The right of lawful self-defense shall not allow premeditated killing unless it is meant to ward off one of the matters: First: An act feared to cause death or deep wounds, if such fear is based on plausible reasons. Second: Lying with a woman or assaulting a person indecently by force. Third: Kidnapping a person. Article 250: The lawful right of defending the property and funds shall not allow premeditated killing unless it is meant to ward off one of the following matters: ... Third: Entering at night into a tenanted house or one of its appurtenances;
Penal Code, art. 251
Whoever exceeds in good faith the limits of the right of lawful defense, while using this right, without having the intent to cause a bigger harm than the demands of this defense shall not be fully exempted from punishment. However, the judge, in case the act constitutes a felony, may consider it excusable if there is place for that, and pass a ruling sentencing him/her to detention instead of the penalty prescribed in the law.

  • Legitimate Defense (Egypt) (Mondaq / Andersen in Egypt (Maher Milad Iskander), 23 June 2022)

b62ddd403072155e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Uzbekistan

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 37 of the Uzbek Criminal Code says an act done in necessary defence of oneself, another person, or public or state interests against an unlawful attack is not a crime, provided the limits of necessary defence were not exceeded. Exceeding the limits means a clear mismatch between the defence and the nature and danger of the attack. The code states that the right of defence belongs to a person regardless of any chance to seek help from others or the authorities or to avoid the attack in another way, so there is no duty to retreat. Deliberately provoking an attack in order to harm the attacker is not defence. Intentionally killing while exceeding the limits is a separate, lighter offence (article 100) punished by up to three years.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Republic of Uzbekistan, art. 37 (Russian text)
Не является преступлением действие, совершенное в состоянии необходимой обороны, то есть при защите личности или прав обороняющегося либо другого лица, интересов общества или государства от противоправного посягательства путем причинения посягающему вреда, если при этом не было допущено превышение пределов необходимой обороны. Превышением пределов необходимой обороны признается явное несоответствие защиты характеру и опасности посягательства. Право на необходимую оборону принадлежит лицу независимо от имевшейся возможности обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или органам власти либо избежать посягательства иным способом. Не является необходимой обороной умышленная провокация посягательства с целью нанесения вреда.
Criminal Code, art. 100
Умышленное причинение смерти, совершенное при превышении пределов необходимой обороны, — наказывается исправительными работами до трех лет или ограничением свободы от одного года до трех лет либо лишением свободы до трех лет.

7db3274502d33a44.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ecuador

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 33 of the Comprehensive Organic Criminal Code (COIP, 2014) says self-defence exists when a person acts in defence of any right, their own or another's, if three conditions are met: a current and unlawful aggression, "rational necessity of the defence", and no sufficient provocation by the defender. The Code does not mention retreat. A 2024 article by an Azuay provincial prosecutor in the University of Cuenca law review expresses the scholarly view that the person attacked should prefer strictly defensive means or, "if possible, opt for a prudent retreat", as long as this does not put them at risk or dishonour; this is legal writing, not a code rule or court ruling. According to El Comercio (2023), the COIP (art. 31) punishes excessive self-defence with a penalty reduced to one third of the minimum for the offence. The sources opened here did not show a special rule for the home.

What the law says
Código Orgánico Integral Penal (COIP), art. 33
Artículo 33.- Legítima defensa.- Existe legítima defensa cuando la persona actúa en defensa de cualquier derecho, propio o ajeno, siempre y cuando concurran los siguientes requisitos: a) Agresión actual e ilegítima; b) Necesidad racional de la defensa; c) Falta de provocación suficiente por parte de quien actúa en defensa del derecho.
COIP, art. 31 (exceso), as quoted by El Comercio
una pena reducida en un tercio de la mínima prevista en el respectivo tipo penal

50afdaa53e486664.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ivory Coast

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Côte d'Ivoire's current Penal Code (Law No. 2019-574) says there is no offence when the acts are commanded by the current necessity of defending oneself, another person or legally protected property against an unjust attack, 'on condition that the attack cannot be averted otherwise' and that the defence is simultaneous with and proportionate to the circumstances, including the danger and gravity of the attack and the value of the property (art. 97). The word 'retreat' does not appear, but the condition that the attack could not be averted in any other way means defence is lawful only when there was no other way to avoid the attack. The 1981 Penal Code (art. 100) used the same wording. No Ivorian court decision applying this condition to a chance to escape was found.

At home

Article 98 of the 2019 Code (art. 101 of the 1981 Code, same wording) presumes legitimate defence for a person who kills or wounds while repelling at night the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of a house or inhabited flat or their outbuildings, or while defending against people committing violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n° 2019-574), art. 97 (Section 1 : Légitime défense)
Il n’y a pas d’infraction lorsque les faits sont commandés par la nécessité actuelle de défense de soi-même ou d’autrui ou d’un bien juridiquement protégé contre une attaque injuste, à condition que cette dernière ne puisse être écartée autrement et que la défense soit concomitante et proportionnée aux circonstances, notamment au danger et à la gravité de l’attaque, à l’importance et à la valeur du bien attaqué. [English rendering, not an official translation: There is no offence when the acts are commanded by the current necessity of defending oneself or another or legally protected property against an unjust attack, on condition that the attack cannot be averted otherwise and that the defence is simultaneous with and proportionate to the circumstances, in particular to the danger and gravity of the attack and to the importance and value of the property attacked.]
Code pénal (Loi n° 2019-574), art. 98
Est présumé agir en état de légitime défense, celui qui commet un homicide, porte volontairement des coups ou fait des blessures soit en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d’une maison, d’un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances, soit en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence. [English rendering, not an official translation: A person is presumed to act in legitimate defence who commits homicide or intentionally strikes or wounds either while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of the fences, walls or entrances of a house, an inhabited flat or their outbuildings, or while defending against the perpetrators of thefts or looting carried out with violence.]
Code pénal (1981), art. 100 — superseded by Loi n° 2019-574
Il n'y a pas d'infraction lorsque les faits sont commandés par la nécessité actuelle de défense de soi-même ou d'autrui ou d'un bien juridiquement protégé contre une attaque injuste, à condition que cette dernière ne puisse être écartée autrement et que la défense soit concomitante et proportionnée aux circonstances, notamment au danger et à la gravité de l'attaque, à l'importance et à la valeur du bien attaqué.
Code pénal (1981), art. 101 — superseded
Est présumé agir en état de légitime défense, celui qui commet un homicide, porte volontairement des coups ou fait des blessures soit en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d'une maison, d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances, soit en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

1704a111e9b3142d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Falkland Islands

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

The Crimes Ordinance 2014 (No. 13 of 2014), section 120, governs self-defence. It keeps the common-law defences of self-defence and defence of property and sets out how the reasonableness of the force is judged: by the circumstances as the accused genuinely believed them to be (s. 120(3)-(4)), with force that is disproportionate in those circumstances treated as not reasonable (s. 120(6)). On retreat, s. 120(8) says in words that the possibility that the accused could have retreated is only a factor to be taken into account, 'rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat'. The section is annotated as copied from s. 76 of the UK Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 as amended by s. 148 of LASPO 2012. The consolidated text read (version valid from 3 February 2025) contains no separate 'householder' rule: s. 120(6) applies the disproportionate-force bar to every case, and no dwelling exception appears in the section.

What the law says
Crimes Ordinance 2014 (Falkland Islands), s. 120(8)
(8) In deciding the question mentioned in subsection (3), a possibility that D could have retreated is to be considered (so far as relevant) as a factor to be taken into account, rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat.
Crimes Ordinance 2014 (Falkland Islands), s. 120(2)-(3)
(2) The defences are — (a) the common law defence of self-defence; (b) the common law defence of defence of property; and (c) the defence provided by section 119. (3) The question whether the degree of force used by D was reasonable in the circumstances is to be decided by reference to the circumstances as D believed them to be, and subsections (4) to (8) also apply in connection with deciding that question.
Crimes Ordinance 2014 (Falkland Islands), s. 120(6)
(6) The degree of force used by D is not to be regarded as having been reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them to be if it was disproportionate in those circumstances.

b2a67fabc19e8cb4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Guinea

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

In the new Penal Code of Guinea (Ministry of Justice text dated February 2016; the law was enacted later in 2016, and article numbers in the final version could not be checked), there is no crime or offence when the act was required by the necessity of legitimate defence of oneself or another (art. 21(4)). The code text found does not mention retreat, and this article also does not spell out a proportionality test. Defence at night against forced or tricked entry into an inhabited place, and defence against violent robbery, are presumed to be legitimate defence. No specific rule on excessive self-defence was found.

At home

Article 22 presumes legitimate defence for a person who acts to repel at night entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, or to defend against violent theft or looting; article 292 applies the same presumption to killing or wounding while repelling night-time climbing or break-in into a house or inhabited flat.

What the law says
Nouveau Code pénal (Ministère de la Justice, février 2016), art. 21(4)
Il n'y a ni crime ni délit, lorsque : ... 4. l'action du prévenu est commandée par la nécessité de sa légitime défense ou de celle d'autrui.
Nouveau Code pénal (2016), art. 22
Est présumé agir en état de légitime défense, celui qui accomplit l’acte : 1. pour repousser de nuit l’entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2. pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vol ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Nouveau Code pénal (2016), art. 292
Est présumé agir en état de légitime défense, celui qui commet un homicide, porte volontairement des coups ou fait des blessures soit en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d’une maison, d’un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances, soit en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exercés avec violence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

30bdb361ec12be70.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Central African Republic

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The Central African Republic's Penal Code (Law No. 10.001 of 2010) says killing, wounding and blows are justified when they were required by the 'present necessity of legitimate defence' of oneself or others, or of one's own or others' property. The article does not mention proportionality or retreat; its test is present necessity. It names two situations that count as such necessity: repelling night-time climbing or break-in into a home, and defending against violent theft or looting. No provision on excessive self-defence was found in the article.

At home

Article 49 counts as legitimate defence killing, wounding or striking while repelling at night the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of a house, inhabited flat or their outbuildings, and defence against violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal centrafricain (Loi n° 10.001), art. 49
L’homicide, les blessures et les coups sont justifiés et n’entraînent pas condamnation lorsqu’ils étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi ou d’autrui, de ses biens ou de ceux d’autrui. Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de défense, les deux cas suivants : 1. Si l’homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites ou si les coups ont été portés en repoussant pendant la nuit l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d’une maison, d’un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances ; 2. Si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vol ou de pillage exécutés avec violence.

6f0103560e86e49d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Angola

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Angola's Penal Code (Law No. 38/20 of 11 November 2020) defines legitimate defence as an act carried out 'as a necessary means' to repel a current and unlawful attack on legally protected interests of the defender or a third party. The code does not mention retreat or a duty to flee; the test is whether the means used were necessary. If the means used were excessive, the act is unlawful but the penalty may be specially reduced (art. 31). A person who exceeded the means because of non-blameworthy disturbance, fear or fright acts without guilt (art. 36). No separate home-defence rule was found.

What the law says
Código Penal (Lei n.º 38/20, de 11 de Novembro), art. 31.º (Legítima Defesa)
Constitui legítima defesa o facto praticado como meio necessário para repelir a agressão actual e ilícita de interesses juridicamente protegidos do agente ou de terceiro. Se houver excesso dos meios empregados em legítima defesa o facto é ilícito, mas a pena pode ser especialmente atenuada.
Código Penal (Lei n.º 38/20), art. 36.º (Excesso de Legítima Defesa Desculpante)
Age sem culpa quem exceder os meios empregues em legítima defesa, sempre que o excesso resultar de perturbação, medo ou susto não censuráveis.

d20c06634619fbaa.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Baja California Sur

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Baja California Sur's Penal Code (art. 31-VI) allows a person to repel a real, current or imminent attack on their own or another's legal interests, if the defence is rationally necessary and proportionate and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. The code does not mention retreating or fleeing. Intruders into a dwelling are presumed to be lawful targets of defence unless shown otherwise. Against attackers under 18, the defender must avoid injuring them and use only the defence needed against serious attacks; breaching this counts as excessive self-defence. Excess in self-defence is punished with one quarter of the penalty for the offence (art. 87). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 31-VI presumes legitimate defence, unless proven otherwise, when harm is caused to someone who tries to enter or enters without right the place where the defender lives (temporarily or permanently), their family's home, the home of anyone they must protect, its outbuildings, or a place holding property they must protect; the same presumption applies to harm caused to an intruder caught there in circumstances suggesting a possible attack.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Baja California Sur, art. 31, fracc. VI
VI. Legítima defensa como causa de justificación. Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad racional y proporcional de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. Se presume que existe legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, cuando se cause un daño a quien por cualquier medio trate de penetrar o penetre, sin derecho, al lugar en que habite de forma temporal o permanente el que se defiende, al de su familia o al de cualquier persona respecto de las que el agente tenga la obligación de defender, a sus dependencias o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que exista la misma obligación. Igual presunción existirá cuando el daño se cause a un intruso al momento de sorprenderlo en alguno de los lugares antes citados en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión. En los casos de agresiones provenientes de menores de 18 años se evitará lesionar al agresor y sólo se ejercerá la defensa necesaria ante ataques graves. La contravención a esta disposición será considerada un exceso en la legítima defensa conforme a lo dispuesto en el artículo 87 de este Código;
Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Baja California Sur, art. 87
Artículo 87. Exceso en las causas de justificación y de inculpabilidad. A quien incurra en exceso en los casos previstos en las fracciones VI, VII, VIII y X del artículo 31 de este Código, se le impondrá la cuarta parte de la pena o medida de seguridad correspondiente al delito de que se trate, siempre que con relación al exceso no se actualice otra causa de exclusión del delito.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Baja California Sur, compilation by H. Congreso del Estado de Baja California Sur, Oficialía Mayor (última reforma BOGE 14-05-2026) (H. Congreso del Estado de Baja California Sur (copy hosted by HIV Justice Network))
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

b0be165ef0c47595.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Afghanistan

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The Penal Code of 2017 (Official Gazette No. 1260, 15 May 2017; presidential decree of 4 March 2017), in the Justice Sector Support Program translation held by FAOLEX, makes legitimate defence a justification (art. 125) but allows it only when, among other conditions, 'Defense is the only way to avoid the danger' (art. 127(2)(5)) and the right does not arise at all 'When it is possible to resort to security official to avert the danger' (art. 130). Killing in defence is allowed only against listed acts: an act with obvious fear of death or serious injury, rape, kidnapping or hostage-taking, dangerous arson, felony larceny, and unauthorised night entry into a dwelling (art. 129). Good-faith excess reduces the offence by one grade (art. 132). The word 'retreat' does not appear; the 'only way' and 'possible to resort to officials' conditions are what place it in the retreat category. The 1976 Penal Code (SHERLOC copy) had the same conditions at arts. 60(3) and 62. Status under the Taliban: the Afghanistan Analysts Network's February 2026 translation of the Islamic Emirate's 'Penal Code for Courts' (119 articles, circulated to courts, not yet in the Official Gazette) contains no self-defence article and its art. 119 annuls all codes the Commander of the Faithful has not ratified; AAN's companion report (2 March 2026) does not say in words that the 2017 code is suspended. Zan Times (27 Jan 2026) says the Taliban 'annulled the former national penal code'. An 8am.media report (30 March 2023) says Taliban courts were ordered to re-evaluate judgments 'based on the previous penal code'. No source opened states which self-defence rule Taliban courts apply.

At home

Art. 129(6): killing is permitted in defence 'against unauthorized entry at night into residential house and/or its annexes'.

What the law says
Penal Code 2017 (OG 1260), art. 125
(1) Commission of act for the purpose of exercising the legitimate right of defense shall not be considered crime. (2) Legitimate right of defense permits the threatened person to make use of necessary means for the purpose of defending against any criminal act that poses a danger to life, honor, freedom or distraction of property to defender or another person.
Penal Code 2017, art. 127(2)
Legitimate right of defense arises under all of the following conditions: 1- Defense is against an illegal and unjust act; 2- Defense is against a current or imminent attack and aggression; 3- Defense is concurrent with the attack of transgressor; 4- Defense is proportionate to the danger of the threat; 5- Defense is the only way to avoid the danger; 6- The defender did not deliberately cause the opposite side to perpetrate a criminal act
Penal Code 2017, art. 129
Commission of murder on the basis of exercising the legitimate right of defense is not permitted, unless it takes place for defense against one of the following acts: 1- Defense against an act which fear of death or serious injury is obvious due to logical reasons. 2- Defense against rape or imminent threat of rape. 3- Defense against kidnapping or taking hostage. 4- Defense against intentional and dangerous arson. 5- Defense against that act of larceny which is considered felony based on provisions of this law. 6- Defense against unauthorized entry at night into residential house and/or its annexes.
Penal Code 2017, art. 130
When it is possible to resort to security official to avert the danger, the legitimate right of defense shall not come into existence.
Penal Code 2017, art. 132
If a person has exceeded the limits of legitimate right of defense with good faith, his/her punishment may be reduced to misdemeanor if it is a felony and to petty crime if it is a misdemeanor.
Penal Code 1976 (OG 347), arts. 60 and 62
Article 60 Legitimate right of defense comes into presence under the following conditions: 1– Defense should be against aggression and assaults; 2– Defense should be proportionate to the danger of threat; 3– Defense should be the only way of removing the danger; ... Article 62 Legitimate right of defense does not come into existence if it is possible to resort to officials of public services to ward off the danger.
Islamic Emirate 'Penal Code for Courts', art. 119 (AAN unofficial translation, Feb 2026)
This Code is to be enacted from the date of its approval, and published in the official journal, and all Codes that the exalted Commander of the Faithful, Sheikh al-Quran and Hadith Mawlawi Hibatullah Akhundzada, may Allah protect him, has not ratified, sanctioned or approved, are hereby annulled.
AAN, 'Inside the Islamic Emirate's Penal Code' (2 March 2026)
The Code has not been published (yet) in the Official Gazette, but it has been circulated to the nation's courts
Zan Times, 27 Jan 2026
The Taliban introduced its new Penal Code of the Taliban Courts as a replacement for Afghanistan's national penal code.

bbff172a3cd5dcb7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mali

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Mali adopted a new Penal Code in December 2024 (Law No. 2024-027). Under article 122-4, a person is not criminally responsible for an act required, at the same moment, by the need to defend themselves or another against an unjustified attack, unless the means of defence are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. Defence of property may never extend to intentional homicide and must be strictly necessary and proportionate. The code says nothing about retreat or flight, and no Malian court decision on the point was found. No provision on excessive self-defence was found in the sections searched.

At home

A person is presumed to have acted in self-defence when repelling, at night, entry into an inhabited place by break-in, violence or trickery, or when defending against violent theft or looting (art. 122-5). Article 321-56 likewise counts as 'current necessity of defence' a homicide or injury committed while repelling, at night, an intrusion into a dwelling or its outbuildings, notably by climbing or breaking through fences, walls or enclosures.

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n°2024-027 du 13 décembre 2024), art. 122-4
N’est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d’elle-même ou d’autrui, sauf s’il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l’atteinte. N’est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l’exécution d’un crime ou d’un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu’un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l’infraction.
Code pénal 2024, art. 122-5
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l’acte : 1°) pour repousser, de nuit, l’entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2°) pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal 2024, arts. 321-55 and 321-56
Article 321-55 : N’est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui commet un homicide, fait des blessures, porte des coups ou exerce des violences lorsque ceux-ci étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle ou la légitime défense de soi-même ou d’autrui. Article 321-56 : Sont compris dans le cas de nécessité actuelle de défense, les deux cas suivants : 1°) si l’homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites et les coups ont été portés ou si les violences ont été exercées en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l’intrusion dans une habitation ou ses dépendances, notamment par escalade ou effraction des clôtures, murs ou enclos. 2°) si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

cf4ed00d6c3b5d6b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cameroon

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Cameroon's Penal Code (Law No. 2016/007 of 12 July 2016) says criminal liability cannot arise from an act required by the immediate necessity of defending oneself, another person, or one's own or another's right against an unlawful attack, provided the defence is proportionate to the seriousness of the attack (s. 84(1)). Killing or serious injury is always treated as proportionate to an attack that gives reason to fear death, serious injury, rape or sodomy (s. 84(2)). The code does not mention retreat. No separate provision on excessive self-defence or on home defence was found; section 85 gives a mitigating excuse for offences provoked by an unlawful act against the offender or close persons.

What the law says
Loi n° 2016/007 du 12 juillet 2016 portant Code pénal, art. 84 (Légitime défense) — text from an OCR-scanned copy, accents missing; 'centre' in the scan corrected to 'contre'
(1) La responsabilite penale ne peut resulter d'un acte commande par la necessite immediate de la defense de soi-meme ou d'autrui, ou d'un droit appartenant a soi-meme ou a autrui contre une atteinte illegitime a condition que la defense soit proportionnee a la gravite de l'atteinte. (2) Il y a toujours juste proportion entre l'homicide et l'atteinte qui donne lieu de craindre soit la mort soit les blessures graves telles que prevues au present Code, soit le viol ou la sodomie.

773605d5987c28d4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Portugal

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Article 32 of the Portuguese Penal Code defines legitimate defence as the act carried out as the 'necessary means' to repel a present and unlawful aggression against legally protected interests of the agent or a third party; excess of means makes the act unlawful but allows a specially mitigated penalty, and no punishment if the excess came from non-blameworthy disturbance, fear or fright (Article 33). The Supreme Court of Justice (STJ), 3rd Section, judgment of 18 April 2018 in case 1603/14.1JAPRT.G1.S1 (rapporteur Gabriel Catarino, unanimous), states in its headnote (point XIX) that when weighing whether the defensive means were necessary 'the possibility of flight must not be taken into account; escaping is not repelling the aggression', citing Figueiredo Dias and Claus Roxin; the same judgment also says the necessity test is made ex ante and does not involve weighing the proportionality of the legal interests involved, and that the defence may be intense enough to end the attack quickly, the defender not being required to use timid attempts at defence. So Portugal's highest criminal court says there is no duty to retreat. The code itself does not mention retreat or the home.

What the law says
Código Penal, artigo 32.º (Legítima defesa)
Constitui legítima defesa o facto praticado como meio necessário para repelir a agressão actual e ilícita de interesses juridicamente protegidos do agente ou de terceiro. [Our rendering: Legitimate defence is the act carried out as the necessary means to repel a present and unlawful aggression against legally protected interests of the agent or of a third party.]
Código Penal, artigo 33.º (Excesso de legítima defesa)
1 - Se houver excesso dos meios empregados em legítima defesa, o facto é ilícito mas a pena pode ser especialmente atenuada. 2 - O agente não é punido se o excesso resultar de perturbação, medo ou susto, não censuráveis. [Our rendering: 1 - If there is excess in the means used in legitimate defence, the act is unlawful but the penalty may be specially mitigated. 2 - The agent is not punished if the excess results from non-blameworthy disturbance, fear or fright.]
Supremo Tribunal de Justiça, 3.ª Secção, Acórdão de 18-04-2018, Processo 1603/14.1JAPRT.G1.S1 (Relator Gabriel Catarino), sumário XVII–XX
XVII - A ponderação da necessidade (menor lesividade) tem, porém, de ser compreendida nas circunstâncias do caso: a defesa pode ser intensa para fazer terminar rápida e completamente a agressão ou a eliminação do perigo, não sendo exigível que o agredido apenas utilize tímidos intentos de defesa que podem fazer correr o risco de continuação ou de intensificação da agressão. [...] XIX - Na ponderação sobre a necessidade dos meios não deve, porém, entrar-se em linha de conta com a possibilidade de fuga; escapar não é repelir a agressão (cf. Figueiredo Dias, ob. cit., pág. 419, e Claus Roxin, ob. cit., pág. 631-633). XX - A necessidade e o exame sobre a necessidade surgem ex ante e não supõem uma ponderação de proporcionalidade dos bens jurídicos implicados. [Our rendering: XVII - The weighing of necessity (least harm) must be understood in the circumstances of the case: the defence may be intense so as to end the aggression or eliminate the danger quickly and completely, and the person attacked is not required to use only timid attempts at defence that may risk the aggression continuing or intensifying. XIX - In weighing the necessity of the means, however, the possibility of flight must not be taken into account; escaping is not repelling the aggression. XX - Necessity and the examination of necessity arise ex ante and do not involve weighing the proportionality of the legal interests involved.]

HOMICÍDIO, LEGÍTIMA DEFESA) (DGSI – Bases Jurídico-Documentais (Instituto de Gestão Financeira e Equipamentos da Justiça / Ministério da Justiça, Portugal))

9bf7974dc0c4cf41.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Gabon

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Gabon's Penal Code (Law No. 042/2018, promulgated 5 July 2019) says a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means of defence are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack (art. 34). The code does not mention retreat or flight, and no Gabonese court decision on the point was found; the test is necessity and proportion. Defence of property against a crime or offence may never include intentional homicide and must be strictly necessary and proportionate (art. 34, second paragraph). The earlier code (art. 51 as amended in 1993) likewise required the defence to be 'legitimate and proportionate to the nature and seriousness of the aggression'. No specific rule on excessive self-defence or civil immunity was found in the articles opened.

At home

Article 36 presumes self-defence for a person who acts to repel, at night, entry by break-in, climbing, violence or trickery into an inhabited place or its outbuildings, or to defend against people committing theft or looting with violence.

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n°042/2018 du 05 juillet 2019), art. 34
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi et que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal 2019, art. 36
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense, celui qui accomplit l'acte : pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, escalade, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ou les dépendances d'un tel lieu ; pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Former Code pénal, art. 51 (as amended by Law 19/93 of 27 Aug. 1993)
Il n'y a ni crime ni délit lorsque l'acte était commandé par la nécessité actuelle de la défense de soi-même ou d'autrui, à condition que cette défense soit légitime et proportionnée à la nature et à la gravité de l'agression.

85cc281be6e7857a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Queensland

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Queensland's Criminal Code 1899 lets a person who is unlawfully assaulted and did not provoke it use force reasonably necessary for defence, and force causing death or grievous bodily harm if the assault causes reasonable fear of death or grievous bodily harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise preserve themselves (s 271). The Code imposes no retreat requirement on someone who did not start or provoke the fight. A person who started or provoked the conflict keeps the defence for deadly force only if, before the necessity arose, they 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' (s 272). A separate partial defence (s 304B) reduces murder to manslaughter for killings in an abusive domestic relationship.

At home

s 267: a person in peaceable possession of a dwelling may use force to prevent or repel unlawful entry or remaining if they believe on reasonable grounds the intruder intends to commit an indictable offence in the dwelling and that the force is necessary; the section does not set an upper limit on the degree of force.

What the law says
Criminal Code 1899 (Qld), s 271 Self-defence against unprovoked assault
(1) When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for the person to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault, if the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous bodily harm. (2) If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable grounds, that the person can not otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous bodily harm, it is lawful for the person to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous bodily harm.
Criminal Code 1899 (Qld), s 272(2) Self-defence against provoked assault
This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous bodily harm first begun the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous bodily harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous bodily harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous bodily harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself or herself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Criminal Code 1899 (Qld), s 267 Defence of dwelling
It is lawful for a person who is in peaceable possession of a dwelling, and any person lawfully assisting him or her or acting by his or her authority, to use force to prevent or repel another person from unlawfully entering or remaining in the dwelling, if the person using the force believes on reasonable grounds— (a) the other person is attempting to enter or to remain in the dwelling with intent to commit an indictable offence in the dwelling; and (b) it is necessary to use that force.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Code Act 1899 (current in-force version) (Queensland Legislation, Office of the Queensland Parliamentary Counsel)
Australia as a whole

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).

58b453cf5efef3e0.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bolivia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 11 of the Penal Code (as amended by Ley 1768 of 1997), a person is exempt from liability if, in defence of any right of their own or of another, they repel an unjust or current aggression, provided there was "rational necessity of the defence" and no "evident disproportion" in the means used. The Code does not mention retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Excess is punished with the penalty for the negligent (culpable) offence, and a person whose excess came from excitement or disturbance justified by the circumstances is exempt from punishment. No special rule for the home appears in art. 11. The text used here is a 2008 compilation published by the University of Fribourg's criminal-law site; later amendments to art. 11 were not checked.

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley 1768 de modificaciones), art. 11
Art. 11°.- I. Está exento de responsabilidad: 1) (LEGITIMA DEFENSA).- El que en defensa de cualquier derecho, propio o ajeno, rechaza una agresión injusta o actual, siempre que hubiere necesidad racional de la defensa y no existiese evidente desproporción del medio empleado. ... II. El exceso en las situaciones anteriores será sancionado con la pena fijada para el delito culposo. Cuando proviniere de una excitación o turbación justificables por las circunstancias concomitantes en el momento del hecho, estará exento de pena.
