551aa67a40b6bfb5.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Zambia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Section 17 of Zambia's Penal Code (as amended in 1990) excuses force used to repel an unlawful attack on person or property if the means and degree of force are no more than is necessary in the circumstances; it does not mention retreat. The High Court of Zambia settled the retreat point in People v Zimba (HJ 2 of 2011, Matibini J, SC, February 2011): the court said the defence of self-defence has two aspects, retreat and the degree of retaliation; that a failure to retreat is an element in considering the reasonableness of the accused's conduct; that the obligation to retreat rather than strike down is not absolute; and that it is not the law that a person threatened must take to his heels, though he must show by his actions that he does not want to fight and is prepared to temporize and disengage. The court relied on the English cases R v Julien and R v McInnes, the Australian case R v Howe, Archbold 2010 para 19-42 ('The old rule of law that a man attacked must retreat as far as he can has disappeared') and Mwale v R ('The obligation on a man so assailed to retreat rather than to strike down his assailant is not absolute'). A ZambiaLII summary of People v Simwanza (HK 90 of 2011, High Court, 31 Dec 2010) lists 'Retreat/disengagement' among the factors considered, but that judgment was not opened. Where excessive force is honestly believed necessary, murder is reduced to manslaughter (People v Zimba, citing R v Howe and Jackson v R).

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 87), s. 17
Subject to any other provisions of this Code or any other law for the time being in force, a person shall not be criminally responsible for the use of force in repelling an unlawful attack upon his person or property, or the person or property of any other person, if the means he uses and the degree of force he employs in doing so are no more than is necessary in the circumstances to repel the unlawful attack.
People v Zimba (HJ 2 of 2011) [2011] ZMHC 62, Matibini J, SC (judgment)
The defence of self-defence has two aspects. The first is a question of retreat. And the second is the degree of retaliation. A failure to retreat is an element in considering the reasonableness of an accused conduct. The obligation to retreat rather to strike down is not absolute. Thus, it is not the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in a dramatic fashion. What is necessary is that a person threatened, or attacked must demonstrate by his actions that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporize, and to disengage. And perhaps to make some physical withdrawal.
People v Zimba (2011), quoting Archbold, Criminal Pleading, Evidence and Practice 2010, para. 19-42
The old rule of law that a man attacked must retreat as far as he can has disappeared. Whether the accused did retreat is only one element for the jury to consider on the question of whether the force was reasonably necessary.
People v Zimba (2011), quoting Mwale v R (as cited by defence counsel)
The obligation on a man so assailed to retreat rather than to strike down his assailant is not absolute. If by retreating he enhances rather than avoids the danger to himself, and it is easy to envisage circumstances in which this would be the case, it would not be reasonable to expect him to retreat.

5ba1ee210c19fe03.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Western Australia

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Western Australia's Criminal Code (s 248, rewritten in 2008) treats a harmful act as self-defence if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or another from a harmful act, even one that is not imminent, the act is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they believe them to be, and there are reasonable grounds for those beliefs. The Code does not mention retreat; no duty to retreat is stated. If a killing would have been self-defence except that the response was not reasonable, the person is guilty of manslaughter instead of murder (s 248(3), excessive self-defence). A separate home-invasion provision (s 244) gives occupants wider latitude inside their home.

At home

s 244 (home invasion, inserted 2000): an occupant may use any force they believe on reasonable grounds is necessary to keep out or remove a home invader or defend against violence; force intended or likely to cause death is lawful only if the occupant believes on reasonable grounds that violence is being or is likely to be used or is threatened against a person (s 244(1A)).

What the law says
Criminal Code (WA), s 248(3)–(4) Self-defence
(3) If — (a) a person unlawfully kills another person in circumstances which, but for this section, would constitute murder; and (b) the person’s act that causes the other person’s death would be an act done in self‑defence under subsection (4) but for the fact that the act is not a reasonable response by the person in the circumstances as the person believes them to be, the person is guilty of manslaughter and not murder. (4) A person’s harmful act is done in self‑defence if — (a) the person believes the act is necessary to defend the person or another person from a harmful act, including a harmful act that is not imminent; and (b) the person’s harmful act is a reasonable response by the person in the circumstances as the person believes them to be; and (c) there are reasonable grounds for those beliefs.
Criminal Code (WA), s 244(1A) Home invasion
Despite subsection (1), it is not lawful for the occupant to use force that is intended, or that is likely, to cause death to a home invader unless the occupant believes, on reasonable grounds, that violence is being or is likely to be used or is threatened in relation to a person by a home invader.

d2c31ce60a58e668.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tajikistan

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 40 of the Tajik Criminal Code says harm done to an attacker in necessary defence is not a crime when the attack involved violence dangerous to life or an immediate threat of it. Against less dangerous attacks, defence is lawful unless it exceeded the limits, meaning deliberate acts clearly out of line with the nature and danger of the attack; reactions caused by the surprise of an attack are not an excess. The article states that the right of defence exists regardless of any possibility of avoiding the attack or asking others or the authorities for help (wording added in 2004), so there is no duty to retreat. Killing while exceeding the limits is a separate, lighter offence (article 107) punished by up to two years. This is based on a consolidated text hosted by FAOLEX that includes amendments to at least 2008; later changes were not checked.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Republic of Tajikistan, art. 40(1), (2), (4)
1) Не является преступлением действие, совершенное в состоянии необходимой обороны, то есть при защите личности и прав обороняющегося или другого лица, охраняемых законом интересов общества или государства от общественно опасного посягательства, путем причинения посягающему вреда если это посягательство было сопряжено с насилием, опасным для жизни обороняющегося или другого лица, либо с непосредственной угрозой применения такого насилия. 2) Защита от посягательства, не сопряженного с насилием, опасным для жизни обороняющегося или другого лица, либо с непосредственной угрозой применения такого насилия, является правомерной, если при этом не было допущено превышения пределов необходимой обороны, то есть умышленных действий, явно не соответствующих характеру и опасности посягательства. ... 4) Право на необходимую оборону принадлежит лицу независимо от возможности избежать посягательства, независимо от профессиональной или иной специальной подготовки или служебного положения лица, либо обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или органам власти. (зрт 17.05.04г.N35)
Criminal Code, art. 107(1)
Убийство, совершенное при превышении пределов необходимой обороны, ‐ наказывается ограничением свободы на срок до двух лет или лишением свободы на тот же срок.

59bdb96e518e8916.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Sudan

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Under Sudan's Criminal Act 1991, the right of private defence arises only when a person faces an immediate or imminent assault on their own or another's person, property or honour and it is 'not possible to evade the danger by having recourse to the public authorities, or in any other manner' (s. 12(2)). The wording of the Act therefore makes defence available only where the danger cannot be avoided another way, and the defender may use only what is necessary and appropriate. Deliberately killing is allowed only against a danger of death, grievous hurt, rape, abduction, kidnapping, robbery, armed robbery (hiraba) or certain kinds of arson, sinking or poisoning damage (s. 12(4)). A person who kills by exceeding in good faith the legal limits of self-defence is treated as committing semi-intentional homicide instead of murder (s. 131(2)(b)). No court decisions on how strictly the 'evade' condition is applied were found.

What the law says
Criminal Act 1991, s. 12 – Right of private defence (English translation)
12.(1) No act shall be deemed an offence if done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. (2) The right of private defence arises when a person is confronted with the danger of an immediate or imminent assault upon his person, property or honour the person, property, or honour of any other person, and when it is not possible to evade the danger by having recourse to the public authorities, or in any other manner and the said person may combat the danger by what is necessary to combat it and by the appropriate means. (3) No right of private defence arises against a public servant, acting within the limits of the powers of his post, unless there is apprehension of causing death, or grievous hurt. (4) The right of private defence shall not extend to willfully causing death, unless the danger to be repelled is apprehended to cause death, grievous hurt, rape, abduction, kidnapping, robbery, armed robbery (hiraba), criminal mischief or damage to public property or establishment or criminal mischief by sinking or by setting fire or by using poisonous, or explosive materials.
Criminal Act 1991, s. 131(2)(b) – Semi-intentional homicide
(2) Notwithstanding the provision of section 130(1), culpable homicide shall be deemed to be semi- intentional in any of the following cases :- ... (b) where the offender commits culpable homicide by exceeding, in good-faith, the limits prescribed by law for the exercise of the right of self-defence;
Who makes criminal law here

The 2019 Constitutional Charter repealed the 2005 Interim Constitution and the state constitutions but kept the laws made under them in force. The 2005 constitution's Schedule C had given each state exclusive power over 'Statutes enacted under the penal law power, save for the penalization for the breach of National laws relating to the national competencies'. No source opened in 18 October states that the Criminal Act 1991 is Sudan's only criminal law.

Constitutional Charter for the Transitional Period, 2019 (Constitute Project translation), art. 2 (repeal clause)
The Transitional Constitution of Sudan of 2005 and state constitutions are repealed, while the laws issued thereunder remain in force, unless they are repealed or amended.
Interim National Constitution of the Republic of the Sudan, 2005, Schedule C (Powers of States)
The exclusive executive and legislative powers of a state of the Sudan shall be as follows:- ... Statutes enacted under the penal law power, save for the penalization for the breach of National laws relating to the national competencies;

Flag: the 2005 constitution gave each state its own penal-law power, and the 2019 Charter kept laws made under it in force, so state penal statutes may exist. Whether any state has used that power, and what the post-2019/post-war arrangements are, was not checked. South Sudan has been separate since 2011 (it has its own entry, SDS).

6def197880e5b272.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kyrgyzstan

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Kyrgyzstan's Criminal Code of 2021 (art. 46) allows necessary defence of the person, property, home and other rights; against an attack involving violence dangerous to life or health (or an immediate threat of it) there is no proportionality limit. Against lesser attacks the defence is lawful unless the defender intentionally went beyond the limits, causing excessive serious harm not called for by the situation. The article applies 'regardless of the possibility of avoiding the socially dangerous attack or of seeking help from other persons or authorities', so there is no duty to retreat. Defence against a sudden attack, a violent home intrusion, an armed attacker or a group attack is never excessive. Killing in excess of necessary defence is a separate offence punishable by up to five years' imprisonment (art. 124).

At home

Art. 46(5): defending against an unlawful and violent entry into a dwelling against the will of a lawful occupant is never an excess of necessary defence, even if the intruder is injured or killed.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Kyrgyz Republic No. 127 of 28 October 2021 (edition of 24.07.2026), art. 46(1), (5)–(7) (Russian)
1. Не является преступлением действие, за которое настоящим Кодексом предусмотрена ответственность, но совершенное в состоянии необходимой обороны, то есть в целях защиты личности, имущества человека, жилища и иных объектов, находящихся у него в собственности или ином праве, а также других прав обороняющегося либо другого лица, охраняемых законом интересов общества и государства от общественно опасного посягательства, если это посягательство было сопряжено с насилием, опасным для жизни и здоровья обороняющегося или другого лица, либо с непосредственной угрозой применения такого насилия. ... 5. Не являются превышением пределов необходимой обороны действия обороняющегося лица при защите от незаконного и насильственного проникновения посягающего лица в жилище, совершаемого против воли проживающего (пребывающего) в нем на законных основаниях лица, с причинением нападающему телесных повреждений, в том числе повлекших его смерть. 6. Независимо от тяжести вреда, причиненного посягающему, также не является превышением пределов необходимой обороны и не влечет уголовной ответственности применение оружия или любых других средств либо орудия для: 1) защиты от нападения вооруженного лица; 2) защиты от группового нападения. ... 7. Положения настоящей статьи в равной мере распространяются на всех лиц независимо от их профессиональной или иной специальной подготовки и служебного положения, а также независимо от возможности избежать общественно опасного посягательства или обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или органам власти.
Criminal Code (Kyrgyzstan), art. 46(2)–(3) (Russian)
2. Защита от посягательства, не сопряженного с насилием, опасным для жизни и здоровья обороняющегося или другого лица, либо с непосредственной угрозой применения такого насилия, а также защита от посягательства на завладение чужим имуществом являются правомерными, если при этом не было допущено превышение пределов необходимой обороны, то есть умышленных действий, не соответствующих характеру и опасности посягательства. 3. Превышением пределов необходимой обороны признается несоответствие защиты характеру и степени общественной опасности посягательства, в результате чего посягающему причиняется чрезмерный, не вызываемый обстановкой тяжкий вред.
Criminal Code (Kyrgyzstan), art. 124 (Russian)
Убийство, совершенное при превышении пределов необходимой обороны, а равно при превышении мер, необходимых для задержания лица, совершившего преступление, – наказывается лишением свободы на срок до пяти лет.

0ee4cff356ac2932.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Poland

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Article 25 § 1 of the Polish Criminal Code says a person who, in necessary defence, repels a direct, unlawful attack on any legally protected interest does not commit a crime. The statute does not mention retreat, and the Supreme Court has held that necessary defence is an independent right, not a last resort: a 2013 article by Prof. Marek Mozgawa (Maria Curie-Skłodowska University) quotes Supreme Court rulings that 'the principle of subsidiarity does not apply to necessary defence' and that an attacked person 'has no duty to save themselves by flight, nor to hide from the attacker in a closed room', but may repel the attack with all available necessary means. If the limits are exceeded, especially by a means of defence out of proportion to the danger, the court may extraordinarily mitigate the penalty or waive it; there is no punishment when the excess was caused by fear or agitation justified by the circumstances of the attack. Excess while repelling a home break-in is not punished unless the excess was gross.

At home

Article 25 § 2a (added by amendment to the 1997 Code): a person who exceeds the limits of necessary defence while repelling an attack consisting of breaking into a flat, premises, house or the adjoining fenced area, or an attack preceded by such a break-in, is not punished unless the excess was 'gross' (rażące).

What the law says
Kodeks karny (Act of 6 June 1997, consolidated Dz.U. 2025 poz. 383), art. 25
§ 1. Nie popełnia przestępstwa, kto w obronie koniecznej odpiera bezpośredni, bezprawny zamach na jakiekolwiek dobro chronione prawem. § 2. W razie przekroczenia granic obrony koniecznej, w szczególności gdy sprawca zastosował sposób obrony niewspółmierny do niebezpieczeństwa zamachu, sąd może zastosować nadzwyczajne złagodzenie kary, a nawet odstąpić od jej wymierzenia. § 2a. Nie podlega karze, kto przekracza granice obrony koniecznej, odpierając zamach polegający na wdarciu się do mieszkania, lokalu, domu albo na przylegający do nich ogrodzony teren lub odpierając zamach poprzedzony wdarciem się do tych miejsc, chyba że przekroczenie granic obrony koniecznej było rażące. § 3. Nie podlega karze, kto przekracza granice obrony koniecznej pod wpływem strachu lub wzburzenia usprawiedliwionych okolicznościami zamachu.
Sąd Najwyższy (Supreme Court) judgment, as quoted by M. Mozgawa (2013)
Osoba napadnięta nie ma obowiązku ani ratowania się ucieczką, ani ukrywania się przed napastnikiem w zamkniętym pomieszczeniu, ani też znoszenia napaści ograniczającej jej swobodę, lecz ma prawo odpierać zamach wszelkimi dostępnymi środkami, które są konieczne do zmuszenia napastnika do odstąpienia od kontynuowania zamachu.

9c10bcb13090e888.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Senegal

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Senegal's Penal Code (Law 65-60, on the old French model) says there is no crime when homicide, wounds or blows were 'commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence of oneself or another' (art. 316). The code then lists two situations that automatically count as such necessity: repelling a night-time break-in into an inhabited home, and defending against violent theft or looting. The code does not mention retreat or proportionality, and no Senegalese court decisions on whether a person must avoid the attack were found. Killing or injuring someone after being provoked by serious blows or violence is 'excusable' (art. 309), which reduces the penalty when the excuse is proven (art. 314).

At home

The code counts as 'current necessity of defence' a homicide, wounding or blows committed while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or the entrance of an inhabited house or flat or its outbuildings. Killings or injuries committed while repelling such a break-in when it is not at night are not justified but are 'excusable' (reduced penalty) under the provision that follows article 309, which refers night-time cases to article 317.

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n° 65-60), art. 316
Il n'y a ni crime ni délit, lorsque l'homicide, les blessures et les coups étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d'autrui.
Code pénal, art. 317 (numbering as it appears in the ICNL copy, whose two-column layout splits the article)
Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de défense, les deux cas suivants: 1° Si l'homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites, ou si les coups ont été portés en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d'une maison ou d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances; 2° Si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vo[l]s ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal, art. 309 and following article (excuses)
Le meurtre ainsi que les blessures et les coups sont excusables, s'ils ont été provoqués par des coups ou violences graves envers les personnes. ... Les crimes et délits mentionnés au précèdent article sont également excusables, s'ils ont été commis en repoussant pendant l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d'une maison ou d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances. ... Si le fait est arrivé pendant la nuit, ce cas est réglé par l'article 317.

7f65a7936a0f2b83.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Michigan

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Under Michigan's Self-Defense Act (2006 Public Act 309, effective 1 October 2006), a person who is not engaged in a crime may use deadly force 'anywhere he or she has the legal right to be with no duty to retreat' if they honestly and reasonably believe it is necessary to prevent imminent death, imminent great bodily harm, or imminent sexual assault of themselves or another (Mich. Comp. Laws § 780.972(1)). The Act keeps the earlier common-law rules on retreat for situations it does not cover (§ 780.973), so a person engaged in a crime, or one outside a place they have a legal right to be, falls back on case law. In homes and business premises, a 2006 companion law creates a rebuttable presumption of honest and reasonable fear when the other person was breaking in, committing home invasion, or abducting someone, with exceptions including domestic-violence situations where the defender has a prior history as the aggressor (§ 780.951). A person who uses force in compliance with the Act and is not engaged in a crime 'commits no crime' (§ 780.961(1)); if a prosecutor charges such a person anyway, the prosecutor must present evidence that the force was not justified at the warrant stage, at any preliminary examination and at trial (§ 780.961(2)), but Michigan has no separate pretrial immunity hearing. A person who used force in compliance with the Act is immune from civil liability to the person they used it against and to that person's relatives (§ 600.2922b, 2006 PA 314).

At home

Mich. Comp. Laws § 780.951 (2006): in civil and criminal cases there is a rebuttable presumption that a person using force under the Self-Defense Act honestly and reasonably believed death, sexual assault or great bodily harm was imminent if the other person was breaking and entering (or had broken in and remained in) a dwelling or business premises, committing home invasion, or unlawfully removing someone from a dwelling, business or occupied vehicle. The presumption does not apply against someone with a legal right to be there (absent a protective, no-contact, probation or parole order), a parent or guardian taking their own child, a peace officer acting lawfully, where the defender is committing a crime, or against a spouse, ex-spouse, dating partner, co-parent or household member if the defender has a prior history of domestic violence as the aggressor.

What the law says
Mich. Comp. Laws § 780.972(1)
An individual who has not or is not engaged in the commission of a crime at the time he or she uses deadly force may use deadly force against another individual anywhere he or she has the legal right to be with no duty to retreat if either of the following applies: (a) The individual honestly and reasonably believes that the use of deadly force is necessary to prevent the imminent death of or imminent great bodily harm to himself or herself or to another individual. (b) The individual honestly and reasonably believes that the use of deadly force is necessary to prevent the imminent sexual assault of himself or herself or of another individual.
Mich. Comp. Laws § 780.973
Except as provided in section 2, this act does not modify the common law of this state in existence on October 1, 2006 regarding the duty to retreat before using deadly force or force other than deadly force.
Mich. Comp. Laws § 780.951(1)
it is a rebuttable presumption in a civil or criminal case that an individual who uses deadly force or force other than deadly force under section 2 of the self-defense act has an honest and reasonable belief that imminent death of, sexual assault of, or great bodily harm to himself or herself or another individual will occur if both of the following apply: (a) The individual against whom deadly force ... is used is in the process of breaking and entering a dwelling or business premises or committing home invasion ...
Mich. Comp. Laws § 780.961
(1) An individual who uses deadly force or force other than deadly force in compliance with section 2 of the self-defense act and who has not or is not engaged in the commission of a crime at the time he or she uses that deadly force or force other than deadly force commits no crime in using that deadly force ... (2) ... the prosecutor ... shall present evidence to the judge or magistrate at the time of warrant issuance, at the time of any preliminary examination, and at the time of any trial establishing that the individual's actions were not justified ...
Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2922b
An individual who uses deadly force or force other than deadly force in self-defense or in defense of another individual in compliance with section 2 of the self-defense act is immune from civil liability for damages caused to either of the following by the use of that deadly force ...

  • MCL 780.951 (presumption), 780.961 (2006 PA 310), 600.2922b (2006 PA 314) (Michigan Legislature)

04e5d86c53686ab1.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Belarus

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 34 of the Belarus Criminal Code gives every citizen the right to defend against a socially dangerous attack, and says this right exists regardless of whether the person could avoid the attack or call others or the authorities for help, so there is no duty to retreat. Harm caused in defence of life, health, property, dwelling or other rights is not a crime unless the limits of necessary defence were exceeded. Excess means a mismatch, obvious to the defender, between the defence and the danger of the attack, where death or grave bodily injury is caused intentionally and without need. Acts done when the surprise of the attack prevented the defender from judging the danger are not an excess. Killing while exceeding the limits is a separate, lighter offence (article 143) punished by up to two years.

At home

Article 34(2) lists defence of the 'жилища' (dwelling) among the interests that may be defended, under the same rules as any other defence.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Republic of Belarus, art. 34(1)-(4)
1. Каждый гражданин имеет право на защиту от общественно опасного посягательства. Это право принадлежит лицу независимо от возможности избежать посягательства либо обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или органам власти. 2. Не является преступлением действие, совершенное в состоянии необходимой обороны, то есть при защите жизни, здоровья, собственности, жилища, прав обороняющегося или другого лица, интересов общества или государства от общественно опасного посягательства путем причинения посягающему вреда, если при этом не было допущено превышения пределов необходимой обороны. 3. Превышением пределов необходимой обороны признается явное для обороняющегося лица несоответствие защиты характеру и опасности посягательства, когда посягающему без необходимости умышленно причиняется смерть или тяжкое телесное повреждение. 4. Не являются превышением пределов необходимой обороны действия обороняющегося лица, если это лицо вследствие неожиданности посягательства не могло объективно оценить характер и опасность посягательства.
Criminal Code, art. 143
Убийство, совершенное при превышении пределов необходимой обороны, – наказывается исправительными работами на срок до двух лет, или ограничением свободы на тот же срок, или лишением свободы на срок до двух лет.

59ef097ece7b934c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Sudan

Self-defense narrowly allowed

South Sudan's Penal Code Act 2008 (in the Indian Penal Code tradition) says no act is an offence if done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence of one's own or another's body or property (s 40). The right never extends to inflicting more harm than necessary (s 42), and there is no right of private defence at all 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities' (s 43). The Act does not mention retreat. Intentionally causing death is allowed only to repel an attack causing reasonable fear of death or grievous hurt, rape or an assault for 'unnatural lust', or abduction or kidnapping (s 45). A person who in good faith exceeds the power of private defence and kills, without premeditation and without intending more harm than necessary, commits culpable homicide not amounting to murder rather than murder (s 210(3)), punishable by up to life imprisonment, a fine or both. The Act is listed here as restrictive because of the s 43 bar whenever police protection could be sought in time.

At home

The right of private defence of property extends to intentionally causing death only against robbery, house-breaking by night, arson of a building, tent or vessel used as a dwelling, or theft, mischief or house-trespass that reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt (Penal Code Act 2008, s 46).

What the law says
Penal Code Act 2008 (Act 9), ss 40(1), 42, 43
40. (1) No act is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. ... 42. The right of private defence shall, in no case, extend to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 43. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Act 2008, s 45 When Right of Private Defence of the Body Extends to Causing Death
The right of private defence of the body extends, under the limitations mentioned in sections 43 and 44 of this Act, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repulsed is any of the following— (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Penal Code Act 2008, s 210(3) Culpable Homicide (excess of private defence)
Whoever, in good faith, exercises the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him or her by law and causes the death of the person against whom he or she is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence, commits the offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

5ede5894fcb2f9c9.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Northern Territory

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The Northern Territory Criminal Code (s 43BD, which applies to Schedule 1 and declared offences) follows the Commonwealth model: conduct is self-defence only if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or another (or for listed property and trespass purposes) and it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceive them. The section does not mention retreat and no duty to retreat is stated. Intentionally inflicting death or serious harm only to protect property or deal with trespassers is excluded.

At home

No home-specific rule in s 43BD; force intentionally causing death or serious harm may not be used only to protect property or to prevent or remove a criminal trespasser (s 43BD(3)).

What the law says
Criminal Code Act 1983 (NT), s 43BD Self-defence
(1) A person is not criminally responsible for an offence if the person carries out the conduct constituting the offence in self-defence. (2) A person carries out conduct in self-defence only if: (a) the person believes the conduct is necessary: (i) to defend himself or herself or another person; or (ii) to prevent or terminate the unlawful imprisonment of himself or herself or another person; or (iii) to protect property from unlawful appropriation, destruction, damage or interference; or (iv) to prevent criminal trespass to any land or premises; or (v) to remove from any land or premises a person who is committing criminal trespass; and (b) the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as he or she perceives them. (3) However, the person does not carry out conduct in self-defence if: (a) the person uses force that involves the intentional infliction of death or serious harm: (i) to protect property; or (ii) to prevent criminal trespass; or (iii) to remove a person who is committing criminal trespass; ...
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Code Act 1983, as in force at 12 October 2026 (Northern Territory Legislation)
Australia as a whole

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).

Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book — Self-defence (Judicial Commission of New South Wales)

3a0d30925b1e6787.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Estonia

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Under section 28 of the Estonian Penal Code, a person acts lawfully when they fight off a direct or immediate unlawful attack on their own or someone else's legal rights, as long as they do not exceed the limits of self-defence. The statute says outright that having the chance to avoid the attack or to ask someone else for help does not take away the right to self-defence, so there is no duty to retreat. The limits are exceeded only if the defender deliberately uses means 'evidently incongruous' with the danger or deliberately causes evidently excessive harm to the attacker. Committing an offence in excess of the limits of self-defence is listed as a mitigating circumstance for sentencing (section 57).

At home

No separate home-defence rule; section 28 covers an unlawful attack against any legal rights of the person or another person.

What the law says
Penal Code (Karistusseadustik), § 28 (official English translation)
(1) An act is not unlawful if the person combats a direct or immediate unlawful attack against the legal rights of the person or of another person by violating the legal rights of the attacker and without exceeding the limits of self-defence. (2) A person is deemed to have exceeded the limits of self-defence if the person with deliberate or direct intent carries out self-defence by means which are evidently incongruous with the danger arising from the attack or if the person with deliberate of direct intent causes evidently excessive damage to the attacker. (3) An opportunity to avoid an attack or to request assistance from another person shall not preclude the right to self-defence.
Penal Code, § 57(1) point 8 (official English translation)
Mitigating circumstances are: ... 8) commission of the offence in excess of the limits of self-defence;
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Penal Code (Karistusseadustik), English translation, version in force from 19.07.2026 (Riigi Teataja (Estonian State Gazette))

881e2c4374041a55.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Guinea-Bissau

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Guinea-Bissau's Penal Code (1993) says acting in legitimate defence removes the unlawfulness of the act, and defines legitimate defence as action necessary to repel an unlawful attack that is imminent or under way but not yet over, against any legally protected interest of the defender or a third party. The code does not mention retreat; the test is whether the defensive action was necessary. If the defender uses means that are manifestly excessive in kind or degree, the act is unlawful but the penalty may be specially reduced, and excess caused by understandable disturbance, fear or fright removes guilt. No specific home-defence rule was found.

What the law says
Código Penal (1993), arts. 33–34 (text transcribed by OCR from a scanned copy; minor spelling may differ)
Artigo 33.º Legítima defesa: 1. A actuação do agente em legítima defesa exclui a ilicitude da conduta. 2. Considera-se legítima defesa a actuação necessária ao afastamento de uma agressão ilícita, iminente ou em início de execução mas ainda não terminada, a quaisquer interesses protegidos pela ordem jurídica e pertencentes ao agente ou a terceiro. Artigo 34.º Excesso de legítima defesa: 1. A conduta do agente é ilícita se empregar meios que pela sua espécie e grau de utilização forem manifestamente excessivos para a acção defensiva, mas a pena pode ser especialmente atenuada. 2. O excesso de meios utilizados devido a perturbação, medo ou susto compreensíveis, exclui a culpa do agente.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Código Penal da Guiné-Bissau (1993), Portuguese (policinglaw.info)

34595fbc4a9385b8.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Honduras

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Honduras's Penal Code (Decree 130-2017, published in La Gaceta on 10 May 2019) exempts from criminal liability a person who defends their own or another's person or rights against a current unlawful attack, if the means used were reasonably necessary to prevent or repel it and the defender did not sufficiently provoke it (art. 30(4)). Repelling a break-in to an inhabited home, or using violence against an intruder found inside, is automatically treated as meeting these requirements. The code does not mention retreat, and no Honduran court decision on retreat was found. If a non-essential requirement is missing, the defence counts as a 'qualified mitigating circumstance' that reduces the penalty (art. 31(1)).

At home

Penal Code art. 30(4) deems all three requirements of self-defence met for a person who repels the climbing over or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of an inhabited house or apartment or its outbuildings, or who uses violence against a stranger caught inside those places.

What the law says
Código Penal (Decreto 130-2017), art. 30(4) – Legítima defensa
Legítima defensa. Quien obra en defensa de la persona o derechos propios o extraños, siempre que concurran los requisitos siguientes: a) Agresión ilegítima actual; b) Necesidad razonable de los medios empleados para impedir o repeler la agresión; y, c) Falta de provocación suficiente de quien se defiende. Se entiende que concurren las tres (3) circunstancias anteriores respecto de quien rechaza el escalamiento o fractura de cercados, paredes, entradas de una casa o apartamento habitado o de sus dependencias o, emplea violencia contra la persona extraña a ella cuando sea sorprendido dentro de los indicados lugares
Código Penal (Decreto 130-2017), art. 31(1) – Circunstancias atenuantes
Las causas de exención de la responsabilidad criminal cuando no concurra alguno de los requisitos no esenciales exigidos para su apreciación. Estas causas tienen la consideración de atenuantes cualificadas
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

c1727c21a9448082.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Vanuatu

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Vanuatu's Penal Code (Cap. 135, s 23), which follows a French-style formula, removes criminal responsibility for an act 'dictated by the immediate necessity of defence' of oneself, another person or any right, against an unlawful action, provided the means of defence are not disproportionate to the seriousness of the threatened action. Intentional killing can be justified in defence against an attack causing a reasonable apprehension of death, grievous harm, rape or sodomy (s 23(2)). The Code does not mention retreat, and the Supreme Court decisions opened here (e.g. Public Prosecutor v Vakau, 2016, where three defendants were acquitted) applied the necessity and proportionality tests without discussing whether the defendants could have escaped. The prosecution must disprove self-defence once it is raised (s 9 of the Code). No special rule for the home and no partial 'excessive self-defence' rule appear in the Code text read.

What the law says
Penal Code [Cap. 135], s 23(1)–(2) (Consolidated Edition 2006)
(1) No criminal responsibility shall attach to an act dictated by the immediate necessity of defence of the person acting or of another, or of any right of himself or another, against an unlawful action, provided that the means of defence be not disproportionate to the seriousness of the unlawful action threatened. (2) Without prejudice to the generality thereof, subsection (1) shall apply to the intentional killing of another in defence of an attack causing a reasonable apprehension of death, grievous harm, rape or sodomy.
Public Prosecutor v Vakau [2016] VUSC 22 (Supreme Court, Fatiaki J, 11 March 2016)
The force used in self-defence must not be disproportionate
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Penal Code [Cap. 135], Laws of the Republic of Vanuatu, Consolidated Edition 2006 (Police Human Rights Resources (copy of official consolidation))
  • Public Prosecutor v Vakau [2016] VUSC 22 (PacLII)

d812669134807edf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cambodia

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Cambodia's Criminal Code of 2009 (art. 33) removes criminal responsibility for an offence committed in self-defence if it was compelled by the necessity to defend oneself, others or property against an unjustified assault, happened at the same time as the assault, and the means used were not disproportionate to its seriousness. Art. 34 presumes self-defence against night-time forced entry into a dwelling and against violent theft or pillage, but the presumption can be rebutted. The code does not mention retreat or flight. A second English translation (CJAD, University of Nottingham, from the 2014 EN/Khmer edition) was opened and has the same three conditions. No Cambodian court decision, bench book or law-faculty commentary on whether the defender must first try to avoid the attack was found, so the retreat question stays unsettled.

At home

Art. 34: self-defence is presumed where the act was done at night to repel an entry into a dwelling by forced entry, violence or deception, or against perpetrators of theft or pillage with violence; the presumption is rebuttable.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Kingdom of Cambodia (2009), art. 33 (English translation, Open Development Cambodia)
A person who committed an offence under a legitimate defence is not criminally responsible. Legitimate defence must fulfil the following conditions: 1. The offence is justified by the necessity to engage in defence against an unjustified aggression; 2. The offence and the aggression must happen at the same time; 3. There is no disproportion between the means of defence used and the severity of the aggression.
Criminal Code 2009 (2014 EN/Khmer edition), art. 33 Self-defence, as published by CJAD
A person who commits an offence in self- defence shall not be criminally responsible. Self-defence must meet the following conditions: - the offence was compelled by the necessity to defend oneself or others or to defend property against an unjustified assault; - the offence and the assault must occur at the same time; and - the means used in defence were not disproportionate to the seriousness of the assault.
Criminal Code 2009 (2014 edition), art. 34 Presumption of self-defence, as published by CJAD
A person shall be presumed to have acted in self-defence if he or she acted: (1) at night, to repel an entry into a dwelling place committed by forced entry, violence or deception; (2) to defend himself or herself against the perpetrators of theft or pillaging with violence. The presumption of self-defence is not absolute. It may be rebutted by contrary evidence.
What was tried

web search: 'Cambodia Criminal Code article 33 legitimate defence commentary retreat/flee/escape' (results: CJAD page, policehumanrightsresources PDF of the code, unrelated Canadian/Maltese material); 'Cambodia Criminal Code 2009 legitimate defence JICA annotated textbook Royal University of Law' (Japanese MOJ PDF opened: it is a Japanese translation of the code's promulgation decree, no commentary on retreat); 'Cambodia self-defence killing intruder court acquitted Article 33 Phnom Penh Post/Khmer Times' (Cambodia Daily news items only, not opened); 'Code pénal cambodgien doctrine fuite article 33' (Lextenso 'Droit du Cambodge' chapter behind paywall, not opened). No court ruling or commentary on avoidance located.

55c656d8104ce710.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Algeria

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Algeria's Penal Code (Ordinance 66-156 of 1966, as amended) says there is no offence when the act was required by the present necessity of legitimate defence of oneself, another person, or one's own or another's property, 'provided that the defence is proportionate to the seriousness of the attack' (art. 39). The code does not mention retreat. Article 40 lists cases that count as present necessity: repelling an attack on life or bodily integrity, repelling night-time climbing or break-in into a home, and defending against violent theft or looting. The code text found does not contain a specific 'excessive self-defence' rule in these articles.

At home

Article 40 counts as legitimate defence killing, wounding or blows used to repel an attack on a person's life or bodily integrity, or to repel at night the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of an inhabited house or flat or their outbuildings, and acts against perpetrators of violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal (Ordonnance n° 66-156), art. 39(2°)
Il n'y a pas d'infraction: ... 2°) Lorsque le fait était commandé par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d’autrui ou d’un bien appartenant à soi-même ou à autrui, pourvu que la défense soit proportionnée à la gravité de l’agression.
Code pénal (Ordonnance n° 66-156), art. 40
Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de légitime défense: 1°) L’homicide commis, les blessures faites ou les coups portés en repoussant une agression contre la vie ou l’intégrité corporelle d’une personne ou en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d’une maison ou d’un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances; 2°) L’acte commis en se défendant ou en défendant autrui contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Code pénal, 4e édition (bilingual French/Arabic), Ministère de la Justice (Ministère de la Justice, Algérie (hosted by rightofassembly.info))

b5b91b05dc680881.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Morocco

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Morocco's Penal Code (consolidated text of 5 July 2018) says there is no offence when it was 'commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence' of oneself, another person, or one's own or another's property, 'provided the defence is proportionate to the seriousness of the aggression' (art. 124(3)). Repelling a night-time break-in into a home and defending against violent theft or looting are presumed to be legitimate defence (art. 125). The code does not mention retreat or flight, and no Moroccan court decisions on the point were found. When an excuse applies (for example, killing provoked by serious blows or violence, art. 416, or repelling a daytime break-in, art. 417), a crime punishable by death or life imprisonment is reduced to one to five years' imprisonment (art. 423).

At home

Killing, wounding or blows committed while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or the entrance of an inhabited house or flat or its outbuildings are presumed to be legitimate defence (art. 125(1)). The same acts by day are not presumed justified but are 'excusable' (art. 417), which reduces the penalty.

What the law says
Code pénal (version consolidée au 5 juillet 2018), art. 124(3)
Il n'y a ni crime, ni délit, ni contravention : ... 3° Lorsque l'infraction était commandée par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d'autrui ou d'un bien appartenant à soi-même ou à autrui, pourvu que la défense soit proportionnée à la gravité de l'agression.
Code pénal, art. 125
Sont présumés accomplis dans un cas de nécessité actuelle de légitime défense : 1° L'homicide commis, les blessures faites ou les coups portés, en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d'une maison ou d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances; 2° L'infraction commise en défendant soi-même ou autrui contre l'auteur de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal, arts. 417 and 423
Article 417 Le meurtre, les blessures et les coups sont excusables s'ils ont été commis en repoussant pendant le jour l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d'une maison ou d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances. S'ils ont été commis pendant la nuit, les dispositions de l'article 125, alinéa 1, sont applicables. ... Article 423 Lorsque le fait d'excuse est prouvé, la peine est réduite : 1° A un emprisonnement d'un à cinq ans s'il s'agit d'un crime légalement puni de mort ou de la réclusion perpétuelle; 2° A un emprisonnement de six mois à deux ans s'il s'agit de tout autre crime; 3° A un emprisonnement d'un à trois mois s'il s'agit d'un délit.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

a30b95d13a5ab9a8.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Romania

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 19 of the Romanian Criminal Code (Law 286/2009) justifies an act done to remove a material, direct, immediate and unjust attack on oneself, another, their rights or a general interest, 'if the defence is proportionate to the seriousness of the attack'; a person repelling an unlawful, violent, fraudulent, break-in or night-time entry into a dwelling is presumed to act in legitimate defence (art. 19(3)). The code does not mention retreat. A 2025 Romanian legal textbook (Dunea and Anghel, Fise de drept penal, vol. 1, 8th ed., Hamangiu, sheet no. 8) says that, unlike necessity, the law does not require the act to be the only way of removing the attack, and that 'doctrine constantly points out' that if the perpetrator could have hoped to avoid the attack by fleeing, hiding or begging the attacker's mercy, the possibility of using those alternatives does not exclude legitimate defence; the court may still look at other alternatives, but as a rule this goes to the proportionality of the defence to the attack. An earlier doctoral-thesis summary (Nicolae Titulescu University) described the question as controversial in doctrine and proposed an express no-retreat clause. No Înalta Curte de Casație și Justiție decision stating the retreat rule was opened. Excess of proportionate limits caused by disturbance or fear is not imputable (art. 26).

At home

Article 19(3) presumes legitimate defence for a person who acts to repel someone entering a dwelling, room, outbuilding or enclosed place belonging to it without right, by violence, deceit, break-in or similar unlawful means, or at night. The textbook adds that the presumption applies while the intruder is still inside and not withdrawing; if the intruder has left or is in a non-offensive retreat, the presumption can/should be set aside.

What the law says
Codul penal (Law 286/2009), art. 19
(2) Este în legitimă apărare persoana care săvârşeşte fapta pentru a înlătura un atac material, direct, imediat şi injust, care pune în pericol persoana sa, a altuia, drepturile acestora sau un interes general, dacă apărarea este proporţională cu gravitatea atacului. (3) Se prezumă a fi în legitimă apărare, în condiţiile alin. (2), acela care comite fapta pentru a respinge pătrunderea unei persoane într-o locuinţă, încăpere, dependinţă sau loc împrejmuit ţinând de aceasta, fără drept, prin violenţă, viclenie, efracţie sau alte asemenea modalităţi nelegale ori în timpul nopţii. [Our rendering: (2) A person is in legitimate defence who commits the act to remove a material, direct, immediate and unjust attack endangering their person, another's, their rights or a general interest, if the defence is proportionate to the seriousness of the attack. (3) A person who commits the act to repel the entry of someone into a dwelling, room, outbuilding or enclosed place belonging to it, without right, by violence, deceit, break-in or other such unlawful means, or at night, is presumed to be in legitimate defence.]
Mihai Dunea and Simona Anghel, Fișe de drept penal pentru admiterea în magistratură și avocatură, vol. 1 Partea generală, ed. 8 (Hamangiu, 2025), Fișa nr. 8 'Legitima apărare', condition that the defence be necessary
spre deosebire de starea de necesitate, nu se prevede expres/nu este necesar ca săvârșirea faptei prevăzute de legea penală să fie singura cale de înlăturare a atacului; • doctrina evidențiază constant că, dacă făptuitorul putea spera să evite atacul recurgând la fugă sau ascunzându-se ori implorând mila agresorului, aceste alternative nu sunt viabile, în sensul că posibilitatea recurgerii la ele nu exclude reținerea legitimei apărări; desigur, existența unor alte alternative care să nu conducă la comiterea unei fapte prevăzute de legea penală poate fi analizată de instanță, cu posibila consecință a refuzului acordării beneficiului legitimei apărări, dar, de regulă, aceasta privește condiția proporționalității apărării față de atac; [Our rendering: unlike the state of necessity, it is not expressly provided / not necessary that committing the act be the only way of removing the attack; doctrine constantly points out that if the perpetrator could have hoped to avoid the attack by fleeing, hiding or begging the aggressor's mercy, these alternatives are not viable, in the sense that the possibility of resorting to them does not exclude a finding of legitimate defence; of course, the existence of other alternatives not involving a criminal act may be examined by the court, possibly leading to refusal of legitimate defence, but as a rule this concerns the condition that the defence be proportionate to the attack.]
Sources (read 2026-10-17, 2026-10-18)

6938bba5083b6b0c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

French Southern and Antarctic Lands

Part of France, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The French Southern and Antarctic Lands (TAAF) have no permanent population and no criminal code of their own. Article 1-1 of the TAAF statute (Law no. 55-1052 of 6 August 1955, as amended in 2007) makes French laws on 'droit pénal et ... procédure pénale' (criminal law and criminal procedure) apply there automatically, so the French Penal Code applies. Under art. 122-5, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack; defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Neither article mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not say whether flight is expected. Art. 122-6 presumes self-defence against night-time break-ins into inhabited places and against violent theft.

At home

French Penal Code art. 122-6 applies: a person is presumed to have acted in self-defence when repelling, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, or when defending against perpetrators of violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Loi n° 55-1052 du 6 août 1955, art. 1-1, 5° (text as proposed in the 2006 government bill that inserted it)
Par dérogation au premier alinéa, sont applicables de plein droit dans les Terres australes et antarctiques françaises, sans préjudice de dispositions les adaptant à l'organisation particulière du territoire, les dispositions législatives et réglementaires qui sont relatives : [...] 5° Au droit pénal et à la procédure pénale ;
Assemblée nationale, amendment CL53 (7 September 2017), exposé sommaire (confirming art. 1-1, 5° is in force)
pour les Terres australes et antarctiques françaises, le code de procédure pénale est applicable de plein droit sans mention expresse en vertu du 5° de l'article 1-1 de la loi n° 55-1052
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité, 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Projet de loi portant dispositions statutaires et institutionnelles relatives à l'outre-mer (Sénat, n° 360, 2005-2006) (Sénat (France))

476e5483754a1bff.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Paraguay

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Paraguay's Penal Code (Law 1160/97) says a person does not act unlawfully when their conduct was necessary and rational to repel or deflect a present, unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interest (art. 19). The code does not mention retreat or give a special rule for defending a home, and no Paraguayan court decision on retreat was found. A person who goes beyond the limits of self-defence out of confusion or terror is exempt from punishment (art. 24), and the code also allows exemption or reduced punishment where no other conduct could be expected of someone facing a present danger to life, body or liberty (art. 25).

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley N° 1160/97), art. 19 – Legítima defensa
No obra antijurídicamente quien realizara una conducta descrita en el tipo legal de un hecho punible, cuando ella fuera necesaria y racional para rechazar o desviar una agresión, presente y antijurídica, a un bien jurídico propio o ajeno.
Código Penal (Ley N° 1160/97), art. 24 – Exceso por confusión o terror
El que realizara un hecho antijurídico excediéndose por confusión o terror en los límites de la legítima defensa o de un estado de necesidad justificante, será eximido de pena.
Código Penal (Ley N° 1160/97), art. 25 – Inexigibilidad de otra conducta
El que realizara un hecho antijurídico para rechazar o desviar de sí mismo, de un pariente o de otra persona allegada a él, un peligro presente para su vida, su integridad física o su libertad, será eximido de pena cuando, atendidas todas las circunstancias, no le haya sido exigible otra conducta. En caso de haber sido exigible otra conducta, la pena podrá ser atenuada con arreglo al artículo 67.

6fac31dffef9ebe2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Texas

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

The Texas Penal Code allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is immediately necessary to protect against another's unlawful deadly force, or to prevent an imminent aggravated kidnapping, murder, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, robbery or aggravated robbery (§ 9.32(a)). Senate Bill 378, in force 1 September 2007, removed the duty to retreat: a person who has a right to be where the force is used, did not provoke the attacker and is not engaged in criminal activity 'is not required to retreat', and a jury may not consider failure to retreat when judging whether the belief was reasonable (§ 9.32(c)-(d)). This applies anywhere the person lawfully is, including vehicles and workplaces. The same law created a presumption that the belief was reasonable when the attacker was forcibly entering or trying to drag someone out of the actor's occupied home, vehicle, or place of business or employment, or was committing one of the listed violent crimes. Texas also allows deadly force to protect property in limited cases, including theft or criminal mischief at night, if the property cannot be protected another way (§ 9.42). A defendant whose force was justified under Penal Code chapter 9 is immune from civil liability for resulting injury or death (Civil Practice and Remedies Code § 83.001, added 1995, amended 2007). No statutory pretrial criminal immunity hearing exists; justification is decided at trial. Force is not justified for someone who provoked the other's use or attempted use of unlawful force, unless they abandoned the encounter (§ 9.31(b)).

At home

The belief that deadly force was immediately necessary is presumed reasonable when the person against whom it was used was unlawfully and with force entering, or trying to enter, the actor's occupied habitation, vehicle, or place of business or employment, or forcibly removing the actor from it, provided the actor did not provoke them and was not engaged in criminal activity other than a traffic Class C misdemeanor (Penal Code § 9.32(b), 2007). Texas also allows deadly force to protect property against arson, burglary, robbery and night-time theft or criminal mischief in some circumstances (§ 9.42).

What the law says
Texas Penal Code § 9.32(c)-(d) (S.B. 378, 2007)
(c) A person who has a right to be present at the location where the deadly force is used, who has not provoked the person against whom the deadly force is used, and who is not engaged in criminal activity at the time the deadly force is used is not required to retreat before using deadly force as described by this section. (d) For purposes of Subsection (a)(2), in determining whether an actor described by Subsection (c) reasonably believed that the use of deadly force was necessary, a finder of fact may not consider whether the actor failed to retreat.
Texas Penal Code § 9.32(a)
A person is justified in using deadly force against another: (1) if the actor would be justified in using force against the other under Section 9.31; and (2) when and to the degree the actor reasonably believes the deadly force is immediately necessary: (A) to protect the actor against the other's use or attempted use of unlawful deadly force; or (B) to prevent the other's imminent commission of aggravated kidnapping, murder, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, robbery, or aggravated robbery.
Texas Penal Code § 9.32(b) (presumption)
The actor's belief under Subsection (a)(2) that the deadly force was immediately necessary as described by that subdivision is presumed to be reasonable if the actor: (1) knew or had reason to believe that the person against whom the deadly force was used: (A) unlawfully and with force entered, or was attempting to enter unlawfully and with force, the actor's occupied habitation, vehicle, or place of business or employment ...
Civil Practice and Remedies Code § 83.001
A defendant who uses force or deadly force that is justified under Chapter 9, Penal Code, is immune from civil liability for personal injury or death that results from the defendant's use of force or deadly force, as applicable.

8616a0f4f8ebdbaf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New Caledonia

Part of France, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

New Caledonia applies the French Penal Code: art. 711-1 makes Books I to V applicable there, subject to the adaptations in that title, so self-defence is governed by arts. 122-5 and 122-6 (necessity, simultaneity, no disproportion; presumption for repelling night-time entry into an inhabited place and violent theft). Neither article mentions retreat. In the one Cour de cassation decision found that discusses flight (Crim., 28 February 2006, no. 05-87400), the defendant argued that 'la fuite n'est pas une obligation légale' (flight is not a legal obligation) after the investigating chamber found later shots disproportionate partly because the pharmacist 'pouvait alors se mettre à l'abri à l'arrière de l'officine' (could then have taken shelter at the back of the shop), when the robbers were already fleeing; the Cour de cassation rejected the appeal on the ground that the investigating chamber's assessment of the facts was sovereign, without ruling on whether flight is required. The retreat question therefore remains unsettled by the sources opened.

At home

Art. 122-6 presumes self-defence for a person who repels, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, or defends against violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal (France), art. 711-1
Sous réserve des adaptations prévues au présent titre, les livres Ier à V du présent code sont applicables, dans leur rédaction résultant de la loi n° 2026-813 du 24 août 2026 ..., en Nouvelle-Calédonie, en Polynésie française et dans les îles Wallis et Futuna.
Code pénal (France), art. 122-5, first paragraph
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte.
Cass. crim., 28 février 2006, n° 05-87400 (appellant's ground, not the Court's holding)
4 / alors que si l'existence d'un choix autre que la violence exclut la légitime défense, la fuite n'est pas une obligation légale ; qu'en affirmant que la riposte était disproportionnée dès lors que le commerçant pouvait fuir pour se mettre à l'abri à l'arrière de l'officine, la chambre de l'instruction a violé les textes susvisés [English rendering, mine: 4. whereas, although the existence of a choice other than violence excludes self-defence, flight is not a legal obligation; by holding that the response was disproportionate because the shopkeeper could flee to shelter at the back of the pharmacy, the investigating chamber breached the above provisions]
Cass. crim., 28 février 2006, n° 05-87400 (Court's answer)
Qu'en effet, les juridictions d'instruction apprécient souverainement si les faits retenus à la charge de la personne mise en examen sont constitutifs d'une infraction, la Cour de cassation n'ayant d'autre pouvoir que de vérifier si, à supposer ces faits établis, la qualification justifie la saisine de la juridiction de jugement ; Que, dès lors, les moyens ne peuvent qu'être écartés ; [English rendering, mine: Investigating courts assess sovereignly whether the facts charged constitute an offence, the Cour de cassation having no power other than to check whether, assuming those facts proven, the legal characterisation justifies sending the case to trial; the grounds must therefore be dismissed.]

dc40a716225669f3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Azerbaijan

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Azerbaijan's Criminal Code (1999) makes harm caused in 'necessary defence' of life, health or rights not a crime, as long as the defence stays within allowed limits. Article 36.2 says the right exists regardless of whether the person could have called the authorities or others for help, or could have avoided the attack, so there is no duty to retreat. Force that is deliberate and obviously out of line with the nature and danger of the attack counts as 'excess of the limits of necessary defence', which remains a (lesser) crime. The code text found does not contain a separate home-defence rule.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Republic of Azerbaijan (1999, as amended 2018), art. 36 (Necessary defence)
36.2. All persons irrespective of their professional or other special preparation and service position shall have right on necessary defence in an equal measure. This right shall be distributed on persons irrespective to an opportunity to address for the help to the state bodies or other persons, and also an opportunity to avoid publicly dangerous encroachment. 36.3. The deliberate actions, which are obviously not appropriate to nature and a degree of public danger of an encroachment, shall be admitted as excess of limits on necessary defense.

00461309521e953b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Burkina Faso

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Burkina Faso's Penal Code (Law No. 025-2018/AN) says a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same moment out of the necessity of legitimate defence, unless the means used were disproportionate to the seriousness of the attack. The code does not mention retreat or a duty to avoid the attack. Defence against a crime or offence against property may never include an intentional killing and must be strictly necessary and proportionate. Night-time defence of an inhabited place against forced or tricked entry, and defence against violent robbery, are named as legitimate defence.

At home

Article 132-2 lists as acts required by the immediate necessity of legitimate defence those committed to repel, at night, entry by climbing, break-in, violence or trickery into a house, inhabited flat, their outbuildings or any other inhabited place, and those committed against perpetrators of violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n° 025-2018/AN), art. 132-2
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction. Sont notamment commandés par la nécessité immédiate de la légitime défense les actes commis : ‑ pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par escalade, effraction, violence ou ruse dans une maison, un appartement habité ou leurs dépendances ou dans tout autre lieu habité ; ‑ pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

a231e42a94db93a7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Yemen

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Under art. 27 of Yemen's Criminal Code (Republican Decree Law No. 12 of 1994, English translation published by CJAD), self-defence arises when a person faces an immediate danger from a crime to themselves, their honour or property, or those of others, and cannot turn to the public authorities to avert the danger in time; the defender may then repel it 'by any appropriate means or any appropriate method'. The code does not mention retreat or flight, and no Yemeni court decision or commentary on avoidance was found, so the retreat question is left unsettled. Intentional killing is lawful in self-defence only to repel a reasonably feared murder or serious injury, attempted forced rape or sodomy, or armed kidnapping of the defender or close relatives (art. 28); strong evidence is required, and if self-defence is proved there is no qisas, blood money or compensation.

At home

Art. 29 allows intentional killing in defence of property only to repel certain acts, including "Unlawful entry at night to an inhabited house or any of its auxiliaries" (English translation).

What the law says
Criminal Code 1994 (English translation), art. 27
Legitimate Self-defense arises when a person faces an immediate danger from a crime to himself/herself,his/her honor or his/her property, or the lives, honor and property of others without resorting to the public authorities to evade this danger in due time. Accordingly the defending person may repel such danger by any appropriate means or any appropriate method.
Criminal Code 1994, art. 28
Intentional murder is not lawful in self-defense, unless it was intended to repulse any act that threatens to lead to any of the following crimes, with such fear being reasonable: 1. Murder or serious injury, if such injuries fall on the defendant or any of his relatives. 2. Attempted forced rape or sodomy on the defendant thereof, his spouse or any person who is considered his kin or relative. 3. Forced or threatened armed kidnapping of the defendant, his spouse, children or one of his “sanctified relations” to whom the latter's marriage is forbidden. Strong evidence must be presented for all forms of self-defense; if they prove as such, there is no punishment by In-Kind retribution [qisas], blood money or compensation for injury to be meted out to the defendant accordingly.
Criminal Code 1994, art. 29
The right of self-defense for the defense of property does not allow for intentional murder, unless it is intended to repulse any of the following: 1. Intentional arsenals. 2. Serious robbery cases. 3. Unlawful entry at night to an inhabited house or any of its auxiliaries.

09e30e78906a8791.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Oman

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Oman's Penal Code issued by Royal Decree 7/2018 allows legitimate defence only if all of these conditions are met: the defender faces a present danger from a crime against their own or another's life, honour or property (or reasonably believes so); it is impossible to reach the public authorities in time; 'there is no other means to repel this danger'; the defence is necessary and proportionate; and it is aimed at the source of the attack (art. 46). The 'no other means' condition is written into the law itself; no Omani court decision explaining whether it requires escape was found. If the defender in good faith goes beyond the limits of self-defence, or mistakenly believes they are in a self-defence situation, they remain liable, but the court may impose the penalty for a lesser category of offence (misdemeanour instead of felony) (art. 47). Self-defence is available even against an attacker who is not criminally responsible, such as a child or mentally ill person (art. 48).

At home

The 2018 Penal Code has no separate home or night-time break-in rule in its self-defence chapter (arts. 46–48). The former Penal Law of 1974 (art. 253) had treated repelling a night-time break-in of an inhabited house as self-defence; that law was replaced in 2018.

What the law says
Penal Code (Royal Decree 7/2018), art. 46
لا جريمة إذا وقع الفعل استعمالا لحق الدفاع الشرعي، ويقوم هذا الحق إذا توافرت الشروط الآتية: أ – إذا واجه المدافع خطرا حالا من جريمة على نفسه أو عرضه أو ماله أو نفس غيره أو عرضه أو ماله، أو اعتقد قيام هذا الخطر، وكان اعتقاده مبنيا على أسباب معقولة. ب – أن يتعذر على المدافع الالتجاء إلى السلطات العامة في الوقت المناسب لدفع هذا الخطر. ج – ألا توجد وسيلة أخرى لدفع هذا الخطر. د – أن يكون الدفاع لازما لدفع الاعتداء، ومتناسبا معه. هـ – أن يكون الدفاع موجها إلى مصدر الاعتداء.
Penal Code 2018, art. 47
إذا تجاوز المدافع بحسن نية حدود حق الدفاع الشرعي، أو اعتقد خطأ أنه في حالة دفاع شرعي، فإنه يكون مسؤولا عن الجريمة التي ارتكبها. وللمحكمة في هذه الحالة أن تحكم بعقوبة الجنحة بدلا من عقوبة الجناية، وأن تحكم بعقوبة المخالفة بدلا من عقوبة الجنحة.
Penal Code 2018, art. 48
تقوم حالة الدفاع الشرعي، ولو كان الشخص المستعمل ضده هذا الحق غير مسؤول جزائيا، وفقا لأحكام موانع المسؤولية المقررة قانونا.
