b328d11c5a434a11.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Florida

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Florida allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to themselves or another, or to prevent the imminent commission of a forcible felony (Fla. Stat. § 776.012(2)). There is no duty to retreat anywhere a person has a right to be, as long as they are not engaged in criminal activity; Florida's 2005 law (ch. 2005-27) was the first modern 'stand your ground' statute, and it was rewritten in 2014 (ch. 2014-195) to cover threatened force too. In a home, residence or occupied vehicle the law presumes reasonable fear of death or great bodily harm when the other person was unlawfully and forcibly entering, but that presumption does not apply against another lawful resident (absent a protective injunction or no-contact order), against a parent or guardian taking their own child, against an identified police officer, or if the defender was engaged in crime. A person who used force lawfully is immune from arrest, criminal prosecution and civil suit by the attacker or the attacker's heirs (§ 776.032), and a court must award attorney's fees and lost income to a defendant found immune in a civil case. Since a 2017 amendment (ch. 2017-72), once the defendant raises a prima facie claim at a pretrial immunity hearing, the prosecution must disprove immunity by clear and convincing evidence. Police may investigate but may not arrest unless there is probable cause that the force was unlawful. The justification is not available to someone committing or escaping from a forcible felony, or to an initial provoker, unless the provoker faced imminent deadly danger after exhausting every reasonable means of escape, or withdrew in good faith and clearly said so (§ 776.041).

At home

Fla. Stat. § 776.013: a person in a dwelling or residence where they have a right to be has no duty to retreat and may use deadly force if they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent imminent death, great bodily harm or a forcible felony. The law presumes a reasonable fear of death or great bodily harm when the person against whom force is used was unlawfully and forcibly entering (or had entered) a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle, or was trying to remove someone from it, and presumes an intruder who forcibly enters intends violence. 'Dwelling' includes an attached porch and a tent.

What the law says
Fla. Stat. § 776.012(2)
A person who uses or threatens to use deadly force in accordance with this subsection does not have a duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground if the person using or threatening to use the deadly force is not engaged in a criminal activity and is in a place where he or she has a right to be.
Fla. Stat. § 776.013(1)–(2)
A person who is in a dwelling or residence in which the person has a right to be has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground ... A person is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or great bodily harm to himself or herself or another when using or threatening to use defensive force that is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm to another if: (a) The person against whom the defensive force was used or threatened was in the process of unlawfully and forcefully entering, or had unlawfully and forcibly entered, a dwelling, residence, or occupied vehicle ...
Fla. Stat. § 776.032(1), (4)
A person who uses or threatens to use force as permitted in s. 776.012, s. 776.013, or s. 776.031 is justified in such conduct and is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action ... (4) In a criminal prosecution, once a prima facie claim of self-defense immunity from criminal prosecution has been raised by the defendant at a pretrial immunity hearing, the burden of proof by clear and convincing evidence is on the party seeking to overcome the immunity from criminal prosecution provided in subsection (1).
Fla. Stat. § 776.041
The justification described in the preceding sections of this chapter is not available to a person who: (1) Is attempting to commit, committing, or escaping after the commission of, a forcible felony; or (2) Initially provokes the use or threatened use of force against himself or herself, unless ...

9c7e399b58ab22aa.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ethiopia

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Ethiopia's Criminal Code (2005) allows defence of oneself or another against an unlawful or imminent unlawful attack only 'if the attack or imminent attack could not have been otherwise averted' and if the defence was proportionate. The code does not use the word 'retreat', but this wording makes legitimate defence conditional on there being no other way to avert the attack; no court ruling interpreting it was found. If the defender used disproportionate means or went beyond what was needed, the court must reduce the penalty, and may impose no punishment if the excess was due to excusable fear, surprise or excitement caused by the attack. No separate home-defence rule was found.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Ethiopia (2005), art. 78 (Legitimate Defence)
An act done in self-defence or the defence of another person against an unlawful attack or an imminent and unlawful attack against a legally protected right shall not be punishable if the attack or imminent attack could not have been otherwise averted and if the defence was proportionate to the needs of the case.
Criminal Code of Ethiopia (2005), art. 79 (Excess in Legitimate Defence)
(1) When a person in repelling an unlawful attack or an imminent and unlawful attack exceeded the limits of legitimate defence by using disproportionate means or going beyond the acts necessary for averting the danger, the Court shall, without restriction, reduce the penalty (Art. 180). (2) The Court may impose no punishment when the excess committed was due to excusable fear, surprise or excitement caused by the attack.
Who makes criminal law here

Under the Constitution of Ethiopia (1994), art. 55(5), the federal House of Peoples' Representatives 'shall enact a penal code', but the regional states 'may, however, enact penal laws on matters that are not specifically covered by Federal penal legislation.' The Criminal Code that governs homicide and self-defence is federal.

Constitution of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, art. 55(5)
It shall enact a penal code. The States may, however, enact penal laws on matters that are not specifically covered by Federal penal legislation.

Flag: the constitution lets the regional states make penal laws on matters the federal code does not cover; whether any region has done so was not checked. Homicide and self-defence are covered by the federal Criminal Code.

118a9be09b482e49.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Baja California

Part of Mexico, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Código Penal para el Estado de Baja California, art. 23(B)(II): a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence used is necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. No avoidance or 'no other means' condition appears in the article, and it does not say the defender need not flee. National Supreme Court (SCJN) theses point both ways: a 1940 thesis (registro 814826) says flight should not be imposed as a condition, while a 1946 thesis (registro 806596) denied the defence where the accused 'could well have avoided the aggression by other means'. No state-specific thesis was found (web search budget ran out), so whether retreat is required is not settled. Excess (art. 79) is punished as a vencible mistake about the law (error de prohibición vencible) but still counts as intentional; it is not excess where a woman facing physical, sexual or femicidal violence acted in fear, terror or confusion.

At home

Art. 23(B)(II) presumes the requirements are met for whoever causes harm, injury or death to someone who by violence, climbing in or any other means tries to enter or has entered their home or its outbuildings without right (even if not their usual home), their family's, their office, business, or where they find such a person there in circumstances showing a possible attack. A further presumption covers a woman repelling physical, sexual or femicidal violence, and a third person defending her.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Baja California, art. 23, apartado B, fracción II
II. Legítima defensa: Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte de la persona agredida o de la persona defensora; Se presumirá que concurren los requisitos de la legítima defensa, respecto de aquél que cause un daño, lesión o privación de la vida, a quien a través de la violencia, del escalamiento o por cualquier otro medio trate de penetrar o ya haya penetrado sin derecho, su hogar o sus dependencias, aunque no sea su hogar habitual, a los de su familia o los de cualquier persona que tenga el mismo deber de defender o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos de los que tenga la misma obligación; dentro de la casa donde se encuentre su familia, en su oficina de trabajo, su negocio comercial, o bien, cuando lo encuentre en alguno de esos lugares, en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión;
Código Penal para el Estado de Baja California, art. 79
ARTÍCULO 79.- Casos de exceso.- Al que incurra en exceso en alguna de las causas de justificación se le impondrá la sanción correspondiente al error de prohibición vencible, pero quedará subsistente la atribución del hecho a título doloso. ... No se considerará exceso en la legítima defensa cuando la mujer sea víctima de violencia física, sexual o feminicida, o en el hecho haya estado en peligro de serlo y al momento en que ésta se concretice acredite haber estado en un estado miedo o terror o se encuentren en un estado de confusión que afecte su capacidad para determinar el límite adecuado de su respuesta o la racionalidad de los medios empleados.
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 814826 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA. EVITABILIDAD DEL PELIGRO), Informe 1940, p. 42
no debe imponerse como condición al injustamente agredido la posibilidad de la fuga, pues en esas condiciones el ejercicio de la legítima defensa se tornaría en imposible en la mayoría de los casos
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 806596 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA), S.J.F. Tomo LXXXVIII, p. 721 (1946)
no puede aceptarse la defensa legítima, si el procesado no estuvo en inminente peligro de perder la vida o en condiciones de suponer este peligro, y pudo muy bien evitar la agresión de que fue víctima por otros medios, o en último extremo, preverla.

Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

1a8268f952832e89.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Chad

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Chad's Penal Code (2017) says there is no criminal responsibility for an act required by the immediate need to protect one's own or another's life or physical integrity against an unlawful attack, provided the defence is proportionate to the seriousness of the attack. It adds that killing is always considered proportionate to an unlawful attack that gives reason to fear death, rape or serious injury. The code does not mention retreat. Article 69 gives a mitigating excuse (reduced penalty) to someone who commits an offence immediately provoked by another's unlawful act against them or close relatives, if the reaction was not disproportionate. No separate home-defence rule was found in these articles.

What the law says
Code pénal (2017), art. 68
La responsabilité pénale ne peut résulter d’un acte commandé par la nécessité immédiate de la protection de sa vie ou de son intégrité physique ou de celle d’autrui contre une atteinte illégitime, à condition que la défense soit proportionnée à la gravité de l’atteinte. Il y a toujours juste proportion entre l’homicide et l’atteinte illégitime qui donne lieu de craindre la mort, le viol ou des blessures graves telles que prévues au présent Code.
Code pénal (2017), art. 69
Bénéficie de l’excuse atténuante, s’il n’y a pas disproportion entre la provocation et la réaction, tout auteur d’une infraction immédiatement provoquée par l’acte illégitime d’autrui contre lui‐même ou, en sa présence, contre son conjoint, son descendant ou ascendant, son frère ou sa sœur, son employeur ou son employé, le mineur ou l’incapable dont il a la garde.

7daf434f8087c12d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Netherlands

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Article 41 of the Dutch Criminal Code says a person is not punishable for an act 'required by the necessary defence' of their own or another's body, sexual integrity or property against an immediate, unlawful attack. In its 2016 overview judgment (ECLI:NL:HR:2016:456) the Supreme Court explained that self-defence fails the necessity (subsidiarity) test if the defendant not only could have escaped the attack but also should have; a court may not reject self-defence merely because escape was possible, since there must have been a real and reasonable chance to withdraw and it must have been fair to expect it (it is not expected where the situation is so threatening that escape is no real alternative). The defence must also not be out of reasonable proportion to the attack; for example, forcefully inflicting a deep, potentially fatal stab wound is in principle not proportionate to an attack with bare hands or fists. Exceeding the limits of necessary defence is not punishable if it was the immediate result of a violent emotion caused by the attack (noodweerexces, Article 41(2)), which the Supreme Court says applies only to a disproportionate defence, not where there was no need to defend at all.

At home

No separate home-defence rule was found; Article 41 protects one's own or another's body, sexual integrity or property.

What the law says
Wetboek van Strafrecht, artikel 41
1 Niet strafbaar is hij die een feit begaat, geboden door de noodzakelijke verdediging van eigen of eens anders lijf, eerbaarheid of goed tegen ogenblikkelijke, wederrechtelijke aanranding. 2 Niet strafbaar is de overschrijding van de grenzen van noodzakelijke verdediging, indien zij het onmiddellijk gevolg is geweest van een hevige gemoedsbeweging, door de aanranding veroorzaakt.
Hoge Raad 22 March 2016, ECLI:NL:HR:2016:456, r.o. 3.5.2
Aan de subsidiariteitseis is niet voldaan indien de verdachte zich niet behoefde te verdedigen en er dus geen noodzaak tot verdediging bestond. Daarvan is bijvoorbeeld sprake indien de verdachte zich niet alleen aan de aanranding had kunnen, maar zich daaraan ook had moeten onttrekken. Bij de verwerping van een beroep op noodweer kan dus niet worden volstaan met het enkele argument dat de verdachte zich aan de aanranding had kunnen onttrekken. Het zich aan de aanranding kunnen onttrekken houdt in dat daartoe voor de verdachte een reële en redelijke mogelijkheid moet hebben bestaan. [...] Onttrekking aan de aanranding moet voorts van de verdachte kunnen worden gevergd. Dit behoeft bijvoorbeeld niet het geval te zijn wanneer de situatie zo bedreigend is dat zich onttrekken aan de aanranding geen reëel alternatief is.

92e941cccc1642ff.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Eritrea

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Eritrea's Penal Code (2015) excuses an act of self-defence or defence of another against an imminent and unlawful assault only 'where the assault or threat could not have been otherwise averted' and the defence was proportionate to the danger and gravity of the assault. The code does not use the word 'retreat', but this wording makes defence conditional on there being no other way to avert the assault; no court ruling interpreting it was found. Defence of property can never justify intentional killing or serious injury. A person who used disproportionate means gets a reduced sentence, may receive no punishment if the excess came from excusable fear, surprise or excitement, and remains civilly liable for injury caused by the excess.

At home

Article 30 allows a person in peaceable possession of property to use force to prevent unlawful taking or trespass, to retake just-taken property, or to remove a trespasser from land, but not to intentionally kill or seriously injure, and not with more force than is reasonable.

What the law says
Penal Code of Eritrea (2015), art. 29 (Self-Defense and Defense of Another)
An act done under the necessity of self-defense or the defense of another person against an imminent and unlawful assault or a threat of an assault directed against a legally protected belonging shall not be punishable where the assault or threat could not have been otherwise averted and where the defense was proportionate to the needs of the case, in particular to the danger and gravity of the assault and the importance of the belonging to be defended.
Penal Code of Eritrea (2015), art. 30(2)
Sub-Article (1) does not apply where the person: (a) intentionally kills or inflicts serious bodily injury on another person; or (b) uses more force than is reasonable for the purposes described in that subsection.
Penal Code of Eritrea (2015), art. 31 (Excess in Self-Defense)
(1) Where a person, in fending off an unlawful assault, exceeds the limits of self-defense by using disproportionate means or by going beyond the acts necessary for averting the danger, the Court shall without restriction reduce the penalty. (2) The Court may impose no punishment where the excess committed was due to excusable fear, surprise or excitement caused by the assault. (3) Where a person has exceeded strict self-defense, he shall remain civilly liable for the injury caused by his excess.

0e7ddc21a873bfae.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nepal

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Nepal's National Criminal Code (Muluki Aparadh Samhita) 2074 (2017) was opened in its official Nepali PDF from the Nepal Law Commission. Sections 24-26 of the General Part deal with private defence: s. 24 says an act done in exercise of the right of private defence under this chapter is not an offence, that every person has the right to protect their own or another's body, life or property from unlawful harm, and that the right may be used only where there is a reasonable belief that without immediate action the body, life or property cannot be saved; s. 25 withdraws the right where protection or help of a public authority is immediately available at the time of the unlawful act and provides that no more force may be used than is reasonably necessary for the defence (s. 25(3)); s. 26 says the right does not in general include taking life, except, subject to s. 25(3), where without immediate defence against an attack one's own or another's life would be lost or grievous harm suffered (and other listed cases). The pattern follows the Indian Penal Code's ss. 96-106. The code does not use the word retreat, and no Nepal Supreme Court decision or commentary on whether the 'public authority available' limit requires running away was opened, so the retreat question stays unsettled. The PDF's text layer is damaged by a legacy Nepali font, so the readings above are a rough English rendering from partly garbled text and the quoted extract is given as extracted.

At home

No dwelling-specific rule was identified in ss. 24-26 as read; the list in s. 26(2) of cases where causing death is allowed could not be read in full because of the font damage.

What the law says

de010721c9b49861.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Austria

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Section 3 of the Criminal Code (StGB) makes defence lawful when it is the defence 'that is necessary' to repel a present or imminent unlawful attack on life, health, bodily integrity, sexual integrity, freedom or property; it is not justified if the person attacked obviously faced only a minor harm and the defence is inappropriate. There is no general duty to retreat: the Supreme Court (OGH) has held that the right of self-defence is not lost because one could perhaps escape further attacks by moving away (RS0088885, 1962). But the OGH has also said defence must be the last resort, and that a person should give way to attacks by children, the mentally ill or drunk people (RS0089005, 1972), and that someone who culpably provoked the attack must try to avoid it (RS0088713, 1977). Under section 3(2), a person who goes beyond the justified limit only out of confusion, fear or fright is punished only if the excess was negligent and negligence is a crime for that act.

What the law says
Strafgesetzbuch (StGB), § 3
(1) Nicht rechtswidrig handelt, wer sich nur der Verteidigung bedient, die notwendig ist, um einen gegenwärtigen oder unmittelbar drohenden rechtswidrigen Angriff auf Leben, Gesundheit, körperliche Unversehrtheit, sexuelle Integrität und Selbstbestimmung, Freiheit oder Vermögen von sich oder einem anderen abzuwehren. Die Handlung ist jedoch nicht gerechtfertigt, wenn es offensichtlich ist, daß dem Angegriffenen bloß ein geringer Nachteil droht und die Verteidigung, insbesondere wegen der Schwere der zur Abwehr nötigen Beeinträchtigung des Angreifers, unangemessen ist. (2) Wer das gerechtfertigte Maß der Verteidigung überschreitet oder sich einer offensichtlich unangemessenen Verteidigung (Abs. 1) bedient, ist, wenn dies lediglich aus Bestürzung, Furcht oder Schrecken geschieht, nur strafbar, wenn die Überschreitung auf Fahrlässigkeit beruht und die fahrlässige Handlung mit Strafe bedroht ist.
OGH Rechtssatz RS0088885 (9 Os 50/62, 17 Jan 1962)
Weder durch das Vorhersehen eines tätlichen Angriffes noch durch die Möglichkeit, sich unter Umständen durch Ausweichen weiterer Angriffe zu entziehen, wird das Recht auf Notwehr verwirkt.
OGH Rechtssatz RS0089005 (13 Os 83/72, 23 Nov 1972)
Aus dem Hinweis des Gesetzes auf die "nötige" Verteidigung (nunmehr : "Verteidigung, die notwendig ist") ist abzuleiten, daß die Notwehrhandlung das letzte Mittel zur Verteidigung der genannten Rechtsgüter sein müsse. Stehen andere Möglichkeiten zu deren Erhaltung zur Verfügung, so liegt grundsätzlich eine Notwehrsituation nicht vor. ... Ein Ausweichen vor einem rechtswidrigen Angriff ist insbesondere gegenüber Unreifen, Geisteskranken, Betrunkenen (ohne Rücksicht auf verschuldete Trunkenheit) geboten, da es hier einer Bewährung der Rechtsordnung nicht bedarf.
OGH Rechtssatz RS0088713 (13 Os 158/77, 10 Nov 1977)
Eine schuldhafte Provokation verpflichtet zwar zum Ausweichen vor dem provozierten Angriff, schließt aber (anders als Absichtsprovokation) Notwehr als letztes Mittel ... nicht grundsätzlich aus.
Who makes criminal law here

Under the Austrian Federal Constitutional Law (B-VG), art. 10(1) no. 6, legislation and execution in criminal law ('Strafrechtswesen') belong to the Federation, except administrative penal law and procedure in matters within the Länder's own sphere. The Criminal Code (StGB) is federal; the Länder can only attach administrative penalties to their own laws.

B-VG art. 10(1) no. 6 (official German, extract)
(1) Bundessache ist die Gesetzgebung und die Vollziehung in folgenden Angelegenheiten: ... 6. ... Strafrechtswesen mit Ausschluss des Verwaltungsstrafrechtes und des Verwaltungsstrafverfahrens in Angelegenheiten, die in den selbständigen Wirkungsbereich der Länder fallen;
B-VG art. 10(1) no. 6 (English translation)
criminal law, excluding administrative penal law and administrative penal procedure in matters which fall within the autonomous sphere of competence of the Laender;
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • RIS Justiz Rechtssätze RS0088885, RS0089005, RS0088713 (RIS, Austrian Federal Chancellery)

ecb66549ce649c7a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kenya

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Kenya's Penal Code does not set out its own self-defence rules: section 17 says criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property is decided by the principles of English common law. Kenyan courts apply the Privy Council case Palmer v R (1971): a person who is attacked may do what is reasonably necessary to defend themselves, judged on the facts, and force wholly out of proportion is not covered. The High Court in Republic v Faris Wakhungu (2020) stated that Palmer was approved and followed in the English case R v McInnes; McInnes, as quoted with approval by Nigeria's Supreme Court, holds that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run' but should show they do not want to fight. No Kenyan judgment ruling directly on retreat could be opened (the Kenya Law website refused access), so the retreat position here rests on the English authorities Kenyan courts say they follow. Where the force was excessive, Kenyan courts have convicted of manslaughter instead of murder (Wakhungu: 10 years' imprisonment), and Mungai v Republic (1984) treats acts done in excess of self-defence or under provocation as rebutting malice.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 63), s. 17 – Defence of person or property
Subject to any express provisions in this Code or any other law in operation in Kenya, criminal responsibility for the use of force in the defence of person or property shall be determined according to the principles of English Common Law.
Republic v Faris Wakhungu [2020] eKLR (High Court, Bungoma), quoting Palmer v R [1971] AC 814
It is both good law and good sense that a man who is attacked may defend himself. It is both good law and common sense that he may do, but may only do, what is reasonably necessary. But everything will depend upon the particular facts and circumstances.
Republic v Faris Wakhungu [2020] eKLR, quoting Mungai v Republic (1984) KLR 85
it matters little whether the circumstances relied on are regarded as acts done in excess of the right of self-defence of person or property or as acts done under the stress of provocation. The essence of crime of murder is malice aforethought and if the circumstances show that the fatal blow was given in the heat of passion on a sudden attack or threat of attack which is near enough and serious enough to cause loss of control, then the inference of malice is rebutted and the offence will be manslaughter.
R v McInnes [1971] 3 All ER 295 (England), as quoted in Laoye v The State (Nigeria SC, 1985)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal

  • Republic v Faris Wakhungu [2020] eKLR (Sheriaplex)

2cc53f2cd26b7dda.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Veracruz

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Veracruz's Penal Code (art. 25-III) treats as a justification repelling a current or imminent unlawful attack on one's own or another's property or interests, if there is a reasonable need for the defence and the defender did not sufficiently provoke it. The code does not mention retreating, fleeing or avoiding the attack. Home intruders are presumed to be lawful targets only when their presence evidently reveals an attack. No separate rule on excessive self-defence was found in the text checked. The only full text that could be opened is an older consolidation (last reform shown: 7 January 2009); the Veracruz Congress and State Prosecutor sites refused connections, so later amendments are not reflected. A news report describes a bill by deputy Astrid Sánchez Moguel to add a presumption of self-defence for women repelling physical, sexual or feminicidal attacks to art. 25; whether it passed was not checked. Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 25-III presumes legitimate defence when harm is caused to someone who by any means tries to enter or enters without right the place where the defender, their family or anyone they must defend lives (temporarily or permanently), or where property they must protect is kept, provided the stranger's presence 'evidently reveals an attack'.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave, art. 25, fracc. III
III. Repeler una agresión actual o inminente y contraria a derecho, en protección de bienes propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad razonable de la defensa y no medie provocación suficiente por parte del que rechaza la agresión o de la persona a quien defiende. Se presumirá la legítima defensa cuando se cause un daño a quien, por cualquier medio, trate de penetrar o penetre sin derecho al lugar en que, temporal o permanentemente, habite el que se defiende, su familia o cualquier persona a la que tenga obligación de defender, o donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que tenga igual obligación de defensa, siempre que la presencia del extraño revele evidentemente una agresión;
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave (consolidation with last reform 7 January 2009) (Justia México)
  • Proponen presumir legítima defensa para mujeres agredidas en Veracruz (news on a bill to amend art. 25) (El Congresista)
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • IUS 814826 – Legítima defensa. Evitabilidad del peligro (SDV compendium of SCJN theses (secondary reproduction))
  • IUS 806596 – Legítima defensa (SDV compendium of SCJN theses (secondary reproduction))

d644949db04b2762.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nicaragua

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 34(4) of Nicaragua's Penal Code (Law 641), a person is exempt from criminal liability when acting in legitimate defence of their own or another's person or rights, if there is an unlawful attack, the means used are rationally necessary to prevent or repel it, and the defender did not sufficiently provoke it. For property, only an attack that is a crime and puts the property in serious danger of imminent loss counts; for a home, improper entry counts as the attack. The code does not mention retreat, and no Nicaraguan court decision on retreat was found. If not all requirements are met, the defence becomes an 'incomplete exemption' that mitigates the penalty (art. 35(1)).

At home

Penal Code art. 34(4)(a) says that, for an unlawful attack on a dwelling and its outbuildings, improper entry into them counts as the unlawful attack, so a resident may defend against an intruder subject to the rational-necessity and no-provocation requirements.

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley N° 641), art. 34(4)
Está exento de responsabilidad penal quien: [...] 4. Actúe en legítima defensa de la persona o derechos propios o ajenos, siempre que concurran los requisitos siguientes. a) Agresión ilegítima; en caso de defensa de los bienes se considerará agresión ilegítima, el ataque a los mismos que constituya delito y los ponga en grave peligro de deterioro o pérdida inminentes. En caso de agresión ilegítima a la morada y sus dependencias, se considerará la entrada indebida en una u otras; b) Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedir o repeler la agresión; c) Falta de provocación suficiente por parte del defensor.
Código Penal (Ley N° 641), art. 35(1)
Son circunstancias atenuantes: 1. Eximentes incompletas. Las causas expresadas en el capítulo anterior, cuando no concurran todos los requisitos necesarios para eximir de responsabilidad penal en sus respectivos casos.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Código Penal (Ley N° 641), Nicaragua (WIPO Lex (World Intellectual Property Organization))
  • WIPO Lex record: Código Penal (Ley Nº 641), Nicaragua (WIPO Lex)

4c68af814f094f32.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Sonora

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Sonora's Penal Code (art. 13(B)(II)) lists legitimate defence as a justification: a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence used was necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. The code does not mention retreating or fleeing. Its presumption is unusually broad: it covers harming or killing anyone who enters any property without the owner's or occupant's consent, not just a home. A person who exceeds the limits of self-defence, because of an emotional state the judge finds understandable or by using means that were not rationally necessary or not the most practicable or least harmful, gets three days to five years in prison and a fine (art. 68). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 13(B)(II) creates a legal presumption of legitimate defence, unless proven otherwise, for causing harm, injury 'or even death' to anyone who by any means enters the bounds of a property (inmueble) without right or without the consent of its lawful owner, possessor or occupant, or that of their family or of anyone they must defend, or a place holding property they must protect; or who is found there in circumstances revealing a possible attack. It is not limited to dwellings.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Sonora, art. 13, apartado B, fracc. II
II.- Legítima defensa: Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. Existe presunción legal de defensa legítima, salvo prueba en contrario, por el hecho de causar daño, lesione o incluso se prive de la vida a quien por cualquier medio se introduzca a los límites de un inmueble, sin derecho o sin consentimiento de quien legítimamente sea propietario, posesionario u ocupante, al de su familia, o al de cualquier persona que tenga la obligación de defender, así como al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que exista la misma obligación; o bien, lo encuentre en alguno de aquellos lugares en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión.
Código Penal para el Estado de Sonora, art. 68
Artículo 68.- Al que se exceda en los límites impuestos por la legítima defensa, estado de necesidad, cumplimiento de un deber legal, ejercicio de un derecho u obediencia jerárquica legítima, debido a un proceso emocional explicable a juicio del juez, al empleo de medios no necesarios [...] racionalmente o que no sean los más practicables o menos perjudiciales, se le impondrán de tres días a cinco años de prisión y multa de diez a ciento cincuenta Unidades de Medida y Actualización.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal para el Estado de Sonora (file dated September 2026) (Supremo Tribunal de Justicia del Estado de Sonora, marco normativo)
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

5b973f18622a78b6.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Namibia

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Namibia has no criminal code; 'private defence' is a common-law defence inherited from South Africa and applied by the courts. The test used by Namibian courts (restated in S v Simataa, High Court Main Division, 30 March 2017, paras 30-31, quoting Snyman and S v Naftali) is that the defensive act must be necessary to avert the attack, directed at the attacker and reasonably proportionate, and the means used must be necessary in the circumstances. On retreat, the High Court in Simataa found against the accused on the ground that 'the shooting could have been easily avoided had the accused retreated as that could have exposed the accused to no threat or danger', after counsel had put Burchell's statement that defence is not necessary if the attack can be avoided by retreat or escape, but that one may stand one's ground if fleeing would worsen one's chances; counsel also relied on the Supreme Court's decision in S v Jonkers 2006 (2) NR 432 for the point that a person need not retreat if retreating would threaten their life (that is the fetch tool's paraphrase of Simataa, not a quotation from Jonkers, which could not be opened). The word 'retreat' therefore does appear, and the rule as applied is that a safe avenue of escape counts against the necessity of force; this rests on one High Court judgment, and the Supreme Court decisions (Jonkers; S v Matheus [2002] NASC 7) were not opened. Gregory v State [2013] NAHCMD 46 (Shivute J) states the test as whether the accused reasonably believed life was in danger or was using reasonable means to ward off the attack, without discussing retreat.

What the law says
S v Simataa (2) (CC 3 of 2014) [2017] NAHCMD 104, para 30, quoting Snyman, Criminal Law
A person acts in private defence, and her act in therefore lawful, if she uses force to repel an unlawful attack which has commenced, or is imminently threatening, upon her or somebody else's life, bodily integrity, property or other interest which deserves to be protected, provided the defensive act is necessary to protect the interest threatened, is directed against the attacker, and is reasonably proportionate to the attack.
S v Simataa (2017), para 31, quoting S v Naftali
(b) The defence must be directed against the attacker and necessary to avert the attack and the means used must be necessary in the circumstances.
S v Simataa (2017), para 27 (counsel's submission quoting Burchell)
Where the threat is one of personal injury, defence is not necessary if the attack can be avoided by retreat or escape. Indeed some legal systems, concerned about the preservation of human life, impose on the victim of an attack a duty to retreat in so far as this is possible and would not expose the defender to even greater danger. Clearly, if to flee would be to worsen the accused's chances of avoiding the injury, he would be justified in standing his ground and defending himself
S v Simataa (2017), court's finding on retreat
In casu, the shooting could have been easily avoided had the accused 'retreated' as that could have exposed the accused to no threat or danger.
Gregory v State (CA 142/2007) [2013] NAHCMD 46, Shivute J, para 15
The test for private defence is whether the accused reasonably believed that his life was in danger or that he was using reasonable means to ward off the attack.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • Gregory v State (CA 142/2007) [2013] NAHCMD 46 (25 February 2013) (NamibLII)

c7ee51adc341581b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Botswana

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Botswana's Penal Code (1964, as amended) says a person is not criminally responsible for using force to repel an unlawful attack on their own person or property, or that of someone they have a moral or legal duty to protect, if the means and degree of force are 'no more than is reasonably necessary in the circumstances' (s. 16). The Constitution (s. 4(2)) likewise does not treat a death as a breach of the right to life if it results from reasonably justifiable force used to defend any person from violence or to defend property. The statute does not mention retreat; a 2024 High Court acquittal reported by the government Daily News applied section 16 and found the response proportionate, but no ruling on a duty to retreat was found.

At home

Section 16 of the Penal Code covers repelling an unlawful attack on one's 'person or property', with the same 'reasonably necessary' limit; no separate dwelling rule was found.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 08:01), s. 16 (Defence of person or property)
Subject to the express provisions of this Code or any other law for the time being in force, a person shall not be criminally responsible for the use of force in repelling an unlawful attack upon his person or property or the person or property of anyone whom it is his moral or legal duty to protect if the means he uses and the degree of force he employs in so doing are no more than is reasonably necessary in the circumstances.
Constitution of Botswana, s. 4(2)(a)
A person shall not be regarded as having been deprived of his or her life in contravention of subsection (1) of this section if he or she dies as the result of the use, to such extent and in such circumstances as are permitted by law, of such force as is reasonably justifiable- (a) for the defence of any person from violence or for the defence of property;
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Self-defence - national proceedings: Botswana (Penal Code 1964 (2005); Constitution 1966 (2006)) (National Implementing Legislation Database (Case Matrix / University of Nottingham))
  • Gaborone High Court Judge frees Machete (18 May 2024) (Daily News (Botswana Government / BOPA))

774ce2fb8ff962ce.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ghana

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Ghana's Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29) allows force or harm 'reasonably necessary' to prevent or defend against a crime, 'extending in case of extreme necessity, even to killing' (s. 37), and no force can be justified beyond what is reasonably necessary (s. 32). The statute does not mention retreat, but the Court of Appeal in Yeboah v The State (1967) held that killing is justified only if there was no other means of saving one's life, and that a person who 'could have avoided the act, say by easily escaping from his assailant' cannot justify killing the assailant. Force used in an unlawful fight cannot be justified (s. 38). No statutory 'excessive self-defence' reduction was found.

At home

Section 39 lets a person in actual possession of a house, land, vessel or goods use 'such force as is reasonably necessary' to repel someone trying to enter forcibly and unlawfully, or to remove someone who refuses to leave; it does not separately authorise killing.

What the law says
Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29), s. 37
For the prevention of, or for the defence of himself or any other person against any crime, or for the suppression or dispersion of a riotous or unlawful assembly, a person may justify any force or harm which is reasonably necessary extending in case of extreme necessity, even to killing.
Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29), s. 32
Notwithstanding the existence of any matter of justification for force, force cannot be justified as having been used in pursuance of that matter— (a) which is in excess of the limits hereinafter prescribed in the section of this Chapter relating to that matter; or (b) which in any case extends beyond the amount and kind of force reasonably necessary for the purpose for which force is permitted to be used.
Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29), s. 39(a)
a person in actual possession of a house, land, or vessel, or goods, or his servant or any other person authorised by him, may use such force as is reasonably necessary for repelling a person who attempts forcibly and unlawfully to enter the house, land, or vessel, or to take possession of the goods;
Yeboah v The State [1967] GLR 512 (Court of Appeal, 10 July 1967)
... that short of killing the deceased, there was no other means of saving his own life. ... could have avoided the act, say by easily escaping from his assailant ... he cannot justify the killing of his assailant.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29) (Republic of Ghana (hosted by policinglaw.info))
  • Yeboah v. The State [1967] GLR 512 (SuperLaw Ghana)
  • Self-defence - national proceedings: Ghana (National Implementing Legislation Database (Case Matrix / University of Nottingham))

b23e75555ac9c186.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Republic of Serbia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 19 of the Serbian Criminal Code says an act done in necessary defence is not a crime, where the defence is 'absolutely necessary' to repel a simultaneous unlawful attack on one's own or another's interests. The code does not mention retreat, and a 2017 article by Igor Vuković (University of Belgrade Faculty of Law) reports that Serbian courts do not impose a duty to retreat: one court called it 'unacceptable' to say the accused should have called neighbours for help or escaped through a window. Courts do expect the defender to avoid or give way to attacks by children, mentally ill or drunk people, and a person who willingly joins a fight cannot claim self-defence; the same article says courts accept self-defence 'very restrictively', especially when the attacker died. A person who exceeds the limits of necessary defence may receive a reduced sentence, or no sentence if the excess came from strong agitation or fright caused by the attack. In 2022 the Interior Ministry proposed widening the definition to cover attacks that are about to happen; the code text checked here still has the old wording.

At home

The Criminal Code has no special home-defence rule: the same test (defence 'absolutely necessary' to repel a simultaneous unlawful attack) applies inside and outside the home. A Belgrade law professor argues the home should be treated separately and criticises courts for applying the test very restrictively in home-defence cases.

What the law says
Krivični zakonik (Criminal Code), član 19
(1) Nije krivično delo ono delo koje je učinjeno u nužnoj odbrani. (2) Nužna je ona odbrana koja je neophodno potrebna da učinilac od svog dobra ili dobra drugoga odbije istovremen protivpravan napad. (3) Učiniocu koji je prekoračio granice nužne odbrane može se kazna ublažiti. Ako je učinilac prekoračio granice nužne odbrane usled jake razdraženosti ili prepasti izazvane napadom može se i osloboditi od kazne.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Krivični zakonik (consolidated text) (Paragraf Lex)
  • Doktrine „Stand Your Ground“ i „Castle“ – nužna odbrana stana i drugih prostora iz ugla angloameričkog i evropskog prava (Igor Vuković), Crimen 2017 (University of Belgrade Faculty of Law (Crimen journal))
  • Samoodbrana i pre napada: U Krivičnom zakoniku biće proširena definicija pojma "nužna odbrana" (24 Sept 2022) (Večernje novosti)
b23e75555ac9c186.t: Republic of Serbia · No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

8db6d12de610ec16.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Czechia

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Section 29 of the Criminal Code (Act No. 40/2009) says an act that repels a directly threatening or continuing attack on an interest protected by criminal law is not a crime, unless the defence was 'quite obviously disproportionate' to the manner of the attack. The code says nothing about retreat, but the Supreme Court has held that, unlike necessity, self-defence does not require that the defender could not have avoided the attack in another way (6 Tdo 339/2008), and that failing to use a chance to flee cannot by itself be the basis for finding the defence excessive (5 Tdo 162/2007). The court also says the defence may be stronger than the attack, since otherwise it would have no chance of success, and that it is judged partly by how the attack appeared to the defender. Defence that was quite obviously disproportionate ('intensive excess') is not justified and can be punished.

What the law says
Trestní zákoník (Act No. 40/2009 Coll.), § 29
(1) Čin jinak trestný, kterým někdo odvrací přímo hrozící nebo trvající útok na zájem chráněný trestním zákonem, není trestným činem. (2) Nejde o nutnou obranu, byla-li obrana zcela zjevně nepřiměřená způsobu útoku.
Supreme Court, resolution 6 Tdo 339/2008 (26 Mar 2008), headnote as published by epravo.cz
Podmínkou nutné obrany není, že se bránící nemohl vyhnout útoku jinak. Obrana ale nesmí být zcela zjevně nepřiměřená způsobu útoku. ... obrana musí být, má-li být způsobilá k jistému odvrácení útoku bez rizika pro napadeného, silnější než útok.
Supreme Court, resolution 5 Tdo 162/2007 (28 Feb 2007), as summarised in epravo.cz article
sama skutečnost, že napadený nevyužil možnost útěku, ale aktivně se útoku bránil, nemůže být podkladem pro závěr, že spáchal trestný čin v důsledku překročení mezí nutné obrany. Podle Nejvyššího soudu ČR tak nikdo není povinen snášet útok vůči své osobě a vůči zájmům chráněným trestním zákoníkem, ale má právo se bránit i v případě, že je možné se teoreticky útoku vyhnout jinak.

f4b98e1aa541a934.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tunisia

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Tunisia's Penal Code (1913, official 2012 edition) has a short general rule in article 39: there is no offence when the person was forced to act by a circumstance that exposed their own life, or that of a close relative (ascendants, descendants, siblings, spouse), to imminent danger, 'and when this danger could not otherwise be averted'. If the person threatened is not a close relative, the judge assesses the degree of responsibility. The wording therefore makes the defence depend on there being no other way to avoid the danger, and on a threat to life. Article 40 separately says there is no offence when a killing or injury happens while repelling a night-time break-in to a dwelling or defending against violent theft or looting. No Tunisian court decisions on how the 'no other way' condition applies to flight, and no provision on excessive defence, were found.

At home

There is no offence where homicide, wounds or blows occur while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of a dwelling or its outbuildings, or while defending against violent theft or looting (art. 40).

What the law says
Code pénal (Décret du 9 juillet 1913, édition officielle 2012), art. 39
Il n'y a pas d'infraction lorsque l'auteur y a été contraint par une circonstance qui exposait sa vie ou celle de l’un de ses proches à un danger imminent, et lorsque ce danger ne pouvait être autrement détourné. Sont considérés comme proches : 1°- les ascendants et descendants, 2°- les frères et sœurs, 3°- les époux. Si la personne menacée n’est pas un proche, le juge appréciera le degré de responsabilité.
Code pénal, art. 40
Il n'y a pas d'infraction : 1) si l'homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites ou les coups portés en repoussant, la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d'une habitation ou de ses dépendances. 2) si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

6afef7a4694b0929.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mauritania

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Mauritania's Penal Code (Ordinance 83-162 of 9 July 1983) keeps the old French self-defence wording alongside Islamic-law offences: there is no crime when homicide, wounds or blows were 'commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence of oneself or another' (art. 304). Article 305 lists two situations that automatically count as such necessity: repelling a night-time break-in into an inhabited home, and defending against violent theft or looting. The code says nothing about retreat or proportionality, and no Mauritanian court decisions on whether a person must avoid the attack were found. A killing provoked by serious blows or violence, or done while repelling a daytime break-in, is 'excusable' (arts. 297–298); when the excuse is proven, a crime carrying death or life hard labour is reduced to one to five years' imprisonment (art. 302).

At home

Article 305 counts as 'current necessity of defence' a homicide, wounding or blows committed while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or the entrance of an inhabited house or flat or its outbuildings. Repelling such a break-in by day is not justified but 'excusable' (art. 298), which lowers the penalty.

What the law says
Code pénal (Ordonnance n° 83-162 du 9 juillet 1983), art. 304
Il n'y [a] ni crime ni délit lorsque l'homicide, les blessures et les coups étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d'autrui.
Code pénal, art. 305
Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de défense, les deux cas suivants : 1. Si l'homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites, ou si les coups ont été portés en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d'une maison ou d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances; 2. Si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal, arts. 297, 298 and 302
ART. 297. - Le meurtre ainsi que les blessures et les coups sont excusables, s'ils ont été provoqués par des coups ou violences graves envers les personnes. ART. 298. - Les crimes ou délits mentionnés au précédent article sont également excusables, s'ils ont été commis en repoussant pendant le jour l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d'une maison ou d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances. Si le fait est arrivé pendant la nuit, ce cas est réglé par l'article 305. ... ART. 302. - Lorsque le fait d'excuse sera prouvé, s'il s'agit d'un crime emportant la peine de mort, ou celle des travaux forcés à perpétuité, la peine sera réduite à un emprisonnement d'un an à cinq ans.

b525eb88bef592ad.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Malawi

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Malawi's Penal Code section 17 says criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property is decided by the principles of common law. Malawian courts apply the Privy Council case Palmer v R: a person who is attacked may do what is reasonably necessary, a person cannot be expected to weigh the exact measure of defensive force, and force used after the danger has passed is revenge, not self-defence. The Supreme Court of Appeal in Paison v Republic (1998) added that a person needing to defend themselves cannot be expected to choose the right weapon or target. No Malawian statute or judgment found says whether a person must retreat, so the retreat question is not settled by the sources found. Where self-defence fails only because the force was more than reasonably necessary, Malawian courts convict of manslaughter instead of murder (Jackson v Reginam; Paison; Republic v Smart John Phiri, 2021).

At home

In Ngozo v Republic (High Court, 1997) the trial court had thought self-defence was unavailable because the complainant was injured at his own house; the High Court said that was wrong, because the necessity to protect one's body 'can arise anywhere even in the victim's house'. No specific home or castle rule was found.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 7:01), s. 17 – Defence of person or property
Subject to any express provisions in this Code or any other law in operation in Mala[w]i, criminal responsibility for the use of force in the defence of person or property shall be determined according to the principles of common law.
Republic v Smart John Phiri, Homicide Case No. 28 of 2020 (High Court, 17 Feb 2021), citing Jackson v Reginam, Paison v Rep [1998] MLR 302 (SCA) and Nyirenda v Rep
where the defence of self-defence fails merely because the person used excessive force than was reasonably necessary ... that person would normally be entitled to be convicted for the lesser offence of manslaughter.
Republic v Smart John Phiri (2021), citing Paison v Rep [1998] MLR 302 (SCA)
the law also recognizes that when a person finds himself in a situation which demands self-defence ... he cannot be expected to have time to select the right weapon and to target the correct part of the body.
Francisco Macloud Ngozo v Republic, Criminal Appeal No. 106 of 1996 (High Court, 31 Jan 1997)
The defence is based on necessity to protect ones limb or body or that of another. Such necessity can arise anywhere even in the victim's house.
What was tried

MalawiLII search API (direct download): '"self defence" retreat', '"self-defence" "retreat"', 'self defence "duty to retreat"', 'retreat self-defence Julien', 'McInnes retreat', 'Mwale retreat self defence'. Only R v Nomale & Ors [2008] MWHC 158 (bail pending appeal, 13 Aug 2008) discusses retreat; its search snippet reads 'Whether the accused did retreat is only one element for the jury to consider. ... It is stated that the ‘duty to retreat’ factor was perhaps given too much weight' (search snippet only). the web reader of that judgment was refused (robots) on malawilii.org and www.malawilii.org; direct download gets a bot check. R v Kefa [2009] MWHC 48 opened by the web reader: no retreat discussion.

bc63a9fbd4a91787.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

United Arab Emirates

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The UAE's federal Crimes and Penalties Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, in force 2 January 2022) says there is no crime when an act is done in the use of the right of legitimate defence (art. 58). According to the official English text, as summarised when it was opened, the right applies when the defender faces an immediate threat of a forcible crime against themselves, their property or another person or their property (or reasonably believes so), cannot get timely help from the authorities, and has no other way to stop the danger; the defence must also be necessary and proportionate. Intentional killing is justified only to repel a reasonably feared act causing death or serious injury, forced intercourse or 'disgracing' a person, kidnapping, arson, destruction or theft felonies, or a night-time entry into an inhabited house (art. 59). Exceeding the limits in good faith is treated as an extenuating excuse, and the judge may pardon the person (art. 61). The full article texts could only be read in short excerpts, so the wording of the 'no other way' condition is paraphrased here, not quoted.

At home

Article 59 lists 'entering at night an inhabited house or any of its annexes' among the five situations in which legitimate defence may extend to intentional killing.

What the law says
Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021 (Crimes and Penalties Law), art. 58 (official English translation; excerpts)
There is no crime if the act is committed in the use of the right of legitimate defence. ... If the defence is necessary in order to repel the attack and is proportionate thereto.
Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, art. 59 (excerpts)
The right of legitimate defence does not justify premeditated murder, unless ... Entering at night an inhabited house or any of its annexes.
Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, art. 61 (excerpt)
Exceeding the limits of justification in good faith is considered an extenuating excuse
Who makes criminal law here

Under the UAE Constitution the federation has exclusive legislative power over 'Major legislation relating to the penal, civil, and commercial codes' (art. 121), and federal laws prevail over emirate legislation (art. 151). But art. 149 lets the emirates, as an exception, legislate on art. 121 matters so long as they do not conflict with federal law.

Constitution of the UAE, art. 121
Without prejudice to the provisions of the preceding Article, the UAE has exclusive legislative jurisdiction in the following matters: ... Major legislation relating to the penal, civil, and commercial codes; company law, civil and criminal procedure codes;
Constitution of the UAE, art. 149
As an exception to the provisions of Article 121 of this Constitution, the Emirates may promulgate legislations necessary for the regulation of the matters set out in the said Article without violation of the provisions of Article 151 of this Constitution.
Constitution of the UAE, art. 151
The provisions of this Constitution shall prevail over the Constitutions of the member Emirates of the UAE and the federal laws which are issued in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution shall have priority over the legislations, regulations and decisions issued by the authorities of the Emirates.

Caution for the owner: art. 149 allows emirate-level legislation on penal matters that does not conflict with federal law, so the constitution does not rule out emirate penal laws. Whether any emirate penal code is still in force alongside Federal Decree-Law 31/2021 was not checked (uaelegislation.gov.ae returned 403; web-search budget exhausted).

0477a62e7d20bc1c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Washington

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Washington has no stand-your-ground statute; RCW 9A.16.050 makes homicide justifiable in lawful defence of oneself or others against an imminent felony or great personal injury but says nothing about retreat. The rule is judicial. In State v. Redmond, 150 Wn.2d 489 (2003), the Washington Supreme Court said: 'The law is well settled that there is no duty to retreat when a person is assaulted in a place where he or she has a right to be', and reversed a conviction because the trial court refused to give the no-duty-to-retreat instruction. The pattern instruction, WPIC 16.08, as quoted by the Court of Appeals in State v. Williams, 81 Wn. App. 738 (1996), reads: 'It is lawful for a person who is in a place where that person has a right to be and who has reasonable grounds for believing that he is being attacked to stand his ground and defend against such attack by the use of lawful force. The law does not impose a duty to retreat.' Redmond holds the instruction must be given whenever a jury could conclude that flight was a reasonably effective alternative. RCW 9A.16.110 adds that no one shall be placed in legal jeopardy for protecting themselves by reasonable means and requires the state to reimburse a defendant acquitted on self-defence.

At home

RCW 9A.16.050(2) makes homicide justifiable 'in the actual resistance of an attempt to commit a felony upon the slayer, in his or her presence, or upon or in a dwelling, or other place of abode, in which he or she is.' No separate castle presumption was found.

What the law says
State v. Redmond, 150 Wn.2d 489 (2003) (Fairhurst, J.)
The law is well settled that there is no duty to retreat when a person is assaulted in a place where he or she has a right to be. State v. Studd, 137 Wn.2d 533, 549, 973 P.2d 1049 (1999). An instruction should be given to this effect when sufficient evidence is presented to support it. State v. Allery, 101 Wn.2d 591, 598, 682 P.2d 312 (1984). ... the no duty to retreat instruction is required where, as in this case, a jury may objectively conclude that flight is a reasonably effective alternative to the use of force in self-defense.
WPIC 16.08 (No Duty to Retreat), as set out in State v. Williams, 81 Wn. App. 738 (1996), footnote
WPIC 16.08 reads as follows: It is lawful for a person who is in a place where that person has a right to be and who has reasonable grounds for believing that he is being attacked to stand his ground and defend against such attack by the use of lawful force. The law does not impose a duty to retreat.
State v. Williams, 81 Wn. App. 738 (1996)
In Washington, one who is assaulted in a place he has a right to be has no duty to retreat. Allery, 101 Wn.2d at 598. Flight, however reasonable an alternative to violence, is not required.
RCW 9A.16.050
Homicide is also justifiable when committed either: (1) In the lawful defense of the slayer, or his or her husband, wife, parent, child, brother, or sister, or of any other person in his or her presence or company, when there is reasonable ground to apprehend a design on the part of the person slain to commit a felony or to do some great personal injury to the slayer or to any such person, and there is imminent danger of such design being accomplished; or (2) In the actual resistance of an attempt to commit a felony upon the slayer, in his or her presence, or upon or in a dwelling, or other place of abode, in which he or she is.

df7bac817aae487a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Sinaloa

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Sinaloa's Penal Code (art. 26-IV) excludes liability when a person defends their own or another's legal interests by repelling a current, violent, unlawful attack that creates imminent danger, unless it is proven that the defender provoked it, that they 'foresaw the attack and could easily have avoided it by other legal means', that the means used were not rationally necessary, or that the threatened harm was easily repairable or minor compared with the harm caused. Avoiding a foreseen attack is therefore part of the written test, but only when it was easy and lawful; there is no general duty to flee. For break-ins into an inhabited home, the presumption applies 'whatever the harm caused to the aggressor'. A person who exceeds self-defence is punished as for a negligent (culposo) offence (art. 86). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 26-IV presumes the requirements of legitimate defence are met for anyone who repels, at the very moment it happens, the climbing over or breaking of the fences, walls or entrance of their inhabited house or flat or its outbuildings, 'whatever the harm caused to the aggressor'. The same presumption favours anyone who harms a stranger found inside their home, a house where their family is, or premises holding property they must protect, when the intruder uses violence against people or things there.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Sinaloa, art. 26, fracc. IV
IV. Obre el acusado en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, repeliendo una agresión actual, violenta, sin derecho y de la cual resulte un peligro inminente, a no ser que se pruebe que intervino alguna de las circunstancias siguientes: PRIMERA. Que el agredido provocó la agresión, dando causa inmediata y suficiente para ella; SEGUNDA. Que previó la agresión y pudo fácilmente evitarla por otros medios legales; TERCERA. Que no hubo necesidad racional del medio empleado en la defensa; y [...] CUARTA. Que el daño que iba a causar el agresor, era fácilmente reparable después por medios legales o era notoriamente de poca importancia comparado con el que causó la defensa. Se presumirá que concurren los requisitos de la legítima defensa respecto de aquél que rechazare, en el momento mismo de estarse verificando, el escalamiento o fractura de los cercados, paredes, o entrada de su casa o departamento habitado, o de sus dependencias, cualquiera que sea el daño causado al agresor. Igual presunción favorecerá al que causare cualquier daño a un extraño a quien encontrare dentro de su hogar; en la casa en que se encuentre su familia, aún cuando no sea su hogar habitual; en el local en que aquél tenga sus bienes o donde se encuentren bienes ajenos que tenga obligación legal de defender; y el intruso ejerza violencia sobre las personas o sobre las cosas que en tales sitios se hallen;
Código Penal para el Estado de Sinaloa, art. 86
ARTÍCULO 86. Al que se exceda en casos de legítima defensa, estado de necesidad, obediencia jerárquica, cumplimiento de un deber o ejercicio de un derecho será penado como delincuente por delito culposo.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal para el Estado de Sinaloa, texto vigente (última reforma P.O. No. 093, 1 de agosto de 2025), copy published by the Municipality of Elota (H. Ayuntamiento de Elota, Sinaloa (copy of the official text))
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

de331268ba451c47.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Niger

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Niger's Penal Code (Law 61-27 of 1961 as amended by Law 2003-025 of 13 June 2003) follows the old French model: there is no offence when the act was 'commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence of oneself or another' (art. 43). Article 44 lists two situations that automatically count as such necessity: repelling a night-time break-in into an inhabited home, and defending against violent theft or looting. The code does not mention retreat or proportionality, and no Nigerien court decisions on whether a person must avoid the attack were found. Killing or injuring after being provoked by serious blows or violence, or while repelling a daytime break-in, is 'excusable' (art. 245), which reduces the penalty; a spouse who kills the other spouse or their partner on catching them in adultery in the marital home is also excused (art. 246).

At home

Article 44 counts as 'current necessity of defence' a homicide, wounding or blows committed while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or the entrance of an inhabited house or flat or its outbuildings. If the same thing happens by day, the killing or injury is not justified but is 'excusable', which lowers the penalty (art. 245(2)).

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n° 61-27, modifiée par Loi n° 2003-025), art. 43
Il n’y a pas d’infraction lorsque le fait a été commandé par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d’autrui.
Code pénal, art. 44
Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de défense les deux cas suivants : 1) si l’homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites ou si les coups ont été portés en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs, ou entrée d’une maison, ou d’un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances ; 2) si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols, ou pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal, art. 245
Le meurtre ainsi que les blessures et les coups sont excusables : 1) s’ils ont été provoqués par des coups et violences graves envers les personnes ; 2) s’ils ont été commis en repoussant, pendant le jour, l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d’une maison ou d’un appartement habité, ou de leurs dépendances. Toutefois le parricide, le génocide et les crimes contre l’humanité ne sont jamais excusables
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

b0fbcf1c3789165a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Costa Rica

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 28 of the Penal Code (Ley 4573 of 1970), a person does not commit a crime when defending their own or another's person or rights, if there is an unlawful aggression and a "reasonable necessity of the defence used" to repel or prevent it. The Code does not mention retreat, and the sources opened here did not settle whether flight is expected. A separate article (art. 29, headed "Excess in defence") deals with defenders who go beyond these limits; its text could not be read in the source opened. The home rule added in 1975 covers intruders inside a building who endanger the occupants.

At home

Since Ley 5743 of 1975, art. 28 states that self-defence applies to anyone who commits violent acts against a stranger who, without any right and endangering the inhabitants or occupants, is inside a building or its outbuildings, "whatever the harm caused to the intruder".

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley 4573), art. 28, as amended by Ley 5743 of 4 August 1975
No comete delito el que obra en defensa de la persona o derechos, propios o ajenos, siempre que concurran las siguientes circunstancias: a) Agresión ilegítima; y b) Necesidad razonable de la defensa empleada para repeler o impedir la agresión. Se entenderá que concurre esta causal de justificación para aquel que ejecutare actos violentos contra el individuo extraño que, sin derecho alguno y con peligro para los habitantes u ocupantes de la edificación o sus dependencias, se hallare dentro de ellas, cualquiera que sea el daño causado al intruso.

  • Código Penal de Costa Rica (Ley 4573), consolidated (Bufete de Costa Rica (legal library))
  • Reforma del Artículo 28 del Código Penal de Costa Rica (Ley N° 5743) (Bufete de Costa Rica)

596ce604d88de048.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

California

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

California Penal Code § 197 makes homicide justifiable when resisting an attempt to murder, to commit a felony or to do great bodily injury, and is silent on retreat except that an assailant or mutual combatant must in good faith try to decline further struggle. The no-retreat rule is judicial and is carried in the official instruction. CALCRIM No. 505 (Judicial Council of California, 2024 edition) tells the jury: 'A defendant is not required to retreat. He or she is entitled to stand his or her ground and defend himself or herself and, if reasonably necessary, to pursue an assailant until the danger of (death/great bodily injury/ <insert forcible and atrocious crime>) has passed. This is so even if safety could have been achieved by retreating.' The Authority list cites People v. Hughes (1951) 107 Cal.App.2d 487, 493 and People v. Hatchett (1942) 56 Cal.App.2d 20, 22 for 'No Duty to Retreat'. The instruction requires a reasonable belief in imminent danger of death or great bodily injury, a reasonable belief that immediate deadly force was necessary, and no more force than reasonably necessary; the People must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the killing was not justified. An honest but unreasonable belief reduces murder to voluntary manslaughter (CALCRIM No. 571).

At home

Cal. Penal Code § 198.5 (Stats. 1984, ch. 1666): a person using deadly force within their residence against someone who unlawfully and forcibly entered is presumed to have reasonably feared imminent death or great bodily injury. Penal Code § 197(2) also covers defence of habitation against a violent or riotous entry.

What the law says
CALCRIM No. 505 Justifiable Homicide: Self-Defense or Defense of Another (Judicial Council of California Criminal Jury Instructions, 2024 ed.; New January 2006; Revised ... September 2022)
[A defendant is not required to retreat. He or she is entitled to stand his or her ground and defend himself or herself and, if reasonably necessary, to pursue an assailant until the danger of (death/great bodily injury/ <insert forcible and atrocious crime>) has passed. This is so even if safety could have been achieved by retreating.] ... The People have the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the [attempted] killing was not justified.
CALCRIM No. 505, Authority
Justifiable Homicide. Pen. Code, §§ 197–199. ... No Duty to Retreat. People v. Hughes (1951) 107 Cal.App.2d 487, 493 [237 P.2d 64]; People v. Hatchett (1942) 56 Cal.App.2d 20, 22 [132 P.2d 51].
Cal. Penal Code § 197(1), (3)
Homicide is also justifiable when committed by any person in any of the following cases: (1) When resisting any attempt to murder any person, or to commit a felony, or to do some great bodily injury upon any person. ... (3) ... but such person, or the person in whose behalf the defense was made, if he or she was the assailant or engaged in mutual combat, must really and in good faith have endeavored to decline any further struggle before the homicide was committed.
