f7a49e3fab722b28.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tasmania

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Tasmania's Criminal Code (s 46, substituted in 1987) justifies the force that, in the circumstances as the person believes them to be, it is reasonable to use in defence of themselves or another. The section says nothing about retreat and no duty to retreat is stated in the Code. No Tasmanian provision on excessive self-defence was found in the Code text consulted.

At home

s 40: a person in peaceable possession of a dwelling-house may use the force they believe on reasonable grounds is necessary to prevent forcible breaking and entering by someone they believe intends to commit a crime there, or to eject such a person.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act 1924 (Tas), Schedule 1, s 46 Self-defence and defence of another person
A person is justified in using, in the defence of himself or another person, such force as, in the circumstances as he believes them to be, it is reasonable to use.
Criminal Code Act 1924 (Tas), s 40 Defence of dwelling-house
It is lawful for any person who is in peaceable possession of a dwelling-house, and for any person lawfully assisting him or acting by his authority, to use such force as the person using the same believes on reasonable grounds to be necessary to prevent the forcible breaking and entering of the dwelling-house by any person whom he believes on reasonable grounds to be attempting to break or enter the dwelling-house with intent to commit any crime therein, or to eject therefrom any person who has unlawfully entered the dwelling-house, and whom he believes on reasonable grounds to intend to commit a crime therein.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Code Act 1924 (current version) (Tasmanian Legislation, Office of Parliamentary Counsel)
Australia as a whole

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).

Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book — Self-defence (Judicial Commission of New South Wales)

09bba2a41db54367.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Republika Srpska

Part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Republika Srpska has its own Criminal Code (Krivični zakonik Republike Srpske, 2017, amended up to 2026). Article 26 says an act done in necessary defence is not a crime, and defines necessary defence as defence that is absolutely necessary to repel a simultaneous or imminent unlawful attack on one's own or another's interests ('dobro'). Unlike the codes of the Federation and Brčko District, this article does not add the words 'proportionate to the attack'; it still requires that the defence be 'absolutely necessary'. The code does not mention retreat or the home, and no court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits may get a lighter sentence, or none if the excess came from strong irritation or fright caused by the attack.

What the law says
Krivični zakonik Republike Srpske (Sl. glasnik RS 64/2017 ... 78/2026), član 26 – Nužna odbrana
(1) Nije krivično djelo ono djelo koje je izvršeno u nužnoj odbrani. (2) Nužna je ona odbrana koja je neophodno potrebna da se od svog dobra ili od dobra drugog odbije istovremeni ili neposredno predstojeći protivpravni napad. (3) Učinilac koji je prekoračio granice nužne odbrane može se blaže kazniti, a ako je prekoračenje učinio usljed jake razdraženosti ili prepasti izazvane napadom, može se i osloboditi od kazne.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Krivični zakonik Republike Srpske (consolidated text) (Paragraf Lex BA)
Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole

Bosnia and Herzegovina has four criminal codes: one for the state level and one each for the Federation of BiH, Republika Srpska and Brčko District; ordinary crimes such as homicide are mostly tried under the entity codes, which were not checked here. The state-level Criminal Code (article 24) says an act committed in necessary defence is not a crime, and defines necessary defence as one that is absolutely necessary to repel a simultaneous or directly imminent unlawful attack on oneself or another and that is proportionate to the attack. The code does not mention retreat, and no court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits may receive a lighter sentence, and may be spared punishment entirely if the excess was caused by strong irritation or fright caused by the attack.

Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Krivični zakon Bosne i Hercegovine / The Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina (bilingual edition) (BH novinari (hosted copy))

49198c9d0571f124.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Jalisco

Part of Mexico, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Jalisco's Penal Code (art. 22-IV(e)) treats as legitimate defence the repelling of a current, real, violent and unlawful attack on one's own or another's person, honour, rights or property that creates imminent danger. The defence does not apply if the defender deliberately provoked the attack, foresaw it, 'or could easily have avoided it by other means', so easy avoidance is written into the code as a condition. The defence applies only partly if the means were not rationally necessary or the threatened harm was easily repairable or minor; such excess is punished with three days to eight years in prison. Intruders breaking into or found inside a dwelling are presumed to be lawful targets, and the public prosecutor must decide on its own motion during the investigation whether self-defence applies. Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 22-IV(e) presumes legitimate defence for anyone who repels and harms an intruder climbing over or breaking the fences, walls or entrances of their inhabited house or flat or its inner outbuildings, where there is an evident presumption of an attack or crime, or the possibility of entering or causing harm; the same presumption covers harming an intruder found in one's own or family's dwelling, that of someone one must defend, or a place holding property one must look after, when the circumstances reveal a possible attack.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Jalisco, art. 22, fracc. IV, inciso e)
e) La legítima defensa de la persona, honor, derechos o bienes del activo; así como de la persona, honor, derechos o bienes de otro; entendiéndose que se encuentra en tal hipótesis quien rechace una agresión actual, real, violenta e ilegítima que genere un peligro inminente. No operará tal excluyente, si el activo provocó dolosa, suficiente e inmediata la agresión o la previó o pudo evitarla fácilmente por otros medios. Operará parcialmente dicha excluyente, si no hubo necesidad racional del medio empleado en la defensa o si el daño que iba a causar el agresor era fácilmente reparable por otro medio o era notoriamente de poca importancia, comparado con el que causó la defensa. Se presumirá que actúa en legítima defensa quien rechace y dañe a un intruso que realice un escalamiento o fractura de las cercas, paredes o entradas de su casa o departamento habitado o de sus dependencias interiores, y que exista la presunción evidente de cometer una agresión o la comisión de un delito, o revele la posibilidad de penetrar al inmueble o causar daño. La misma presunción favorecerá al que dañe a un intruso que encontrare en la habitación propia o familiar, o de aquella persona a quien tenga obligación de defender, o en lugar donde se encuentren sus bienes propios o ajenos que deba cuidar, siempre que la presencia del extraño ocurra en circunstancias que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión por el intruso. El Ministerio Público en la investigación resolverá de oficio si opera o no la legítima defensa. En el caso de exceso en la legítima defensa que se menciona en este artículo, se aplicará al infractor la pena de tres días a ocho años de prisión.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Jalisco (file dated 25 Nov 2025), published on the transparency portal of the Zoológico Guadalajara (Zoológico Guadalajara transparency portal (copy of the state code; the Jalisco Congress library page returned an error))
  • Leyes Federales y Estatales (Jalisco transparency listing) (Gobierno de Jalisco)
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Código Penal Federal (texto vigente) (Cámara de Diputados, Mexico)

d98a79824daefcc3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Iraq

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Iraq's Penal Code (No. 111 of 1969) says there is no crime when an act is committed in legal defence, but only if the person could not take refuge with the public authorities in time and 'has no other means with which to ward off such threat' (art. 42). The code does not use the word 'retreat'; these conditions make defence available only when there is no other way out, and no court ruling interpreting them was found. Killing in self-defence is allowed only against a reasonably feared risk of death or serious injury, rape or sodomy by force, or kidnapping (art. 43), and in defence of property only against arson, theft, night-time entry into a home, or a feared risk of death or injury (art. 44). A person who deliberately or negligently goes beyond the limits of the right is responsible for the offence, but the court must impose the lower penalty class (misdemeanour instead of felony) (art. 45).

At home

Paragraph (article) 44 allows killing in defence of property when warding off, among other things, 'entering at night a residential building or part thereof'.

What the law says
Penal Code No. 111 of 1969, para. 42 (Ministry of Justice English translation)
There is no crime if the act is committed while exercising a right of legal defense. This right exists if the following conditions apply: (1) If a person defends himself and his property against the threat of a criminal act or reasonably believes that such threat exists. (2) If he is unable to take refuge with the public authorities in order to protect himself from such threat at the appropriate time. (3) If he has no other means with which to ward off such threat.
Penal Code No. 111 of 1969, paras. 43–45
Paragraph 43 - The right of legal self-defense does not permit murder unless it is intended that one of the following situations is to be avoided: (1) An act as a result of which it is reasonably feared that death or serious injury may occur. (2) Rape or buggery of a man or woman against his or her will. (3) Kidnapping. ... Paragraph 45 - The right of legal defense does not permit the infliction of greater harm than is necessary and if the person concerned oversteps the limits of that right either deliberately or negligently or if he mistakenly thinks that he is in a situation of legal defense, then he will be responsible for the offence he commits. In this case, the court is only permitted to impose the penalty for a misdemeanor rather than that prescribed for a felony and the penalty for an infraction rather than that prescribed for a misdemeanor.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Penal Code No. 111 of 1969 with amendments, third edition (Ministry of Justice English translation) (Iraq Ministry of Justice (hosted by policinglaw.info))

41a6cad06047fc02.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Hungary

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Hungary's Criminal Code (Act C of 2012) says an act necessary to fend off an unlawful attack, or a direct threat of one, against one's own or another's person or property or the public interest is not punishable. The statute states directly that the person attacked is not obliged to step aside from the unlawful attack, so there is no duty to retreat. Certain attacks (at night, armed, by a group, or home intrusions of those kinds) must be treated as if they were aimed at killing the defender, which widens what force counts as necessary. A person who goes beyond the necessary degree of defence out of fright or excusable agitation is not punishable.

At home

Section 22(2) of the Criminal Code treats an unlawful intrusion into a home at night, with a weapon displayed or carried, or by a group, and an armed unlawful intrusion into the fenced area belonging to a home, as if it were also aimed at killing the defender. Section 21 also allows non-lethal protective devices installed in advance, if the owner did everything reasonable to prevent them causing harm.

What the law says
Büntető Törvénykönyv (Act C of 2012), 22. § (1)-(4)
(1) Nem büntetendő az a cselekmény, amely a saját, illetve más vagy mások személye, javai vagy a közérdek ellen intézett, illetve ezeket közvetlenül fenyegető jogtalan támadás elhárításához szükséges. (2) A jogtalan támadást úgy kell tekinteni, mintha az a védekező életének kioltására is irányult volna, ha a) azt személy ellen aa) éjjel, ab) fegyveresen, ac) felfegyverkezve vagy ad) csoportosan követik el, b) az a lakásba ba) éjjel, bb) fegyveresen, bc) felfegyverkezve vagy bd) csoportosan történő jogtalan behatolás, vagy c) az a lakáshoz tartozó bekerített helyre fegyveresen történő jogtalan behatolás. (3) Nem büntethető, aki az elhárítás szükséges mértékét ijedtségből vagy menthető felindulásból lépi túl. (4) A megtámadott nem köteles kitérni a jogtalan támadás elől.
Criminal Code, section 22(3)-(4) (English translation in CJAD database)
(3) Any person who exceeds the reasonable force of self-defense due to shock or justifiable aggravation shall not be prosecuted. (4) The person assaulted shall not be liable to take evasive action so as to avoid the unlawful attack.
Büntető Törvénykönyv (Act C of 2012), 21. §
Nem büntetendő annak a cselekménye, aki a saját, illetve a mások személye vagy javai elleni jogtalan támadás megelőzése céljából telepített, az élet kioltására nem alkalmas védelmi eszközzel a jogtalan támadónak sérelmet okoz, feltéve, hogy a védekező mindent megtett, ami az adott helyzetben elvárható annak érdekében, hogy az általa telepített védelmi eszköz ne okozzon sérelmet.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • 2012. évi C. törvény a Büntető Törvénykönyvről (Wolters Kluwer Jogtár (free legislation service))
  • Self-defence - national proceedings: Hungary (University of Nottingham, CJAD database)

503f255456c2a0fb.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Sri Lanka

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Sri Lanka's Penal Code (Cap. 19, Ordinance No. 2 of 1883 as amended; the copy read lists amendments up to Act No. 29 of 1998) gives a right of private defence of body and property (ss. 89–90), allows causing death against assaults reasonably causing fear of death or grievous hurt, rape, kidnapping and similar (s. 93) and against robbery, house-breaking by night, arson of a dwelling and dangerous theft or trespass (s. 96). Section 92(3) removes the right 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities', and s. 92(4) limits harm to what is necessary. In The Queen v. A. O. Rodrigo (Court of Criminal Appeal, 1962, 66 NLR) the court held that s. 92(3) does not apply where a person is set upon and in imminent danger, only where the attack is known beforehand with time to seek the authorities, and that on the appellant's version 'there was no legal obligation on him to have run away'. Good-faith excess of private defence reduces murder to culpable homicide (s. 294, Exception 2).

At home

S. 96: private defence of property extends to causing death against robbery, house-breaking by night, and mischief by fire or explosives on a building used as a human dwelling.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 19), s. 89
89. Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.
Penal Code, s. 92(3)–(4)
(3) There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. (4) The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.
Penal Code, s. 93
93. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in the last preceding section, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the assailant, if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right be of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely— Firstly—Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Secondly—Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Thirdly—An assault with the intention of committing rape; ...
Penal Code, s. 96
96. The right of private defence of property extends, under the restrictions mentioned in section 92, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the wrong-doer, if the offence, the committing of which, or the attempting to commit which, occasions the exercise of the right, be an offence of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely— Firstly—Robbery; Secondly—House-breaking by night; Thirdly—Mischief by fire, or explosives committed on any building, tent, or vessel, which building, tent, or vessel is used as a human dwelling, or as a place for the custody of property ; Fourthly—Theft, mischief, or house-trespass under such circumstances as may reasonably cause apprehension that death or grievous hurt will be the consequence if such right of private defence is not exercised.
Penal Code, s. 294, Exception 2
Exception 2.—Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law, and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
The Queen v. A. O. Rodrigo (1962) 66 NLR, Court of Criminal Appeal
Section 92 (3) of the Penal Code does not apply to a case where a person is set upon by his assailant and there is imminent danger of death or grievous hurt, but to a case where the attack is known beforehand and the time is sufficient to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. ... According to appellant's version, there was no legal obligation on him to have run away. ... He was justified in law in holding his ground and defending his body.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Penal Code [Cap. 19] (as amended) – PDF, 166 pages, amendments listed to Act No. 29 of 1998 (Policinglaw.info)
  • The Queen v. A. O. Rodrigo, 66 NLR (LawNet, Ministry of Justice, Sri Lanka)

0f2c10ff8ae7794a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Louisiana

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Louisiana makes a homicide justifiable when committed in self-defence by someone who reasonably believes they are in imminent danger of losing their life or receiving great bodily harm and that the killing is necessary to save themselves, or to prevent a violent or forcible felony involving danger to life or great bodily harm (La. R.S. 14:20(A)). A person who is not engaged in unlawful activity and is in a place where they have a right to be has no duty to retreat before using deadly force and may stand their ground and meet force with force (§ 14:20(C)). Louisiana goes further than most states: the judge or jury is not allowed to consider the possibility of retreat at all when deciding whether the person's belief that deadly force was necessary was reasonable (§ 14:20(D)). These retreat provisions and the home presumption were added by Acts 2006, No. 141, and amended by Acts 2014, No. 163; the parallel non-deadly force section (§ 14:19) was extended to churches and places of worship and last amended in 2026 (Acts 2026, No. 148). A person who is the aggressor or 'who brings on a difficulty' cannot claim self-defence unless they withdraw in good faith in a way the adversary knows or should know (§ 14:21). The sources consulted for this entry show no statutory immunity from criminal prosecution or pretrial immunity hearing; civil immunity was not checked.

At home

La. R.S. 14:20(A)(4) and (B): a homicide is justifiable when committed by a person lawfully inside a dwelling, place of business or motor vehicle when the conflict began, against someone trying to enter unlawfully or who has entered unlawfully, if the person reasonably believes deadly force is necessary to prevent the entry or make the intruder leave; the law presumes that belief was reasonable if the intruder was unlawfully and forcibly entering and the person knew or had reason to believe it. This home/business/vehicle rule does not apply to someone who is at that time engaged in acquiring or distributing illegal drugs or possessing them with intent to distribute. § 14:20(A)(3) also allows deadly force against someone reasonably believed likely to use unlawful force against a person in a dwelling, business or vehicle while committing burglary or robbery there.

What the law says
La. R.S. 14:20(C)–(D)
C. A person who is not engaged in unlawful activity and who is in a place where he or she has a right to be shall have no duty to retreat before using deadly force as provided for in this Section, and may stand his or her ground and meet force with force. D. No finder of fact shall be permitted to consider the possibility of retreat as a factor in determining whether or not the person who used deadly force had a reasonable belief that deadly force was reasonable and apparently necessary to prevent a violent or forcible felony involving life or great bodily harm or to prevent the unlawful entry.
La. R.S. 14:20(A)(1)–(2)
A homicide is justifiable: (1) When committed in self-defense by one who reasonably believes that he is in imminent danger of losing his life or receiving great bodily harm and that the killing is necessary to save himself from that danger. (2) When committed for the purpose of preventing a violent or forcible felony involving danger to life or of great bodily harm by one who reasonably believes that such an offense is about to be committed and that such action is necessary for its prevention.
La. R.S. 14:20(B)
there shall be a presumption that a person lawfully inside a dwelling, place of business, or motor vehicle held a reasonable belief that the use of deadly force was necessary to prevent unlawful entry thereto, or to compel an unlawful intruder to leave the dwelling, place of business, or motor vehicle when the conflict began, if both of the following occur: (1) The person against whom deadly force was used was in the process of unlawfully and forcibly entering or had unlawfully and forcibly entered ...
La. R.S. 14:21
A person who is the aggressor or who brings on a difficulty cannot claim the right of self-defense unless he withdraws from the conflict in good faith and in such a manner that his adversary knows or should know that he desires to withdraw and discontinue the conflict.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • La. R.S. 14:20, Justifiable homicide (Acts 1976 No. 655 … Acts 2006 No. 141; Acts 2014 No. 163) (Louisiana State Legislature)
  • La. R.S. 14:19, Use of force or violence in defense (Acts 2006 No. 141; 2014 No. 163; 2026 No. 148) (Louisiana State Legislature)
  • La. R.S. 14:21, Aggressor cannot claim self defense (Louisiana State Legislature)

5f580ab6e9a29373.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Zimbabwe

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Zimbabwe's Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act 2004 makes defence of a person a complete defence only if the attack had begun or was imminent, the defender's conduct was necessary to avert it "and he or she could not otherwise escape from or avert the attack" (or reasonably believed so), the means used were reasonable, and the harm was not grossly disproportionate and fell on the attacker rather than an innocent third party. So the law expressly builds in a duty to escape or avoid the attack where that is possible. Courts must take account of the defender's circumstances, including stress or fear. If everything else is met but the means used were unreasonable, a person charged with murder is instead guilty of culpable homicide (s. 254). A genuine and reasonable mistaken belief in an attack counts as if it were true (s. 255). The sources opened here did not show a separate home rule.

What the law says
Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act [Chapter 9:23], s. 253(1)
the fact that a person accused of a crime was defending himself or herself or another person against an unlawful attack ... shall be a complete defence to the charge if— (a) when he or she did or omitted to do the thing, the unlawful attack had commenced or was imminent or he or she believed on reasonable grounds that the unlawful attack had commenced or was imminent, and (b) his or her conduct was necessary to avert the unlawful attack and he or she could not otherwise escape from or avert the attack or he or she, believed on reasonable grounds that his or her conduct was necessary to avert the unlawful attack and that he or she could not otherwise escape from or avert the attack, and (c) the means he or she used to avert the unlawful attack were reasonable in all the circumstances; and (d) any harm or injury caused by his or her conduct— (i) was caused to the attacker and not to any innocent third party; and (ii) was not grossly disproportionate to that liable to be caused by the unlawful attack.
Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act, s. 254
If a person accused of murder was defending himself or herself or another person against an unlawful attack ... he or she shall be guilty of culpable homicide if all the requirements for defence of person specified in section two hundred andfifty-three are satisfied in the case except that the means he or she used to avert the unlawful attack were not reasonable in all the circumstances.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Self-defence - national proceedings: Zimbabwe (Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act 2004) (Case Matrix Network / University of Nottingham, Criminal Justice and Armed Defence (CJAD) legislation database)

705ee286201f60b8.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Georgia and the Islands

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands has no permanent population. Its official laws website says English common law and some English statutes apply through several routes, and that working out exactly which apply is ultimately for the courts. No local Ordinance or court decision on self-defence or retreat was found, so the retreat rule is not settled here.

What the law says
SGSSI Laws website, 'English Statutory Law' (from previous entry)
There are several ways in which English statute law either applied or continues to apply in South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

2f476281628ec2dd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina

Part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina has its own Criminal Code (Krivični zakon FBiH, 2003, last amended 2025), which covers ordinary crimes such as homicide there. Article 26 says an act done in necessary defence is not a crime, and defines necessary defence as defence that is absolutely necessary to repel a simultaneous or directly imminent unlawful attack on oneself or another and that is proportionate to the attack. The code does not mention retreat or the home, and no court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits of necessary defence may get a lighter sentence, and may be spared punishment entirely if the excess came from strong irritation or fear caused by the attack.

What the law says
Krivični zakon Federacije Bosne i Hercegovine (Sl. novine FBiH 36/2003 ... 58/2025), član 26 – Nužna odbrana
(1) Nije krivično djelo ono djelo koje je učinjeno u nužnoj odbrani. (2) Nužna je ona odbrana koja je neophodno potrebna da učinitelj od sebe ili od drugog odbije istovremeni ili direktno predstojeći protivpravni napad, a koja je srazmjerna napadu. (3) Učinitelj koji prekorači granice nužne odbrane može se blaže kazniti, a ako je prekoračenje učinio zbog jake razdraženosti ili straha izazvanog napadom, može se i osloboditi kazne.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole

Bosnia and Herzegovina has four criminal codes: one for the state level and one each for the Federation of BiH, Republika Srpska and Brčko District; ordinary crimes such as homicide are mostly tried under the entity codes, which were not checked here. The state-level Criminal Code (article 24) says an act committed in necessary defence is not a crime, and defines necessary defence as one that is absolutely necessary to repel a simultaneous or directly imminent unlawful attack on oneself or another and that is proportionate to the attack. The code does not mention retreat, and no court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits may receive a lighter sentence, and may be spared punishment entirely if the excess was caused by strong irritation or fright caused by the attack.

bb93503f1a7df878.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Switzerland

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 15 of the Swiss Criminal Code entitles the person attacked, and anyone else, to ward off an unlawful attack or imminent threat of attack 'by means that are reasonable in the circumstances'. According to a 2023 article by Prof. Felix Bommer (University of Zurich) reviewing Swiss doctrine and Federal Supreme Court case law, there is no duty to flee or step aside in a self-defence situation, but Swiss practice requires that there be no obvious imbalance between the value of what is attacked and the harm done to the attacker; a person who negligently provoked the attack may, in some decisions, be required to step aside. If a defender exceeds the limits of self-defence, the court must reduce the sentence (Art. 16(1)); if the excess came from excusable excitement or panic caused by the attack, the defender is not guilty (Art. 16(2)), though courts rarely find an excess excusable.

At home

No separate home-defence rule. The right to exclude others from one's home (Hausrecht) can be defended, but Swiss practice still requires that the harm caused not be grossly out of proportion; Prof. Bommer gives the example that a homeowner may not fire a warning shot to chase an uninvited guest out of an office.

What the law says
Schweizerisches Strafgesetzbuch, Art. 15 (German text)
Wird jemand ohne Recht angegriffen oder unmittelbar mit einem Angriff bedroht, so ist der Angegriffene und jeder andere berechtigt, den Angriff in einer den Umständen angemessenen Weise abzuwehren.
Swiss Criminal Code, Art. 15-16 (English translation)
Art. 15 If any person is unlawfully attacked or threatened with imminent attack, the person attacked and any other person are entitled to ward off the attack by means that are reasonable in the circumstances. Art. 16 1 If a person in defending himself exceeds the limits of self-defence as defined in Article 15 and in doing so commits an offence, the court shall reduce the sentence. 2 If a person in defending himself exceeds the limits of self-defence as a result of excusable excitement or panic in reaction to the attack, he does not commit an offence.
Who makes criminal law here

Under the Swiss Federal Constitution, art. 123(1), 'The Confederation is responsible for legislation in the field of criminal law and the law of criminal procedure'; the cantons run the courts and carry out sentences (art. 123(2)). The Swiss Criminal Code is federal.

Federal Constitution of the Swiss Confederation, art. 123 (Criminal law)
The Confederation is responsible for legislation in the field of criminal law and the law of criminal procedure. The Cantons are responsible for the organisation of the courts, the administration of justice in criminal cases as well as for the execution of penalties and measures, unless the law provides otherwise.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Das deutsche Notwehrrecht – Ein knapper Blick von außen (Felix Bommer), KriPoZ 6/2023 (Kriminalpolitische Zeitschrift (KriPoZ))
  • Self-defence - national proceedings: Switzerland (Criminal Code 1937 (2017) EN) (University of Nottingham, CJAD database)

7abd6df26dda10b4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Quintana Roo

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Quintana Roo's Penal Code (art. 20(B)(II)) lists legitimate defence as a justification: a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence used was necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. The code does not mention retreating, fleeing or avoiding the attack. Home intruders are presumed to be lawful targets of defence. Since November 2023 the code also presumes 'self-defence with a gender perspective', unless proven otherwise, when a woman defends herself while being, or in imminent danger of being, a victim of physical, sexual or feminicidal violence, or when someone acts to help such a woman. Under arts. 56-57, exceeding a justification keeps the offence intentional but the penalty is one third of that for the offence. Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 20(B)(II) presumes the requirements of legitimate defence are met for anyone who harms a person who, by violence, climbing in or any other means, tries to enter without right their home or its outbuildings, those of their family or of anyone they must defend, or a place holding property they must protect; or who is found there in circumstances revealing a possible attack.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Quintana Roo, art. 20, apartado B, fracc. II
II. Legítima defensa: Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de [...] la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. Se presumirá que concurren los requisitos de la legítima defensa, respecto de aquél que cause un daño, a quien a través de la violencia, del escalamiento o por cualquier otro medio trate de penetrar sin derecho, a su hogar o sus dependencias, a los de su familia o los de cualquier persona que tenga el mismo deber de defender o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos de los que tenga la misma obligación; o bien, cuando lo encuentre en alguno de esos lugares, en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión; También se presumirá la legítima defensa con perspectiva de género, salvo prueba en contrario, en los supuestos siguientes: [...] Cuando quien ejerza la legitima defensa, sea una mujer, y al momento de desplegar la conducta, sea víctima, o esté en peligro inminente de ser víctima, de violencia física, sexual o feminicida, y [...] Cuando una persona despliegue la conducta en auxilio de una mujer en el momento, sea víctima de violencia física, sexual o feminicida, a fin de repeler el acto violento de que se trate.
Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Quintana Roo, arts. 56 (second paragraph) and 57
En casos de error de prohibición vencible quedará subsistente la atribución del hecho a título doloso, pero la penalidad será de una tercera parte del delito de que se trate. [...] ARTICULO 57.- Al que incurra en exceso en alguna de las causas de justificación se le impondrá la sanción correspondiente al error de prohibición vencible, pero quedará subsistente la atribución del hecho a título doloso.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Quintana Roo (última reforma P.O. 9 de octubre de 2024) (H. Congreso del Estado de Quintana Roo)
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

a889242b56c252a2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kurdistan Region

Part of Iraq, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The Kurdistan Region applies Iraq's Penal Code No. 111 of 1969 'as amended', with changes made by its own parliament: its laws list amendments or suspensions of particular articles, for example article 41(1) (2001), articles 128, 130 and 131 on 'honourable motives' (Law No. 14 of 2002), article 156 (2003), articles 144 and 408(1) (2004) and article 409 (Law No. 3 of 2015). None of the Kurdistan Parliament laws listed on its website for the years checked amends the legitimate-defence articles (42–46), so these appear to apply unchanged; no court ruling from the Region was found. Under article 42, legitimate defence exists only if the person could not get help from the public authorities in time and had no other means of warding off the threat. Killing is allowed only against a reasonably feared risk of death or serious injury, rape or sodomy by force, or kidnapping (art. 43). A person who goes beyond the limits of the right is still responsible but receives a lower penalty class (art. 45).

At home

Article 44 of the Iraqi Penal Code, applied in the Region, allows killing in defence of property against, among other things, night-time entry into an inhabited house.

What the law says
Penal Code No. 111 of 1969, para. 42 (Ministry of Justice English translation)
There is no crime if the act is committed while exercising a right of legal defense. This right exists if the following conditions apply: (1) If a person defends himself and his property against the threat of a criminal act or reasonably believes that such threat exists. (2) If he is unable to take refuge with the public authorities in order to protect himself from such threat at the appropriate time. (3) If he has no other means with which to ward off such threat.
Penal Code No. 111 of 1969, paras. 43–45
Paragraph 43 - The right of legal self-defense does not permit murder unless it is intended that one of the following situations is to be avoided: (1) An act as a result of which it is reasonably feared that death or serious injury may occur. (2) Rape or buggery of a man or woman against his or her will. (3) Kidnapping. ... Paragraph 45 - The right of legal defense does not permit the infliction of greater harm than is necessary and if the person concerned oversteps the limits of that right either deliberately or negligently or if he mistakenly thinks that he is in a situation of legal defense, then he will be responsible for the offence he commits. In this case, the court is only permitted to impose the penalty for a misdemeanor rather than that prescribed for a felony and the penalty for an infraction rather than that prescribed for a misdemeanor.
Kurdistan Region Law No. 14 of 2002 (as quoted by Amnesty International, 2007)
The perpetration of a crime with respect to women under the pretext of honourable motives shall not be considered an extenuating legal excuse for the purposes of applying the rules of articles 128, 130 and 131 of the Penal Code, number 111, 1969, amended
Kurdistan Parliament legislation lists (examples)
Law No. 6 (2002) to Amend Fines Defined in Amended Law No. 111 (1969) of the Penal Code ... Law No. 21 (2003) An act to annul Article 156 of the Iraqi Penal Code ... Law No. 42 (2004) An act to suspend Article 408, paragraph 1 of Law No. 111 (1969) Amended the Penal Code ... Law No. 43 (2004) An act to suspend punishment for crimes committed against spouses described in Article 144 of Law No. 111 (1969) the Penal Code
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • Kurdistan Parliament – Legislation by year (2001–2025 pages checked) (Kurdistan Parliament)
  • Iraq: Stoning to death of Yezidi girl – public statement (MDE 14/029/2007) (Amnesty International)
  • Law No. 3 of 2015 amending the application of Iraqi Penal Code No. 111 of 1969 in the Kurdistan Region (Kurdish text) (Kurdistan Parliament)
Iraq as a whole

Iraq's Penal Code (No. 111 of 1969) says there is no crime when an act is committed in legal defence, but only if the person could not take refuge with the public authorities in time and 'has no other means with which to ward off such threat' (art. 42). The code does not use the word 'retreat'; these conditions make defence available only when there is no other way out, and no court ruling interpreting them was found. Killing in self-defence is allowed only against a reasonably feared risk of death or serious injury, rape or sodomy by force, or kidnapping (art. 43), and in defence of property only against arson, theft, night-time entry into a home, or a feared risk of death or injury (art. 44). A person who deliberately or negligently goes beyond the limits of the right is responsible for the offence, but the court must impose the lower penalty class (misdemeanour instead of felony) (art. 45).

563a7393793d9adf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Libya

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under Libya's Penal Code (1953, as amended by Law No. 48 of 1956), there is no punishment for an act committed in exercise of the right of lawful defence, which covers 'any act that is necessary in order to avert a crime' that would harm oneself or others (art. 70). The right does not exist when it would have been possible to seek the protection of the public authorities in time. The code text found does not mention retreat or escape, and no Libyan court decisions on the point were found. Wilful killing is justified only to avert a reasonably feared act causing death or severe injury, forcible sexual intercourse or violation, kidnapping, felony theft, or night-time entry into an inhabited residence (art. 70 bis (b)). If the limits imposed by necessity are negligently exceeded, the person is punished under the rules for negligent offences where they exist (art. 73).

At home

Article 70 bis (b) lists 'entry by night of an inhabited residence or any of its appurtenances' among the situations in which lawful defence may extend to wilful killing.

What the law says
Penal Code (as amended by Law No. 48 of 1956), art. 70 – Lawful Defence (DCAF English translation)
There is no punishment if the act is committed during exercise of the right to lawful defence. This right exculpates a person for commission of any act that is necessary in order to avert a crime that would cause damage to himself or others. This right does not exist when it would have been possible to seek the protection of the public authorities in a timely manner.
Penal Code, art. 70 bis (b)
The right to lawful defence does not exculpate wilful murder unless it was intended in order to avert the following situations: An act that it is feared would cause death or severe injury, when this fear rests on reasonable grounds. Sexual intercourse or violation by force or under threat. Kidnapping. Felony theft. Entry by night of an inhabited residence or any of its appurtenances.
Penal Code, art. 73 – Transgression of the Limits of Lawful Defence
If in the commission of any of the acts set forth in the preceding articles, the limits prescribed by law, by the order of an authority, or imposed by necessity are negligently exceeded, the perpetrator shall be punished by the penalties for negligent offences, if the law provides that the commission of such offences may constitute negligence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

Zacatecas

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Zacatecas's Penal Code (art. 13(B)(II)) lists legitimate defence as a justification: a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence used was necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. The code does not mention retreating, fleeing or avoiding the attack. Home intruders are presumed to be lawful targets of defence. Since a 2019 reform, excess in any justification is punished like an avoidable mistake of law (art. 14): one third of the minimum and maximum penalty for the offence (art. 58 Ter). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

Art. 13(B)(II) presumes the requirements of legitimate defence are met for anyone who harms a person who, by violence, climbing in or any other means, tries to enter without right their home or its outbuildings, those of their family or of anyone they must defend, or a place holding property they must protect; or who is found there in circumstances revealing a possible attack.

Código Penal para el Estado de Zacatecas, art. 13, apartado B, fracc. II
II. Legítima defensa: Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. Artículo 14.- Al que incurra en exceso en alguna de las causas de justificación se le impondrá la sanción correspondiente al error de prohibición vencible. [...] En caso de que sea vencible el error de prohibición, a que se refiere el artículo señalado en el párrafo anterior, la penalidad será de una tercera parte del mínimo y del máximo del delito que se trate.

404f1753ef66bcc0.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bulgaria

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 12 of the Criminal Code says an act done in 'necessary defence' to protect state or public interests, oneself or another from an immediate unlawful attack, by harming the attacker within the necessary limits, is not socially dangerous (not a crime). The limits are exceeded when the defence is clearly out of line with the nature and danger of the attack. The code does not mention retreat, unlike the necessity defence in article 13, which requires a danger that 'could not be avoided in another way'; no court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits is not punished if the excess was due to fright or confusion (article 12(4)).

At home

Article 12(3): there is no excess of self-defence if the attack was made by forcibly entering, or breaking into, a dwelling. This survives from a 1997 amendment; the Constitutional Court (Decision No. 19 of 21 Nov 1997) struck down other parts of that amendment (for example those covering holiday homes and business premises) as allowing killing regardless of the real danger, but upheld the dwelling clause. The current wording dates from a 2006 amendment.

What the law says
Наказателен кодекс (Criminal Code), чл. 12
(1) Не е общественоопасно деянието, което е извършено при неизбежна отбрана - за да се защитят от непосредствено противоправно нападение държавни или обществени интереси, личността или правата на отбраняващия се или на другиго чрез причиняване вреди на нападателя в рамките на необходимите предели. (2) Превишаване пределите на неизбежната отбрана има, когато защитата явно не съответствува на характера и опасността на нападението. (3) (Изм. - ДВ, бр. 62 от 1997 г., изм. - ДВ, бр. 75 от 2006 г., в сила от 13.10.2006 г.) Няма превишаване пределите на неизбежната отбрана, ако нападението е извършено чрез проникване с насилие или с взлом в жилище. (4) ... Деецът не се наказва, когато извърши деянието при превишаване пределите на неизбежната отбрана, ако това се дължи на уплаха или смущение.
Наказателен кодекс, чл. 13(1) (necessity, for contrast)
Не е общественоопасно деянието, което е извършено от някого при крайна необходимост - за да спаси държавни или обществени интереси, както и свои или на другиго лични или имотни блага от непосредствена опасност, която деецът не е могъл да избегне по друг начин, ако причинените от деянието вреди са по-малко значителни от предотвратените.
Constitutional Court, Decision No. 19 of 21 November 1997 (case 13/1997), operative part
Обявява за противоконституционни разпоредбите на т. 1, т. 2, т. 3 относно думите "вилен имот или стопански обект", т. 4 и т. 5 от ал. 3 на чл. 12 от Наказателния кодекс ... Отхвърля искането за установяване на несъответствие с чл. 6, ал. 1 от Международния пакт за гражданските и политическите права на разпоредбите на т. 3 относно израза "нападението е извършено чрез проникване с насилие или с взлом в жилище" и на т. 6 от ал. 3 на чл. 12

4abba1d8f2a97693.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Suriname

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Suriname's Penal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht, 1910, Dutch-based) says a person is not punishable for an act required by the necessary defence of their own or another's body, sexual integrity or property against an immediate, unlawful attack (art. 66). Going beyond the limits of necessary defence is also not punishable if it was the direct result of a violent emotion caused by the attack ('noodweerexces'). The code does not mention retreat or contain a special home-defence rule, and no Surinamese court decision on retreat was found. The text used is the National Assembly's consolidated version amended up to 2004 (listed under laws in force to 2005); later amendments were not checked.

What the law says
Wetboek van Strafrecht (Suriname), art. 66
Niet strafbaar is hij die een feit begaat, geboden door de noodzakelijke verdediging van eigen of eens anders lijf, eerbaarheid of goed tegen ogenblikkelijke, wederrechtelijke aanranding. Niet strafbaar is de overschrijding van de grenzen van noodzakelijke verdediging, indien zij het onmiddellijk gevolg is geweest van een hevige gemoedsbeweging, door de aanranding veroorzaakt.

146eecc01fe62537.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Liberia

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Liberia's Penal Law (Title 26, approved 1976, published 1978) follows the American Model Penal Code. Force is justified when the person believes it is immediately necessary to protect themselves against unlawful force on the present occasion (§ 5.3(1)). Deadly force is justified only against death, serious bodily harm, kidnapping, or rape or sodomy compelled by force or threat, and is not justified if the person knows they can avoid the need for it 'with complete safety by retreating' or by handing over property or complying with a demand (§ 5.3(3)). The retreat duty does not apply in one's own dwelling or place of work (with exceptions for initial aggressors and co-workers). Using more force than the person believes necessary and appropriate is not justified (§ 5.1(5)), and justification under the criminal law does not bar a civil action (§ 5.1(4)).

At home

A person 'is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling or place of work', unless they are the initial aggressor, or are attacked at work by someone whose place of work they know it also is (§ 5.3(3)(a)).

What the law says
Penal Law (Liberian Codes Revised, Title 26), § 5.3(1) and (3) – Self-defense
1. Use of force justifiable in self-defense. Subject to the provisions of this section and of section 5.9 the use of force upon or toward another person is justifiable when the actor believes that such force is immediately necessary for the purpose of protecting himself against the use of unlawful force by such other person on the present occasion. ... 3. Deadly force. The use of deadly force is not justifiable under this section unless the person using force believes that such force is necessary to defend himself against death, serious bodily harm, kidnapping, rape or sodomy compelled by force or threat; nor is it justifiable if the person using force knows that he can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating or by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim of right thereto or by complying with a demand that he abstain from any action which he has no duty to take, except that: (a) The person using force is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling or place of work, unless he is the initial aggressor or is assailed in his place of work by another person whose place of work the person using force knows it to be
Penal Law, § 5.1(4)–(5) – General provisions
4. Civil remedy unimpaired. That conduct may be justified within the meaning of this subchapter does not abolish or impair any remedy for such conduct which is available in any civil action. 5. Excessive force. A person is not justified in using more force than he believes to be necessary and appropriate under the circumstances.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

8c41834f855e24f3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tamaulipas

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Tamaulipas's Penal Code (art. 32-II) justifies defending one's own or another's legal interests by repelling a real, violent, current and unlawful attack that creates imminent danger, unless it is proven that the defender provoked it, that they 'foresaw the attack and could easily have avoided it by other legal means', that the means were not rationally necessary, or that the threatened harm was easily repairable or minor compared with the harm caused. Avoiding a foreseen attack is therefore part of the written test, but only when it was easy and lawful; there is no general duty to flee. A May 2025 reform requires cases involving women victims of gender violence to be judged with a gender perspective, treats defending a woman from physical, sexual or feminicidal violence as self-defence, and says it is not excess when fear or terror impaired the person's ability to judge the limits of their response. Otherwise, excess (lack of rational necessity, or disproportion to a minor or repairable harm) is punished as a negligent (imprudencial) offence (art. 34). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 32-II presumes, unless proven otherwise, that the requirements of legitimate defence are met for anyone who harms a person who, by violence, climbing in or any other means, tries to enter without right their home, their family's home, its outbuildings or those of anyone they must defend, or a place holding property they must protect; or who is found there in circumstances revealing a possible attack.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Tamaulipas, art. 32, fracc. II
II.- Obrar en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, repeliendo una agresión real, violenta, actual, sin derecho y de la cual resulte un peligro inminente, a no ser que se pruebe que intervino alguna de las circunstancias siguientes: a).- PRIMERA: Que el agredido provocó la agresión, dando causa inmediata y suficiente para ella; b).- SEGUNDA: Que previó la agresión y pudo fácilmente evitarla por otros medios legales; [...] c).- TERCERA: Que no hubo necesidad racional del medio empleado en la defensa; y d).- CUARTA: Que el daño que iba a causar el agresor, era fácilmente reparable después por medios legales o era notoriamente de poca importancia comparado con el que causó la defensa. Se presumirá que concurren los requisitos de la legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, respecto de aquél que cause un daño a quien a través de la violencia, del escalamiento o por cualquier otro medio, trate de penetrar, sin derecho, a su hogar, al de su familia, a sus dependencias o a los de cualquier persona que tenga el mismo deber de defender o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que tenga la misma obligación; o bien, lo encuentre en alguno de aquellos lugares en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión. En los casos relacionados con mujeres víctimas de violencia de género, se deberá juzgar en todo momento bajo esta perspectiva. [...] También se considerará legítima defensa cuando una persona actúe para proteger a una mujer que se encuentre en una situación de violencia de género, abarcando la violencia física, sexual y/o feminicida, conforme a lo previsto en la legislación general y local en la materia, y cause un daño al agresor, con el propósito de hacer cesar dicha conducta.
Código Penal para el Estado de Tamaulipas, art. 34
ARTÍCULO 34.- El que exceda en el caso de legítima defensa, por intervenir la tercera o cuarta circunstancia enumeradas en la fracción II del artículo 32, será sancionado como delincuente imprudencial. No se considerará exceso en la legítima defensa, cuando al momento en que ésta se concrete concurran circunstancias en las que la persona agredida sufra miedo o terror que afecte su capacidad para determinar el límite adecuado de su respuesta o la racionalidad de los medios empleados, conforme a las valoraciones psicológicas conducentes.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal para el Estado de Tamaulipas, documento de consulta (última reforma aplicada P.O. No. 19, 12 de febrero de 2026) (H. Congreso del Estado de Tamaulipas)
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

61ae97c27516407b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Moldova

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 36 of Moldova's Criminal Code (2002) says an act committed in legitimate defence is not a crime, where it repels a direct, immediate, material and real attack on oneself, another or a public interest that seriously endangers the person, their rights or the public interest; preventing a violent entry into a dwelling or other room also counts (art. 36(3)). The code does not say whether the defender must avoid the attack if they can. The Supreme Court of Justice (Colegiul penal), in decision 1ra-579/13 of 29 May 2013, upheld the Court of Appeal's reasoning that for art. 36 to apply 'there must be a relationship of proportionality between attack and defence, in the sense that the result produced by the defence should not be more serious than the consequence of the attack', and rejected the plea because the victim had already been disarmed when struck with an axe; the decision does not discuss retreat. A Moldova State University student paper (Tabarcea, supervised by Daniel Martin) proposes adding to art. 36 an express rule that legitimate defence applies 'regardless of the possibility of avoiding or not the attack', which shows the statute does not now say so; another CSJ decision (1ra-982/13 of 23 October 2013) also turned on proportionality (three knife wounds). No source states whether retreat is required, so the entry stays unclear.

At home

Article 36(3) treats as legitimate defence an act done to prevent someone from violently entering a dwelling or other space, where this endangers life or health or is accompanied by a threat of such violence.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Republic of Moldova (2002), Article 36(2)-(3) (English translation)
(2) A person who commits an act in order to repel a direct, immediate, material, and real attack against him/herself, against another person, or against a public interest and which seriously endangers the person or the rights of the attacked person or the public interest shall be in a state of legitimate defense. (3) A person who commits an act set forth in paragraph (2) in order to prevent someone violently entering into a house or other space thus endangering a person's life or health or by a threat of such violence shall be in a state of legitimate defense.
Curtea Supremă de Justiţie, Colegiul penal, Decizie din 29 mai 2013, dosarul nr. 1ra-579/13 (quoting the Court of Appeal reasoning it upheld)
Pentru a fi aplicate dispoziţiile art. 36 Cod penal este necesar ca între atac şi apărare să existe un raport de proporţionalitate, în sensul că rezultatul produs în urma apărării să nu fie mai grav decît cel ce reprezintă urmarea atacului. [...] Este cert dovedit că în momentul în care inculpatul intenţionat a lovit victima cu toporul, ultimul era deja deposedat de lopată şi nu mai putea să exercite nici un atac asupra inculpatului [Our rendering: For art. 36 of the Criminal Code to apply, there must be a relationship of proportionality between attack and defence, in the sense that the result produced by the defence must not be more serious than the consequence of the attack. ... It is clearly proven that when the accused deliberately struck the victim with the axe, the latter had already been stripped of the shovel and could no longer carry out any attack on the accused]
Cătălina Tabarcea, 'Legitima apărare în dreptul penal al Republicii Moldova' (student paper, Moldova State University; recommended by Daniel Martin, dr., conf. univ.)
De asemenea, o altă completare care ar fi una bine-venită este cea care se referă la așa-zisa posibilitate de a evita atacul. [...] ar fi bine-venită completarea art. 36 CP RM cu un nou alineat care ar stabili dreptul persoanei de a considera faptele sale săvârșite în stare de legitimă apărare, indiferent de posibilitatea acestuia de a evita sau nu atacul [Our rendering: Another welcome addition would concern the so-called possibility of avoiding the attack. ... it would be welcome to add to art. 36 of the Criminal Code a new paragraph establishing the person's right to have their acts treated as committed in legitimate defence regardless of whether or not they could have avoided the attack]
What was tried

web search 'Moldova legitima apărare posibilitatea de a evita atacului art. 36 CSJ' → four CSJ decisions opened (1ra-982/13, 1ra-579/13, 1ra-1548/2022, 1ra-1391/14), none discusses a duty to avoid/flee; USM article 'Legitima apărare. Condiţii referitoare la atac' record and ibn.idsi.md article page returned no text. No CSJ explanatory decision (hotărâre explicativă) on legitimate defence found.

076bd680b052f470.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Sierra Leone

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The only Sierra Leonean text on self-defence found was the 1991 Constitution: a death does not breach the right to life if it results from force 'reasonably justifiable in the circumstances of the case' for the defence of any person from unlawful violence or for the defence of property, without affecting liability under any other law (s. 16(2)(a)). No criminal statute or court decision setting the rules of self-defence, the retreat question, defence of the home, or the result of excessive force was found in this research pass. The retreat question is therefore not settled by the sources found.

What the law says
Constitution of Sierra Leone 1991, s. 16(2)(a)
Without prejudice to any liability for a contravention of any other law with respect to the use of force in such cases as are hereinafter mentioned, a person shall not be regarded as having been deprived of his life in contravention of this section if he dies as a result of the use of force to such extent as is reasonably justifiable in the circumstances of the case, that is to say — a. for the defence of any person from unlawful violence or for the defence of property ;

7d71fa0a74dca630.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Aceh

Part of Indonesia, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Aceh has its own Islamic criminal law, the Qanun Jinayat (Qanun Aceh No. 6 of 2014), but it covers only ten listed offences (alcohol, gambling, seclusion, intimacy, adultery, sexual harassment, rape, false accusation of adultery, and same-sex acts) and does not cover homicide or assault. Its only defences are acting under official duty (art. 9) and duress or mental illness (art. 10); it has no self-defence provision. Killing and violence in Aceh are therefore tried under Indonesia's national Criminal Code. Indonesia's new Criminal Code (Law No. 1 of 2023), in force from 2026, says a person who is forced to do a prohibited act in defence against an immediate unlawful attack or threat of attack on themselves or another, sexual honour, or property is not punished (art. 34); the old code (art. 49) said the same. The official elucidation of article 34 lists four conditions, including that the defence was made 'because there was no other way' to repel the attack (subsidiarity) and that it was proportionate to the attack. The law does not use the word 'retreat', but the 'no other way' condition means that avoiding the attack, where possible, comes first; Indonesian commentators discuss this as a duty to avoid. A person who exceeds the limits of defence is not punished if the excess was directly caused by severe emotional shock from the attack (art. 43, formerly art. 49(2)).

What the law says
Qanun Aceh No. 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat, Pasal 3(2)
Jarimah sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) meliputi: a. Khamar; b. Maisir; c. khalwat; d. Ikhtilath; e. Zina; f. Pelecehan seksual; g. Pemerkosaan; h. Qadzaf; i. Liwath; dan j. Musahaqah.
Qanun Aceh No. 6 Tahun 2014, Pasal 9 and 10 (Alasan Pembenar dan Alasan Pemaaf)
Pasal 9: Petugas yang sedang melaksanakan tugas atau perintah atasan sesuai dengan peraturan perundang-undangan tidak dikenakan 'Uqubat. ... Pasal 10: Tidak dikenakan 'Uqubat, seseorang yang melakukan Jarimah karena: a. dipaksa oleh adanya ancaman, tekanan, kekuasaan atau kekuatan yang tidak dapat dihindari, kecuali perbuatan tersebut merugikan orang lain; dan/atau b. pada waktu melakukan Jarimah menderita gangguan jiwa, penyakit jiwa atau keterbelakangan mental, kecuali perbuatan tersebut merugikan orang lain.
UU No. 1 Tahun 2023 tentang KUHP (new Criminal Code, in force 2026), Pasal 34
Setiap orang yang terpaksa melakukan perbuatan yang dilarang tidak dipidana, jika perbuatan tersebut dilakukan karena pembelaan terhadap serangan atau ancaman serangan seketika yang melawan hukum terhadap diri sendiri atau orang lain, kehormatan dalam arti kesusilaan, atau harta benda sendiri atau orang lain.
Penjelasan (Elucidation) Pasal 34 UU 1/2023, as summarised by Hukumonline
harus ada serangan atau ancaman serangan yang melawan hukum yang bersifat seketika; pembelaan dilakukan karena tidak ada jalan lain (subsidiaritas) untuk menghalau serangan; pembelaan hanya dapat dilakukan terhadap kepentingan yang ditentukan secara limitatif yaitu kepentingan hukum diri sendiri atau orang lain, kehormatan dalam arti kesusilaan, atau harta benda; dan keseimbangan antara pembelaan yang dilakukan dan serangan yang diterima (proporsionalitas).
UU 1/2023, Pasal 43 (excessive defence)
Setiap orang yang melakukan pembelaan terpaksa yang melampaui batas yang langsung disebabkan keguncangan jiwa yang hebat karena serangan atau ancaman serangan seketika yang melawan hukum, tidak dipidana.
Old KUHP (Wetboek van Strafrecht, in force until 2025), Pasal 49
(1) Tidak dipidana, barang siapa melakukan perbuatan pembelaan terpaksa untuk diri sendiri maupun untuk orang lain, kehormatan kesusilaan atau harta benda sendiri maupun orang lain, karena adanya serangan atau ancaman serangan yang sangat dekat pada saat itu yang melawan hukum. (2) Pembelaan terpaksa yang melampaui batas, yang langsung disebabkan oleh keguncangan jiwa yang hebat karena serangan atau ancaman serangan itu, tidak dipidana.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat (PPID Pemerintah Aceh)
  • Kriteria Pembelaan Terpaksa atau Noodweer (Klinik Hukumonline) (Hukumonline)
  • Lawan atau Lari? Batasan Pembelaan Diri dalam Hukum Pidana (Hukumonline)
Indonesia as a whole

Indonesia's new Criminal Code (Law No. 1 of 2023), which according to Hukumonline takes effect in 2026, says a person who is forced to commit a prohibited act to defend against an immediate, unlawful attack is not punished (art. 34); the old code's article 49 had the same rule ('noodweer'). According to Hukumonline's summary of the official elucidation of article 34, the defence must be used because there is 'no other way (subsidiarity) to repel the attack', and must be in balance with the attack received (proportionality). A Supreme Court news article (MARINews, February 2026) explains that defending oneself is 'not required if one can still avoid' the attack, and that someone who provoked the attack cannot claim self-defence. If the defence goes beyond the limits because of severe mental shock caused directly by the attack ('noodweer exces'), the person is also not punished (art. 43 new code; art. 49(2) old code); the act stays unlawful but the person is excused, and the excuse fails if the excess was driven by old grudges rather than sudden fear. The full official text of the new code could not be opened here (official databases blocked), so the new articles are quoted only as excerpted by these sources.

52ecd466c06940c3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Aland

Part of Finland, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Åland is a self-governing region of Finland, but under section 27 of the Act on the Autonomy of Åland (1144/1991) criminal law is a matter for Finland's national legislature, except that Åland may set penalties within its own fields of law (section 18, point 25). So the Finnish Criminal Code's self-defence rule applies in Åland. Chapter 4, section 4 of that code allows a defensive act that is necessary to repel a begun or directly threatening unlawful attack, unless it obviously exceeds what is justifiable overall, considering the nature and strength of the attack, the persons of defender and attacker, and other circumstances. The code does not mention retreat, and no Finnish court ruling on retreat was checked. If the limits were exceeded, the defender is still free from criminal liability if, given the danger and surprise of the attack and the situation as a whole, no other reaction could reasonably have been required.

What the law says
Rikoslaki (Criminal Code of Finland, 39/1889), 4 luku 4 § Hätävarjelu
Aloitetun tai välittömästi uhkaavan oikeudettoman hyökkäyksen torjumiseksi tarpeellinen puolustusteko on hätävarjeluna sallittu, jollei teko ilmeisesti ylitä sitä, mitä on pidettävä kokonaisuutena arvioiden puolustettavana, kun otetaan huomioon hyökkäyksen laatu ja voimakkuus, puolustautujan ja hyökkääjän henkilö sekä muut olosuhteet. Jos puolustuksessa on ylitetty hätävarjelun rajat (hätävarjelun liioittelu), tekijä on kuitenkin rangaistusvastuusta vapaa, jos olosuhteet olivat sellaiset, ettei tekijältä kohtuudella olisi voinut vaatia muunlaista suhtautumista, kun otetaan huomioon hyökkäyksen vaarallisuus ja yllätyksellisyys sekä tilanne muutenkin.
Ahvenanmaan itsehallintolaki (Act on the Autonomy of Åland, 1144/1991), 27 § (extract)
Valtakunnalla on lainsäädäntövalta asioissa, jotka koskevat: ... rikosoikeutta 18 §:n 25 kohdassa säädetyin poikkeuksin;
Självstyrelselag för Åland (1144/1991), 27 § (Swedish, extract)
straffrätt med undantag av vad som stadgas i 18 § 25 punkten,

be8ef1ef9a800ed2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New South Wales

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Self-defence in NSW is set out in Part 11 (ss 418–423) of the Crimes Act 1900, inserted by the Crimes Amendment (Self-defence) Act 2001. A person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them; the prosecution must disprove self-defence beyond reasonable doubt (s 419). There is no stated duty to retreat: the judges' Bench Book tells juries that the availability of retreat is one matter they may consider when judging whether the response was reasonable. If a person who believed deadly force was necessary used force that was not a reasonable response, the result is manslaughter rather than murder ('excessive self-defence', s 421).

At home

The Bench Book notes that the 2001 amending Act repealed the Home Invasion (Occupants Protection) Act 1998; home defence now falls under the general self-defence test in Part 11 of the Crimes Act 1900 (the official statute site could not be opened from here).

What the law says
NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book, Self-defence [6-460] (suggested jury direction)
[It may be necessary to give directions on such matters as arise on the evidence relating to, for example, the imminence of a threatened attack or the availability of other remedies to the accused, such as retreat. It should, however, be made emphatically clear to the jury that it is the accused’s perception of the circumstances which must be considered.]
NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book, Self-defence [6-455] (summary of Crimes Act ss 418, 421)
A direction for self-defence in cases of murder must contain all the above numbers 1–5 essential components. The difference is that they are applied to the facts in a sequential way to accommodate the offence of manslaughter by excessive self-defence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book — Self-defence (Judicial Commission of New South Wales)
  • Self-defence (Australia) — used only as a pointer to Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) ss 418–423 (Wikipedia), CC BY-SA 4.0
Australia as a whole

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).
