a515a502b122a930.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Togo

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Togo's Penal Code of 2015 (Law No. 2015-010 of 24 November 2015) lists self-defence as a justification (art. 18). A person is not criminally responsible for an act required, at the same moment, by the need to defend themselves or another against an unjustified attack, unless the means of defence are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack (art. 19). Defence of property can never extend to intentional homicide and must be strictly necessary and proportionate (art. 20). The code does not mention retreat or flight, and no Togolese court decisions on the point were found. No provision on excessive self-defence was found in the sections searched.

At home

A person is presumed to have acted in self-defence when repelling, at night, entry by climbing, break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, a shop, a farm or business building or any other outbuilding of rented premises, or when defending against violent theft or looting (art. 21).

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n° 2015-010 du 24 novembre 2015), art. 19
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, commet, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte.
Code pénal 2015, art. 20
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, commet un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal 2015, art. 21
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui commet l’infraction : 1) pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par escalade, effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité, dans un magasin, dans un bâtiment d’exploitation ou dans toute autre dépendance d’un lieu loué ; 2) pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

4d93061d609071c6.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Maine

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Maine allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is necessary and reasonably believes the other person is about to use unlawful deadly force against them or a third person, or is committing or about to commit a kidnapping, robbery or gross sexual assault by compulsion against them or a third person (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(2)(A)). Maine keeps a duty to retreat: deadly force is not justified if the person knows that they or the third person can, with complete safety, retreat from the encounter, surrender property to someone with a colourable claim to it, or comply with a demand to stop doing something they are not obliged to do (§ 108(2)(C)(3)). The only place exception is the person's own dwelling place, and only if they were not the initial aggressor; Maine has no workplace exception. The retreat rule has been part of the code since 1975 (PL 1975, c. 499) and was restated in 2007 (PL 2007, c. 173). Deadly force is also not justified for someone who provoked the other, intending to cause harm, into using deadly force, or to defend someone the person knows intentionally and unlawfully provoked the attack; non-deadly force is barred for a provoker, an initial aggressor who has not withdrawn and clearly communicated it, or in a fight by agreement (§ 108(1)–(2)). Since 2019 (PL 2019, c. 462), force is not justified when based solely on discovering the victim's gender, gender identity or sexual orientation, including after an unwanted non-forcible advance. The sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit and no pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(2)(B): deadly force is justified when a person reasonably believes another has entered or is trying to enter a dwelling place (or has secretly stayed inside) without licence or privilege, and that deadly force is necessary to prevent that person from inflicting bodily injury on someone present in the dwelling. The duty to retreat does not apply in one's own dwelling place if one was not the initial aggressor (§ 108(2)(C)(3)(a)). There is no statutory presumption of reasonable fear.

What the law says
Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(2)(C)(3)
However, a person is not justified in using deadly force as provided in paragraph A if: ... (3) The person knows that the person or a 3rd person can, with complete safety: (a) Retreat from the encounter, except that the person or the 3rd person is not required to retreat if the person or the 3rd person is in the person's dwelling place and was not the initial aggressor; (b) Surrender property to a person asserting a colorable claim of right thereto; or (c) Comply with a demand that the person abstain from performing an act that the person is not obliged to perform.
Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(2)(A)
A person is justified in using deadly force upon another person: A. When the person reasonably believes it necessary and reasonably believes such other person is: (1) About to use unlawful, deadly force against the person or a 3rd person; or (2) Committing or about to commit a kidnapping, robbery or a violation of section 253, subsection 1, paragraph A, against the person or a 3rd person ...
Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(2)(B)
When the person reasonably believes: (1) That such other person has entered or is attempting to enter a dwelling place or has surreptitiously remained within a dwelling place without a license or privilege to do so; and (2) That deadly force is necessary to prevent the infliction of bodily injury by such other person upon the person or a 3rd person present in the dwelling place ...
Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(3)
A person is not justified in using force against another based solely on the discovery of, knowledge about or potential disclosure of the victim's actual or perceived gender, gender identity, gender expression or sexual orientation ...

81ac7293a00f2f46.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Marshall Islands

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The Marshall Islands Criminal Code 2011 (31 MIRC Ch. 1), modelled on the US Model Penal Code, allows force a person believes immediately necessary to protect themselves against unlawful force. Deadly force is allowed only against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or forced sexual intercourse, and not if the person knows they can avoid the need for it with reasonable safety by retreating, handing over property, or complying with a demand to stop doing something they have no duty to do. There is no duty to retreat from one's own home or workplace, except for an initial aggressor or when attacked at work by a co-worker. Outside the deadly-force rule, a person may judge the need for force without retreating (§3.04(2)(c)).

At home

No duty to retreat from one's own dwelling or place of work, unless the person was the initial aggressor or is attacked at work by someone whose workplace it also is (§3.04(2)(b)(ii)(A)).

What the law says
Criminal Code 2011 (31 MIRC Ch. 1), §3.04(2)(b)
The use of deadly force is not justifiable under this Section unless the actor believes that such force is necessary to protect himself or herself against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat; nor is it justifiable if: (i) the actor, with the purpose of causing death or serious bodily injury, provoked the use of force against himself or herself in the same encounter, unless the actor completely withdraws from the conflict and successfully communicates that to the victim; or (ii) the actor knows that he or she can avoid the necessity of using such force with reasonable safety by retreating or by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim or right thereto or by complying with a demand that the actor abstain from any action that he or she has no duty to take, except that: (A) the actor is not obliged to retreat from the actor’s dwelling or place of work, unless he or she was the initial aggressor or is assailed in his or her place of work by another person whose place of work the actor knows it to be; ...
Criminal Code 2011, §3.04(2)(c)
Except as required by paragraphs (a) and (b) of this Subsection, a person employing protective force may estimate the necessity of such force under the circumstances as the person believes them to be when the force is used, without retreating, surrendering possession, doing any other act that the person has no legal duty to do, or abstaining from any lawful action.

901694eedabf1959.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Durango

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Durango's Penal Code (art. 28(B)(II)) lists legitimate defence as a justification: a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence used was necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. The code does not mention retreating, fleeing or avoiding the attack. A 2021 reform states that a person who harms, injures or kills a home intruder is presumed to meet the requirements of self-defence. Exceeding any justification, including self-defence, is punished with one quarter of the penalty for the offence (art. 86). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 28(B)(II), as reformed in December 2021, presumes the requirements of legitimate defence are met for anyone who causes harm, injury or death to a person who, by violence, climbing in or any other means, tries to enter without right their home or its outbuildings, those of their family or of anyone they must defend, or a place holding property they must protect; or who is found there in circumstances revealing a possible attack.

What the law says
Código Penal del Estado Libre y Soberano de Durango, art. 28, apartado B, fracc. II
II. Legítima defensa: Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. Se presumirá que concurren los requisitos de la legítima defensa, respecto de aquél que cause un daño, lesión o privación de la vida a quien a través de la violencia, del escalamiento o por cualquier otro medio trate de penetrar sin derecho, a su hogar o sus dependencias, a los de su familia o los de cualquier persona que tenga el mismo deber de defender o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos de los que tenga la misma obligación; o bien, cuando lo encuentre en alguno de esos lugares, en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión; FRACCION REFORMADA POR DEC. 78, P.O. 103 BIS DEL 26 DE DICIEMBRE DE 2021.
Código Penal del Estado Libre y Soberano de Durango, art. 86
ARTÍCULO 86. Punibilidad en casos de exceso en las causas de justificación. Al que incurra en exceso en alguna de las causas de justificación previstas en el artículo 28 de este Código, se le impondrá la cuarta parte de las penas o medidas de seguridad, correspondientes al delito de que se trate.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal del Estado Libre y Soberano de Durango (última reforma Dec. 404, P.O. 46 bis, 7 de junio de 2026) (H. Congreso del Estado de Durango)
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

9e3d40343020e8ee.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Niger

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.
Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963), on ss. 59-65
When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Zamfara Shari'a Penal Code 2000, s. 204(c), as reproduced in Peters (2001), Appendix Five
204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC 430/1962) [1963] NGSC 24 (25 March 1963) (NigeriaLII)

  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Michoacán

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Michoacán's Penal Code (art. 27-VI) excludes liability when a person repels a real, current or imminent attack on their own or another's legal interests, if there was a reasonable need for the defence used and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. The code says nothing about retreating or fleeing. Intruders into a dwelling are presumed to be lawful targets of defence unless shown otherwise. Excess in self-defence is punished with one quarter of the penalty for the offence (art. 75). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 27-VI presumes legitimate defence, unless proven otherwise, when harm is caused to someone who by any means tries to enter without right the home of the defender or their family, its outbuildings, the home of anyone they must defend, or a place holding property they must protect; or who is found there in circumstances showing a probable attack.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Michoacán, art. 27, fracc. VI
VI. Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad razonable de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. Se presumirá como legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, el hecho de causar daño a quien por cualquier medio trate de penetrar sin derecho al hogar del agente, al de su familia, a sus dependencias, o a los de cualquier persona que ésta tenga la obligación de defender, al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que exista la misma obligación o bien lo encuentre en alguno de aquellos lugares en circunstancias tales que revelen la probabilidad de una agresión;

Artículo 75. Exceso en las causas de justificación A quien incurra en exceso en los casos previstos en las fracciones V, VI y VII del artículo 27 de este Código, se le impondrá la cuarta parte de la pena o medida de seguridad correspondiente al delito de que se trate, siempre que con relación al exceso no se actualice otra causa de exclusión del delito.

f7d6d5b7119ebcad.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New York

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

New York's Penal Law (section 35.15) allows deadly physical force only when the person reasonably believes the other person is using or about to use deadly force, or is committing a kidnapping, forcible rape, forcible aggravated sexual abuse or robbery, or a burglary in the circumstances set out in section 35.20. Against deadly force, New York keeps a duty to retreat: the person may not use deadly force if they know they can avoid it with complete personal safety, to themselves and others, by retreating. The only exceptions are being in one's own dwelling and not the initial aggressor, or being a police or peace officer (or assisting one). There is no exception for vehicles, workplaces or public places, and the retreat rule does not apply to the separately listed cases of kidnapping, rape, robbery and burglary. Physical force is not justified when the person provoked the other with intent to cause injury, was the initial aggressor (unless they withdrew and communicated it), or the force came from an agreed fight. The occupant of a dwelling or occupied building may use deadly force they reasonably believe necessary to prevent or end a burglary (35.20(3)). No presumption of reasonable fear, civil immunity or pretrial immunity hearing exists in current law; bills such as S1473 (2025) would remove the retreat duty, bar jurors from considering retreat and grant criminal and civil immunity, but they had not been enacted in the compiled law checked (last modified 6 September 2024).

At home

No duty to retreat in one's dwelling if not the initial aggressor (Penal Law 35.15(2)(a)(i)). A person in possession or control of, or licensed or privileged to be in, a dwelling or occupied building may use deadly force when they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent or end a burglary of it (35.20(3)); deadly force against a burglar is also allowed by cross-reference in 35.15(2)(c).

What the law says
Penal Law § 35.15(2)(a)
The actor reasonably believes that such other person is using or about to use deadly physical force. Even in such case, however, the actor may not use deadly physical force if he or she knows that with complete personal safety, to oneself and others he or she may avoid the necessity of so doing by retreating; except that the actor is under no duty to retreat if he or she is: (i) in his or her dwelling and not the initial aggressor; or (ii) a police officer or peace officer ...
Penal Law § 35.15(2)(b)
He or she reasonably believes that such other person is committing or attempting to commit a kidnapping, forcible rape, forcible aggravated sexual abuse, a crime formerly defined in section 130.50 of this chapter by force, or robbery
Penal Law § 35.20(3)
A person in possession or control of, or licensed or privileged to be in, a dwelling or an occupied building, who reasonably believes that another person is committing or attempting to commit a burglary of such dwelling or building, may use deadly physical force upon such other person when he or she reasonably believes such to be necessary to prevent or terminate the commission or attempted commission of such burglary.
Senate Bill S1473 (2025) – proposed, not law
A person who is justified in threatening or using physical force against another person in defense of themself, another person, or property pursuant to this section is immune from criminal and civil liability ...

39bb7c42161d7b7a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Guerrero

Part of Mexico, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Guerrero No. 499, art. 31(IV): a person may repel a real, current or imminent attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence used is reasonably necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. No avoidance or 'no other means' condition appears in the article, and it does not say the defender need not flee. National Supreme Court (SCJN) theses point both ways: a 1940 thesis (registro 814826) says flight should not be imposed as a condition, while a 1946 thesis (registro 806596) denied the defence where the accused 'could well have avoided the aggression by other means'. No state-specific thesis was found (web search budget ran out), so whether retreat is required is not settled. Against attacks by minors, the defender must avoid injuring the attacker and use only necessary and proportionate defence against serious attacks. Excess (art. 87) is punished with one quarter of the penalty; it is not excess if the defender was in confusion, fear or terror.

At home

Art. 31(IV), second paragraph (added P.O. No. 99, 10 Dec 2019): causing harm, injury or death, unless proven otherwise, to someone who tries to enter or enters without right the property where the home or workplace is (including communal, ejido and small-holding land) of the defender, their family, 'comunidad afectiva' or anyone they must defend, or a place with property they must protect, is legitimate defence.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Guerrero No. 499, art. 31, fracción IV
IV. Legítima defensa como causa de justificación. Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad razonable de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de quien lo defienda; Existe defensa legítima propia al ejercicio del derecho de defenderse, al hecho de causar daño, lesión o privación de la vida, salvo prueba en contrario, a quien por cualquier medio trate de penetrar o se introduzca sin derecho al inmueble donde se encuentre el hogar o lugar de trabajo, incluidos inmuebles ubicados en bienes comunales, ejidales y de pequeña propiedad, del agente pasivo, víctima o víctimas, al de su familia, comunidad afectiva o a las de cualquier persona que tenga la obligación de defender. ... En los casos de agresiones provenientes de menores se evitará lesionar al agresor y sólo se ejercerá la defensa necesaria y proporcional ante ataques graves. La contravención a esta disposición será considerada un exceso en la legítima defensa conforme a lo dispuesto en el artículo 87 de este código;
Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Guerrero No. 499, art. 87 (reformed P.O. No. 99, 10 Dec 2019)
A quien incurra en exceso en los casos previstos en las fracciones V y VI del artículo 31 de este código, se le impondrá la cuarta parte de la pena o medida de seguridad correspondiente al delito de que se trate, siempre que con relación al exceso no se actualice otra causa de exclusión del delito. No se considerará exceso en la defensa legítima propia, cuando concurran circunstancias en las que la persona que se defiende se encuentre en estado de confusión, miedo o terror, que afecte su capacidad para determinar el límite adecuado de su respuesta o racionalidad de los medios empleados para defenderse.
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 814826 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA. EVITABILIDAD DEL PELIGRO), Informe 1940, p. 42

b5d9171988226fcb.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Chiapas

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Chiapas's Penal Code (art. 25(B)(II)) lists legitimate defence as a justification: a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary, the means are rational and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. 'Rational means' is defined as the least harmful one, or the least harmful use of it when only one means is available; the code does not mention retreating or fleeing. Home intruders are presumed to be lawful targets unless shown otherwise. Excess exists when the defender needlessly prolongs the justified conduct, keeps going with non-rational means, or causes unnecessary or irrational harm (art. 27), and is punished with between the minimum and half the maximum penalty for the offence (art. 95). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 25(B)(II) presumes legitimate defence, unless proven otherwise, when harm is caused to someone who by any means tries to enter or enters without right the place where the defender, their family or anyone they must defend lives (temporarily or permanently), or the defender's outbuildings or a place holding property they must protect; the same applies to harm caused to an intruder surprised there in circumstances revealing a probable attack.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Chiapas, art. 25, apartado B, fracc. II
II.- Legítima defensa.- En defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, repela una agresión real, actual o inminente realizada sin derecho, siempre que exista la necesidad de la defensa, se utilicen medios racionales y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de la persona que se defiende. Se entenderá por medio racional, el menos dañoso o el uso menos dañoso, del mismo, cuando únicamente se disponga de un medio de defensa. Se presumirá como defensa legítima, salvo prueba en contrario, la causación de un daño a quien por cualquier medio trate de penetrar o penetre sin derecho al lugar en que habite de manera temporal o permanente la persona que se defiende, su familia, o cualquier otra persona cuyos derechos y bienes jurídicos tutelados, el agente tenga obligación de defender, o bien en las mismas circunstancias trate de penetrar o penetre a las dependencias del agente, al sitio en donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que tenga la misma obligación de defensa. Igual presunción existirá cuando el daño se cause a un intruso, al momento de sorprenderlo en alguno de los lugares antes citados, en circunstancias tales que revelen la probabilidad de una agresión.
Código Penal para el Estado de Chiapas, arts. 27 and 95
Artículo 27.- Exceso.- Existe exceso, cuando el sujeto activo en los supuestos de la fracción III, del apartado A, y fracciones II y III, del apartado B, prolonga innecesariamente la conducta típica que originalmente fue justificada, o continúa la conducta justificada haciendo uso de medios no racionales, o genere en el pasivo un daño innecesario o irracional. [...] Artículo 95.- Al que incurra en exceso en la legítima defensa, estado de necesidad justificante, en el cumplimiento de un deber o en el ejercicio de un derecho, se le impondrá del mínimo hasta la mitad de la pena máxima o medidas de seguridad que correspondan al delito de que se trate.

5f06416a8b31bd86.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Albania

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 19 of the Criminal Code (Law No. 7895 of 1995) says a person bears no criminal liability for an act done when 'compelled' to defend the life, health, rights or interests of himself or another against an unjust, real and immediate attack, provided the defence is proportionate to the danger of the attack; an obvious mismatch between them is an excess of the limits of necessary defence. The code does not mention retreat, and no court ruling on retreat was found; by contrast, the necessity defence (article 20) covers only harm that is unavoidable by other means. Killing while exceeding the limits of necessary defence is a separate offence (article 83) punished by up to seven years in prison.

What the law says
Kodi Penal i Republikës së Shqipërisë (Law No. 7895, 27.1.1995, as amended), neni 19
Nuk ka përgjegjësi penale personi që ka kryer veprën duke qenë i detyruar të mbrojë jetën, shëndetin, të drejtat dhe interesat e tij ose të një tjetri, nga një sulm i padrejtë, i vërtetë dhe i çastit me kusht që, karakteri i mbrojtjes të jetë në proporcion me rrezikshmërinë e sulmit. Mospërputhja haptazi ndërmjet tyre përbën kapërcim të kufijve të mbrojtjes së nevojshme.
Kodi Penal, neni 20 (necessity, for contrast)
Nuk ka përgjegjësi penale personi që ka kryer veprën nga nevoja për të përballuar një rrezik real dhe të çastit që e kërcënon atë, një person tjetër apo pasurinë nga një dëmtim i rëndë dhe i pashmangshëm me mënyra të tjera, me kusht që të mos jetë i provokuar prej tij dhe dëmi i shkaktuar të mos jetë më i madh së dëmi i zmbrapsur.
Kodi Penal, neni 83
Vrasja e kryer në kushtet e kapërcimit të kufijve të mbrojtjes së nevojshme dënohet me burgim gjer në shtatë vjet.

b18f0b5eb6ada258.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Federated States of Micronesia

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The national criminal code (Title 11 FSMC) has no self-defence section; the rule comes from FSM Supreme Court decisions annotated in the Code. Deadly force is allowed if necessary against imminent serious harm or death, and force must be reasonable in light of the aggressor's force (Alik v. Kosrae, 1994); a person may use no more force than necessary against an intruder (FSM v. Ruben, 1981; Tosie v. FSM, 1991). The annotations, re-checked in this run, never mention retreat or escape. The four state codes were checked: none has a self-defence section (Pohnpei's chapter on justification is marked 'Reserved').

At home

Reasonable force to protect oneself, family, home and property from an intruder and to expel the intruder (FSM v. Ruben, 1981; Tosie v. FSM, 1991).

What the law says
Title 11 FSMC, Chapter 1, case annotations — Alik v. Kosrae, 6 FSM Intrm. 469, 473 (App. 1994)
There are two different standards used when reviewing a claim of self-defense. When one is threatened with imminent serious bodily harm or death by another he may justifiably use deadly force if necessary to protect himself from great bodily harm or death.

1f5ae901cda80b50.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Slovakia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Section 25 of the Slovak Criminal Code (Act 300/2005) says an act done to avert an impending or ongoing attack on an interest protected by the Code is not a crime. Self-defence is excluded only if the intensity of the defence 'clearly exceeds' the intensity of the attack, judged by the manner, place and time of the attack and the circumstances of attacker and defender. The statute says nothing about retreat; a Slovak legal article on necessity contrasts the two defences, explaining that under necessity (§ 24) the danger must not be avertable in another way, so the defender would first have to try to avoid it, whereas self-defence carries no such requirement. A person who exceeds the limits is not criminally liable if they acted in intense agitation caused by the attack, such as confusion, fear or fright. The English text quoted is the 2010 version in a university database; the current official text could not be opened to check later changes.

What the law says
Criminal Code (Trestný zákon, Act 300/2005), Section 25 (English translation, 2010 version)
(1) An act, which otherwise gives rise to criminal liability, shall not be considered as a criminal offence if it is performed in order to avert an impending or actual attack on an interest protected under this Act. (2) Necessary self-defence shall not be invoked if the intensity of defence clearly exceeds the intensity of an attack, in particular in view of the mode, place, time of an attack, the circumstances related to an assailant or a defender. (3) Any person who averts an attack in a manner referred to in paragraph 2 shall not be held criminally liable if he acted in a state of intense agitation caused by an attack, in particular as a consequence of confusion, fear or fright.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

af8d1484eeb1f520.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

San Luis Potosí

Part of Mexico, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Código Penal del Estado de San Luis Potosí, art. 28(IV): a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack if the defence used is necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. No avoidance or 'no other means' condition appears in the article, and it does not say the defender need not flee. National Supreme Court (SCJN) theses point both ways: a 1940 thesis (registro 814826) says flight should not be imposed as a condition, while a 1946 thesis (registro 806596) denied the defence where the accused 'could well have avoided the aggression by other means'. No state-specific thesis was found (web search budget ran out), so whether retreat is required is not settled. Excess (art. 89, reformed P.O. 14 May 2026) is punished with one quarter of the penalty; since 14 May 2026 it is not excess for a woman facing physical, sexual or femicidal violence who acted in fear, terror or confusion.

At home

Art. 28(IV) presumes legítima defensa, unless proven otherwise, when harm is caused to someone who by any means tries to break into, or breaks into, without right the place where the defender lives temporarily or permanently, their family's or that of anyone they must defend, outbuildings or a place with property they must protect; and to an intruder surprised there in circumstances showing a possible attack. a762085a606e89c2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

French Guiana

An overseas region of France, part of France itself. Shown with the entry for France, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 122-5 of the Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. The defence must be simultaneous with the attack; a blow struck after the attacker has left is treated as ordinary violence. Neither art. 122-5 nor art. 122-6 mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Judges decide whether the defence was disproportionate; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes that an excessive response may lead to mitigating circumstances or a conviction for a lesser offence rather than full exoneration.

At home

Art. 122-6 of the Penal Code presumes self-defence for a person who acts "to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place", and against perpetrators of violent theft or looting. The presumption is rebuttable and does not cover daytime intrusions, which fall under the general rule of art. 122-5.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

2d0f303f351a4899.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Northern Ireland

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Northern Ireland has its own criminal law but shares much of England's approach. Self-defence is a common-law defence: force is lawful if it was necessary and reasonable, judged on the facts as the defendant honestly believed them to be, and section 76 of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 (which extends to Northern Ireland) says force is not reasonable if it was disproportionate. There is no duty to retreat, but this comes from the courts, not statute: the Northern Ireland Crown Court Bench Book tells judges that failing to retreat when it was possible and safe 'is not conclusive' and is 'simply a factor' (citing R v Bird). The statutory wording in s. 76(6A) that retreat is only a factor, and the 2013 householder rule, apply only in England and Wales. If the force was unreasonable, the bench book directs that it 'would not be lawful'; no partial 'excessive self-defence' verdict appears in the sources opened.

At home

No special householder rule applies: the 'grossly disproportionate' test for householders in section 76(5A) of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 is marked on the official text as extending to England and Wales only, so in Northern Ireland the ordinary rule that disproportionate force is unreasonable (s. 76(6)) applies inside the home too.

What the law says
Northern Ireland Crown Court Bench Book (3rd ed. 2010), 5.8 Self-defence, note (3)
Failure to retreat when attacked and when it is possible and safe to do so, is not conclusive. It is simply a factor to be taken into account in deciding whether it was necessary for the defendant to use force and whether the force used was reasonable. It is not necessary that the defendant should demonstrate by his actions that he does not want to fight (see Bird 81 Cr.App.R.110).
Northern Ireland Crown Court Bench Book, 5.8 Self-defence (specimen direction)
A man acts in lawful self-defence if it is necessary for him to defend himself, and the amount of force used in self defence is reasonable. ... If the amount of force used was unreasonable it would not be lawful. Force used in self-defence would be unreasonable if it was out of proportion to the nature of the attack or if it was in excess of what was really required of the defendant to defend himself.
Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s. 76(3), (6) (extent E+W+N.I.; subsections (5A) and (6A) extent E+W only)
(3) The question whether the degree of force used by D was reasonable in the circumstances is to be decided by reference to the circumstances as D believed them to be ... (6) [In a case other than a householder case,] the degree of force used by D is not to be regarded as having been reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them to be if it was disproportionate in those circumstances.
Criminal Law Act (Northern Ireland) 1967, s. 3(1)
A person may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances in the prevention of crime, or in effecting or assisting in the lawful arrest of offenders or suspected offenders or of persons unlawfully at large.

0327b87bfb694bc5.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Campeche

Part of Mexico, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Código Penal del Estado de Campeche, art. 33(B)(II): a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack if the defence used is necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. No avoidance or 'no other means' condition appears in the article, and it does not say the defender need not flee. National Supreme Court (SCJN) theses point both ways: a 1940 thesis (registro 814826) says flight should not be imposed as a condition, while a 1946 thesis (registro 806596) denied the defence where the accused 'could well have avoided the aggression by other means'. No state-specific thesis was found (web search budget ran out), so whether retreat is required is not settled. Excess (art. 91 Bis) is punished under art. 90 and may still be treated as intentional; it is not excess for a woman victim of physical, sexual or femicidal violence acting in fear, terror or confusion.

At home

Art. 33(B)(II) presumes the requirements are met for whoever harms someone trying to enter, by violence, climbing or any means, their home or outbuildings, their family's, or a place holding property they must protect, or whom they find there in circumstances showing a possible attack. A further paragraph presumes legítima defensa for a woman in imminent danger of physical or sexual violence, attempted homicide or femicide, and for a third person helping her.

What the law says
Código Penal del Estado de Campeche, art. 33, apartado B, fracción II
II. Legítima defensa: Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. Se presumirá que concurren los requisitos de la legítima defensa, respecto de aquél que cause un daño, a quien a través de la violencia, del escalamiento o por cualquier otro medio trate de penetrar sin derecho, a su hogar o sus dependencias, a los de su familia o los de cualquier persona que tenga el mismo deber de defender o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos de los que tenga la misma obligación; o bien, cuando lo encuentre en alguno de esos lugares, en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión; Se considerará que actúa en legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, cuando al momento de desplegar la conducta: a) La mujer sea o se encuentre en inminente peligro de ser víctima de violencia física, sexual, tentativa de homicidio o feminicidio; o b) Una tercera persona actúe en auxilio inmediato de la mujer, ante una agresión de la misma naturaleza.
Código Penal del Estado de Campeche, art. 91 Bis
ARTÍCULO 91 Bis.- La persona que incurra en exceso respecto de alguna causa de justificación será sancionada conforme a lo previsto en el artículo 90 de este Código, sin perjuicio de que el hecho se atribuya como realizado con dolo. No se considerará que existe exceso en los casos de legítima defensa ejercida por una mujer, cuando ésta haya sido víctima de violencia física, sexual o feminicida, o se haya encontrado en peligro inminente de serlo, y al momento de los hechos acredite haber actuado bajo un estado de miedo, terror o confusión que le haya impedido valorar adecuadamente los límites de su respuesta o la racionalidad de los medios empleados.
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 814826 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA. EVITABILIDAD DEL PELIGRO), Informe 1940, p. 42
no debe imponerse como condición al injustamente agredido la posibilidad de la fuga, pues en esas condiciones el ejercicio de la legítima defensa se tornaría en imposible en la mayoría de los casos
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 806596 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA), S.J.F. Tomo LXXXVIII, p. 721 (1946)
no puede aceptarse la defensa legítima, si el procesado no estuvo en inminente peligro de perder la vida o en condiciones de suponer este peligro, y pudo muy bien evitar la agresión de que fue víctima por otros medios, o en último extremo, preverla.
What was tried

Current state code opened (see sources). For case law: opened SCJN theses 814826 and 806596 via sdv.com.mx (secondary reproduction); sjf2.scjn.gob.mx and legislacion.scjn.gob.mx are JavaScript apps not readable by direct download; no further searching was possible (session search limit reached).

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. d6d1d00271b39b09.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kentucky

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Kentucky allows deadly force when the defendant believes it is necessary to protect against death, serious physical injury, kidnapping, sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat, a felony involving the use of force, or in the home-intrusion situations covered by § 503.055 (Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.050(2)). Since 2006 Ky. Acts ch. 192 (effective 12 July 2006), 'a person does not have a duty to retreat prior to the use of deadly physical force' (§ 503.050(4)), and a person not engaged in unlawful activity who is attacked in any place where they have a right to be may stand their ground and meet force with force, including deadly force, to prevent death, great bodily harm or a violent felony (§ 503.055(3)). The same 2006 Act created the home, residence and occupied-vehicle presumption of reasonable fear (§ 503.055). Force is not justified to resist a known arrest by an officer using reasonable force (even if the arrest is unlawful), by someone who provoked the other intending to kill or seriously injure, or by an initial aggressor, unless their first force was non-deadly and the response put them in imminent deadly danger, or they withdrew and clearly communicated it (§ 503.060). A person who used permitted force is immune from criminal prosecution (including arrest, detention and charging) and civil action, except against an identified or recognisable on-duty peace officer; police may not arrest without probable cause that the force was unlawful, and a court must award fees, costs and lost income to a civil defendant found immune (§ 503.085). If the defendant's belief in the need for force was wanton or reckless, the justification is unavailable for offences requiring only wantonness or recklessness, such as second-degree manslaughter or reckless homicide (§ 503.120(1)).

At home

Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.055(1) (2006): a person is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent death or great bodily harm when using deadly force against someone who was unlawfully and forcibly entering (or had entered) a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle, or was removing someone from it, if the person knew or had reason to believe that was happening; and an unlawful forcible intruder is presumed to intend violence (§ 503.055(4)). The presumption does not apply against another lawful resident with no domestic-violence injunction or no-contact order, a parent or guardian taking their own child, an identified or recognisable peace officer on duty, or where the defender is engaged in unlawful activity.

What the law says
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.050(4)
A person does not have a duty to retreat prior to the use of deadly physical force.
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.055(3)
A person who is not engaged in an unlawful activity and who is attacked in any other place where he or she has a right to be has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground and meet force with force, including deadly force, if he or she reasonably believes it is necessary to do so to prevent death or great bodily harm to himself or herself or another or to prevent the commission of a felony involving the use of force.
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.055(1)
A person is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or great bodily harm to himself or herself or another when using defensive force that is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm to another if: (a) The person against whom the defensive force was used was in the process of unlawfully and forcibly entering or had unlawfully and forcibly entered a dwelling, residence, or occupied vehicle ...
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.060(2)–(3)
the use of physical force by a defendant upon another person is not justifiable when: ... (2) The defendant, with the intention of causing death or serious physical injury to the other person, provokes the use of physical force by such other person; or (3) The defendant was the initial aggressor, except that ...
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.085(1)
A person who uses force as permitted in KRS 503.050, 503.055, 503.070, and 503.080 is justified in using such force and is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of such force ... As used in this subsection, the term "criminal prosecution" includes arresting, detaining in custody, and charging or prosecuting the defendant.
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.120(1)
but the defendant is wanton or reckless in believing the use of any force, or the degree of force used, to be necessary ... the justification afforded by those sections is unavailable in a prosecution for an offense for which wantonness or recklessness, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.

87bf943f5ef5d83d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Crimea

Part of Ukraine, occupied and annexed by Russia since 2014, which applies its own criminal code there (see Russia). Shown with the entry for Ukraine, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 36 of Ukraine's Criminal Code allows 'necessary defence' of one's own or another's rights, or public or state interests, by causing the harm that is necessary and sufficient to avert or stop an attack. The code states that every person has this right 'notwithstanding any possibility to avoid' the attack or to ask others or the authorities for help, so there is no duty to retreat. Excess of necessary defence means intentionally causing grave harm that is not adequate to the danger, and it is punishable only under two specific lighter offences (Articles 118 and 124, killing or grave injury in excess of defence); there is no liability if high excitement prevented the person judging proportionality. Using weapons against an armed attacker, a group, or a violent intrusion into a home is never treated as excess. The English text quoted is the 2010 version held in a university database; the official Ukrainian site could not be reached to check later amendments.

At home

Article 36(5): using weapons or other means to avert an unlawful violent intrusion into a dwelling or other premises is not treated as excess of necessary defence and carries no criminal liability, whatever the harm caused to the intruder.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Ukraine, Article 36 (English translation, 2010 version)
1. The necessary defense shall mean actions taken to defend the legally protected rights and interests of the defending person or another person, and also public interests and interests of the state, against a socially dangerous trespass, by inflicting such harm upon the trespasser as is necessary and sufficient in a given situation to immediately avert or stop the trespass, provided the limits of the necessary defense are not exceeded. 2. Every person shall have the right to necessary defense notwithstanding any possibility to avoid a socially dangerous trespass or request assistance of other persons or authorities. 3. The excess of necessary defense shall mean an intended causing of a grievous harm to the trespasser, which is not adequate to the danger of the trespass or circumstances of the defense. The excess of necessary defense shall entail criminal liability only in cases specifically prescribed in Articles 118 and 124 of this Code. 4. A person shall not be subject to criminal liability where that person was not able, due to high excitement, to evaluate if the harm caused by that person was proportionate to the danger of the trespass or circumstances of defense. 5. The use of weapons or other means or things for protection against an attack of an armed person or an attack of a group of persons, and also to avert an unlawful violent intrusion upon a dwelling place or other premises, shall not be treated as the excess of necessary defense and shall not entail criminal liability irrespective of the gravity of harm caused to the trespasser.

5fbada19e9f47a64.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Chihuahua

Part of Mexico, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Chihuahua's Penal Code (art. 28-IV) allows a person to repel a real, unlawful, current or imminent attack that creates an immediate danger, but only if the attack 'could not have been easily avoided', the means used were rationally necessary, the defender did not provoke it, and the threatened harm could not easily have been repaired later by legal means. This makes easy avoidance of the attack a written condition of self-defence, but the presumption for home intruders (including killing them) removes that test inside the dwelling unless proven otherwise. A further presumption covers a person who, before repelling the attack, was a victim of feminicidal violence by the attacker. Excess in self-defence is punished with one quarter of the penalty for the offence (art. 80). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 28-IV presumes the requirements of legitimate defence are met for anyone who harms, injures or kills a person who, by violence, climbing in or any other means, tries to enter without right their home or its outbuildings, those of their family or of anyone they must defend, or a place holding property they must protect; or who is found in such places in circumstances revealing a possible attack.

What the law says
Código Penal del Estado de Chihuahua, art. 28, fracc. IV
IV. (Legítima defensa). Se repela una agresión real, ilegítima, actual o inminente, protegiendo bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, de la cual resulte un peligro inmediato, siempre que no haya podido ser fácilmente evitada, exista necesidad racional del medio empleado para repelerla, no mediara provocación suficiente por parte del que se defiende o que el daño que iba a causar el agresor no hubiese podido ser fácilmente reparado después por medios legales. Se presumirá que concurren los requisitos de la legítima defensa, respecto de aquel que cause un daño, lesione o prive de la vida a alguien a quien a través de la violencia, del escalamiento o por cualquier otro medio trate de penetrar sin derecho, a su hogar o sus dependencias, a los de su familia, o los de cualquier persona que tenga el mismo deber de defender, o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos de los que tenga la misma obligación; o bien, cuando lo encuentre en alguno de esos lugares, en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión. También se presumirá legítima defensa, cuando antes de repeler la agresión, fuese víctima de violencia feminicida por parte de la persona agresora.
Código Penal del Estado de Chihuahua, art. 80
Al que incurra en exceso, en los casos previstos en las fracciones IV, V y VI del artículo 28 de este Código, se le impondrá la cuarta parte de las penas o medidas de seguridad, correspondientes al delito de que se trate.

843f80d73e8dc18c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Hawaii

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Hawaii's 1972 penal code (L 1972, c 9), which follows the Model Penal Code, allows deadly force when the actor believes it is necessary to protect themselves against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping, rape or forcible sodomy (Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-304(2)). Hawaii keeps a duty to retreat: deadly force is not justified if the actor knows they can avoid the need for it with complete safety by retreating, by handing over property to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to refrain from something they have no duty to do (§ 703-304(5)(b)). There is no duty to retreat from one's dwelling or place of work, except for an initial aggressor or a person attacked at work by a co-worker; police and people lawfully assisting them need not give up an arrest. For non-deadly force there is no retreat requirement (§ 703-304(3)). Deadly force is also not justified if the actor provoked the use of force in the same encounter intending to cause death or serious injury, and force may not be used to resist a known arrest by an officer even if the arrest is unlawful (§ 703-304(4)–(5)). The test is the actor's own belief, but if that belief was reckless or negligent, the justification is not available for offences that need only recklessness or negligence, such as manslaughter or negligent homicide (§ 703-310). The section was last amended in 2001 (L 2001, c 91); the sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit.

At home

Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-304(5)(b)(i): the actor is not obliged to retreat from their dwelling or place of work, unless they were the initial aggressor or are attacked at work by a co-worker (someone whose place of work the actor knows it to be). There is no statutory presumption of reasonable fear for home intrusions.

What the law says
Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-304(5)
The use of deadly force is not justifiable under this section if: (a) The actor, with the intent of causing death or serious bodily injury, provoked the use of force against himself in the same encounter; or (b) The actor knows that he can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating or by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim of right thereto or by complying with a demand that he abstain from any action which he has no duty to take, except that: (i) The actor is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling or place of work, unless he was the initial aggressor or is assailed in his place of work by another person whose place of work the actor knows it to be ...
Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-304(2)
The use of deadly force is justifiable under this section if the actor believes that deadly force is necessary to protect himself against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping, rape, or forcible sodomy.
Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-310(1)
When the actor believes that the use of force ... is necessary ... but the actor is reckless or negligent in having such belief ..., the justification afforded by those sections is unavailable in a prosecution for an offense for which recklessness or negligence, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.

b18dce766e6dbbfc.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kaduna

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Kaduna re-enacted the Penal Code as the Kaduna State Penal Code Law, 2017, renumbering the private-defence sections: s. 25 limits defence to necessary harm, s. 26 says there is no right of private defence where there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities, and s. 28 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm and the other listed attacks. The wording matches the 1959 Penal Code ss. 62, 63 and 65. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases.

What the law says
Kaduna State Penal Code Law, 2017, ss. 25-26
25. The right of private defence in no case extends to the infliction of more harm than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 26. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Kaduna State Penal Code Law, 2017, s. 28 (opening words)
28. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 25 and 26 of this Law, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely: an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm; or
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Kaduna State Penal Code Law, 2017 (PolicyVault.Africa)
  • Sunday Jackson v The State, SC/CR/1026/2022, Supreme Court of Nigeria, 7 March 2025 (certified true copy, 62 pp., scanned; text obtained by OCR) (CITY LAWYER Magazine (hosting the certified copy, watermarked TheNigeriaLawyer))
  • Sunday Jackson v The State (2025-03) Legalpedia 85898 (SC) - summary (Legalpedia)
  • Laoye v The State, SC 200/1984, 25 October 1985, [1985] 2 N.S.C.C. 1251 (headnote) (vLex Nigeria)
  • Notes on the Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), Second Edition 1963, annotated by S. S. Richardson (reproduces the code text with commentary) (anticor.world (scan of the 1963 Government Printer edition))
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

0de105e5985719f1.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Slovenia

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Article 22 of the Slovenian Criminal Code (KZ-1) says an act committed in self-defence (silobran) is not unlawful, where the defence is 'absolutely necessary' (nujno potrebna) to repel a simultaneous unlawful attack on oneself or another; the code does not mention retreat. Slovenian appellate courts treat the possibility of withdrawing as part of that necessity test. A Tax-Fin-Lex case-law summary of the Celje Higher Court decision Kp 277/99 says the court found the accused did not act in self-defence 'because he could have avoided the attack by withdrawing, instead of using force (throwing a stone)'. In 2026 the Maribor Higher Court, upholding the acquittal of Irena Tihec for the killing of her husband (reported by N1/Večer, 1 June 2026), stressed that everyone has the right to defend their life and found that she 'had no realistic possibility of retreat'; it rejected the prosecution's argument that she could have fled, and, referring to Supreme Court case law, held her defence 'absolutely necessary or unavoidable and, given the intensity of the attack, proportionate'. So the sources show courts asking whether the defender could safely have withdrawn before accepting self-defence; this rests on two Higher Court rulings (one via a database summary, one via press), not on a Supreme Court statement of a general rule. Exceeding the limits may lead to a lighter sentence, which may be waived if the excess came from strong agitation or fright caused by the attack (art. 22(3)).

What the law says
Kazenski zakonik (KZ-1), 22. člen
(1) Dejanje, ki je storjeno v silobranu, ni protipravno. (2) Silobran je obramba, ki je nujno potrebna, da storilec odvrne od sebe ali koga drugega istočasen protipraven napad. [Our rendering: (1) An act committed in self-defence is not unlawful. (2) Self-defence is the defence that is absolutely necessary for the perpetrator to repel a simultaneous unlawful attack on himself or on another.]
VSC sodba Kp 277/99 (Višje sodišče v Celju), as summarised by Tax-Fin-Lex
Sodišče je ocenilo, da obdolženec ni ravnal v silobranu, saj se je napadu lahko izognil z umikom, namesto da bi uporabil silo (metanje kamna). [Our rendering: The court held that the accused did not act in self-defence, since he could have avoided the attack by withdrawing, instead of using force (throwing a stone).]
Višje sodišče v Mariboru, confirmation of acquittal of Irena Tihec (as reported by N1 Slovenija, 1 June 2026, citing Večer)
Višje sodišče je po poročanju Večera poudarilo, da ima vsakdo pravico braniti svoje življenje, ter ocenilo, da Irena Tihec pred napadom moža Aleša Tihca ni imela realne možnosti umika. [...] Senat višjih sodnic je zavrnil trditev tožilstva, da Irena Tihec ni bila resno ogrožena oziroma da bi lahko pobegnila. Ocenil je, da se je znašla v brezizhodnem položaju in da je bila njena obramba nujna. Prav tako ni sledilo očitku, da je bil odziv z nožem nesorazmeren. Sklicevalo se je na sodno prakso vrhovnega sodišča in pritrdilo ugotovitvi, da je bila obramba "nujno potrebna oziroma neizogibna ter glede na intenziteto napada pokojnega tudi sorazmerna" [Our rendering: According to Večer, the Higher Court stressed that everyone has the right to defend their life, and found that Irena Tihec had no realistic possibility of retreat from her husband's attack. [...] The panel of higher-court judges rejected the prosecution's claim that she was not seriously endangered or that she could have fled. It found she was in a hopeless position and her defence was necessary. Nor did it accept the complaint that the response with a knife was disproportionate. It referred to Supreme Court case law and confirmed the finding that the defence was 'absolutely necessary or unavoidable and, given the intensity of the deceased's attack, also proportionate'.]
