bdfb4ecebb09cee7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Rivers

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • Agbonmwanre Omoregie v The State, SC 301/2006, 19 December 2008, (2008-12) Legalpedia (SC) 18215 (summary) (Legalpedia)
  • Emmanuel Ogar Akong Edoko v The State, SC.315/2012, 27 February 2015 (summary; Cross River, Criminal Code s. 286) (Legalpedia)
  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

b118bc3c4159bef3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cabo Verde

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Cabo Verde's Penal Code (2003) defines legitimate defence as an act carried out 'as a necessary means' to repel a current and unlawful attack on legally protected and relevant interests of the defender or another person. The code does not mention retreat or a duty to flee; the test is whether the means used were necessary. Its explanatory preamble says the 'relevant interests' wording was chosen so that very minor or insignificant attacks do not justify defensive harm. If the defender used excessive means the act stays unlawful but the penalty can be freely reduced (art. 37), and a person who exceeded the means because of non-blameworthy disturbance, fear or fright acts without guilt (art. 41). No specific home-defence rule was found.

What the law says
Código Penal (2003), art. 36 (Legítima defesa)
Constitui legítima defesa o facto praticado como meio necessário para afastar a agressão actual e ilícita de interesses juridicamente protegidos e relevantes do agente ou de terceiro.
Código Penal (2003), art. 37 (Excesso de legítima defesa)
Não é excluída a ilicitude do facto, se houver excesso dos meios utilizados pelo defendente, mas a pena pode ser livremente atenuada, nos termos e com os limites referidos no n.º 2 do artigo 22.º.
Código Penal (2003), art. 41 (Excesso de legítima defesa não censurável)
Age sem culpa quem se exceder nos meios empregados em legítima defesa, em virtude de perturbação, medo ou susto não censuráveis.

c846c371ff45cb77.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Guatemala

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 24(1) of the Penal Code, a person who defends their own or another's person, property or rights is justified if there is an unlawful aggression, "rational necessity of the means used" to prevent or repel it, and no sufficient provocation by the defender. The Code does not mention retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. The no-provocation requirement is waived for defence of close relatives, a spouse or partner, parents or adopted children, if the defender took no part in the provocation. Rules on excessive defence were not found in the source opened.

At home

Art. 24(1) deems all three conditions of self-defence to be met for a person who repels someone trying to enter, or who has entered, another's dwelling or its outbuildings, if that person's conduct shows an imminent danger to the life, property or rights of the occupants.

What the law says
Código Penal (Decreto 17-73), art. 24(1)
Son causas de justificación: Legítima defensa 1º. Quien obra en defensa de su persona, bienes o derechos, o en defensa de la persona, bienes o derechos de otra, siempre que concurran las circunstancias siguientes: a) Agresión ilegítima; b) Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla; c) Falta de provocación suficiente por parte del defensor. Se entenderá que concurren estas tres circunstancias respecto de aquel que rechaza al que pretenda entrar o haya entrado en morada ajena o en sus dependencias, si su actitud denota la inminencia de un peligro para la vida, bienes o derechos de los moradores. El requisito previsto en el literal c) no es necesario cuando se trata de la defensa de sus parientes dentro de los grados de ley, de su cónyuge o concubinario, de sus padres o hijos adoptivos, siempre que el defensor no haya tomado parte en la provocación.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

c7599d6cccc2f3a9.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Illinois

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

720 ILCS 5/7-1(a) allows force when a person reasonably believes it necessary to defend against the imminent use of unlawful force, and deadly force only to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm or a forcible felony; the section does not use the word 'retreat'. The no-retreat rule is judicial. The Illinois Supreme Court Committee's pattern instruction IPI Criminal 24-25.09X ('Non-Initial Aggressor—No Duty To Retreat') tells juries: 'A person who has not initially provoked the use of force against himself has no duty to attempt to escape the danger before using force against the aggressor', citing People v. Hughes, 46 Ill. App. 3d 490 (1st Dist. 1977), and People v. Miller, 259 Ill. App. 3d 257 (1st Dist. 1994). In Hughes the appellate court said that the rule that one who is first assaulted 'has a right to stand his ground and has no duty to retreat before defending himself' has been the law in Illinois since 1902, while holding that only one who is first assaulted has that right. An initial aggressor may use deadly force only after exhausting every reasonable means of escape, or after withdrawing in good faith (720 ILCS 5/7-4; IPI 24-25.09). Since P.A. 93-832 (2004) a person using justified force cannot be sued by the aggressor or the aggressor's family unless the force involved willful or wanton misconduct (§ 7-1(b)).

At home

720 ILCS 5/7-2 (defence of dwelling), as set out in IPI Criminal 24-25.07: force to prevent or end an unlawful entry into or attack on a dwelling; deadly force if the entry is violent, riotous or tumultuous and the person reasonably believes it necessary to prevent an assault on someone inside, or to prevent a felony in the dwelling. No statutory presumption of reasonable fear.

What the law says
Illinois Pattern Jury Instructions – Criminal, No. 24-25.09X Non-Initial Aggressor—No Duty To Retreat, with Committee Note
24-25.09X Non-Initial Aggressor--No Duty To Retreat. A person who has not initially provoked the use of force against himself has no duty to attempt to escape the danger before using force against the aggressor. Committee Note: See People v. Hughes, 46 Ill.App.3d 490, 360 N.E.2d 1363, 4 Ill.Dec. 930 (1st Dist.1977); People v. Miller, 259 Ill.App.3d 257, 630 N.E.2d 1125, 197 Ill.Dec. 1 (1st Dist. 1994). ... In appropriate cases, both instruction 24-25.09 and 24-25.09X should be given.
People v. Hughes, 46 Ill. App. 3d 490 (1st Dist. March 2, 1977)
Defendant further contends that his fourth instruction refused by the trial court indicates that one who is first assaulted has a right to stand his ground and has no duty to retreat before defending himself and was improperly refused by the trial court. It is true, as defendant contends, that no instruction was given on this point. It is also true, and acknowledged by the State, that such has been the law in Illinois since 1902. (People v. Harris (1970), 124 Ill. App. 2d 234, 260 N.E.2d 325.) However, nowhere does defendant's proffered instruction on the above point mention that only one who is first assaulted has no duty to retreat. As such, defendant's instruction did not accurately state the law.
720 ILCS 5/7-1(a) Use of force in defense of person (Source: P.A. 93-832, eff. 7-28-04)
A person is justified in the use of force against another when and to the extent that he reasonably believes that such conduct is necessary to defend himself or another against such other's imminent use of unlawful force. However, he is justified in the use of force which is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm only if he reasonably believes that such force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to himself or another, or the commission of a forcible felony.

  • People v. Hughes, 46 Ill. App. 3d 490 (1977), full text (Caselaw Access Project, Harvard Law School Library)

b9d05567b4af1978.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Gambia

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The current text of The Gambia's Criminal Code on self-defence could not be opened. The Criminal Offences Bill, 2020, published by the National Assembly to revise and consolidate criminal law, provides in section 17 that criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property is to be decided by the principles of English common law, subject to any express provisions. Whether that bill has been enacted, and how Gambian courts treat retreat, could not be confirmed from the sources found.

What the law says
Criminal Offences Bill, 2020 (The Gambia), s. 17 (as summarised from the National Assembly copy; full wording not captured)
... criminal responsibility for the use of force in the defence of person or property shall be determined according to the principles of English Common Law.

6f90e36bf84441ba.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

West Virginia

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

West Virginia's stand-your-ground and castle rules are written in W. Va. Code § 55-7-22, a section placed in the civil-actions chapter (first enacted by HB 4658 in 2004 and amended by SB 145 in 2008). In the home or residence, a lawful occupant may use reasonable and proportionate force, including deadly force, against an intruder to prevent or end a forcible entry when they reasonably fear death or serious harm or reasonably believe the intruder means to commit a felony, and has no duty to retreat. Outside the home, a person not engaged in unlawful activity who is attacked anywhere they have a legal right to be may use deadly force 'without a duty to retreat' if they reasonably believe they or another are in imminent danger of death or serious bodily harm that only deadly force can prevent. The force must be 'reasonable and proportionate'. Justified force is a full and complete defence to any civil suit by the intruder or attacker, but that defence is not available to someone committing or escaping a felony, someone who provoked force as an excuse to injure, or an initial aggressor who did not clearly withdraw. The section does not authorise resisting a police officer or setting traps on property. Because the section sits in the civil code, its exact effect in criminal prosecutions (where West Virginia's common law also applies) was not confirmed from a criminal case or jury instruction for this entry. No statutory presumption of reasonable fear or pretrial criminal immunity hearing was found; the bill history page lists a 2024 bill (HB 5621) touching the section, whose outcome was not checked.

At home

A lawful occupant of a home or other residence may use reasonable and proportionate force, including deadly force, to prevent or end a forcible unlawful entry if they reasonably fear death or serious harm to anyone inside, or reasonably believe the intruder intends a felony there and that deadly force is necessary; there is no duty to retreat from the intruder (W. Va. Code § 55-7-22(a)-(b), enacted 2004, amended 2008).

What the law says
W. Va. Code § 55-7-22(c)
A person not engaged in unlawful activity who is attacked in any place he or she has a legal right to be outside of his or her home or residence may use reasonable and proportionate force against an intruder or attacker: Provided, That such person may use deadly force against an intruder or attacker in a place that is not his or her residence without a duty to retreat if the person reasonably believes that he or she or another is in imminent danger of death or serious bodily harm from which he or she or another can only be saved by the use of deadly force against the intruder or attacker.
W. Va. Code § 55-7-22(a)-(b) (home)
(b) A lawful occupant within a home or other place of residence does not have a duty to retreat from an intruder or attacker in the circumstances described in subsection (a) of this section.
W. Va. Code § 55-7-22(d)-(e) (civil defence and limits)
(d) The justified use of reasonable and proportionate force under this section shall constitute a full and complete defense to any civil action brought by an intruder or attacker against a person using such force. (e) The full and complete civil defense created by the provisions of this section is not available to a person who: (1) Is attempting to commit, committing or escaping from the commission of a felony; (2) Initially provokes the use of force against himself herself or another with the intent to use such force as an excuse to inflict bodily harm upon the assailant ...

eb1153b9ad959301.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Minnesota

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Minn. Stat. § 609.065 ('Justifiable taking of life', last amended 1986) allows an intentional killing only 'when necessary' to resist an offence the actor reasonably believes exposes them or another to great bodily harm or death, or to prevent a felony in the actor's home; it says nothing about retreat. The duty comes from the courts. In State v. Glowacki, 630 N.W.2d 392 (Minn. 2001), the Minnesota Supreme Court said 'Generally, the law mandates a duty to retreat if reasonably possible when acting in self-defense', and held there is no duty to retreat from one's own home. In State v. Blevins, No. A22-0432 (Minn. July 31, 2024), the court restated that 'the absence of a reasonable possibility of retreat to avoid the danger' is one of four elements of self-defence under § 609.06, subd. 1(3) (citing State v. Basting, 1997), called the duty 'judicially created', and extended it to a person who only brandishes a dangerous weapon (felony second-degree assault-fear); the vote was 4–2. A later 2024 ruling, State v. Valdez, 121 N.W.3d 191 (Minn. 2024), reportedly held that a person defending someone else has no personal duty to retreat (that opinion was not opened here; only a news summary). Minnesota has no stand-your-ground statute.

At home

State v. Glowacki (Minn. 2001): no duty to retreat from one's own home when acting in self-defence there, whether the aggressor is an intruder or a co-resident. Minn. Stat. § 609.065 also permits a killing to prevent a felony in the actor's place of abode. No statutory presumption of reasonable fear.

What the law says
State v. Glowacki, 630 N.W.2d 392 (Minn. July 12, 2001)
Generally, the law mandates a duty to retreat if reasonably possible when acting in self-defense. Carothers, 594 N.W.2d at 899. However, in Carothers we held that when there is an intruder in one's home, there is no duty to retreat when acting either in defense of dwelling or in self-defense. ... Thus we adopt the following rule: There is no duty to retreat from one's own home when acting in self-defense in the home, regardless of whether the aggressor is a co-resident. But the lack of a duty to retreat does not abrogate the obligation to act reasonably when using force in self-defense.
State v. Blevins, No. A22-0432 (Minn. Sup. Ct., filed July 31, 2024), syllabus para. 1 and opinion
1. The duty to retreat when reasonably possible—a judicially created element of self-defense—applies to persons who claim they were acting in self-defense when they committed the felony offense of second-degree assault-fear with a device designed as a weapon and capable of producing death or great bodily harm. ... We have read section 609.06, subdivision 1(3), to include four elements: (1) [T]he absence of aggression or provocation on the part of the defendant; (2) the defendant's actual and honest belief that he or she was in imminent danger of . . . great bodily harm; (3) the existence of reasonable grounds for that belief; and (4) the absence of a reasonable possibility of retreat to avoid the danger. Basting, 572 N.W.2d at 285–86 (emphasis added). ... Accordingly, we hold that a person claiming self-defense has a duty to retreat when reasonably possible before committing the felony offense of second-degree assault-fear with a dangerous weapon, specifically, a device designed as a weapon and capable of producing death or great bodily harm.
CRIMJIG 7.08 (10 Minn. Dist. Judges Ass'n, Minnesota Practice—Jury Instruction Guides, Criminal, 4th ed. 1999), as quoted in Glowacki, footnote
The modified version of CRIMJIG 7.08, as given to the jury, read, "The legal excuse of self-defense is available only to those who act honestly and in good faith and this includes the duly to [retreat or] avoid the danger if reasonably possible." (Omitted words in brackets.)
Minn. Stat. § 609.065 Justifiable taking of life (History: 1963 c 753 art 1 s 609.065; 1978 c 736 s 1; 1986 c 444)
The intentional taking of the life of another is not authorized by section 609.06, except when necessary in resisting or preventing an offense which the actor reasonably believes exposes the actor or another to great bodily harm or death, or preventing the commission of a felony in the actor's place of abode.

f9c5d1b0d7db12be.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nayarit

Part of Mexico, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Código Penal para el Estado de Nayarit, art. 39(VI): a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack if the defence used is necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. No avoidance or 'no other means' condition appears in the article, and it does not say the defender need not flee. National Supreme Court (SCJN) theses point both ways: a 1940 thesis (registro 814826) says flight should not be imposed as a condition, while a 1946 thesis (registro 806596) denied the defence where the accused 'could well have avoided the aggression by other means'. No state-specific thesis was found (web search budget ran out), so whether retreat is required is not settled. Excess in fractions IV–VI of the same article is punished with one quarter of the penalty.

At home

Art. 39(VI), second paragraph (reformed P.O. 22 Nov 2019), presumes legítima defensa, unless proven otherwise, when any harm, injury or death is caused to someone who tries to enter or enters without right the place where the defender lives temporarily or permanently, their family's or that of anyone they must defend, outbuildings or a place with property they must protect; and to an intruder surprised in those places.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Nayarit, art. 39, fracción VI
VI. Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. (REFORMADO, P.O. 22 DE NOVIEMBRE DE 2019) Se presume que existe legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, cuando se cause cualquier daño, lesión o se prive de la vida, a quien por cualquier medio trate de penetrar o penetre, sin derecho, al lugar en que habite de forma temporal o permanente el que se defiende, al de su familia o al de cualquier persona respecto de las que el agente tenga la obligación de defender, a sus dependencias o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que exista la misma obligación. Igual presunción existirá cuando el daño, lesión o privación de la vida se cause a un intruso al momento de sorprenderlo en alguno de los lugares antes citados;
Código Penal para el Estado de Nayarit, art. 39 (paragraph on exceso, within the error/exceso provisions)
Al que incurra en exceso, en los casos previstos en las fracciones IV, V y VI de este artículo, se le impondrá la cuarta parte de las penas o medidas de seguridad, correspondientes al delito de que se trate, siempre y cuando con relación al exceso, no exista otra causa de exclusión del delito;
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 814826 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA. EVITABILIDAD DEL PELIGRO), Informe 1940, p. 42
no debe imponerse como condición al injustamente agredido la posibilidad de la fuga, pues en esas condiciones el ejercicio de la legítima defensa se tornaría en imposible en la mayoría de los casos
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 806596 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA), S.J.F. Tomo LXXXVIII, p. 721 (1946)
no puede aceptarse la defensa legítima, si el procesado no estuvo en inminente peligro de perder la vida o en condiciones de suponer este peligro, y pudo muy bien evitar la agresión de que fue víctima por otros medios, o en último extremo, preverla.
What was tried

Article number taken from the chapter heading 'ARTÍCULO 39.- El delito y la responsabilidad penal se excluyen cuando:'. The exceso paragraph refers to 'fracciones IV, V y VI de este artículo', while legítima defensa is fraction VI. Current state code opened (see sources). Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

1ee259bdeab6e8d7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kebbi

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.
Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963), on ss. 59-65
When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Zamfara Shari'a Penal Code 2000, s. 204(c), as reproduced in Peters (2001), Appendix Five
204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.

Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

52681488dbf4652d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bhutan

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Bhutan's Penal Code 2004 treats self-defence as a justification: force to protect oneself or a third person is allowed if it is the same or a lesser degree of force, the defendant believes it necessary, and it is no greater than necessary (s 95). Deadly force is justified only against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or rape, and not if the defendant provoked it with intent to kill or seriously injure, or knew how to or could avoid the need for deadly force by retreating, handing over property or complying with a demand (s 98). There is no duty to retreat from one's home or workplace except for an initial trespasser or someone attacked at work by another person (s 102). This is the 2004 English text; the 2011 and 2021 amendment Acts were not checked for changes to these sections.

At home

s 102: a defendant is not obliged to retreat from an abode or place of work, except when the defendant is the initial trespasser or is attacked at their place of work by another person.

What the law says
Penal Code of Bhutan 2004, s 95
A defendant shall have the defence of justification, when the defendant uses force upon or towards another person to protect the defendant or a third person if: (a) The defendant uses the same or a lesser degree of force to protect oneself or the third person; (b) The defendant believes that the force is necessary for the protection of oneself or the third person; and (c) The force used is no greater than that which is necessary.
Penal Code of Bhutan 2004, s 98
A defendant shall not have the defence of justification, if the defendant uses deadly force unless the defendant believes that the use of deadly force was necessary to protect the defendant or a third person from death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping, or rape except, if the defendant: (a) With the purpose of causing death or serious bodily injury, provoked the use of deadly force against the person; or (b) Knew how to or could avoid the necessity of using deadly force by retreating or by surrendering possession of a item or by complying with a demand that the defendant abstain from an action which is not a duty the defendant is bound to perform by law.
Penal Code of Bhutan 2004, s 102
A defendant is not obliged to retreat from an abode or place of work except: (a) When the defendant is the initial trespasser; or (b) The defendant is attacked in the defendant’s place of work by another person.

0ccc41d1358319b9.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Guanajuato

Part of Mexico, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Código Penal del Estado de Guanajuato, art. 33(V): the offence is excluded where a person acts in defence of their own or another's legal interests against an unlawful, current or imminent attack, provided the defence used to repel or prevent it is reasonably necessary. The text has no provocation clause and no avoidance or 'no other means' condition. No avoidance or 'no other means' condition appears in the article, and it does not say the defender need not flee. National Supreme Court (SCJN) theses point both ways: a 1940 thesis (registro 814826) says flight should not be imposed as a condition, while a 1946 thesis (registro 806596) denied the defence where the accused 'could well have avoided the aggression by other means'. No state-specific thesis was found (web search budget ran out), so whether retreat is required is not settled. Excess (art. 34) is punished with one third of the minimum to one third of the maximum penalty for the offence.

At home

Art. 33(V), second paragraph (added P.O. 24 Sep 2018): causing harm, unless proven otherwise, to someone who by violence, climbing or any other means tries to enter without right the defender's dwelling, their family's, outbuildings, those of anyone they must defend, or a place with property they must protect, or whom they find there in circumstances showing the probability of an attack, is presumed to be legitimate defence.

What the law says
Código Penal del Estado de Guanajuato, art. 33, fracción V
V. Se obre en defensa de bienes jurídicos, propios o ajenos, contra agresión ilegítima, actual o inminente, siempre que exista necesidad razonable de la defensa empleada para repelerla o impedirla; (ADICIONADO, P.O. 24 DE SEPTIEMBRE DE 2018) Se presumirá como legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, el hecho de causar daño a quien a través de la violencia, del escalamiento o por cualquier otro medio trate de penetrar sin derecho, a la casa habitación del agente, al de su familia, a sus dependencias, o a los de cualquier persona que tenga la obligación de defender, al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que exista la misma obligación; o bien, lo encuentre en alguno de aquellos lugares en circunstancias tales que revelen la probabilidad de una agresión;
Código Penal del Estado de Guanajuato, art. 34
Artículo 34.- A quien actúa justificadamente, en los términos de las fracciones III, IV, V y VI del artículo anterior, pero excede los límites impuestos por la ley o por la necesidad, se le aplicará de un tercio del mínimo a un tercio del máximo de la punibilidad señalada al tipo penal de que se trate.
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 814826 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA. EVITABILIDAD DEL PELIGRO), Informe 1940, p. 42
no debe imponerse como condición al injustamente agredido la posibilidad de la fuga, pues en esas condiciones el ejercicio de la legítima defensa se tornaría en imposible en la mayoría de los casos
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 806596 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA), S.J.F. Tomo LXXXVIII, p. 721 (1946)
no puede aceptarse la defensa legítima, si el procesado no estuvo en inminente peligro de perder la vida o en condiciones de suponer este peligro, y pudo muy bien evitar la agresión de que fue víctima por otros medios, o en último extremo, preverla.
What was tried

www.congresogto.gob.mx and congresogto.gob.mx: TLS failure / no response from direct download; the web reader refused (robots.txt); congresogto.s3.amazonaws.com returned 403; Wayback API rate-limited (429). The Congress compilation was found on the state judiciary site. Current state code opened (see sources). For case law: opened SCJN theses 814826 and 806596 via sdv.com.mx (secondary reproduction); sjf2.scjn.gob.mx and legislacion.scjn.gob.mx are JavaScript apps not readable by direct download; no further searching was possible (session search limit reached).

Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. 6863b107c98c7a17.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bauchi

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.
Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963), on ss. 59-65
When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Zamfara Shari'a Penal Code 2000, s. 204(c), as reproduced in Peters (2001), Appendix Five
204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.

520836bdb2a1cd03.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Israel

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Under Israel's Penal Law, 5737-1977, a person bears no criminal responsibility for an act that was immediately necessary to repel an unlawful attack posing a real danger of harm to their own or another's life, liberty, body or property, unless they brought on the attack by their own wrongful conduct while foreseeing how things might develop (s. 34J). The defence does not apply where the act was not reasonable in the circumstances for preventing the harm (s. 34P). The statute does not use the word retreat. An Israel Democracy Institute commentary (2024) says the Supreme Court has held that self-defence does not license weapon carriers to use them against someone who is not a clear and immediate danger to life. Hebrew legal literature treats retreat as part of the 'necessity' requirement (an article by Shai Akiva Wozner, 'Self-defence, the necessity requirement and the duty to retreat: on the margins of the Shai Dromi affair', Mehkarei Mishpat 27 (2011) 315, is cited on Hebrew Wikipedia), but that article and any Supreme Court ruling on retreat could not be opened in this pass, so the retreat question is left unsettled.

At home

Section 34J1, added in 2008 (known as the 'Dromi Law'), removes criminal responsibility for an act immediately necessary to repel someone breaking into or entering, or trying to, one's own or another's dwelling, business or fenced farm with intent to commit an offence, unless the act was 'clearly unreasonable' in the circumstances or the person's own wrongful conduct brought about the break-in while foreseeing it.

[Rendering by the researcher:] A person shall not bear criminal responsibility for an act that was immediately necessary to repel an unlawful attack that posed a real danger of harm to his life, liberty, body or property, or those of another; however, a person does not act in self-defence where by his wrongful conduct he brought about the attack while foreseeing the possible development of events.

(א) לא יישא אדם באחריות פלילית למעשה שהיה דרוש באופן מיידי כדי להדוף מי שמתפרץ או נכנס לבית המגורים, בית העסק או המשק החקלאי המגודר, שלו או של זולתו, בכוונה לבצע עבירה, או מי שמנסה להתפרץ או להיכנס כאמור. (ב) הוראת סעיף קטן (א) לא תחול אם – (1) המעשה היה לא סביר בעליל, בנסיבות העניין, לשם הדיפת המתפרץ או הנכנס; (2) האדם הביא בהתנהגותו הפסולה להתפרצות או לכניסה תוך שהוא צופה מראש את אפשרות התפתחות הדברים.

Israel Democracy Institute, Mirit Lavi and Amir Fuchs, 24 Jan 2024 (lead paragraph)
בית המשפט העליון קבע בעבר שעקרון ההגנה העצמית אינו נותן אישור לנושאי נשק לעשות בו שימוש נגד מי שאינו מהווה סכנת חיים ברורה ומידית. [Rendering: The Supreme Court has held in the past that the principle of self-defence does not authorise weapon carriers to use them against someone who does not pose a clear and immediate danger to life.]

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kwara

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

6dec5633ec044344.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

El Salvador

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 27(2) of the Penal Code excludes criminal liability for self-defence when there is an unlawful aggression, a "reasonable necessity of the defence used to prevent or repel it", and no sufficient provocation by the defender. Salvadoran appeal chambers (2002 decisions collected by the Supreme Court's jurisprudence centre) explain that the defence must be necessary, meaning the person "was not obliged to carry out another less harmful or harmless conduct" instead, and that there can be no enormous disproportion between defence and attack. The code text quoted does not mention retreat. When the defence was necessary but the defender used disproportionate means or kept going too long, the courts describe this as "excess of defence" rather than full self-defence. The sources opened here did not show a special rule for the home.

What the law says
Código Penal, art. 27 num. 2 (requirements as quoted by the Cámaras de lo Penal)
a) Agresión ilegítima; b) necesidad razonable de la defensa empleada para impedirla o repelerla; ... c) no haber sido provocada la agresión, de modo suficiente, por quien ejerce la defensa
Cámara de la 2ª Sección de Occidente, sentencia de 27/06/2002
Cita la doctrina que la defensa para ser legítima debe ser ante todo necesaria; es decir, que el sujeto no haya estado obligado a realizar otra conducta menos lesiva o inocua en lugar de la conducta típica.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Aspectos de Derecho Penal, Cámaras de lo Penal 2002 (Centro de Documentación Judicial, Corte Suprema de Justicia de El Salvador)

fcffd4303a09deb2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Turks and Caicos Islands

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The Turks and Caicos Islands, a British Overseas Territory, have their own criminal statutes, but none of those opened sets out self-defence rules. The Criminal Law Ordinance (Cap. 3.01, revised to 31 March 2018) allows 'such force as is reasonable in the circumstances' to prevent crime or make an arrest and says this replaces the common-law rules on that question (s 4); self-defence itself is left to the common law. The Offences Against the Person Ordinance (Cap. 3.08) opened here contains no self-defence section. A Court of Appeal judgment (Elsaieh v The Crown) found in an earlier pass confirms only that self-defence must be left to the jury whenever the evidence raises it. No TCI source found says whether a person must retreat, so the retreat question is not settled by the sources found, and nothing is assumed from English case law.

What the law says
Criminal Law Ordinance (Cap. 3.01), s 4 Use of force in making arrest, etc (Revised Edition, law as at 31 March 2018)
(1) A person may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances in the prevention of crime, or in effecting or assisting in the lawful arrest of offenders or suspected offenders or of persons unlawfully at large. (2) Subsection (1) shall replace the rules of the common law on the question when force used for a purpose mentioned in the subsection is justified for that purpose.

87cb42feab7df03b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

México (State of Mexico)

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The State of Mexico's Penal Code (art. 15-III(b)) excludes liability when a person repels a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests, if the defence was necessary, the means were rational, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. The code says nothing about retreating or fleeing. Intruders into a dwelling are presumed to be lawful targets of defence unless shown otherwise. Under art. 66, someone who goes beyond the limits of defence (because the threatened harm was easily repairable by legal means, was smaller than the harm caused, or the means used were not rationally needed) gets six months to seven years in prison, never more than two thirds of the normal penalty. Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 15-III(b) presumes legitimate defence, unless proven otherwise, when harm is caused to someone who by any means tries to enter or has entered without right the home of the defender or their family, its outbuildings, the home of anyone they must defend, or a place holding property they must protect; or who is found in those places in circumstances showing a probable attack.

What the law says
Código Penal del Estado de México, art. 15, fracc. III, inciso b)
b) Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho en protección de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa y racionalidad de los medios empleados y no medie provocación dolosa, suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de la persona a quien se defiende. Se presumirá como defensa legítima, salvo prueba en contrario, el hecho de causar daño a quien por cualquier medio trata de penetrar o haya penetrado sin derecho al hogar del agente, al de su familia, o sus dependencias o a los de cualquier persona que tenga la obligación de defender, al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos, respecto de los que exista la misma obligación; o lo encuentre en alguno de aquellos lugares en circunstancias tales que revelen la probabilidad de una agresión.
Código Penal del Estado de México, art. 66
Artículo 66.- A quien se excediere en los límites señalados para la defensa o la necesidad, porque el daño que iba a sufrir era fácilmente reparable por medios legales o era de menor magnitud que el que causó o bien por no haber tenido necesidad racional del medio empleado, se le impondrá prisión de seis meses a siete años y de treinta a noventa días multa, sin que en ningún caso la pena exceda de las dos terceras partes de la que correspondería al delito simple.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal del Estado de México (última reforma POGG 16 de junio de 2026), copy published by the Municipality of Ecatepec (H. Ayuntamiento de Ecatepec de Morelos (copy of the State of Mexico's official text; official site legislacion.edomex.gob.mx refused the connection))
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

78a823fa07366126.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ogun

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.

  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

c61a25cac9a7d83b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Taraba

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.

When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.

It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
