204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.

88228f958a7f4b42.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Missouri

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Missouri allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to protect themselves, their unborn child or another against death, serious physical injury or any forcible felony (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.031.2(1)), and also against someone unlawfully entering or remaining in a dwelling, residence or vehicle the defender lawfully occupies, or private property the defender owns or leases. A person has no duty to retreat from a dwelling, residence or vehicle where they are lawfully present, from private property they own or lease, or 'in any other location such person has the right to be' (§ 563.031.3). The version history on the Revisor's site shows the steps: in 2007 (S.B. 62 & 41) deadly force against intruders in a dwelling, residence or vehicle and no duty to retreat from them were added; in 2010 (H.B. 1692 et al.) the same was extended to private property the defender owns or leases; and the 'any other location' stand-your-ground rule was added by S.B. 656, enacted in 2016 over the governor's veto (effective 14 October 2016). Self-defence is not available to an initial aggressor unless they withdrew and clearly communicated it and the other person kept attacking, nor to someone attempting, committing or escaping from a forcible felony (§ 563.031.1). The defendant must raise the issue, after which the state bears the burden of proof. Since 2007, justified force is 'an absolute defense to criminal prosecution or civil liability', and a court must award fees and costs to a civil defendant who has that defence (§ 563.074); the statute does not set out a separate pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.031.2(2)–(3): deadly force may be used against a person who unlawfully enters, remains after unlawfully entering, or attempts to unlawfully enter a dwelling, residence or vehicle lawfully occupied by the defender, or private property owned or leased by the defender (or occupied with the owner's specific authority), without separately showing fear of death or serious injury. If the defendant relies on the dwelling/vehicle rule, the state must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant did not reasonably believe force was necessary (§ 563.031.5). There is no duty to retreat from such a dwelling, residence, vehicle or private property (§ 563.031.3).

What the law says
Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.031.3
A person does not have a duty to retreat: (1) From a dwelling, residence, or vehicle where the person is not unlawfully entering or unlawfully remaining; (2) From private property that is owned or leased by such individual; or (3) If the person is in any other location such person has the right to be.
Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.031.2
A person shall not use deadly force upon another person under the circumstances specified in subsection 1 of this section unless: (1) He or she reasonably believes that such deadly force is necessary to protect himself, or herself or her unborn child, or another against death, serious physical injury, or any forcible felony; (2) Such force is used against a person who unlawfully enters, remains after unlawfully entering, or attempts to unlawfully enter a dwelling, residence, or vehicle lawfully occupied by such person ...
Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.031.1
unless: (1) The actor was the initial aggressor; except that in such case his or her use of force is nevertheless justifiable provided: (a) He or she has withdrawn from the encounter and effectively communicated such withdrawal to such other person but the latter persists ...; (3) The actor was attempting to commit, committing, or escaping after the commission of a forcible felony.
Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.074.1
a person who uses force as described in sections 563.031, 563.041, 563.046, 563.051, 563.056, and 563.061 is justified in using such force and such fact shall be an absolute defense to criminal prosecution or civil liability.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Missouri Revised Statutes § 563.031 (L. 1977 S.B. 60 … A.L. 2007 S.B. 62 & 41, A.L. 2010 H.B. 1692, A.L. 2016 S.B. 656, veto overridden 14 Sept 2016) (Missouri Revisor of Statutes)
  • Missouri Revised Statutes § 563.031, versions effective 28 Aug 2007 and 28 Aug 2010 (Missouri Revisor of Statutes)
  • Missouri Revised Statutes § 563.074 (L. 2007 S.B. 62 & 41) (Missouri Revisor of Statutes)

Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. d5a39c3182011118.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mississippi

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Mississippi Code § 97-3-15 (headed 'Homicide; justifiable homicide; use of defensive force; duty to retreat') makes homicide justifiable when resisting an attempt to kill or to commit a felony on the person or in a dwelling, occupied vehicle, business or workplace (§ 97-3-15(1)(e)), and in lawful defence of oneself or another where there is reasonable ground to fear a felony or great personal injury and imminent danger of it (§ 97-3-15(1)(f)). Subsection (4), as it reads in the 2025 code, says a person who is not the initial aggressor and is not engaged in unlawful activity 'shall have no duty to retreat before using deadly force under subsection (1)(e) or (f) of this section if the person is in a place where the person has a right to be', and no finder of fact may treat failure to retreat as evidence that the force was unnecessary, excessive or unreasonable. Subsection (3) presumes reasonable fear when the other person was unlawfully and forcibly entering a dwelling, occupied vehicle, business or workplace. The history line lists Laws 1983, ch. 382; 2006, ch. 492, § 1; 2016, ch. 421, § 4; 2023, ch. 458, § 3 (eff. July 1, 2023). A defendant acquitted under (1)(e) or (f) is immune from civil damages for the same conduct (§ 97-3-15(5)(b)).

At home

Miss. Code § 97-3-15(3): a person who uses defensive force is presumed to have reasonably feared imminent death, great bodily harm or a felony when the other person was unlawfully and forcibly entering, or had entered, the person's dwelling, an occupied vehicle, or their business or place of employment or its immediate premises.

What the law says
Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-15(4) (2025 Mississippi Code 1972)
A person who is not the initial aggressor and is not engaged in unlawful activity shall have no duty to retreat before using deadly force under subsection (1)(e) or (f) of this section if the person is in a place where the person has a right to be, and no finder of fact shall be permitted to consider the person's failure to retreat as evidence that the person's use of force was unnecessary, excessive or unreasonable.
Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-15(1)(e)-(f)
(e) When committed by any person in resisting any attempt unlawfully to kill such person or to commit any felony upon him, or upon or in any dwelling, in any occupied vehicle, in any place of business, in any place of employment or in the immediate premises thereof in which such person shall be; (f) When committed in the lawful defense of one's own person or any other human being, where there shall be reasonable ground to apprehend a design to commit a felony or to do some great personal injury, and there shall be imminent danger of such design being accomplished;

Laws, 1983, ch. 382; 2006, ch. 492, § 1; 2016, ch. 421, § 4 (effective from and after passage, approved April 15, 2016); 2023, ch. 458, § 3 (effective from and after July 1, 2023).

5a470b8952495161.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bougainville (Autonomous Region)

Part of Papua New Guinea, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The Autonomous Bougainville Government may adopt the national Criminal Code and make other criminal laws, but under the PNG Constitution (s. 291, inserted by Constitutional Amendment No. 23) the national Criminal Code applies in Bougainville until the Bougainville Government adopts it, and a Bougainville version can be changed only with national consent or under agreed procedures. No adoption or Bougainville-specific self-defence law was found, so the Papua New Guinea rules apply: deadly force is lawful only against an attack causing reasonable fear of death or grievous bodily harm when the defender reasonably believes there is no other way to save the person defended (Criminal Code s. 269). Retreat is not a separate requirement, but whether the accused could have retreated is weighed when judging reasonableness (State v Pondros Laki, 2010).

What the law says
Constitution of Papua New Guinea, s. 291 (Constitutional Amendment No. 23 – Peace-Building in Bougainville), as summarised from PacLII
The Criminal Code shall apply in and to Bougainville until adopted under Subsection (2)(a).
Bougainville Peace Agreement (2001), key points
Until Bougainville establishes its equivalent, the National Court will hear cases under the Criminal Code ... a Bougainvillean Criminal Code can only come into effect on agreement with the national government.
Criminal Code Act 1974 (PNG), s. 269 – Self-defence against unprovoked assault (as quoted in Henry v State [2022] PGSC 75)
(1) When a person is unlawfully assaulted and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make an effectual defence against the assault, if the force used is not intended to cause, and is not likely to cause, death or grievous bodily harm. (2) If– (a) the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm; and (b) the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable grounds, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous bodily harm, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even if it causes death or grievous bodily harm.
The State v Pondros Laki [2010] PGNC 260 (National Court, Bialla), para. 35
retreating before employing a force is not an independent and imperative condition when self defence is raised as a defence. ... Whether he should have retreated or run away is a matter for the court to consider ... in deciding on the reasonableness of the conduct of the accused. ... Here the court finds that the accused could have simply retreated before employing a deadly force.

Papua New Guinea as a whole

Papua New Guinea's Criminal Code 1974 (based on the Queensland code) sets out self-defence in section 269. A person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke the assault may use force reasonably necessary to make an effectual defence; force that causes death or grievous bodily harm is lawful only if the assault caused reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm and the defender believes on reasonable grounds that they cannot otherwise preserve themselves (s 269(2)); section 270 covers provoked assaults. The Code does not mention retreat, but the 'cannot otherwise preserve' test means the courts look at whether escape was realistic: in State v Ambrose (1997) the National Court asked 'Should the accused have retreated. I do not think so', because he was sitting down when attacked and the next blow could have been fatal, and acquitted him. In Henry v State (2022) the Supreme Court quashed a murder conviction and entered an acquittal on self-defence. The sources opened here did not cover a special rule for the home or what happens when the force was excessive.

1e579ddd179ec875.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Idaho

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Idaho makes homicide justifiable when resisting an attempt to murder, to commit a felony or to do great bodily injury, and in defence of a home, place of business or employment, occupied vehicle, property or person against someone who clearly intends a violent felony or a violent entry (Idaho Code § 18-4009(1)). A person 'need not retreat from any place that person has a right to be' and may stand their ground using all force that would appear necessary to a reasonable person in the same situation 'without the benefit of hindsight' (§ 19-202A(3)); this rule does not apply to jail or prison inmates dealing with staff. The current wording, including the stand-your-ground sentence and the presumption of reasonable fear in homes, businesses and occupied vehicles, comes from a 2018 amendment (2018 ch. 222). A person may act on appearances as a reasonable person would, without waiting to learn whether the danger is real (§ 19-202A(2)). An assailant or a person who joined in mortal combat must really and in good faith try to decline further fighting before a killing is justified (§ 18-4009(1)(c)). In a criminal case the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the force was not justified (§ 19-202A(4)); Idaho's statutes do not create immunity from prosecution or a pretrial immunity hearing. A person who used justified force is immune from civil liability (except toward a law enforcement officer they knew or should have known was acting officially), and the court must award fees and costs to a defendant found immune (§ 6-808, added 2006).

At home

Idaho Code § 19-202A(5) (2018): a person using force or deadly force in defence of a habitation, place of business or employment, or occupied vehicle is presumed to have acted reasonably and to have had a reasonable fear of imminent death or serious bodily injury if the other person's entry or attempted entry was unlawful and made by force, in a violent and tumultuous manner, surreptitiously or by stealth, or to commit a felony. § 18-4009(2) also presumes that anyone who unlawfully enters such a place by force or stealth intends to commit a felony. 'Habitation' includes a tent and the curtilage of a dwelling.

What the law says
Idaho Code § 19-202A(3)
In the exercise of the right of self-defense or defense of another, a person need not retreat from any place that person has a right to be. A person may stand his ground and defend himself or another person by the use of all force and means which would appear to be necessary to a reasonable person in a similar situation and with similar knowledge without the benefit of hindsight.
Idaho Code § 19-202A(4)–(5)
the burden is on the prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the use of force, attempted use of force or threat to use force was not justifiable. (5) A person using force or deadly force in defense of a habitation, place of business or employment or occupied vehicle ... is presumed to have acted reasonably and had a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or serious bodily injury if the force is used against a person whose entry or attempted entry therein is unlawful ...
Idaho Code § 18-4009(1)(a), (c)
Homicide is justifiable when committed by any person in any of the following cases: (a) When resisting any attempt to murder any person, or to commit a felony, or to do some great bodily injury upon any person; ... but such person, or the person in whose behalf the defense was made, if he was the assailant or engaged in mortal combat, must really and in good faith have endeavored to decline any further struggle before the homicide was committed ...
Idaho Code § 6-808(1)
A person who uses force as justified in section 18-4009, Idaho Code, or as otherwise permitted in sections 19-201 through 19-205, Idaho Code, is immune from any civil liability for the use of such force except when the person knew or reasonably should have known that the person against whom the force was used was a law enforcement officer acting in the capacity of his or her official duties.

Montenegro

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

3617c0bbd59b4b46.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bayelsa

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.

1f143dcfc21b2d4d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Puntland

Part of Somalia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Puntland, a self-governing state in northern Somalia, applies the Somali Penal Code of 1962 (Legislative Decree No. 5 of 16 December 1962), according to the introduction to the English text published by somalilandlaw.com; no separate Puntland penal code was found. Under article 34, a person who acts because they were compelled by the necessity of defending their own or another's right against an actual danger of unlawful injury is not punishable, provided the defence is proportionate to the injury. The code does not mention retreat, and no Puntland court decisions were found. If the limits imposed by necessity are exceeded through negligence, the person is punished under the rules for negligent crimes where such a crime exists (art. 37).

What the law says
Penal Code 1962, English text, publisher's introduction
This Code is still applied in the Republic of Somaliland and in the northern Somalia region of Puntland. It is still current in South and Central Somalia.
Penal Code (Legislative Decree No. 5 of 16 December 1962), art. 34 – Private Defence
Whoever has committed an act, having been compelled by the necessity of defending his own or another person's right against the actual danger of an unlawful injury, shall not be punishable provided that the defence is proportionate to the injury
Penal Code 1962, art. 37 – Excess Committed With Culpa
Where, in committing any of the acts referred to in articles 33, 34, 35 and 36, the limits imposed by necessity are exceeded with culpa, and where the act constitutes a crime committed with culpa, the provisions relating to crimes committed with culpa shall apply.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Penal Code, Legislative Decree No. 5 of 16 December 1962 (English text) (Somalilandlaw.com)
Somalia as a whole

Somalia's Penal Code (Legislative Decree No. 5 of 16 December 1962), based on the Italian Penal Code of 1930, is still applied in south and central Somalia, Puntland and Somaliland according to the publisher of the English text. A person who acts because they were 'compelled by the necessity of defending' their own or another's right against an actual danger of unlawful injury is not punishable, 'provided that the defence is proportionate to the injury' (art. 34). The code does not mention retreat, and no Somali court decisions on whether a person must avoid the attack were found. If the limits imposed by necessity are exceeded through negligence (culpa), the person is punished under the rules for negligent crimes where such a crime exists (art. 37).

b379ddf2f5ad9c00.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Indiana

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Indiana Code § 35-41-3-2(c) allows reasonable force to protect oneself or a third person from the imminent use of unlawful force and says a person 'is justified in using deadly force; and does not have a duty to retreat' if they reasonably believe the force is necessary to prevent serious bodily injury to themselves or a third person or the commission of a forcible felony. Subsection (d) says the same, with no duty to retreat, for force to prevent or end an unlawful entry into or attack on the person's dwelling, curtilage or occupied motor vehicle. The statute declares that no person 'shall be placed in legal jeopardy of any kind whatsoever' for protecting themselves by reasonable means. Force is not justified for a person committing or escaping a crime, who provoked the other with intent to injure, or who entered into combat or was the initial aggressor unless they withdrew and communicated it (§ 35-41-3-2(g)). The section dates from 1976; the history note lists amendments through P.L.9-2024. Civil immunity is codified separately at IC 34-30-31.

At home

Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2(d): 'A person: (1) is justified in using reasonable force, including deadly force, against any other person; and (2) does not have a duty to retreat; if the person reasonably believes that the force is necessary to prevent or terminate the other person's unlawful entry of or attack on the person's dwelling, curtilage, or occupied motor vehicle.' No presumption of reasonable fear is stated.

What the law says
Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2(c)
(c) A person is justified in using reasonable force against any other person to protect the person or a third person from what the person reasonably believes to be the imminent use of unlawful force. However, a person: (1) is justified in using deadly force; and (2) does not have a duty to retreat; if the person reasonably believes that that force is necessary to prevent serious bodily injury to the person or a third person or the commission of a forcible felony. No person, employer, or estate of a person in this state shall be placed in legal jeopardy of any kind whatsoever for protecting the person or a third person by reasonable means necessary.
Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2(d)
(d) A person: (1) is justified in using reasonable force, including deadly force, against any other person; and (2) does not have a duty to retreat; if the person reasonably believes that the force is necessary to prevent or terminate the other person's unlawful entry of or attack on the person's dwelling, curtilage, or occupied motor vehicle.
Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2(g)
(g) Notwithstanding subsections (c) through (e), a person is not justified in using force if: (1) the person is committing or is escaping after the commission of a crime; (2) the person provokes unlawful action by another person with intent to cause bodily injury to the other person; or (3) the person has entered into combat with another person or is the initial aggressor unless the person withdraws from the encounter and communicates to the other person the intent to do so and the other person nevertheless continues or threatens to continue unlawful action.
Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2 history note (2025 Indiana Code)

1b7b990cbc249953.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Lesotho

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Lesotho's Penal Code Act 2010 writes a retreat requirement into the self-defence section itself: force against an unlawful attack on oneself or another is excused only if it was not reasonable to use a means of retreat the defender knew about, and the force was no more than reasonably necessary (s. 20(1)(a)). The explanatory notes printed with the Act say this does not require retreat in every case; the means of escape only has to have been reasonable, so the defender need not take great risks to avoid the harm. The notes also say the drafters chose not to create a plea of 'excessive defence'; instead, where excessive force kills, courts in practice find provocation, which reduces the seriousness of the charge. Murder carries death, but the court must impose a lesser sentence where there are extenuating circumstances (s. 40(3)).

At home

The Penal Code has no separate home or dwelling rule. Force to protect property (s. 20(1)(b)) is allowed only if the means and degree of force are reasonable; the code's explanatory notes say courts would likely not regard lethal force to protect property as reasonable.

What the law says
Penal Code Act 2010 (Act No. 6 of 2012), s. 20 – Self defence
(1) No person shall be criminally responsible for the use of force in repelling an unlawful attack - (a) upon himself or herself or another person if - (i) it was not reasonable to avail himself or herself of any means of retreat of which he or she was aware; and (ii) the degree of force used in repelling the attack was no greater than that which was reasonably necessary in the circumstances; (b) upon his or her property or the property of another provided that the means he or she chooses and the degree of force he or she uses in so doing are reasonable in the circumstances.
Penal Code Act 2010, explanatory notes on s. 20
The accused must have had no means of escaping from the attack. This does not require retreat in every circumstances, as all that is required is that the means of escape should have been reasonable. The accused need not, therefore, take great risks to avoid the threatened harm. The use of excessive force to repel an attack will not be justified. ... where excessive force results in the death of the attacker, in practice the courts will find that there was provocation, and this will reduce the seriousness of the charge. For these reasons it has not been thought appropriate to introduce the plea of excessive defence ... It is likely that the courts would not regard as reasonable the use of lethal force to protect property
Penal Code Act 2010, s. 40(3)
Notwithstanding subsection (2), the court shall in the conviction for murder impose a lesser sentence where it is satisfied that - ... (c) the offence was committed in the presence of extenuating circumstances.

1b893fd29b771949.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Adamawa

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.
Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963), on ss. 59-65
When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Zamfara Shari'a Penal Code 2000, s. 204(c), as reproduced in Peters (2001), Appendix Five
204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Notes on the Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), Second Edition 1963, annotated by S. S. Richardson (reproduces the code text with commentary) (anticor.world (scan of the 1963 Government Printer edition))
  • Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC 430/1962) [1963] NGSC 24 (25 March 1963) (NigeriaLII)

  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cross River

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.

571883f50d932f1c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Zanzibar

Part of Tanzania, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Zanzibar has its own criminal code, the Penal Act No. 6 of 2018, enacted by the House of Representatives of Zanzibar. Section 16 gives a right to defend oneself, any other person, or property against an unlawful act, assault or violence. Section 17 limits this to 'reasonable force as may be necessary for that defence' and makes excessive force criminal (death from excessive force is manslaughter). Section 18 lists when the right extends to causing death or grievous harm, including apprehension of death or grievous harm, rape, kidnapping, burglary, robbery or arson. The Act does not use the word 'retreat' and nothing in its text says whether a person must try to avoid or escape before using force; the sections were read from the official PDF of the Act (OCR of a scanned copy). A ZanzibarLII search of Zanzibar High Court and Court of Appeal judgments for 'retreat' with 'self defence' returned no judgment whose indexed text mentions retreat, and the judgment pages themselves could not be opened from this shell (HTTP 403), so no court ruling settles the point.

At home

No separate dwelling rule found; s. 18(1)(e) extends the right of defence to causing death where the unlawful act is 'burglary, robbery, arson or any offence, which endangers life or property'.

What the law says
Penal Act No. 6 of 2018 (Zanzibar), s. 16(1)
16.-(1) Subject to the provision of this Act, a person has the right: (a) to defend himself or herself or any other person against any unlawful act or assault or violence to the body; or (b) to defend his or her own property or a property in his or her lawful possession, custody or under his care or the property of any other person against any unlawful act of seizure or destruction or violence.
Penal Act No. 6 of 2018 (Zanzibar), s. 17
17.-(1) In exercising the right of self defence or in defence of another or defence of property, a person shall be entitled only to use reasonable force as may be necessary for that defence. (2) A person shall be criminally liable for any offence resulting from excessive force used in self-defence or in defence of another or in defence of property. (3) A person who causes the death of another as the result of excessive force used in defence is guilty of manslaughter.
Penal Act No. 6 of 2018 (Zanzibar), s. 18(1)
18.-(1) The right of self defence or the defence of another or defence of property shall extend to a person who, in exercising that right, causes death or grievous harm to another and the person so acting, acts in good faith and with an honest belief based on reasonable grounds that his or her act is necessary for the preservation of his or her own life or limb or the life or limb of another or of property, in the circumstances where: (a) the lawful act is of such a nature as may reasonably cause the apprehension that his or her own death or the death of another person could be the consequence of that act; (b) the lawful act is of such a nature as may be reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous harm to his or her own body or the body of another could be the consequence of the unlawful act; (c) the unlawful act is with the intention of committing rape or defilement or an unnatural offence; (d) the unlawful act is with the intention of kidnapping or abducting; or (e) the unlawful act is burglary, robbery, arson or any offence, which endangers life or property.
What was tried

zanzibarlii.org: site search pages are JS-only; the JSON search API works and lists 'the Penal Act, 2018' (gazette legal supplement Part I, 13 Apr 2018, no. 6691) and judgments such as DPP v Malik Moh'd Ali [2017] TZZNZHC 103 (which cites Ratanlal & Dhirajlal on private defence) and Khatibu Sheha Khamis v S.M.Z. [1987] TZCA 130, but every /akn/ document and /source PDF URL returned 403 ('Just a moment' bot-check page); the web reader of the judgment URL was blocked (provenance/permission not granted). Searches 'retreat defence' and '"duty to retreat"' returned 0 hits; 'retreat self defence' returned 12 hits with no snippet containing 'retreat'. archive.org wayback: no snapshot of the ZanzibarLII act page; a snapshot of zanzibarassembly.go.tz/act_2018/act_6.pdf exists but web.archive.org is blocked by egress policy. ecoi.net IRB document TZA106150.FE (opened) linked the old act_6.pdf URL (now 404); the live House of Representatives site lists the Act under /en/acts/acts_2018/2018 with the storage PDF used here.

Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • Acts of the House — 2018 (list linking to the Penal Act PDF) (Zanzibar House of Representatives)
  • ZanzibarLII search API results for 'self-defence', 'private defence', 'retreat self defence' (lists the Penal Act, 2018 gazette supplement of 13 April 2018 no. 6691 and Zanzibar High Court judgments; no snippet mentions retreat) (ZanzibarLII (Judiciary of Zanzibar / Laws.Africa))
United Republic of Tanzania as a whole

Tanzania's Penal Code (sections 18 to 18C, added in 1980) gives every person the right to defend themselves, another person, or property, but only with "such reasonable force as may be necessary for that defence". Deadly force or grievous harm is allowed where the defender acts in good faith with an honest belief, on reasonable grounds, that it is needed to preserve life or limb, including against acts reasonably feared to cause death or grievous harm, rape, kidnapping, burglary, robbery or arson. The Code does not mention retreat, and the sources opened here did not settle whether a chance to escape counts against the defender. A person who uses excessive force is criminally liable, and causing death through excessive defensive force is manslaughter rather than murder.

32a8c6c39b303d95.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Carolina

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

South Carolina's Protection of Persons and Property Act (2006 Act No. 379, in force 9 June 2006) put stand-your-ground and castle rules into statute. A person who is not engaged in unlawful activity and is attacked in any place where they have a right to be, including their place of business, has no duty to retreat and may meet force with force, including deadly force, if they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent death or great bodily injury or a violent crime (S.C. Code § 16-11-440(C)). A person who uses deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering, or dragging someone out of, a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle is presumed to have had reasonable fear; the presumption does not apply against a lawful resident, a parent or guardian taking their child, a law officer identified as such, or a defender who is engaged in unlawful activity. Someone who forces entry in breach of a protection order or bond condition is presumed to intend an unlawful act even if they live there (§ 16-11-440(E)). A person who uses deadly force as permitted is 'immune from criminal prosecution and civil action', police may not arrest them without probable cause that the force was unlawful, and courts must award fees and lost income to a defendant found immune in a civil suit (§ 16-11-450). In State v. Duncan (2011) the Supreme Court held that immunity is decided at a pretrial hearing on a motion to dismiss, where the defendant must prove it by a preponderance of the evidence. The Act's stated purpose is that no one 'should be required to needlessly retreat in the face of intrusion or attack' (§ 16-11-420(E)).

At home

The 2006 Protection of Persons and Property Act states its intent 'to codify the common law Castle Doctrine' and extend it to an occupied vehicle and place of business (S.C. Code § 16-11-420). A person using deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering a dwelling (including an attached porch), residence or occupied vehicle is presumed to have reasonable fear of death or great bodily injury (§ 16-11-440(A)); the intruder is presumed to intend a violent crime (§ 16-11-440(D)).

What the law says
S.C. Code § 16-11-440(C) (2006 Act No. 379)
A person who is not engaged in an unlawful activity and who is attacked in another place where he has a right to be, including, but not limited to, his place of business, has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his ground and meet force with force, including deadly force, if he reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent death or great bodily injury to himself or another person or to prevent the commission of a violent crime as defined in Section 16-1-60.
S.C. Code § 16-11-440(A) (presumption)
A person is presumed to have a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or great bodily injury to himself or another person when using deadly force that is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily injury to another person if the person: (1) against whom the deadly force is used is in the process of unlawfully and forcefully entering, or has unlawfully and forcibly entered a dwelling, residence, or occupied vehicle ...
S.C. Code § 16-11-450(A) (immunity)
A person who uses deadly force as permitted by the provisions of this article or another applicable provision of law is justified in using deadly force and is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of deadly force, unless the person against whom deadly force was used is a law enforcement officer ...
S.C. Code § 16-11-420(A)
It is the intent of the General Assembly to codify the common law Castle Doctrine which recognizes that a person's home is his castle and to extend the doctrine to include an occupied vehicle and the person's place of business.
State v. Duncan (S.C. 2011) (pretrial immunity hearing)
The circuit correctly decided the issue of respondent’s immunity from prosecution by way of a pre-trial hearing on respondent’s motion to dismiss, and the applicable standard of proof was a preponderance of the evidence.

1e925ee1db97209c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Massachusetts

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Massachusetts has no general self-defence statute; the rule is case law. In Commonwealth v. Shaffer, 367 Mass. 508 (1975), the Supreme Judicial Court refused to adopt the majority rule that a person attacked in their own home need not retreat, and restated the Massachusetts rule 'that the right to use deadly force by way of self-defense is not available to one threatened until he has availed himself of all reasonable and proper means in the circumstance to avoid combat', holding that it 'has equal application to one assaulted in his own home'. The court added that this is not 'an absolute duty to retreat regardless of considerations of personal safety', that one 'need only retreat as far as necessary in the circumstances', and that the location of the assault is 'an element of major importance' for the jury. The Legislature then enacted the castle statute, M.G.L. c. 278, § 8A, which gives an occupant of a dwelling a defence against a person unlawfully in the dwelling and says 'There shall be no duty on said occupant to retreat from such person unlawfully in said dwelling.' Outside that statute the duty to use every reasonable avenue of escape remains (Commonwealth v. Pike, 428 Mass. 393 (1998)).

At home

M.G.L. c. 278, § 8A: in a prosecution of an occupant of a dwelling for killing or injuring someone unlawfully in the dwelling, it is a defence that the occupant reasonably believed the intruder was about to inflict great bodily injury or death and used reasonable means; 'There shall be no duty on said occupant to retreat'. It applies only to persons unlawfully in the dwelling; Shaffer's retreat rule otherwise governs assaults by lawful occupants or guests.

What the law says
Commonwealth v. Shaffer, 367 Mass. 508 (April 28, 1975)
The defendant asks us in this case to adopt the majority rule that one assaulted in his own home need not retreat before resorting to the use of deadly force. ... This has never been the law of the Commonwealth, and we see no reason to adopt it now. We prefer instead to follow our long-established rule that the right to use deadly force by way of self-defense is not available to one threatened until he has availed himself of all reasonable and proper means in the circumstance to avoid combat, ... and hold that this rule has equal application to one assaulted in his own home. This rule does not impose an absolute duty to retreat regardless of considerations of personal safety. ... one need only retreat as far as necessary in the circumstances, until there is "no probable means of escape." ... We hold that one assaulted in his own home does not have the unlimited right to react with deadly force without any attempt at retreat. However, the importance of the location of the assault and the surrounding circumstance should be stressed to the jury.
Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 278, § 8A Killing or injuring a person unlawfully in a dwelling; defense
Section 8A. In the prosecution of a person who is an occupant of a dwelling charged with killing or injuring one who was unlawfully in said dwelling, it shall be a defense that the occupant was in his dwelling at the time of the offense and that he acted in the reasonable belief that the person unlawfully in said dwelling was about to inflict great bodily injury or death upon said occupant or upon another person lawfully in said dwelling, and that said occupant used reasonable means to defend himself or such other person lawfully in said dwelling. There shall be no duty on said occupant to retreat from such person unlawfully in said dwelling.
Commonwealth v. Pike, 428 Mass. 393 (1998) (read for the previous entry)
A self-defense instruction is not required unless there is some evidence that the defendant availed himself of all means, proper and reasonable under the circumstances, of retreating from the conflict before resorting to the use of deadly force. ... This rule does not impose an absolute duty to retreat regardless of personal safety considerations ... He must, however, use every reasonable avenue of escape available to him.
Sources (read 2026-10-17, 2026-10-18)
  • Commonwealth v. Shaffer, 367 Mass. 508 (1975), full text (Caselaw Access Project, Harvard Law School Library)
  • General Laws Part IV, Title II, Chapter 278, Section 8A (The 194th General Court of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts)
  • Commonwealth v. Pike, 428 Mass. 393 (1998) (CourtListener (Free Law Project))

0a3de7b3e32ded1a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Burundi

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Burundi's Penal Code (Law No. 1/27 of 29 December 2017) says there is no offence in legitimate defence, defined as the reaction of a person who, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, commits an act that falls under criminal law, provided the means used are proportionate to the seriousness of the attack (art. 31(3°)). The code does not mention retreat or a duty to avoid the attack. No separate rule on excessive self-defence or on defence of the home was found in this article.

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n°1/27 du 29 décembre 2017), art. 31(3°)
Il n’y a pas d’infraction : ... 3° En cas de légitime défense qui est la réaction de celui qui, devant une agression injustifiée envers elle‐même, ou autrui, accomplit un acte qui tombe sous le coup de la loi pénale, à condition que les moyens utilisés soient proportionnels à la gravité de l’agression.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Code pénal 2017 (Loi n°1/27 du 29 décembre 2017), droit-afrique.com edition (droit-afrique.com (hosted by lemandat.org))

e32750d2e0e673f7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cook Islands

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The Cook Islands has its own Crimes Act 1969 (separate from New Zealand's). A person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may repel force with force; they may cause death or grievous bodily harm if acting under reasonable fear of death or grievous bodily harm and believing on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise preserve themselves (s 50). No retreat is required of someone who did not provoke the attack, but a person who started or provoked the fight may justify force only if, before using it, 'he declined further conflict and quitted or retreated from it as far as was practicable' (s 51). Text is from the 1969 Act as enacted (scanned copy, read by OCR); later amendments were not checked, and no court decisions were opened.

At home

s 57: a person in peaceable possession of a dwellinghouse may use such force as is necessary to prevent its forcible breaking and entering by anyone, if they believe on reasonable and probable grounds there is no lawful justification for it.

What the law says
Crimes Act 1969, s 50 Self-defence against unprovoked assault
(1) Every one unlawfully assaulted, not having provoked the assault, is justified in repelling force by force, if the force he uses - (a) Is not meant to cause death or grievous bodily harm; and (b) Is no more than is necessary for the purpose of self-defence. (2) Every one unlawfully assaulted, not having provoked the assault, is justified in repelling force by force although in so doing he causes death or grievous bodily harm, if - (a) He causes it under reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm from the violence with which the assault was originally made or with which the assailant pursues his purpose; and (b) He believes, on reasonable grounds, that he cannot otherwise preserve himself from death or grievous bodily harm.
Crimes Act 1969, s 51(c) Self-defence against provoked assault
(c) Before the force was used, he declined further conflict and quitted or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Crimes Act 1969, s 57 Defence of dwellinghouse
Every one in peaceable possession of a dwellinghouse, and every one lawfully assisting him or acting by his authority, is justified in using such force as is necessary to prevent the forcible breaking and entering of the dwellinghouse by any person if he believes, on reasonable and probable grounds, that there is no lawful justification for the breaking and entering.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Crimes Act 1969 No. 20 (scanned original) (Parliament of the Cook Islands, Acts Library)

df5d8db7af38dc44.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Western Sahara

Part of Disputed (Moroccan-administered in part), or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Western Sahara is disputed: Morocco claims it and administers the part it controls, while the POLISARIO Front seeks independence. The US State Department's 2019 human rights report says Morocco administers the territory it controls 'by the same law and structures' as internationally recognised Morocco, so the Moroccan Penal Code applies there in practice. Under that code (art. 124(3)), there is no offence when it was 'commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence' of oneself, another person or property, provided the defence is proportionate to the seriousness of the aggression; the code does not mention retreat, and no court decisions on the point were found. Night-time break-ins into homes and violent theft are presumed to justify defence (art. 125). The law applied in areas east of the Moroccan-controlled zone and in the Sahrawi refugee camps (administered by POLISARIO) was not found, so this entry covers only the Moroccan-administered part.

At home

In the Moroccan-administered part, Moroccan Penal Code art. 125 presumes legitimate defence for killing or wounding while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of an inhabited house or flat or its outbuildings, and for acts against perpetrators of violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal marocain (consolidated to 5 July 2018), art. 124(3)
Il n'y a ni crime, ni délit, ni contravention : ... 3° Lorsque l'infraction était commandée par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d'autrui ou d'un bien appartenant à soi-même ou à autrui, pourvu que la défense soit proportionnée à la gravité de l'agression.
Code pénal marocain, art. 125
Sont présumés accomplis dans un cas de nécessité actuelle de légitime défense : 1° L'homicide commis, les blessures faites ou les coups portés, en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d'une maison ou d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances; 2° L'infraction commise en défendant soi-même ou autrui contre l'auteur de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
US Department of State, Country Report on Human Rights Practices 2019 – Western Sahara (executive summary)
Morocco administers the territories in Western Sahara by the same law and structures governing the exercise of civil liberties and political and economic rights as in internationally recognized Morocco.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Code pénal (Maroc), version consolidée au 5 juillet 2018 (Policinglaw.info)
  • Country Report on Human Rights Practices 2019 – Western Sahara (US Department of State (via ecoi.net))

6389c2341282bdaa.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Georgia

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Georgia allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it necessary to prevent death or great bodily injury to themselves or a third person, or to prevent a forcible felony (O.C.G.A. § 16-3-21(a)). Since 2006 (Ga. L. 2006, p. 477, § 1, SB 396) a person who uses force lawfully in defence of self, others, habitation or other property 'has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground and use force as provided in said Code sections, including deadly force' (§ 16-3-23.1, headed 'No duty to retreat prior to use of force in self-defense'). The justification is lost for a person who provoked the attack as an excuse to injure, who is committing or fleeing a felony, or who was the aggressor or in a fight by agreement unless they withdrew and communicated it (§ 16-3-21(b)). A person who used force in accordance with these sections is immune from criminal prosecution unless the deadly force involved a weapon they could not lawfully carry (§ 16-3-24.2).

At home

O.C.G.A. § 16-3-23 (defence of habitation) allows deadly force against a violent and tumultuous entry, against a non-household member who unlawfully and forcibly enters, or to prevent a felony inside; § 16-3-23.1 adds that there is no duty to retreat.

What the law says
O.C.G.A. § 16-3-23.1 No duty to retreat prior to use of force in self-defense (Code 1981, § 16-3-23.1, enacted by Ga. L. 2006, p. 477, § 1/SB 396)
A person who uses threats or force in accordance with Code Section 16-3-21, relating to the use of force in defense of self or others, Code Section 16-3-23, relating to the use of force in defense of a habitation, or Code Section 16-3-24, relating to the use of force in defense of property other than a habitation, has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground and use force as provided in said Code sections, including deadly force.
O.C.G.A. § 16-3-21(a)
a person is justified in using force which is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm only if he or she reasonably believes that such force is necessary to prevent death or great bodily injury to himself or herself or a third person or to prevent the commission of a forcible felony.
O.C.G.A. § 16-3-24.2
A person who uses threats or force in accordance with Code Section 16-3-20, 16-3-21, 16-3-23, 16-3-23.1, 16-3-24, or 17-4-20 shall be immune from criminal prosecution therefor unless in the use of deadly force, such person utilizes a weapon the carrying or possession of which is unlawful by such person under Part 2 of Article 4 of Chapter 11 of this title.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • 2025 Georgia Code § 16-3-23.1 (Justia, unannotated O.C.G.A.) (Justia)

dbb4b7e092fc6863.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Rwanda

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Rwanda's Law No. 68/2018 determining offences and penalties in general (published in the Official Gazette of 27 September 2018, in Kinyarwanda, English and French) exempts from criminal liability a person who acts in self-defence, defends another person in danger, or acts to interrupt damage to property (art. 86). It names two typical self-defence situations: fending off someone who breaks into or enters an inhabited place by force or trickery, and defending oneself against thieves or other wrongdoers. The exemption applies only if the means used 'are proportional to the gravity of the threat'. The law says nothing about retreat, and no Rwandan court decisions on the point were found. Self-defence does not remove civil liability for damages where appropriate (art. 87).

At home

Article 86 lists among acts done in self-defence 'fending off a person who breaks into or enters by force or trickery an inhabited place'. The general proportionality rule in the same article applies.

What the law says
Law No. 68/2018 determining offences and penalties in general, art. 86 (English version)
Grounds for exemption from criminal liability that are inherent to the act are admitted if : 1º a person acts in self-defence in the following cases: a) fending off a person who breaks into or enters by force or trickery an inhabited place; b) defends himself/herself against thieves or other wrongdoers; 2º a person commits the following acts: a) an act of self-defence in case of danger; b) an act of defending another person in danger; c) an act committed to interrupt the commission of an offence of damage to property in order to protect the property. The exemption of criminal liability due to the grounds referred to under Paragraph 2 of this Article is only admitted if the means used by the offender to ensure self-defence or protect himself/herself or another person from danger or interrupt damage to the property he/she protected are proportional to the gravity of the threat.
Law No. 68/2018, art. 86 (French version, extract)
1º une personne agit en état de légitime défense dans les cas suivants: a) repousser quelqu’un qui entre par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité; b) se défendre contre les voleurs ou d’autres malfaiteurs;
Law No. 68/2018, art. 87
Nor do such grounds entail exemption from civil liability, if necessary.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Law determining Offences and Penalties in general (Law No. 68/2018) (RwandaLII (Laws.Africa))

04c9e69111a6e9ba.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Iowa

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Iowa allows 'reasonable force', which can include deadly force if it is reasonable to believe such force is necessary to avoid injury or risk to one's own or another's life or safety, or to resist a like force or threat (Iowa Code § 704.1(1)). A person may be wrong about the danger or the force needed as long as there was a reasonable basis for the belief and they responded reasonably (§ 704.1(2)). Since 2017 (2017 Acts ch. 69), 'a person who is not engaged in illegal activity has no duty to retreat from any place where the person is lawfully present' before using force (§ 704.1(3)); the same 2017 Act added the presumption of reasonable belief for homes, workplaces and occupied vehicles (§ 704.2A), clarified that merely displaying a weapon is not deadly force (§ 704.2(2)), and added an immunity section. The defence is not available to someone participating in a forcible felony, riot or duel, someone who provoked force as an excuse to injure the other, or someone who provoked force by unlawful acts, unless the response was grossly disproportionate and put them in imminent danger of death or serious injury, or they withdrew and clearly signalled an end to the fight (§ 704.6). Section 704.13 states that a person justified in using reasonable force against an aggressor 'pursuant to section 704.4' is immune from criminal or civil liability for the aggressor's damages; as written it refers to § 704.4 (defence of property), and the sources consulted do not show a pretrial immunity hearing procedure.

At home

Iowa Code § 704.2A (2017 Acts ch. 69): a person is presumed to reasonably believe deadly force is necessary when the other person is unlawfully entering by force or stealth (or has entered and remains in) the defender's dwelling, place of business or employment, or occupied vehicle, or is unlawfully removing someone from it, and the defender knows or has reason to believe this. The presumption does not apply if the defender is engaged in a criminal offence or using the place to further one, against a parent or guardian taking their own child, against a peace officer lawfully entering, or against a lawful resident with no protective or no-contact order.

What the law says
Iowa Code § 704.1(3)
A person who is not engaged in illegal activity has no duty to retreat from any place where the person is lawfully present before using force as specified in this chapter.
Iowa Code § 704.1(1)–(2)
“Reasonable force” means that force and no more which a reasonable person, in like circumstances, would judge to be necessary to prevent an injury or loss and can include deadly force if it is reasonable to believe that such force is necessary to avoid injury or risk to one’s life or safety or the life or safety of another ... 2. A person may be wrong in the estimation of the danger or the force necessary to repel the danger as long as there is a reasonable basis for the belief of the person and the person acts reasonably in the response to that belief.
Iowa Code § 704.2A(1)
a person is presumed to reasonably believe that deadly force is necessary to avoid injury or risk to one’s life or safety or the life or safety of another in either of the following circumstances: a. ... (1) Unlawfully entering by force or stealth the dwelling, place of business or employment, or occupied vehicle of the person using force ...
Iowa Code § 704.6
The defense of justification is not available to the following: 1. One who is participating in a forcible felony, or riot, or a duel. 2. One who initially provokes the use of force against oneself, with the intent to use such force as an excuse to inflict injury on the assailant. 3. One who initially provokes the use of force against oneself by one’s unlawful acts, unless ...
Iowa Code § 704.13
A person who is justified in using reasonable force against an aggressor in defense of oneself, another person, or property pursuant to section 704.4 is immune from criminal or civil liability for all damages incurred by the aggressor pursuant to the application of reasonable force.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Iowa Code 2026, §§ 704.1, 704.2, 704.2A, 704.3, 704.6, 704.13 (Iowa Legislature)
