d20c3e94c1f76a77.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Puerto Rico

Part of United States, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Puerto Rico has its own Penal Code (Act 146-2012). Under Article 25, a person who defends life, dwelling, property or rights, their own or another's, under a reasonable fear of imminent harm is not criminally liable if there was a reasonable need for the means used, there was no provocation by the defender, and no more harm than necessary was inflicted; to justify a killing, the defender must have reasonably believed they were in imminent or immediate danger of death or serious bodily harm. Article 25 itself does not mention retreat, so outside homes, vehicles and workplaces the test is necessity and proportionality. Act 92-2018 (S.B. 39, approved 17 April 2018) added Article 25A, which creates rebuttable presumptions in favour of a person who uses force, including deadly force, against someone unlawfully entering an occupied dwelling, vehicle, place of business or employment, or kidnapping someone there. The presumptions do not apply against someone with a legal right to be there, a parent or guardian taking their own child, a law enforcement officer, or when the defender provoked the other or was committing a crime. Article 25A(e) says the trier of fact 'shall not take into consideration the possibility of the actor could have avoided the confrontation'; because it sits in the article on dwellings, vehicles and workplaces, whether it reaches public places is not settled by the text. A person who acts in self-defence under Article 25A is not criminally or civilly liable for the harm or death caused to the aggressor; no pretrial immunity hearing procedure was found.

At home

Article 25A of the Penal Code (added by Act 92-2018, approved 17 April 2018) presumes reasonable belief of imminent harm, no provocation and reasonable need for the means used when the actor knew or had reason to believe the other person was unlawfully entering, or trying to enter, the occupied dwelling, vehicle, place of business or employment, or kidnapping someone inside; a parallel presumption covers killings where the actor faced imminent risk of death or serious harm. The fact-finder may not consider whether the actor could have avoided the confrontation, and the defender is not criminally or civilly liable.

The separate country-level file PRI.json classifies Puerto Rico as 'statute'; this entry uses 'proportional' because the no-retreat sentence is confined to Article 25A (dwelling, vehicle, business or workplace) and Article 25's general rule rests on reasonable necessity and proportionality.

What the law says
Puerto Rico Penal Code (Act 146-2012), art. 25, as amended by Act 92-2018 (official English translation)
Any person who defends his life, dwelling, property or rights, or the life, dwelling, property, or rights of another under circumstances where there is a reasonable fear of imminent harm shall not be criminally liable, provided that there was a reasonable need for the means used to prevent or avoid harm, there was no provocation by the party claiming self-defense, and that no more harm than necessary is inflicted to avoid or prevent harm. When alleging self-defense to justify causing death to a human being, it is necessary to have reasonable belief that when causing death to the aggressor, the aggrieved or defending person was in imminent or immediate danger of death or serious bodily harm.
Penal Code art. 25A(e) (Act 92-2018)
In order to determine the validity of self-defense, the trier of fact shall not take into consideration the possibility of the actor could have avoided the confrontation.
Penal Code art. 25A(a) (presumption)
It shall be presumed that the actor had a reasonable belief that he or another person was at risk of suffering imminent physical harm, that there was no provocation by the actor, and that there was a reasonable need for the means used and for the harm caused to prevent or avoid harm if: (1) the actor knew or had reason to believe that the person against whom force or violence was used: (i) unlawfully entered or was attempting to unlawfully enter the dwelling, vehicle, place of business or employment occupied at that moment by the actor or the person the actor protects ...
Penal Code art. 25A(g) (immunity)
A person who acting in self-defense uses force against or causes death to a human being in accordance with the provisions of this Article shall not be criminally or civilly liable for the harm or death caused to the aggressor.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Act No. 92-2018 (S.B. 39), official English translation (Oficina de Gerencia y Presupuesto, Puerto Rico (Biblioteca Virtual))

a4953d10f799f0b0.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Hong Kong S.A.R.

Part of China, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Hong Kong's Criminal Procedure Ordinance (Cap. 221, s 101A) allows 'such force as is reasonable in the circumstances' to prevent crime or make an arrest; self-defence remains a common-law defence, tested by whether the defendant honestly believed force was needed and whether the force was reasonable on the facts as they believed them. In HKSAR v Kei Cheuk-yin (紀卓言), [2020] HKCFI 2111 (HCMA 567/2019, 1 September 2020), the Court of First Instance allowed an appeal where the magistrate had relied on the defendant being able to walk away; the judge said that 'retreat as far as he can' is not a necessary condition of self-defence, only one factor the fact-finder may consider in deciding whether force was needed and whether it was reasonable. This is a single-judge appeal ruling, not a Court of Final Appeal decision.

What the law says
Criminal Procedure Ordinance (Cap. 221), s 101A(1) (from previous entry)
(1) A person may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances in the prevention of crime or in effecting or assisting in the lawful arrest of offenders or suspected offenders or of persons unlawfully at large.
HKSAR v 紀卓言 (Kei Cheuk-yin), [2020] HKCFI 2111, HCMA 567/2019 (Deputy High Court Judge Yau Tak-hong 游德康, 1 Sept 2020), para. 20
20. 本席認為必須清楚指出，「退無可退 (retreat as far as he can)」不是自衛的必要條件，而只是其中一個事實裁斷者可以考慮上訴人是否需要使用武力及所使用的武力是否合理的元素。 [English rendering, not an official translation: 20. I consider it must be clearly stated that 'retreat as far as he can' is not a necessary condition of self-defence, but only one element the fact-finder may consider in deciding whether the appellant needed to use force and whether the force used was reasonable.]
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • 香港特別行政區 訴 紀卓言 [2020] HKCFI 2111 (judgment text sourced from the Hong Kong Judiciary) (vLex Hong Kong)

db9a58723b521a72.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kuwait

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Kuwait's Penal Code (Law No. 16 of 1960) says there is no crime when an act is done in defence of one's own or another's person or property (art. 32), but legitimate defence exists only where the danger is present and cannot be repelled by turning in time to the protection of the public authorities (art. 33). Intentional killing is permitted only to repel a crime feared to cause death or serious wounds (on reasonable grounds), rape or indecent assault by force, or abduction by force or threat (art. 34). Exceeding the limits in good faith may be treated as an excuse with a misdemeanour penalty (art. 36). A 2021 bulletin of the Ministry of Justice's Kuwait Institute for Judicial and Legal Studies says the defence must be proportionate to the attack and cites Court of Cassation appeal no. 567/2005 (29 July 2006) restating art. 33; neither the code nor these sources say whether a person must flee or retreat.

What the law says
قانون الجزاء (Penal Code, Law No. 16 of 1960), المادة 32
لا جريمة إذا ارتكب الفعل دفاعاً عن نفس مرتكبه أو ماله، أو دفاعاً عن نفس الغير أو ماله. [English rendering, not an official translation: There is no crime if the act is committed in defence of the actor's own person or property, or in defence of another's person or property.]
Penal Code, المادة 33
لا تقوم حالة الدفاع الشرعي إلا إذا كان الخطر الذي يهدد النفس أو المال خطراً حالاً، لا يمكن دفعه بالالتجاء في الوقت المناسب إلى حماية السلطات العامة. [English rendering, not an official translation: A state of legitimate defence exists only if the danger threatening the person or property is present and cannot be repelled by resorting in good time to the protection of the public authorities.]
Penal Code, المادة 34
لا يبيح الدفاع الشرعي القتل العمد إلا إذا قصد به دفع جريمة من الجرائم الآتية: أولاً: جريمة يتخوف أن يحدث منها الموت أو جراح بالغة، إذا كان لهذا التخوف أسباب معقولة. ثانياً: مواقعة أنثى بغير رضاها أو هتك عرض إنسان بالقوة. ثالثاً: اختطاف إنسان بالقوة أو بالتهديد. [English rendering, not an official translation: Legitimate defence does not permit intentional killing unless it is aimed at repelling one of these crimes: first, a crime feared to cause death or serious wounds, if the fear has reasonable grounds; second, intercourse with a female without her consent or indecent assault by force; third, abduction of a person by force or threat.]
Penal Code, المادة 36
إذا جاوز الشخص بحسن نية حدود الدفاع الشرعي، بأن استعمل لدفع الاعتداء قوة تزيد على القدر الذي كان يستعمله الشخص المعتاد إذا وجد في ظروفه دون أن يكون قاصداً إحداث أذى أشد مما يستلزمه الدفاع، جاز للقاضي، إذا كان الفعل جناية، أن يعده معذوراً وأن يحكم عليه بعقوبة الجنحة بدلاً من العقوبة المقررة في القانون. [English rendering, not an official translation: If a person in good faith exceeds the limits of legitimate defence by using more force than an ordinary person in his circumstances would, without intending more harm than the defence required, the judge may, if the act is a felony, treat him as excused and impose a misdemeanour penalty instead.]
Kuwait Institute for Judicial and Legal Studies, 'ماهية الدفاع الشرعي وفق قانون الجزاء', Institute Bulletin no. 32 (May 2021), citing Court of Cassation appeal no. 567/2005 (criminal), session 29/7/2006
وفي أحكام محكمة التمييز تواترت المبادئ الهامة التي تقوم عليها حالة الدفاع الشرعي حين أقرت أن حالة الدفاع الشرعي طبقا لنص المادة 33 من قانون الجزاء الكويتي لا تقوم إلا إذا كان الخطر الذي يهدد النفس أو المال خطرا حالا لا يمكن دفعه بالالتجاء في الوقت المناسب إلى حماية السلطات العامة وهي لا تتوافر أيضا متى أثبت الحكم أن المتهم هو الذي اعتدى على المجني عليها. ... ولكن أن يكون رد العدوان متناسبا مع العدوان وأن يكون حالا [English rendering, not an official translation: Court of Cassation rulings have consistently held that, under art. 33, legitimate defence exists only if the danger is present and cannot be repelled by resorting in good time to the public authorities, and it does not exist where the judgment establishes that the accused was the one who attacked the victim. ... but the response to the aggression must be proportionate to it and present.]
What was tried

One Arabic web search for the Penal Code self-defence articles. No ruling or commentary on whether the person attacked must flee was found; the PDF text extraction scrambled some line order, and the quotes above were reassembled from it (art. 33 matches the Ministry bulletin's quotation exactly).

a31fef82fa70521c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Somaliland

Part of Somalia (claimed); de facto independent, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991 and governs itself, but most of the world treats it as part of Somalia: Israel became the first UN member state to recognise it, on 26 December 2025, while the African Union, Somalia, IGAD, the EU and others opposed that recognition (sources checked to January 2026). In practice Somaliland applies the 1962 Somali Penal Code (in force since 1964, a near word-for-word copy of the 1930 Italian code), except for articles that conflict with its sovereignty, Islamic Sharia or its constitution. Under article 34 a person who acts because they were 'compelled by the necessity of defending' their own or another's right against an actual danger of unlawful injury is not punishable, 'provided that the defence is proportionate to the injury'. The code says nothing about retreat or the home, and no Somaliland court decisions on whether a person must avoid the attack were found. If the defender exceeds the limits of necessity through negligence (culpa), they are punished under the rules for negligent crimes where such a crime exists (art. 37).

What the law says
Penal Code (Legislative Decree No. 5 of 16 December 1962), art. 34 – Private Defence
Whoever has committed an act, having been compelled by the necessity of defending his own or another person's right against the actual danger of an unlawful injury, shall not be punishable provided that the defence is proportionate to the injury
Penal Code 1962, art. 37 – Excess Committed With Culpa
Where, in committing any of the acts referred to in articles 33, 34, 35 and 36, the limits imposed by necessity are exceeded with culpa, and where the act constitutes a crime committed with culpa, the provisions relating to crimes committed with culpa shall apply.
Somalilandlaw.com, 'Somaliland Criminal Laws' (on continued application of the code)
On reassertion of its independence in 1991, the Republic of Somaliland decided to continue applying the Penal Code ... The Code has been in force in Somaliland since then, but, under Article 130(5) of the Constitution (and prior to that under the Somaliland National Charter), all the articles in the Code which are in conflict with Somaliland sovereignty, Islamic Sharia or the fundamental rights and freedoms enshrined in the Somaliland Constitution are null and void.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • Emergency session on Israel's recognition of Somaliland (6 January 2026) (Amani Africa)
  • International recognition of Somaliland (used as a pointer only) (Wikipedia), CC BY-SA 4.0

a5a3cac37251167b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Northern Mariana Islands

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

The Northern Mariana Islands (a US commonwealth) has its own criminal code, but its no-retreat rule comes from the courts. In Commonwealth v. Demapan (2008 MP 16) the CNMI Supreme Court adopted 'the majority view that defendants are not required to retreat before using reasonable deadly or non-deadly force to defend against unlawful aggressors', and ordered a new trial because the jury had not been told there is no duty to retreat. Self-defence requires a reasonable fear of imminent danger, force used only against an unlawful aggressor, and force that is necessary and proportional; deadly force is justified only if the person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent death or great bodily harm, and 'it is never reasonable to use deadly force against a non-deadly attack'. Once self-defence evidence is presented, the prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt (6 CMC § 251(b), as described by the court). The sources opened did not cover a special home rule, excessive self-defence or civil immunity.

What the law says
Commonwealth v. Demapan, 2008 MP 16 (CNMI Supreme Court, 15 August 2008), ¶¶ 29–30
we adopt the majority view that defendants are not required to retreat before using reasonable deadly or non-deadly force to defend against unlawful aggressors. ... Commonwealth residents have no duty to retreat before using reasonable force in defending against unlawful aggressors.
Commonwealth v. Demapan, 2008 MP 16, ¶ 29 (elements)
(1) the defendant must have a reasonable fear of imminent danger; (2) the defendant may only use force against an unlawful aggressor; (3) the defendant's use of force must be necessary; and (4) the defendant's use of force must be proportional to the aggressor's use of force.
Commonwealth v. Demapan, 2008 MP 16 (deadly force)
Force likely to cause death or great bodily harm is justified in self-defense only if a person reasonably believes that such force is necessary to prevent death or great bodily harm. ... It is never reasonable to use deadly force against a non-deadly attack.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Commonwealth v. Demapan, 2008 MP 16 (CNMI Law Revision Commission (cnmilaw.org))

a5847184442abfe2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kogi

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.
Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963), on ss. 59-65
When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Zamfara Shari'a Penal Code 2000, s. 204(c), as reproduced in Peters (2001), Appendix Five
204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Notes on the Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), Second Edition 1963, annotated by S. S. Richardson (reproduces the code text with commentary) (anticor.world (scan of the 1963 Government Printer edition))
  • Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC 430/1962) [1963] NGSC 24 (25 March 1963) (NigeriaLII)
  • Sunday Jackson v The State, SC/CR/1026/2022, Supreme Court of Nigeria, 7 March 2025 (certified true copy, 62 pp., scanned; text obtained by OCR) (CITY LAWYER Magazine (hosting the certified copy, watermarked TheNigeriaLawyer))
  • Sunday Jackson v The State (2025-03) Legalpedia 85898 (SC) - summary (Legalpedia)
  • Laoye v The State, SC 200/1984, 25 October 1985, [1985] 2 N.S.C.C. 1251 (headnote) (vLex Nigeria)
  • Ruud Peters, The Reintroduction of Islamic Criminal Law in Northern Nigeria: A Study Conducted on Behalf of the European Commission (Lagos, September 2001), Appendix Five: Relevant provisions of the Shari'a Penal Codes (Zamfara text, Kano deviations noted) (ecoi.net (hosting the EC study))
  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

9ab62090152975b9.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

East Timor

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Timor-Leste's Penal Code (Decree-Law 19/2009) defines legítima defesa (art. 44) as the action of the agent necessary to ward off an unlawful, imminent or current attack on any legally protected interest of the agent or a third party; the official-style English translation published by CJAD reads 'committed as the necessary means to repel an imminent or present unlawful attack'. The article has no proportionality wording and does not mention retreat. Excess of means may lead to an extraordinary reduction of sentence, and excess from non-blameworthy disturbance, fear or fright excludes guilt (art. 48). No Timorese court decision, JSMP trial report or commentary on whether flight must be preferred was found, so the retreat question stays unsettled.

At home

No specific home-defence rule; art. 44 covers defence of any legally protected interest of the agent or a third party.

What the law says
Código Penal (Timor-Leste), art. 44 Legítima defesa
Considera-se legítima defesa a actuação do agente necessária ao afastamento de uma agressão ilícita, iminente ou actual, a quaisquer interesses juridicamente protegidos do agente ou de terceiro.
Criminal Code 2009 (English translation), art. 44 Legitimate defense, as published by CJAD
An act constitutes legitimate defense when committed as the necessary means to repel an imminent or present unlawful attack on legally protected interests of the perpetrator or of a third party.
Código Penal (Timor-Leste), art. 48 Excesso de legitima defesa
1. Os meios que, pela sua espécie ou grau de utilização, forem excessivos para a acção defensiva do agente podem determinar a atenuação extraordinária da pena que caberia ao crime. 2. O excesso de meios utilizados na legítima defesa devido a perturbação, medo ou susto, não censuráveis, exclui a culpa do agente.
What was tried

web search: 'Timor-Leste Tribunal de Recurso legítima defesa acórdão meio necessário/fugir JSMP' (only RTP news on unrelated cases and CJAD); 'JSMP Timor-Leste self-defence court decision Article 44 Penal Code trial report' (ICJ 1992 report, Special Panels cases at internationalcrimesdatabase.org, LSE X v Timor-Leste — none on the retreat question, not opened); 'Tribunal de Recurso legítima defesa artigo 44 Código Penal acórdão homicídio' (Brazilian/Portuguese material only). No Timorese decision or commentary found.

Sources (read 2026-10-17, 2026-10-18)

c5f841582451ea1c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

United States Minor Outlying Islands

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

The Minor Outlying Islands (such as Wake, Midway, Johnston, Palmyra, Baker, Howland, Jarvis, Kingman Reef and Navassa) have no local criminal code found here. Federal criminal law reaches places within the 'special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the United States', which 18 U.S.C. § 7 defines to include lands reserved for federal use and guano islands considered as appertaining to the United States; whether each island falls under a given clause was not checked. Federal self-defence law comes from the courts, not a statute: in Brown v. United States (1921) the Supreme Court rejected a jury instruction that a person attacked must always retreat if he safely can. It held that failure to retreat is only 'a circumstance to be considered' and that 'Detached reflection cannot be demanded in the presence of an uplifted knife', so a person who reasonably believes he faces death or grievous bodily harm may stand his ground.

What the law says
18 U.S.C. § 7(3)-(4)
(3) Any lands reserved or acquired for the use of the United States, and under the exclusive or concurrent jurisdiction thereof, or any place purchased or otherwise acquired by the United States by consent of the legislature of the State in which the same shall be, for the erection of a fort, magazine, arsenal, dockyard, or other needful building. (4) Any island, rock, or key containing deposits of guano, which may, at the discretion of the President, be considered as appertaining to the United States.
Brown v. United States, 256 U.S. 335 (1921)
Detached reflection cannot be demanded in the presence of an uplifted knife. Therefore in this Court, at least, it is not a condition of immunity that one in that situation should pause to consider whether a reasonable man might not think it possible to fly with safety or to disable his assailant rather than to kill him ... Rationally the failure to retreat is a circumstance to be considered with all the others in order to determine whether the defendant went farther than he was justified in doing; not a categorical proof of guilt.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • 18 U.S. Code § 7 - Special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the United States defined (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)
  • Brown v. United States, 256 U.S. 335 (1921) (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)

9bb2eef6d4d2851c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Oregon

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Oregon's Criminal Code, largely unchanged since 1971, lets a person use the degree of force they reasonably believe necessary to defend themselves or a third person against imminent unlawful force (ORS 161.209). Deadly force is allowed only if the person reasonably believes the other is committing or attempting a felony involving force against a person, a burglary in a dwelling, or is using or about to use unlawful deadly force (ORS 161.219). The statutes say nothing about retreat. In State v. Sandoval (2007) the Oregon Supreme Court read the 1971 code and held that 'the legislature did not intend to require a person to retreat before using deadly force against the imminent use of deadly physical force by another', so there is no duty to retreat anywhere the person is, by court ruling rather than a stand-your-ground statute. Force is not justified for someone who provoked the other with intent to injure or kill, or who was the initial aggressor unless they withdrew and effectively communicated that (ORS 161.215). A person in lawful possession of premises may use force to stop a criminal trespass, but deadly force only in defence of a person or to prevent arson or a violent felony (ORS 161.225). No statutory presumption of reasonable fear, civil immunity or pretrial immunity hearing was found; the official pattern jury instruction text was not located online.

At home

Deadly force is allowed against someone the defender reasonably believes is committing or attempting a burglary in a dwelling (ORS 161.219(2)). A person in lawful possession of premises may use force to stop a criminal trespass, and deadly force only in defence of a person or to prevent arson or a violent felony by the trespasser (ORS 161.225). No separate castle presumption or immunity statute was found.

What the law says
ORS 161.209 (1971 c.743 §22)
... a person is justified in using physical force upon another person for self-defense or to defend a third person from what the person reasonably believes to be the use or imminent use of unlawful physical force, and the person may use a degree of force which the person reasonably believes to be necessary for the purpose.
ORS 161.219
Notwithstanding the provisions of ORS 161.209, a person is not justified in using deadly physical force upon another person unless the person reasonably believes that the other person is: (1) Committing or attempting to commit a felony involving the use or threatened imminent use of physical force against a person; or (2) Committing or attempting to commit a burglary in a dwelling; or (3) Using or about to use unlawful deadly physical force against a person.
State v. Sandoval, 342 Or 506, 513-14, 156 P3d 60 (2007) (leading case)
The legislature did not intend to require a person to retreat before using deadly force against the imminent use of deadly physical force by another.
ORS 161.215(1)
Notwithstanding ORS 161.209, a person is not justified in using physical force upon another person if: (a) With intent to cause physical injury or death to another person, the person provokes the use of unlawful physical force by that person. (b) The person is the initial aggressor, except that ... the person withdraws from the encounter and effectively communicates to the other person the intent to do so ...
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • ORS Chapter 161 (Oregon State Legislature)
  • Stand Your Ground in Oregon (Giffords Law Center)

The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.
Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963), on ss. 59-65
When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Zamfara Shari'a Penal Code 2000, s. 204(c), as reproduced in Peters (2001), Appendix Five
204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.

Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. a76ac5244fba29bf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tonga

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Tonga's Criminal Offences Act defines assault as force used 'wilfully and without lawful justification', and the courts treat self-defence as a lawful justification governed by common-law principles; no section of the Act setting out self-defence rules was found in the sources opened. In Giles v Police (1999) Chief Justice Ward said the law 'has always recognised a reasonable right to self-defence' and noted that the old common-law requirement to retreat as far as possible before using force is 'no longer a requirement for self defence'. Force must still be reasonable and proportionate: a blow given in anger rather than as reasonable force is not justified, and once self-defence is raised the Crown must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt (R v Malupo, 2023). In Malupo the Supreme Court rejected self-defence where the attacks were disproportionate and driven by 'furious vengeance', and it noted the defendant could have driven away, so a real chance to avoid the fight still counts against the defendant on the facts. No partial 'excessive self-defence' rule was found.

At home

In Giles v Police (1999) the Supreme Court held that an occupier may use reasonable force to remove a trespasser who refuses to leave, using only so much force as is necessary, may 'match force with force' if the trespasser uses force, and has no duty to retreat in the face of a trespasser.

What the law says
Giles v Police [1999] TOSC 24 (Supreme Court, Ward CJ, 15 June 1999)
The same principles apply as to the defence of self defence but, even in the days when the common law required a man to have retreated as far as he could before he could justify force to defend himself [no longer a requirement for self defence], it asked no duty to retreat in the face of a trespasser.
Giles v Police [1999] TOSC 24
The law has always recognised a reasonable right to self-defence as a form of lawful justification of the force used.
R v Malupo [2023] TOSC 46 (Supreme Court, Cooper J, 11 September 2023)
Once self-defence is raised it is for the Crown to rebut that beyond a reasonable doubt.

62cb22b818609842.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ohio

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Ohio law allows a person to act in self-defence, defence of another or defence of their residence, and once there is evidence supporting that, the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the person did not act in self-defence (ORC 2901.05(B)(1), burden shifted by HB 228 effective 28 March 2019). Before 2021 Ohio required retreat outside the home and vehicle; Senate Bill 175, effective 6 April 2021, changed ORC 2901.09 so that a person has no duty to retreat before using force 'if that person is in a place in which the person lawfully has a right to be', which covers public places, workplaces and vehicles. The same law bars juries from considering the possibility of retreat when deciding whether the person reasonably believed force was necessary. Since 2008 there has been a presumption of self-defence when deadly force is used against someone unlawfully entering or inside the residence or vehicle the defender occupies; it can be rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence and does not apply against a lawful resident or to a defender who is unlawfully present. The 2021 law added the same no-retreat rule and the same bar on considering retreat to civil lawsuits (ORC 2307.601), but no separate civil immunity or pretrial immunity hearing was found in these sections. The statutes do not themselves define who may claim self-defence; the 'lawfully has a right to be' condition limits the no-retreat rule.

At home

Since 2008 (SB 184) a person is presumed to have acted in self-defence when using deadly force against someone unlawfully entering, or who has unlawfully entered, the residence or vehicle they occupy (ORC 2901.05(B)(2)). 'Residence' includes a dwelling where one lives or is a guest, including an attached porch and tents. The presumption does not apply against a lawful resident or if the defender is unlawfully there.

What the law says
ORC 2901.09(B)-(C) (amended by SB 175, eff. 6 April 2021)
(B) For purposes of any section of the Revised Code that sets forth a criminal offense, a person has no duty to retreat before using force in self-defense, defense of another, or defense of that person's residence if that person is in a place in which the person lawfully has a right to be. (C) A trier of fact shall not consider the possibility of retreat as a factor in determining whether or not a person who used force in self-defense, defense of another, or defense of that person's residence reasonably believed that the force was necessary to prevent injury, loss, or risk to life or safety.
ORC 2901.05(B)(1) (burden on prosecution, HB 228, 2019)
... the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused person did not use the force in self-defense, defense of another, or defense of that person's residence, as the case may be.
ORC 2901.05(B)(2) (presumption)
... a person is presumed to have acted in self-defense or defense of another when using defensive force that is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm to another if the person against whom the defensive force is used is in the process of unlawfully and without privilege to do so entering, or has unlawfully and without privilege to do so entered, the residence or vehicle occupied by the person using the defensive force.
ORC 2307.601(B) (civil cases)
... the person has no duty to retreat before using force in self-defense, defense of another, or defense of that person's residence if that person is in a place in which the person lawfully has a right to be.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

5530cb55fb0e6b0c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Edo

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.

ca7bd761549bb26b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Yucatán

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Yucatán's Penal Code (art. 21-II(a)) treats legitimate defence as a justification: a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence used was necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. The code does not mention retreating, fleeing or avoiding the attack. Intruders into a dwelling are presumed to be lawful targets of defence unless shown otherwise. A person who exceeds the limits of legitimate defence receives one quarter of the penalty for the offence (art. 22). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 21-II(a) presumes legitimate defence, unless proven otherwise, when harm is caused to someone who tries to enter or enters without right the place where the defender lives (temporarily or permanently), their family's home or that of anyone they must defend, its outbuildings, or a place holding property they must protect; the same applies to harm caused to an intruder surprised there in circumstances suggesting a possible attack.

What the law says
Código Penal del Estado de Yucatán, art. 21, fracc. II, inciso a)
a) La legítima defensa, cuando se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa empleada y no medie [...] provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. Se presume que existe legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, cuando se cause un daño a quien por cualquier medio trate de penetrar o penetre, sin derecho, al lugar en que habite de forma temporal o permanente el que se defiende, al de su familia o al de cualquier persona respecto de las que el agente tenga la obligación de defender, a sus dependencias o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que exista la misma obligación. Igual presunción existirá cuando el daño se cause a un intruso al momento de sorprenderlo en alguno de los lugares antes citados en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión.
Código Penal del Estado de Yucatán, art. 22, third paragraph
Al que se exceda en los casos de defensa legítima, estado de necesidad, cumplimiento de un deber o ejercicio de un derecho se le impondrá la cuarta parte de las penas o medidas de seguridad correspondientes al delito de que se trate, siempre y cuando con relación al exceso, no exista otra causa de exclusión del delito.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal del Estado de Yucatán (última reforma D.O. 28-julio-2026) (H. Congreso del Estado de Yucatán)
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Katsina

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ondo

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.

The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.

9b8727c0eaf6597f.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Montana

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Montana Code Annotated § 45-3-110 (headed 'No duty to summon help or flee', enacted by Ch. 332, L. 2009) says that, except for the aggressor and forcible-felon exclusions in § 45-3-105, 'a person who is lawfully in a place or location and who is threatened with bodily injury or loss of life has no duty to retreat from a threat or summon law enforcement assistance prior to using force', and that this applies to anyone offering evidence of justifiable use of force under §§ 45-3-102 (defence of person), 45-3-103 (occupied structure) or 45-3-104 (other property). Deadly force is justified only when reasonably believed necessary to prevent imminent death or serious bodily harm or a forcible felony (§ 45-3-102). Once the defendant offers evidence of justified force, the state must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the force was not justified (§ 46-16-131). A person whose force was allowable is immune from civil damages (§ 27-1-722).

At home

Mont. Code § 45-3-103: force to prevent or end an unlawful entry into or attack on an occupied structure; deadly force if the entry is made or attempted and the person reasonably believes it necessary to prevent an assault on someone inside, or to prevent a forcible felony in the structure. § 45-3-110 removes any duty to retreat.

What the law says
Mont. Code Ann. § 45-3-110 No duty to summon help or flee (En. Sec. 1, Ch. 332, L. 2009) – MCA 2025
45-3-110. No duty to summon help or flee. Except as provided in 45-3-105, a person who is lawfully in a place or location and who is threatened with bodily injury or loss of life has no duty to retreat from a threat or summon law enforcement assistance prior to using force. The provisions of this section apply to a person offering evidence of justifiable use of force under 45-3-102, 45-3-103, or 45-3-104. History: En. Sec. 1, Ch. 332, L. 2009.
Mont. Code Ann. § 45-3-102
However, the person is justified in the use of force likely to cause death or serious bodily harm only if the person reasonably believes that the force is necessary to prevent imminent death or serious bodily harm to the person or another or to prevent the commission of a forcible felony.
Mont. Code Ann. § 46-16-131
In a criminal trial, when the defendant has offered evidence of justifiable use of force, the state has the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant's actions were not justified.

305bb1c9a0795ecf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Lebanon

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 184 of Lebanon's Penal Code (1943, as amended by Legislative Decree 112 of 16 September 1983) treats as the exercise of a right any act required by a present necessity to repel an unjust, unprovoked attack on one's own or another's person or property; exceeding the limits of defence may bring exemption from punishment under article 228 (acting in a fit of intense emotion). Article 563 counts as self-defence resisting violent theft or pillage, and repelling a person who enters or tries to enter an inhabited house by night by climbing, breaking or using false keys; a daytime entry gives only a mitigating excuse. The code does not mention retreat or escape, and no Lebanese court ruling or commentary on whether a person must flee was found. In 2023 the Court of Cassation upheld the dropping of charges against a man who shot a burglar in his home, as self-defence, with reporting describing the test as proportion between the response and the danger.

At home

Penal Code art. 563(2): repelling a person who enters or attempts to enter an inhabited house or its adjoining annexes by night, by climbing, breaking or false keys, counts as self-defence; if by day, only the mitigating excuse of art. 251 applies.

What the law says

يعد ممارسة حق كل فعل قضت به ضرورة حالية لدفع تعرض غير محق ولا مثار على النفس أو الملك أو نفس الغير أو ملكه ،ويستوي في الحماية الشخص الطبيعي والشخص المعنوي. إذا وقع تجاوز في الدفاع أمكن إعفاء فاعل الجريمة من العقوبة في الشروط المذكورة في المادة 228. [English rendering, not an official translation: Every act required by a present necessity to repel an unjust and unprovoked attack on the person or property, or on the person or property of another, is deemed the exercise of a right; natural and legal persons are equally protected. If the defence is exceeded, the offender may be exempted from punishment under the conditions in article 228.]
Penal Code, المادة 183
لا يعد جريمة الفعل المرتكب في ممارسة حق بغير تجاوز. [English rendering, not an official translation: An act committed in the exercise of a right without excess is not a crime.]
Penal Code, المادة 228 (second paragraph)
على أنه إذا افرط فاعل الجريمة في ممارسة حق الدفاع المشروع لا يعاقب إذا أقدم على الفعل في ثورة انفعال شديد إنعدمت معها قوة وعيه أو إرادته. [English rendering, not an official translation: However, if the offender exceeded the right of legitimate defence, he is not punished if he acted in a fit of intense emotion that deprived him of awareness or will.]
Penal Code, المادة 563
تعد الأفعال الآتية من قبيل الدفاع عن النفس: -1فعل من يدافع عن نفسه أو عن أمواله أو عن نفس الغير أو عن أمواله تجاه من يقدم باستعمال العنف على السرقة أو النهب. -2الفعل المقترف عند دفع شخص دخل أو حاول الدخول ليلا إلى منزل أهل أو إلى ملحقاته الملاصقة بتسلق السياجات أو الجدران أو المداخل أو ثقبها أو كسرها أو باستعمال مفاتيح مقلدة أو أدوات خاصة. وإذا وقع الفعل نهاراً فلا يستفيد الفاعل إلا من العذر المخفف عملاً بالمادة 251. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

0ae1f62d5df8172c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Palau

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Palau's Penal Code (Title 17 of the Palau National Code, as rewritten by an Act passed on 24 February 2014) follows the US Model Penal Code. Force is justified when the actor believes it is immediately necessary to protect themselves against unlawful force, and deadly force when they believe it is necessary to protect against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping, rape or forcible sodomy (17 PNC § 304(a)–(b)). There is a duty to retreat before using deadly force: deadly force is not justified if the actor knows they can avoid the need for it 'with complete safety by retreating', by giving up a thing to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to stop doing something they have no duty to do (§ 304(e)(2)). There is no duty to retreat from one's own home or workplace, except for an initial aggressor or a co-worker attacked at the shared workplace. If the defender's belief that force was necessary was reckless or negligent, the justification is not available for offences that can be committed recklessly or negligently (§ 310(a)), so excessive or mistaken force can still lead to conviction for a lesser offence.

At home

No duty to retreat from one's own dwelling or place of work, unless the defender was the initial aggressor or is attacked at work by someone whose workplace it also is (17 PNC § 304(e)(2)(A)).

What the law says
17 PNC § 304(a)–(c) Use of force in self-protection
(a) Subject to the provisions of this section and of 17 PNC section 308, the use of force upon or toward another person is justifiable when the actor believes that such force is immediately necessary for the purpose of protecting himself or herself against the use of unlawful force by the other person on the present occasion. (b) The use of deadly force is justifiable under this section if the actor believes that deadly force is necessary to protect himself or herself against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping, rape, or forcible sodomy.
17 PNC § 304(e)(2)
(e) The use of deadly force is not justifiable under this section if: ... (2) The actor knows that he or she can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating or by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim of right thereto or by complying with a demand that he or she abstain from any action which he or she has no duty to take, except that: (A) The actor is not obliged to retreat from his or her dwelling or place of work, unless he or she was the initial aggressor or is assailed in his or her place of work by another person whose place of work the actor knows it to be;
17 PNC § 310(a)
When the actor believes that the use of force upon or toward the person of another is necessary for any of the purposes for which such belief would establish a justification under sections 303 to 309 of this Chapter, but the actor is reckless or negligent in having such belief or in acquiring or failing to acquire any knowledge or belief that is material to the justifiability of the actor’s use of force, the justification afforded by those sections is unavailable in a prosecution for an offense for which recklessness or negligence, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.

e4f74a01176a0960.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New Jersey

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

New Jersey's Code of Criminal Justice (N.J.S.A. 2C:3-4) allows deadly force only when the person reasonably believes it is necessary to protect against death or serious bodily harm. It keeps a duty to retreat: deadly force is not justified if the person knows they can avoid the need for it with complete safety by retreating, or by surrendering property to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to stop doing something they have no duty to do. The duty does not apply in one's own dwelling, unless the person was the initial aggressor; it does apply in vehicles, workplaces and public places. The model jury charge tells jurors to judge whether a safe retreat was known by the total circumstances, including the excitement of the moment. A separate rule for intruders in a dwelling (added 1987, amended 1999, L.1999, c.73) lets the occupant use force or deadly force when they reasonably believe it is immediately necessary against an intruder's unlawful force. The State must disprove self-defence beyond a reasonable doubt, and a valid claim fully exonerates the defendant of offences against the aggressor (State v. Rodriguez, 195 N.J. 165 (2008), cited in the charge). Deadly force is not justified for someone who provoked the use of force against themselves in the same encounter with the purpose of causing death or serious harm. No statutory presumption of reasonable fear, civil immunity provision or pretrial immunity hearing was found in the sources checked.

At home

A person is not obliged to retreat from their own dwelling (which the model jury charge says includes the porch) unless they were the initial aggressor (N.J.S.A. 2C:3-4b(2)(b)(i)). Under a 1987 amendment (L.1987, c.120), force or deadly force against an intruder who is unlawfully in a dwelling is justifiable when the occupant reasonably believes it is immediately necessary to protect themselves or others in the dwelling from unlawful force by the intruder (2C:3-4c).

Statute quotes taken through a summarising fetch tool limited to short excerpts; the official legislature site was not reachable.

The actor knows that he can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating ...
N.J.S.A. 2C:3-4b(2)(b)(i) (dwelling exception)
The actor is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling, unless he was the initial aggressor
N.J.S.A. 2C:3-4c(1) (intruder in dwelling; L.1987, c.120)
...the use of force or deadly force upon or toward an intruder who is unlawfully in a dwelling is justifiable ...
Model Criminal Jury Charge, Justification - Self Defense in Self Protection (rev. 8/18/25)
If you find that the defendant knew that they could avoid the necessity of using deadly force by retreating, provided that the defendant knew they could do so with complete safety, then the defense is not applicable to them.
Model Criminal Jury Charge, Justification - Use of Force upon an Intruder (2C:3-4c)
The law exonerates a defendant who uses force (or deadly force) upon or toward an intruder who is unlawfully in a dwelling when the defendant reasonably believes that the force is immediately necessary for the purpose of protecting himself/herself or other person(s) in the dwelling against the use of unlawful force by the intruder on the present occasion.
