92e651b865f80747.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Yobe

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.
Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963), on ss. 59-65
When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Zamfara Shari'a Penal Code 2000, s. 204(c), as reproduced in Peters (2001), Appendix Five
204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.

5fdc4caffb2a9bfa.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Qatar

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Article 49 of Qatar's Penal Code (Law No. 11 of 2004) says there is no crime when an act is done in the exercise of the right of legitimate defence, and lists the conditions: the defender faces (or believes they face) a present danger from a crime against their own or another's person or property; it is impossible to turn in time to the public authority to avert the danger; the defender has no other means of repelling the danger; and the act is necessary to repel the attack and proportionate to it. The word 'retreat' does not appear, but the 'no other means' condition is the kind of wording the map treats as a duty to avoid the attack; no Qatari court ruling interpreting it was found. Article 50 allows intentional killing only to repel an act feared to cause death or serious wounds (on reasonable grounds), rape or forcible indecent assault, abduction, felony arson, destruction or theft, or night-time entry into an inhabited house. Exceeding the limits in good faith may be treated as an excuse with a misdemeanour penalty (art. 51).

At home

Penal Code art. 50: intentional killing in legitimate defence is permitted to repel 'الدخول ليلاً في منزل مسكون أو في أحد ملحقاته' (entering an inhabited house or its annexes by night), subject to the conditions of art. 49.

What the law says
قانون العقوبات (Penal Code, Law No. 11 of 2004), المادة 49 (extracts)
لا جريمة إذا وقع الفعل استعمالاً لحق الدفاع الشرعي. ويقوم حق الدفاع الشرعي إذا توفرت الشروط الآتية: ... إذا واجه المدافع خطراً حالاً من جريمة على نفسه أو ماله أو نفس غيره أو ماله، أو اعتقد قيام هذا الخطر ... أن يتعذر على المدافع الإلتجاء إلى السلطة العامة في الوقت المناسب لاتقاء الخطر. ... ألا يكون أمام المدافع وسيلة أخرى لدفع الخطر. ... أن يكون الفعل لازماً لدفع الاعتداء، ومتناسباً معه. [English rendering, not an official translation: There is no crime if the act is done in exercise of the right of legitimate defence. The right exists if these conditions are met: the defender faces a present danger from a crime against his own or another's person or property, or believes it exists; it is impossible for the defender to resort in time to the public authority to avert the danger; the defender has no other means to repel the danger; the act is necessary to repel the attack and proportionate to it.]
Penal Code, المادة 50 (extracts)
لا يبيح حق الدفاع الشرعي القتل عمداً، إلا إذا أريد به دفع أحد الأمور الآتية: ... فعل يخشى أن يحدث عنه وفاة أو جراح بليغة، إذا كان لهذه الخشية أسباب معقولة. ... مواقعة أنثى كرهاً، أو هتك عرض أي شخص بالقوة. ... اختطاف إنسان. ... جنايات الحريق أو الإتلاف أو السرقة. ... الدخول ليلاً في منزل مسكون أو في أحد ملحقاته. [English rendering, not an official translation: The right of legitimate defence does not permit intentional killing unless intended to repel one of the following: an act feared to cause death or serious wounds, if there are reasonable grounds for the fear; forcible intercourse with a female or forcible indecent assault on any person; abduction of a person; felonies of arson, destruction or theft; entering an inhabited house or one of its annexes by night.] (Note: the fetched extract read 'يحدث عند وفاة'; 'عنه' is the likely reading but was not confirmed.)
Penal Code, المادة 51 (extracts)
إذا جاوز الشخص بحسن نية حدود الدفاع الشرعي، بأن استعمل لدفع الاعتداء قوة تزيد على القدر الذي كان يستعمله الشخص العادي إذا وجد في ظروفه، ودون أن يكون قاصداً إحداث أذىً أشد مما يستلزمه الدفاع ... جاز للقاضي، إذا كان الفعل جناية، أن يَعد الشخص معذوراً ... ويحكم عليه بعقوبة الجنحة بدلاً من العقوبة المقررة في القانون [English rendering, not an official translation: If a person in good faith exceeds the limits of legitimate defence by using more force than an ordinary person in his circumstances would, without intending more harm than the defence required, the judge may, if the act is a felony, treat him as excused and impose a misdemeanour penalty instead of the prescribed one.]

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

692164fab8d89b99.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Querétaro

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Querétaro's Penal Code (art. 25-III) excludes the offence when a person repels a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests, if the defence or means used were rationally necessary and the defender did not provoke it. The code does not require retreat; the code's statement of reasons (exposición de motivos) says the drafters deliberately removed 'the possibility of avoiding the attack' from the formula because such negative elements in practice made the defence unusable. Home intruders (when no immediate help is available) and members of a group of three or more threatening a serious attack are presumed to be lawful targets. Excess exists when the means used and harm caused are not proportionate, and is punished with three days to seven years in prison (art. 71). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 25-III presumes legitimate defence, unless proven otherwise, when, with no possibility of immediate help, harm is caused to someone who by violence or any other means tries to enter without right the home of the agent or their family, its outbuildings, those of anyone they must defend, or a place holding property they must protect; or who is found there in circumstances revealing a possible attack. The presumption also covers harm caused to a member of a group of three or more people whose attitude shows a serious attack is imminent.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Querétaro, art. 25, fracc. III
III. Cuando se repela una agresión real, actual, o inminente, sin derecho, en protección de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad racional de la defensa o medios empleados y no medie provocación suficiente o inmediata por parte del agredido o de la persona a quien se defiende. Se presumirá como legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, cuando no habiendo posibilidad de auxilio inmediato se cause un daño a quien a través de la violencia, o por cualquier otro medio, trate de penetrar sin derecho, al hogar del agente, de la familia de éste, o a sus dependencias, o a las de cualquier persona que tenga el mismo deber de defender, o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que exista la misma obligación; o bien, lo encuentre en alguno de aquellos lugares en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de agresión, o cuando se cause un daño a quien forme parte de un grupo de tres o más personas cuya actitud demuestre la inminencia de una agresión grave. Existe exceso en el caso previsto en esta fracción cuando no haya proporcionalidad en el medio empleado y en el daño ocasionado;
Código Penal para el Estado de Querétaro, art. 71
ARTÍCULO 71.- Al que se exceda en los casos de legítima defensa, estado de necesidad, cumplimiento de un deber, ejercicio de un derecho y obediencia jerárquica en los términos del Artículo 25 de este Código, se aplicará pena de tres días a siete años de prisión.
Código Penal para el Estado de Querétaro, Exposición de motivos (on art. 25-III)
En aras de la exactitud del concepto, se cambia el término "necesidad racional del medio empleado" por "necesidad racional de la defensa" suprimiéndose de la fórmula elementos planteados en forma negativa que en la práctica llegan a hacer nugatoria esta causa de licitud, tales como la posibilidad de evitar la agresión y la estimación de la facilidad para la reparación del daño causado.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal para el Estado de Querétaro (text including reforms to 27 May 2022), copy published by the Municipality of Corregidora (SSPM) (Municipio de Corregidora, Querétaro (copy of the state code))
  • Código Penal para el Estado de Querétaro, with statement of reasons (older consolidation) (Justia México)
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

1a86a5eb7dbe13e6.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Arkansas

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Arkansas allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes the other person is committing or about to commit a felony involving force or violence, is using or about to use unlawful deadly force, or is imminently endangering the person's life as part of a continuing pattern of domestic abuse (Ark. Code § 5-2-607(a)). Until 2021 Arkansas had a duty to retreat outside the home: deadly force was not allowed if the person knew they could avoid it by retreating with complete safety, unless they were in their dwelling or its curtilage and not the original aggressor. Act 250 of 2021 (Senate Bill 24) struck that rule and replaced it with a rule that a person is not required to retreat before using deadly force if they are lawfully present, reasonably believe the other person is imminently threatening death or serious injury, are not the initial aggressor or provoker, are not a felon illegally carrying the gun used (except at home), and are not engaged in crime or gang activity that gave rise to the need for force. The same Act added a matching no-retreat rule for non-deadly force (§ 5-2-606(c)). Force is not justified for a person who provoked the other with the purpose of injuring or killing them, for an initial aggressor who has not withdrawn in good faith and communicated it, or in a fight by agreement (§ 5-2-606(b)). In the home, a 1981 statute presumes any force used against an unlawful intruder was lawful and necessary unless the prosecution or plaintiff overcomes it by clear and convincing evidence (§ 5-2-620). The sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or pretrial immunity hearing in Arkansas.

At home

Ark. Code § 5-2-620 (Acts 1981, No. 880) declares the right to defend oneself, others and property in the home against a person unlawfully entering or trying to enter a 'fundamental right', and creates a legal presumption that any force used for that purpose was lawful and necessary unless overcome by clear and convincing evidence. Before 2021, the dwelling and its curtilage were the main exception to Arkansas's duty to retreat; a felon in possession of a firearm keeps the no-retreat protection only in or at their own dwelling or curtilage (§ 5-2-607(b)(4) as amended 2021).

What the law says
Ark. Code § 5-2-607(b) (as amended by Act 250 of 2021)
A person is not required to retreat before using deadly physical force if the person: (1) Is lawfully present at the location where deadly physical force is used; (2) Has a reasonable belief that the person against whom the deadly physical force is used is imminently threatening to cause death or serious physical injury to the person or another person; (3) Except as provided under § 5-2-606(b)(2)(B), is not the initial aggressor and has not provoked the person against whom the deadly physical force is used; ... (5) Is not engaged in criminal activity that gives rise to the need for the use of deadly physical force at the time the deadly physical force is used; and (6) Is not engaged in any activity in furtherance of a criminal gang, organization, or enterprise ...
Ark. Code § 5-2-607(a)
A person is justified in using deadly physical force upon another person if the person reasonably believes that the other person is: (1) Committing or about to commit a felony involving physical force or violence; (2) Using or about to use unlawful deadly physical force; or (3) Imminently endangering the person's life or imminently about to victimize the person as described in § 9-15-103 from the continuation of a pattern of domestic abuse.
Ark. Code § 5-2-606(b)
A person is not justified in using physical force upon another person if: (1) With purpose to cause physical injury or death to the other person, the person provokes the use of unlawful physical force by the other person; (2)(A) The person is the initial aggressor. ... (3) The physical force involved is the product of a combat by agreement not authorized by law.
Ark. Code § 5-2-620(b)
There is a legal presumption that any force or means used to accomplish a purpose described in subsection (a) of this section was exercised in a lawful and necessary manner, unless the presumption is overcome by clear and convincing evidence to the contrary.

4b529f2b301e42d4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tennessee

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Tennessee's self-defence statute (Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-11-611) says that a person who is not engaged in conduct that would be a felony or Class A misdemeanor, and is in a place where they have a right to be, has no duty to retreat before threatening or using force, including force likely to cause death or serious bodily injury, if they reasonably believe there is imminent danger of death or serious bodily injury, the danger is real or honestly believed, and the belief is founded on reasonable grounds. The no-retreat rule therefore applies in public, at work and in vehicles. A rebuttable presumption of reasonable fear applies when deadly force is used against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering a residence, business, dwelling or vehicle (§ 39-11-611(c)). In State v. Perrier (2017) the Supreme Court held that the 'not engaged in unlawful activity' wording then in the statute was a condition on the no-retreat privilege, that the trial judge decides whether it applies, and that a person engaged in unlawful activity must retreat; the current text now refers to conduct constituting a felony or Class A misdemeanor. Self-defence is not available to someone who provoked the other's use of unlawful force, unless they abandon the encounter or clearly communicate an intent to do so (§ 39-11-611(e)). A person whose use of force is justified is immune from civil liability (§ 39-11-622), and a separate law (§ 39-17-1322) limits arrest for justified use of a weapon, but no general criminal immunity or pretrial immunity hearing was found. In 2026, Public Chapter 1100 widened deadly force to protect property against arson, burglary, robbery and aggravated animal cruelty.

At home

A person using deadly force within a residence, business, dwelling or vehicle is presumed to have held a reasonable belief of imminent death or serious bodily injury when the person against whom force was used was unlawfully and forcibly entering or had entered (Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-11-611(c)). Public Chapter 1100 of 2026 (in force 1 July 2026) amended § 39-11-614 to allow deadly force in defence of property against arson, burglary, robbery, aggravated robbery and aggravated cruelty to animals, for people in a place where they lawfully reside and not engaged in a felony or Class A misdemeanor.

The official Tennessee Code (LexisNexis) could not be opened; statute quotes are short verbatim excerpts obtained through a summarising fetch tool, with bracketed words as connectors. The year the no-retreat rule was first enacted (commonly given as 2007) was not confirmed from a primary source.

What the law says
Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-11-611(b)
Notwithstanding § 39-17-1322, a person who is not engaged in conduct ... [that would constitute] a felony or Class A misdemeanor and is in a place where the person has a right to be ... has no duty to retreat before threatening or using force intended or likely to cause death ...
Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-11-611(c) (presumption)
Any person using force intended or likely to cause death or serious bodily injury within a residence ...
State v. Perrier, 536 S.W.3d 388 (Tenn. 2017) (leading case)
... a person who is not engaged in unlawful activity … has no duty to retreat before threatening or using force against another person[.] ... [The Court held a defendant is entitled to a no-retreat instruction] only when the person was not engaged in unlawful activity and was in a place the person had a right to be.
Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-11-622(a) (civil immunity)
is justified in using such force and is immune from civil liability for the use of such force, unless:

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cyprus

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Cyprus's Criminal Code (Cap. 154) contains a necessity defence in s. 17 (act done only to avert consequences otherwise unavoidable, not exceeding what is reasonably necessary) and s. 3 directs that the Code be interpreted according to the principles of legal interpretation prevailing in England, with its expressions presumed to bear the meaning given to them in English criminal law. No section of Cap. 154 on self-defence as such was found, and no Cypriot Supreme Court judgment stating whether a person must retreat before using defensive force was found: five Supreme Court criminal appeals returned by searches for 'αυτοάμυνα' with retreat terms (Ποινικές Εφέσεις 50/2018 & 137/2018 of 8.4.2020; 208/2015 of 14.11.2018; 71/2018 of 11.9.2019; 4/2020 of 31.1.2022; and a 2025 Court of Appeal decision 136/22) were opened and none deals with self-defence. The retreat question therefore remains unsettled by the sources found.

What the law says
Ποινικός Κώδικας (Criminal Code), Cap. 154, s. 3
Ο Κώδικας αυτός θα ερμηνεύεται σύμφωνα με τις αρχές νομικής ερμηνείας που επικρατούν στην Αγγλία, οι εκφράσεις όμως που χρησιμοποιούνται σε αυτόν θα θεωρούνται ως κατά τεκμήριο ότι χρησιμοποιούνται με την έννοια την οποία απέδωσε σε αυτές το αγγλικό ποινικό δίκαιο [Our rendering: This Code shall be interpreted according to the principles of legal interpretation prevailing in England, and the expressions used in it shall be presumed to be used with the meaning given to them by English criminal law]
Criminal Code, Cap. 154, s. 17 (Κατάσταση ανάγκης — necessity)
Πράξη ή παράλειψη, που διαφορετικά θα συνιστούσε ποινικό αδίκημα, δυνατόν να μη καταλογιστεί σε αυτόν που διέπραξε, αν αυτός μπορέσει να αποδείξει ότι αυτή έγινε ή παραλείφθηκε μόνο για αποτροπή συνεπειών διαφορετικά αναπότρεπτων [...] ότι η πράξη δεν υπερέβη το εύλογα αναγκαίο [Our rendering: An act or omission that would otherwise be a criminal offence may not be imputed to the person who did it if he can prove that it was done or omitted only to avert consequences otherwise unavoidable ... and that the act did not exceed what was reasonably necessary]

b2caeb46e25b65b6.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Equatorial Guinea

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Equatorial Guinea long applied the Spanish Penal Code of 1963, whose article 8(4) excused a person acting in defence of their person or rights if there was an unlawful attack, 'rational necessity of the means used to prevent or repel it', and no sufficient provocation by the defender; it did not mention retreat. On 19 September 2022 the President signed a new penal code (best known for abolishing the death penalty for ordinary crimes), taking effect 90 days after publication. The text of the new code's self-defence article could not be found, so the current position is marked unclear.

At home

Under the 1963 Spanish-era Penal Code (art. 8(4)), in defence of a dwelling or its outbuildings, unlawful entry at night or when the dwelling is in an isolated place counted as an unlawful attack.

What the law says
Código Penal (1963, Spanish text applied in Equatorial Guinea), art. 8(4) — text from an OCR-scanned copy, cleaned of scanning errors; superseded by the 2022 code
4.º El que obra en defensa de su persona o derechos, siempre que concurran las circunstancias siguientes: Primera. Agresión ilegítima. En caso de defensa de los bienes, se reputará agresión ilegítima el ataque a los mismos que constituya delito y los ponga en grave peligro de deterioro o pérdida inminentes. En caso de defensa de la morada o sus dependencias, se reputará agresión ilegítima la entrada indebida en aquella o éstas durante la noche o cuando radiquen en lugar solitario. Segunda. Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla. Tercera. Falta de provocación suficiente por parte del que se defiende.

386ea743149a0831.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Oyo

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.

  • Agbonmwanre Omoregie v The State, SC 301/2006, 19 December 2008, (2008-12) Legalpedia (SC) 18215 (summary) (Legalpedia)
  • Emmanuel Ogar Akong Edoko v The State, SC.315/2012, 27 February 2015 (summary; Cross River, Criminal Code s. 286) (Legalpedia)
  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

ea5a5b2ac0bddfc2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Oklahoma

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Oklahoma's self-defence law is in statute (21 O.S. § 1289.25). A person who is not engaged in an unlawful activity and is attacked in any place where they have a right to be has no duty to retreat and may meet force with force, including deadly force, if they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent death or great bodily harm to themselves or another, or to prevent a forcible felony (subsection D). Inside a dwelling, residence, occupied vehicle, place of business or place of worship, a person using deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering is presumed to have acted from reasonable fear; the presumption does not apply against a lawful resident without a protective order, against a parent or guardian taking their own child, or if the defender is engaged in unlawful activity. A person who uses force as the section permits 'is justified' and 'immune from criminal prosecution and civil action', which includes being charged; police may not arrest without probable cause that the force was unlawful, and a court must award fees and lost income to a defendant found immune in a civil suit. The Court of Criminal Appeals allows a pretrial immunity hearing at which the defendant must prove justification by a preponderance of the evidence (State v. Bradford, 2024 OK CR 3, affirming a grant of immunity). In Dawkins v. State (2011 OK CR 1) the court held the 'unlawful activity' bar covers people actively committing a crime at the time (for example using an illegal weapon or an ongoing assault), not people with minor past infractions. Pointing a weapon to deter a forcible felony is not a crime under the section. The stand-your-ground jury instruction (OUJI-CR 8-15A) is used for attacks outside a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle.

At home

21 O.S. § 1289.25 (the 'Physical or Deadly Force Against Intruder' law) declares that citizens have a right to expect absolute safety in their homes, places of business and places of worship. A person is presumed to have held reasonable fear of death or great bodily harm when using deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering (or who has entered) a dwelling, residence, occupied vehicle, place of business or place of worship, or trying to remove someone from it; the intruder is presumed to intend violence. 'Dwelling' includes an attached porch and tents.

Statute text was read from a 2023 bill that reprints § 1289.25 with proposed amendments (committee bold not visible in extracted text); the quoted subsections D and F match the wording cited in OUJI-CR 8-15A and the 2024 OCCA opinion. Year of original enactment of subsection D was not confirmed from a primary source.

What the law says
21 O.S. § 1289.25(D)
A person who is not engaged in an unlawful activity and who is attacked in any other place where he or she has a right to be has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground and meet force with force, including deadly force, if he or she reasonably believes it is necessary to do so to prevent death or great bodily harm to himself or herself or another or to prevent the commission of a forcible felony.
21 O.S. § 1289.25(F) (immunity)
A person who uses defensive force, as permitted pursuant to the provisions of subsections A, B, D and E of this section, is justified in using such defensive force and is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of such defensive force. As used in this subsection, the term "criminal prosecution" includes charging or prosecuting the defendant.
21 O.S. § 1289.25(A)
The Legislature hereby recognizes that the citizens of the State of Oklahoma have a right to expect absolute safety within their own homes, places of business or places of worship ...
OUJI-CR 8-15A, Defense of Person - Right to Stand Your Ground

01f03ae10993b58c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Jordan

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Jordan's Penal Code (No. 16 of 1960, as amended to Law 8 of 2011 in the version found) treats as the exercise of a right any act required by a present necessity to repel an unjustified and unprovoked attack on oneself, another person, or property (art. 60). For killing or wounding in defence of oneself or one's honour, article 341 adds that the defence must happen during the attack, the attack must be unjust, and the person attacked must be unable to escape or rid themselves of the attack except by killing, wounding or effective force. Article 60 says that where defence was exceeded the offender may be exempted from penalty under the conditions set out elsewhere in the code. Attacks on a dwelling (art. 342) are treated as legitimate defence whether by day or night.

At home

Article 342 makes it legitimate defence to kill, wound or use any force to protect life, honour or property against a person who enters or tries to enter a dwelling, by night or by day, by climbing its fence or walls, being in its yard inside the fence without justification, or forcing its entrances or doors by breaking them or using keys or special tools.

What the law says
قانون العقوبات رقم 16 لسنة 1960 (Penal Code No. 16 of 1960), art. 60
1- يعد ممارسة للحق: كل فعل قضت به ضرورة حالية لدفع تعرض غير محق ولا مثار عن النفس أو المال أو نفس الغير أو ماله. 2- يستوي في الحماية الشخص الطبيعي والشخص المعنوي. 3- اذا وقع تجاوز في الدفاع أمكن إعفاء فاعل الجريمة من العقوبة في الشروط المذكورة في المادة ... [cross-reference illegible in the copy found]

تعد الأفعال الآتية دفاعا ً مشروعاً: 1- فعل من يقتل غيره او يصيبه بجراح او بأي فعل مؤثر دفاعا ً عن نفسه او عرضه او نفس غيره او عرضه، بشرط أن: أ- يقع الدفع حال وقوع الاعتداء. ب- أن يكون الاعتداء غير محق. ج- أن لا يكون في استطاعة المعتدى عليه التخلص من هذا الاعتداء الا بالقتل او الجرح او الفعل المؤثر.

يعد دفاعا مشروعا كل قتل او اصابة بجراح او ارتكاب أي فعل مؤثر يتم لحماية النفس او العرض او المال من اعتداء شخص يدخل او يحاول الدخول، ليلا او نهارا، الى بيت سكن وذلك بتسلق سياج او سور او جدران أي منهما او بالتواجد في ساحته داخل السياج او السور دون مبرر او باقتحام مداخله او ابوابه بثقبها او كسرها او خلعها او باستعمال مفاتيح او ادوات خاصة لهذه الغاية.

8ac92f32e3d8a2b7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Plateau

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.
Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963), on ss. 59-65
When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Zamfara Shari'a Penal Code 2000, s. 204(c), as reproduced in Peters (2001), Appendix Five
204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC 430/1962) [1963] NGSC 24 (25 March 1963) (NigeriaLII)
  • Sunday Jackson v The State, SC/CR/1026/2022, Supreme Court of Nigeria, 7 March 2025 (certified true copy, 62 pp., scanned; text obtained by OCR) (CITY LAWYER Magazine (hosting the certified copy, watermarked TheNigeriaLawyer))
  • Sunday Jackson v The State (2025-03) Legalpedia 85898 (SC) - summary (Legalpedia)
  • Laoye v The State, SC 200/1984, 25 October 1985, [1985] 2 N.S.C.C. 1251 (headnote) (vLex Nigeria)
  • Ruud Peters, The Reintroduction of Islamic Criminal Law in Northern Nigeria: A Study Conducted on Behalf of the European Commission (Lagos, September 2001), Appendix Five: Relevant provisions of the Shari'a Penal Codes (Zamfara text, Kano deviations noted) (ecoi.net (hosting the EC study))
  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

9005ea7744a53689.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Djibouti

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Djibouti's Penal Code says a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves, another person or property, they act at the same moment in a way necessary for legitimate defence, unless the means used or the result obtained were disproportionate to the seriousness of the attack. The code does not mention retreat. Defence is presumed when repelling forced or tricked entry into an inhabited place, or against violent robbery. No specific rule on excessive self-defence was found in these articles.

At home

Article 30 presumes legitimate defence for a person who acts to repel entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place (with no night-time condition), or to defend against violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 30
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, face à une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même, autrui ou un bien, accomplit dans le même temps un acte nécessaire à la défense légitime d'elle-même, d'autrui ou du bien, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés ou le résultat obtenu et la gravité de l'atteinte. Est présumé avoir agi en état de défense légitime celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1 ° pour repousser l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité. 2° pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Pohnpei

Part of Federated States of Micronesia, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The Pohnpei Code (2012 edition), Title 61 Criminal Law, leaves its justification chapter empty: Chapter 3 is headed '[Reserved – Principles of Justification]'. No self-defence section, and no Pohnpei decision on retreat, was found; the FSM national case law (Alik v. Kosrae, 1994) states the necessity test without mentioning retreat.

CHAPTER 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS 2 PRINCIPLES OF PENAL LIABILITY 3 [RESERVED – PRINCIPLES OF JUSTIFICATION] 4 INCHOATE CRIMES 5 OFFENSES AGAINST THE PERSON

The national Revised Criminal Code (Title 11 FSMC, PL 11-72) contains no self-defence section in the chapters checked; self-defence comes from court decisions annotated in the Code. The FSM Supreme Court Appellate Division held that a person threatened with imminent serious bodily harm or death may use deadly force if necessary, while non-deadly threats allow only non-deadly force reasonable in light of the aggressor's force (Alik v. Kosrae, 1994). The annotations do not mention retreat, so the retreat question is not settled by the sources opened. The four states (Chuuk, Kosrae, Pohnpei, Yap) have their own codes, which were not reviewed.

6d583cb48e3c608f.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Colima

Part of Mexico, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Código Penal para el Estado de Colima, art. 31(IV): a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack if the defence used is reasonably necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. No avoidance or 'no other means' condition appears in the article, and it does not say the defender need not flee. National Supreme Court (SCJN) theses point both ways: a 1940 thesis (registro 814826) says flight should not be imposed as a condition, while a 1946 thesis (registro 806596) denied the defence where the accused 'could well have avoided the aggression by other means'. No state-specific thesis was found (web search budget ran out), so whether retreat is required is not settled. Excess (art. 82) is punished with one quarter of the penalty for the offence.

At home

Art. 31(IV) presumes legítima defensa, unless proven otherwise, when 'rationally necessary' harm is caused to someone who tries to enter or enters without right the place where the defender or their family lives, even temporarily, its outbuildings, or a place with property they must protect; the same presumption covers harm to an intruder surprised there in circumstances showing a possible attack.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Colima, art. 31, fracción IV
IV. Legítima defensa. Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en protección de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad razonable de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. Se presume que existe legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, cuando se cause un daño racionalmente necesario a quien por cualquier medio trate de penetrar o penetre sin derecho al lugar donde habite, aunque sea en forma temporal, el que se defiende o su familia o cualquier persona respecto de la que el agente tenga el deber de defender, o a las dependencias de ese lugar o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los cuales se tenga el mismo deber. Igual presunción favorecerá al que cause un daño a un intruso en el momento de sorprenderlo en alguno de los lugares citados en el párrafo anterior, en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión;
Código Penal para el Estado de Colima, art. 82, third paragraph
A quien incurra en exceso en los casos previstos en las fracciones IV, V y VI del artículo 31 de este Código, se le impondrá la cuarta parte de la pena o medida de seguridad correspondiente al delito de que se trate, siempre que con relación al exceso no se actualice otra causa de exclusión del delito.
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 814826 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA. EVITABILIDAD DEL PELIGRO), Informe 1940, p. 42
no debe imponerse como condición al injustamente agredido la posibilidad de la fuga, pues en esas condiciones el ejercicio de la legítima defensa se tornaría en imposible en la mayoría de los casos
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 806596 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA), S.J.F. Tomo LXXXVIII, p. 721 (1946)
no puede aceptarse la defensa legítima, si el procesado no estuvo en inminente peligro de perder la vida o en condiciones de suponer este peligro, y pudo muy bien evitar la agresión de que fue víctima por otros medios, o en último extremo, preverla.
What was tried

Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

1e882db485d85857.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bahrain

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Bahrain's Penal Code (Decree-Law No. 15 of 1976) says the right of self-defence arises when a person faces, or reasonably believes they face, imminent danger to their person or property and there is no time to seek the protection of the public authorities (art. 17). No one may inflict more harm than necessary for defence (art. 18). The code does not mention retreat; the stated limits are the time to call the authorities and necessity. Killing is justified only against an act feared to cause death or serious injury, rape or attack on personal freedom, arson, damage or theft, or breaking into an inhabited house (art. 20). Going beyond the limits of a justified act in good faith is an extenuating circumstance, and the judge may exempt the person from punishment (art. 21).

At home

Article 20 allows killing in defence of self or property against, among other acts, 'breaking into an inhabited house or appurtenances thereof'.

What the law says
Penal Code (Decree-Law No. 15 of 1976), arts. 17–18 (official English translation)
Article 17: The right of self-defence commences when the following two factors are present: 1. If the person is in imminent danger of a threat to his own person or property or if he reasonably believes in the imminence of such danger. 2. If there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. ... Article 18: In the exercise of the right of self-defence, no person may inflict more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defence.
Penal Code (Decree-Law No. 15 of 1976), arts. 20–21
Article 20: Murder in self-defence or in defence of property shall not be justified except in the following cases: 1. An act from which death or serious injury is feared. 2. An act of rape, assault or attack against personal freedom. 3. An act of setting fire, causing damage or theft. 4. An act of breaking into an inhabited house or appurtenances thereof. Article 21: Bypassing the extent of a justified act in good faith shall be deemed as an extenuating circumstance. A judgement for exemption may be passed if the judge finds grounds for such exemption.

7b5940b5f31264c2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Northern Cyprus

Part of Cyprus (claimed); de facto administered by the 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus', or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' declared itself a state in 1983; the UN Security Council called that declaration 'legally invalid' and asked all states not to recognise any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus (Resolution 541), and Turkey is the only country that recognises it. In practice its courts apply the colonial-era Criminal Code (Cap. 154), which has no self-defence section, so self-defence comes from English common law, which the TRNC Courts Law 9/76 (s. 38) tells the courts to apply, and from article 15 of the TRNC constitution. According to a 2015 law thesis at Eastern Mediterranean University, the TRNC Supreme Court requires a person to retreat only when retreat is 'possible and safe': in appeal 3/75 (1975) it acquitted a man whose attacker kept hitting him and gave him no chance to escape, citing the English case R v Julien (1969), while in appeal 21/85 it upheld a conviction where the accused struck a second, fatal blow after the attacker fell instead of using his chance to escape. In a 1989 case the court acquitted two women attacked and raped in their tent, saying it would be 'extremely dangerous' to expect people in such terror to weigh their blows coolly. The same thesis says that, as under English common law, excessive force defeats self-defence entirely and there is no partial 'excessive self-defence' verdict in the TRNC.

What the law says
TRNC Constitution, art. 15(3) (as quoted in Gümüş 2015, p. 24)
(3)Yasa ile konduğu zaman ve gösterildiği şekilde: (a)Kişinin ve malvarlığının, başka türlü kaçınılması ve tamiri olanaksız aynı derecede bir zarara karşı savunulması; ... kesin olarak gerekli olduğu kadar zor kullanmak suretiyle yaşama son verilmesi, (1). ve (2). fıkra kurallarına aykırı sayılmaz.
TRNC Supreme Court, Criminal Appeal No. 3/75 (13 June 1975), as summarised in Gümüş 2015, p. 59
Yüksek Mahkeme, Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi’nin sanığı kaçmak zorundaymış gibi değerlendirdiğini, halbuki meşru müdafaada sanığın her zaman kaçmak zorunda olmadığını, ancak kaçmanın mümkün ve güvenli (possible and safe) hallerde gerektiğini belirterek ... sanığın beraatine karar vermiştir. [The Supreme Court held that the trial court had treated the accused as if he were bound to flee, whereas in self-defence the accused is not always bound to flee, but must do so only where escape is possible and safe, and acquitted him.]
TRNC Supreme Court, Criminal Appeal Y/C 21/85 (D.15/87), as quoted in Gümüş 2015, pp. 85–86

a9bf7681e6e61e45.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Lagos

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Lagos replaced the Criminal Code with the Criminal Law of Lagos State 2011 (Ch. C17, in force 8 August 2011). Section 193 restates the unprovoked-assault rule (reasonably necessary force; deadly force only against an assault causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm) and s. 194 the provoked-assault rule, which excuses the provoker only if, before the necessity arose, he 'declined further conflict, quitted or retreated from it as far as practicable'. The 2011 wording drops the Criminal Code's 'cannot otherwise preserve' clause from the unprovoked rule. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases.

What the law says
Criminal Law of Lagos State 2011, Ch. C17, s. 193
193. Self defence against unprovoked assault (1) When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force as is reasonably necessary to defend himself against the assault, provided that the force used is not intended and is not such as is likely to cause death or grievous harm. (2) When a person is unlawfully assaulted and has not provoked the assault, and the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use such force as is reasonably necessary to defend himself from death or grievous harm even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Law of Lagos State 2011, Ch. C17, s. 194
194. Self defence against provoked assault (1) When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other person assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, it shall be lawful for him to use such force as is reasonably necessary to defend himself from death or grievous harm, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. (2) The provision of subsection (1) of this section does not apply where the person using force which causes death or grievous harm— (a) first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; or (b) endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of defending himself arose, except before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, quitted or retreated from it as far as practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Egheghe v The State (SC, 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • Sunday Jackson v The State, SC/CR/1026/2022, Supreme Court of Nigeria, 7 March 2025 (certified true copy, 62 pp., scanned; text obtained by OCR) (CITY LAWYER Magazine (hosting the certified copy, watermarked TheNigeriaLawyer))
  • Sunday Jackson v The State (2025-03) Legalpedia 85898 (SC) - summary (Legalpedia)
  • Matthew Egheghe v The State, SC.304/2017, 23 January 2020, (2020) Legalpedia (SC) 11101 (summary) (Legalpedia)
  • Laoye v The State, SC 200/1984, 25 October 1985, [1985] 2 N.S.C.C. 1251 (headnote) (vLex Nigeria)
  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

9acf9bb9720bdf3d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Chuuk

Part of Federated States of Micronesia, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The Chuuk State Code, Title 12 (Crimes and Punishment), marked 'DRAFT' on fsmlaw.org, has a Chapter 3 on criminal responsibility covering accomplices, mental disease, intoxication and children, but no self-defence section. The national annotated case FSM v. Ruben (Truk, 1981) holds that no more force than necessary may be used against an intruder. Neither mentions retreat.

At home

No more force than necessary to protect oneself, family, home and property from an intruder and to expel the intruder (FSM v. Ruben, 1 FSM Intrm. 34, 37 (Truk 1981)).

What the law says
Chuuk State Code (draft), Title 12, Chapter 3 Criminal Responsibility — list of sections
2001. Liability for crimes of another. 2002. Physical or mental disease, disorder, or defect excluding criminal responsibility. 2003. Evidence of physical or mental disease, disorder, or defect admissible when relevant to element of the offense. 2004. Physical or mental disease, disorder, or defect excluding fitness to proceed. 2005. Statements for purposes of examination and treatment. 2006. Intoxication. 2007. Presumption as to responsibility of children.
Title 11 FSMC annotations — FSM v. Ruben, 1 FSM Intrm. 34, 37 (Truk 1981)
The general rule is that a person can use no more force than is necessary to protect himself, his family, and his home and property from an intruder and to expel the intruder.

Federated States of Micronesia as a whole

The national Revised Criminal Code (Title 11 FSMC, PL 11-72) contains no self-defence section in the chapters checked; self-defence comes from court decisions annotated in the Code. The FSM Supreme Court Appellate Division held that a person threatened with imminent serious bodily harm or death may use deadly force if necessary, while non-deadly threats allow only non-deadly force reasonable in light of the aggressor's force (Alik v. Kosrae, 1994). The annotations do not mention retreat, so the retreat question is not settled by the sources opened. The four states (Chuuk, Kosrae, Pohnpei, Yap) have their own codes, which were not reviewed.

7552eeb195e0317c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Guadeloupe

An overseas region of France, part of France itself. Shown with the entry for France, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 122-5 of the Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. The defence must be simultaneous with the attack; a blow struck after the attacker has left is treated as ordinary violence. Neither art. 122-5 nor art. 122-6 mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Judges decide whether the defence was disproportionate; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes that an excessive response may lead to mitigating circumstances or a conviction for a lesser offence rather than full exoneration.

At home

Art. 122-6 of the Penal Code presumes self-defence for a person who acts "to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place", and against perpetrators of violent theft or looting. The presumption is rebuttable and does not cover daytime intrusions, which fall under the general rule of art. 122-5.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
