a231d91e2575bf9d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nebraska

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Nebraska's self-defence statute, enacted in 1972 (Laws 1972, LB 895) and modelled on the Model Penal Code, allows deadly force only when the actor believes it is necessary to protect themselves against death, serious bodily harm, kidnapping, or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-1409(4)). Nebraska keeps a duty to retreat: deadly force is not justified if the actor knows they can avoid it with complete safety by retreating, by handing over a thing to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to refrain from something they have no duty to do (§ 28-1409(4)(b)). There is no duty to retreat from one's own dwelling or place of work, except for an initial aggressor or a person attacked at work by a co-worker; police and people lawfully helping them need not abandon an arrest. Deadly force is also not justified if the actor, intending to cause death or serious bodily harm, provoked the use of force in the same encounter, and force may not be used to resist a known arrest by a peace officer even if the arrest is unlawful. The Nebraska Supreme Court requires a reasonable and good-faith belief in the need for force, though a defendant may be mistaken about the extent of the danger (State v. Miller, 281 Neb. 343 (2011); State v. Graham, 234 Neb. 275 (1990)); if the belief was reckless or negligent, the justification is unavailable for offences requiring only recklessness or negligence (§ 28-1414(2)). The sources consulted show no stand-your-ground law, no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit, and no pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-1409(4)(b)(i): the actor is not obliged to retreat from their dwelling or place of work, unless they were the initial aggressor or are attacked at work by a co-worker (someone whose place of work the actor knows it to be). There is no statutory presumption of reasonable fear for home intrusions.

What the law says
Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-1409(4)
The use of deadly force shall not be justifiable under this section unless the actor believes that such force is necessary to protect himself against death, serious bodily harm, kidnapping or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat, nor is it justifiable if: (a) The actor, with the purpose of causing death or serious bodily harm, provoked the use of force against himself in the same encounter; or (b) The actor knows that he can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating or by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim of right thereto or by complying with a demand that he abstain from any action which he has no duty to take, except that: (i) The actor shall not be obliged to retreat from his dwelling or place of work, unless he was the initial aggressor or is assailed in his place of work by another person whose place of work the actor knows it to be ...
Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-1414(2)
When the actor believes that the use of force upon or toward the person of another is necessary ... but the actor is reckless or negligent in having such belief ..., the justification afforded by those sections is unavailable in a prosecution for an offense for which recklessness or negligence, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.
State v. Miller, 281 Neb. 343 (2011) (annotation to § 28-1409)
A defendant's use of deadly force in self-defense is justified if a reasonable ground existed under the circumstances for the defendant's belief that he or she was threatened with death or serious bodily harm, even if the defendant was actually mistaken about the extent of the danger.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Nebraska Revised Statutes § 28-1409, Use of force in self-protection (Laws 1972, LB 895, § 4), with annotations (Nebraska Legislature)
  • Nebraska Revised Statutes § 28-1414 (Nebraska Legislature)

fe980bcf84c9674c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Jamaica

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Self-defence in Jamaica is common law, set out by the Privy Council in two Jamaican appeals: Palmer v R (1971) and Beckford v R (1987). A person may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances as they honestly believe them to be, may strike first if an attack is imminent, and the prosecution must disprove self-defence once it is raised. The judges' Criminal Bench Book says there is no general duty to retreat; whether the accused could have retreated is only one factor the jury may weigh in deciding whether the force was reasonably necessary. There is no 'excessive self-defence' halfway house: if the force was excessive and the intent for murder is proved, the defence fails completely and the verdict is murder, not manslaughter.

At home

The Supreme Court of Jamaica's Criminal Bench Book states that at common law a householder may use reasonable force in defence of property, citing R v Hussey (1925), where defence of property (unlike self-defence at that time) did not require retreat; there is no statutory castle doctrine in the sources found.

What the law says
Supreme Court of Jamaica, Criminal Bench Book, ch. 18-1 (Self-Defence), para. 3, citing R v Stanley Brooks (1987) 24 JLR 166 and R v Garnett Shand SCCA 2/93
There is now no general duty to retreat in all cases where self-defence is raised. The question whether the accused's retreat is an element which the jury may consider in deciding whether the force was reasonably necessary.
Criminal Bench Book, ch. 18-1, para. 4 (excessive force), citing R v Wayne Campbell and Mark Lahoo SCCA 119/00
Where a person kills another with the requisite intent for murder in circumstances in which he would have been entitled to an acquittal on the ground of self-defence but for the use of excessive force the defence fails altogether and he is guilty of murder not manslaughter.
Beckford v R [1988] AC 130 (PC Jamaica), Lord Griffiths, as quoted in the Criminal Bench Book
the test to be applied for self-defence is that a person may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances as he honestly believes them to be in the defence of himself or another.

  • Laing (Delroy) v R [2016] JMCA Crim 11 (Court of Appeal of Jamaica)
  • Williams (Ernie) v R [2011] JMCA Crim 37 (Court of Appeal of Jamaica)

974e513a1a7477d7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Palestine

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Palestinian territory has two different penal codes. In Gaza, the British Mandate Criminal Code Ordinance 1936 excuses an act done 'only in order to avoid consequences which could not otherwise be avoided' and which would have caused grievous harm to the person, honour or property of oneself or others one must protect, provided the person did no more than reasonably necessary and the harm caused was not disproportionate (s. 18). In the West Bank, the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960 applies; in the Jordanian text opened, killing or wounding in defence of oneself, one's honour or another person is legitimate only if done during the attack, the attack is unjust, and the person 'is unable to rid himself of this attack except by killing, wounding or the effective act' (art. 341(1)), and excess in defence may lead to exemption from punishment under the conditions of art. 89 (art. 60(3)). Both texts therefore make the defence depend on there being no other way out. The Jordanian copy opened is Jordan's own text amended to 2011; the West Bank applies the 1960 code without Jordan's post-1967 amendments, so the exact West Bank wording could not be confirmed. No court decisions on retreat were found for either territory.

At home

In the Jordanian Penal Code text opened (art. 342), killing or wounding to protect life, honour or property against a person entering or trying to enter a dwelling by night or day, by climbing a fence or wall, being in its yard without reason, or forcing doors or using keys or tools, counts as legitimate defence. Whether this wording is the version in force in the West Bank could not be confirmed (see summary). No home rule was found in the Gaza code text.

What the law says
Criminal Code Ordinance 1936 (Gaza), s. 18
An act or omission which would otherwise be an offence may be excused if the person accused can show that it was done or omitted to be done only in order to avoid consequences which could not otherwise be avoided, and which if they had followed would have inflicted grievous harm or injury to his person or to his honour or his property or to the person or honour of others whom he was bound to protect or to property placed in his charge: Provided that in so acting he did no more than was reasonably necessary for that purpose, and that the harm inflicted by the act or omission was not disproportionate to the harm avoided.
Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960 (applied in the West Bank), art. 341(1) – text as in Jordan's 2011-amended edition
تعد الأفعال الآتية دفاعا ً مشروعاً: 1 فعل من يقتل غيره او يصيبه بجراح او بأي فعل مؤثر دفاعا ً عن نفسه او عرضه او نفس غيره او عرضه ،بشرط أن: أ -يقع الدفع حال وقوع الاعتداء. ب -أن يكون الاعتداء غير محق. ج -أن لا يكون في استطاعة المعتدى عليه التخلص من هذا الاعتداء الا بالقتل او الجرح او الفعل المؤثر.
Jordanian Penal Code 1960, art. 60 (Jordan's 2011-amended edition)
1 يعد ممارسة للحق: كل فعل قضت به ضرورة حالية لدفع تعرض غير محق ولا مثار عن النفس أو المال أو نفس الغير أو ماله. 2 يستوي في الحماية الشخص الطبيعي والشخص المعنوي. 3 اذا وقع تجاوز في الدفاع أمكن إعفاء فاعل الجريمة من العقوبة في الشروط المذكورة في المادة 89.

4062acebad23962d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Brunei

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Brunei's Penal Code (Chapter 22, 2021 edition) contains a 'right of private defence' chapter. Deadly force in defence of the body is allowed against an assault reasonably causing fear of death or grievous hurt, and against assaults intended to rape, kidnap, abduct or wrongfully confine (s 100). The right never extends to more harm than necessary for defence, and there is no right where there is time to seek protection from the public authorities (s 99). The code does not mention retreat and no Brunei court decision on retreat was opened. A person who in good faith exceeds the right of private defence and kills without premeditation commits culpable homicide, not murder (Exception 2 to murder).

At home

s 103: the right of private defence of property extends to causing death against robbery, house-breaking by night, arson of a building, tent or vessel used as a human dwelling, and theft, mischief or house-trespass that reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 22), s 99(3)–(4) [official PDF is an OCR scan; s 99(3) is garbled in the text layer and is given here as printed in the scan's readable form]
(3) There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. (4) The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.
Penal Code (Cap. 22), s 100
The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in section 99, to the voluntary causing of death, or of any other harm, to the assailant if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right is of any of the following descriptions - (a) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of the assault; (b) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of the assault; (c) an assault with the intention of committing rape; ...
Penal Code (Cap. 22), murder, Exception 2
Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law, and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation, and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Laws of Brunei, Chapter 22, Penal Code (2021 Edition) (Attorney General's Chambers, Brunei Darussalam)

02f95fbf5c6b15af.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Alabama

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Alabama allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes another is using or about to use unlawful deadly force, or is committing or about to commit kidnapping, first- or second-degree assault, burglary, robbery, forcible rape or forcible sodomy, and in those listed situations the law presumes the force was justified (Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(b)). A person who is justified, not engaged in unlawful activity, and in any place they have a right to be has no duty to retreat and may stand their ground (§ 13A-3-23(c)); this rule was added by Act 2006-303, and the statute was amended again in 2013, 2016 and 2023. The home, workplace and car are covered by a presumption: deadly force is presumed justified against someone unlawfully and forcefully entering a dwelling, residence, business property or occupied vehicle, and since Act 2023-493 also against someone attacking a person on business property while the business is closed. Force is not justified for someone who provoked the attack intending to hurt the other person, for an initial aggressor who has not withdrawn and clearly communicated it, or in a fight by mutual agreement. A person who used justified force is immune from both criminal prosecution and civil suit, and the defendant may ask for a pretrial hearing where they must prove immunity by a preponderance of the evidence; if they fail, they can still argue self-defence at trial, where the state must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Since 2023, if the defendant hid, altered or destroyed the weapon (rather than handing it unaltered to police without undue delay), the law presumes the force was not justified, though this can be rebutted. Police may investigate but may not arrest without probable cause that the force was unlawful.

At home

Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(b)(1): deadly force is legally presumed justified against a person who is unlawfully and forcefully entering (or has entered) a dwelling, residence, business property or occupied vehicle, or is trying to remove someone from one, or is using force against an occupant while committing a burglary of a dwelling. The presumption does not apply against another lawful resident (unless there is a domestic-violence protective order or no-contact order), a parent or guardian taking their own child, an on-duty police officer, or where the defender is engaged in unlawful activity.

What the law says
Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(c)
A person who is otherwise justified under this section in using physical force, including deadly physical force, and who is not engaged in an unlawful activity, and who is in any place where he or she has the right to be has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground.
Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(b)(1)
A person may use deadly physical force, and is legally presumed to be justified in using deadly physical force in self-defense or defense of another pursuant to this subdivision, if the person reasonably believes that another person is doing any of the following: a. Using or about to use unlawful deadly physical force. ...
Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(d)
a person is not justified in using physical force if any of the following apply: (1) With intent to cause physical injury or death to another, he or she provoked the use of unlawful physical force by the other person. (2) He or she was the initial aggressor, except that his or her use of physical force upon another person is justifiable if he or she withdraws from the encounter and effectively communicates to the other person his or her intent to do so ... (3) The physical force involved was the product of a combat by agreement not specifically authorized by law.
Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(f)(1)–(2)
A person who uses force, including deadly physical force, as justified and permitted in this section, is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of such force, unless the force was determined to be unlawful. ... During any pretrial hearing to determine immunity, the defendant must show by a preponderance of the evidence that he or she is immune from criminal prosecution.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Code of Alabama § 13A-3-23, Use of Force in Defense of a Person (history: Acts 1977 No. 607; Act 2006-303; Act 2013-283; Act 2016-420; Act 2023-493) (Alabama Legislature (ALISON))

193e1f88e5a6ed5c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Arizona

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Arizona allows deadly force when a reasonable person would believe it is immediately necessary to protect against another's use or attempted use of unlawful deadly force (Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-405(A)), and also to prevent a list of serious crimes including arson of an occupied structure, first- or second-degree burglary, kidnapping, murder, manslaughter, sexual assault, child molestation, armed robbery and certain aggravated assaults (§ 13-411). There is no duty to retreat if the person is in a place where they may legally be and is not engaged in an unlawful act (§ 13-405(B)); the crime-prevention section adds that this covers a home, business, land, vehicle 'or any other place in this state where a person has a right to be', and presumes a person acting to prevent one of the listed crimes is acting reasonably. The current wording of § 13-405 including subsection B was enacted by House Bill 2629, signed 11 May 2010. In a home or occupied vehicle, the law presumes the defender reasonably believed force was necessary and that an unlawful intruder posed a deadly threat (§ 13-419). Force is not justified in response to words alone, to resist a known arrest by police (unless the officer uses unlawful force), or by a person who provoked the fight, unless they withdrew or clearly signalled withdrawal and the other person kept attacking (§ 13-404(B)). Self-defence is not an affirmative defence in Arizona: once the defendant presents evidence of justification, the state must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant did not act with justification (§ 13-205); Arizona has no statutory pretrial immunity hearing. In civil suits by a plaintiff harmed while committing a felony, a person who used force to protect themselves or others is presumed to have acted reasonably (§ 12-716).

At home

Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-418 allows physical or deadly force, with no duty to retreat, against a person unlawfully or forcefully entering (or who has entered) a residential structure or occupied vehicle, or removing someone from it, if the defender reasonably believes someone is in imminent peril of death or serious injury. § 13-419 presumes the defender's belief was reasonable and presumes the intruder poses an imminent threat of deadly harm, except against a lawful resident with no protective order, a parent or guardian taking their own child, an on-duty police officer, or where the defender is engaged in unlawful activity.

What the law says
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-405
A. A person is justified in threatening or using deadly physical force against another: 1. If such person would be justified in threatening or using physical force against the other under section 13-404, and 2. When and to the degree a reasonable person would believe that deadly physical force is immediately necessary to protect himself against the other's use or attempted use of unlawful deadly physical force. B. A person has no duty to retreat before threatening or using deadly physical force pursuant to this section if the person is in a place where the person may legally be and is not engaged in an unlawful act.
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-411(B)–(D)
B. There is no duty to retreat before threatening or using physical force or deadly physical force justified by subsection A of this section. C. A person is presumed to be acting reasonably for the purposes of this section if the person is acting to prevent what the person reasonably believes is the imminent or actual commission of any of the offenses listed in subsection A of this section. D. This section includes the use or threatened use of physical force or deadly physical force in a person's home, residence, place of business, land the person owns or leases, conveyance of any kind, or any other place in this state where a person has a right to be.
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-419(A)–(B)
A person is presumed to reasonably believe that the threat or use of physical force or deadly force is immediately necessary ... if the person knows or has reason to believe that the person against whom physical force or deadly force is threatened or used is unlawfully or forcefully entering or has unlawfully or forcefully entered and is present in the person's residential structure or occupied vehicle.
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-404(B)
The threat or use of physical force against another is not justified: 1. In response to verbal provocation alone; or ... 3. If the person provoked the other's use or attempted use of unlawful physical force, unless: (a) The person withdraws from the encounter or clearly communicates to the other his intent to do so reasonably believing he cannot safely withdraw from the encounter; and (b) The other nevertheless continues or attempts to use unlawful physical force against the person.
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-205(A)
Justification defenses under chapter 4 of this title are not affirmative defenses. ... If evidence of justification pursuant to chapter 4 of this title is presented by the defendant, the state must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant did not act with justification.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Arizona Revised Statutes §§ 13-404, 13-405, 13-411, 13-418, 13-419, 13-205, 12-716 (Arizona State Legislature)
  • Bill Text: AZ HB2629 (2010), Chaptered – amends A.R.S. § 13-405; signed by the Governor 11 May 2010 (LegiScan)

bcafd513fb4badaf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

British Indian Ocean Territory

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

The British Indian Ocean Territory has its own Penal Code (1981, revised to 2020). Section 17 says criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property is decided by the principles of English common law, subject to any express provisions. Under English law there is no duty to retreat: the possibility that the defender could have retreated is a factor in judging whether the force was reasonable, not a duty, and force that was disproportionate in the circumstances as the defender believed them to be is not reasonable (Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s. 76, which says it clarifies the existing common-law defences). The Territory has no permanent civilian population.

At home

English law has a separate 'householder case' rule (Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s. 76(8A) and related subsections) for force used by a non-trespasser inside a dwelling against someone believed to be a trespasser; whether that statutory rule applies in the Territory, as opposed to common-law principles, was not confirmed.

What the law says
BIOT Penal Code 1981 (Ch. C.2, revised edition to 1 September 2020), s. 17
Subject to any express provisions in the Code or any other law in operation in the Territory, criminal responsibility for the use of force in the defence of person or property shall be determined according to the principles of English common law.
Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 (England and Wales), s. 76(6A) and (9)
(6A) In deciding the question mentioned in subsection (3), a possibility that D could have retreated is to be considered (so far as relevant) as a factor to be taken into account, rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat. ... (9) This section, except so far as making different provision for householder cases, is intended to clarify the operation of the existing defences mentioned in subsection (2).
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • The Penal Code 1981, Chapter C.2 (revised edition showing the law as at 1 September 2020) (British Indian Ocean Territory Administration)
  • Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, section 76 (legislation.gov.uk (The National Archives)), Open Government Licence v3.0

2d35103c444d8a56.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

West Bank

Part of Palestine, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The West Bank applies the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960, not the Mandate-era code used in Gaza. In the Jordanian text opened, killing or wounding in defence of oneself, one's honour or another person is legitimate only if done while the attack is happening, the attack is unjust, and the person 'is unable to rid himself of this attack except by killing, wounding or the effective act' (art. 341(1)). An act required by a present necessity to repel an unjust, unprovoked attack on oneself, property or another is treated as the exercise of a right, and a person who exceeds the limits of defence may be exempted from punishment under the conditions of article 89 (art. 60). The copy opened is Jordan's own text amended to 2011; the West Bank applies the 1960 code without Jordan's later amendments, so the exact West Bank wording could not be confirmed. No court decisions on retreat were found. (Text taken from the Palestine file's sources; no new research was done for this split.)

At home

In the Jordanian Penal Code text opened (art. 342), killing or wounding to protect life, honour or property against a person entering or trying to enter a dwelling by night or day, by climbing a fence or wall, being in its yard without reason, or forcing doors or using keys or tools, counts as legitimate defence. Whether this wording is the version in force in the West Bank could not be confirmed (see summary).

What the law says
Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960 (applied in the West Bank), art. 341(1) – text as in Jordan's 2011-amended edition
تعد الأفعال الآتية دفاعا ً مشروعاً: 1 فعل من يقتل غيره او يصيبه بجراح او بأي فعل مؤثر دفاعا ً عن نفسه او عرضه او نفس غيره او عرضه ،بشرط أن: أ -يقع الدفع حال وقوع الاعتداء. ب -أن يكون الاعتداء غير محق. ج -أن لا يكون في استطاعة المعتدى عليه التخلص من هذا الاعتداء الا بالقتل او الجرح او الفعل المؤثر.
Jordanian Penal Code 1960, art. 60 (Jordan's 2011-amended edition)
1 يعد ممارسة للحق: كل فعل قضت به ضرورة حالية لدفع تعرض غير محق ولا مثار عن النفس أو المال أو نفس الغير أو ماله. 2 يستوي في الحماية الشخص الطبيعي والشخص المعنوي. 3 اذا وقع تجاوز في الدفاع أمكن إعفاء فاعل الجريمة من العقوبة في الشروط المذكورة في المادة 89.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • قانون العقوبات رقم 16 لسنة 1960 وجميع تعديلاته (Jordan) (Policinglaw.info)
Palestine as a whole

Palestinian territory has two different penal codes. In Gaza, the British Mandate Criminal Code Ordinance 1936 excuses an act done 'only in order to avoid consequences which could not otherwise be avoided' and which would have caused grievous harm to the person, honour or property of oneself or others one must protect, provided the person did no more than reasonably necessary and the harm caused was not disproportionate (s. 18). In the West Bank, the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960 applies; in the Jordanian text opened, killing or wounding in defence of oneself, one's honour or another person is legitimate only if done during the attack, the attack is unjust, and the person 'is unable to rid himself of this attack except by killing, wounding or the effective act' (art. 341(1)), and excess in defence may lead to exemption from punishment under the conditions of art. 89 (art. 60(3)). Both texts therefore make the defence depend on there being no other way out. The Jordanian copy opened is Jordan's own text amended to 2011; the West Bank applies the 1960 code without Jordan's post-1967 amendments, so the exact West Bank wording could not be confirmed. No court decisions on retreat were found for either territory.

7aababb12364c2f5.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ebonyi

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • Sunday Jackson v The State, SC/CR/1026/2022, Supreme Court of Nigeria, 7 March 2025 (certified true copy, 62 pp., scanned; text obtained by OCR) (CITY LAWYER Magazine (hosting the certified copy, watermarked TheNigeriaLawyer))
  • Sunday Jackson v The State (2025-03) Legalpedia 85898 (SC) - summary (Legalpedia)
  • Matthew Egheghe v The State, SC.304/2017, 23 January 2020, (2020) Legalpedia (SC) 11101 (summary) (Legalpedia)
  • Laoye v The State, SC 200/1984, 25 October 1985, [1985] 2 N.S.C.C. 1251 (headnote) (vLex Nigeria)
  • Agbonmwanre Omoregie v The State, SC 301/2006, 19 December 2008, (2008-12) Legalpedia (SC) 18215 (summary) (Legalpedia)
  • Emmanuel Ogar Akong Edoko v The State, SC.315/2012, 27 February 2015 (summary; Cross River, Criminal Code s. 286) (Legalpedia)
  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

af5baeb5882846bd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Trinidad and Tobago

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Self-defence in Trinidad and Tobago is common law. The Court of Appeal (La Roche v The State, 2011) applies the Privy Council's statement in Palmer v R: a person who reasonably believes their life is in danger or that they face serious bodily harm may use the force they believe on reasonable grounds is necessary, and is not guilty even if they kill intentionally. There is no fixed duty to retreat: the possibility of retreating without danger is one of the circumstances the jury considers when judging whether the force was reasonably necessary. A case cited in Robley v Placide held that no legal duty to retreat arises for a police officer acting in the execution of duty. No statute on home defence and no source on how excessive force is treated were found for this entry.

What the law says
La Roche v The State, Court of Appeal of Trinidad and Tobago, Cr. App. No. 32 of 2009 (20 April 2011), quoting Palmer v R [1971] AC 814 at 823
A man who is attacked in circumstances where he reasonably believes his life to be in danger or that he is in danger of serious bodily harm, may use such force as on reasonable grounds he believes is necessary to prevent and resist the attack and if in using such force he kills his assailant he is not guilty of any crime even if the killing was intentional, and in deciding in a particular case whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as in fact was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Robley v Placide (Trinidad and Tobago), citing a 1966 decision reported at 11 W.I.R. 58
no legal duty to retreat could arise in circumstances where a police officer acted in exec[ution of his duty]

  • Robley v Placide (vLex (free excerpt))
  • Jhardat v The State (Court of Appeal, Trinidad and Tobago) – headnote lists 'Duty to retreat' as an issue (vLex (free excerpt))

1e0ca0348c860d43.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Antigua and Barbuda

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Antigua and Barbuda's self-defence law comes from the common law as stated by the Privy Council in Palmer v R, which the Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal applies (Sherfield Bowen v The Queen, 2007). In Kevil Nelson v The Queen (Court of Appeal, Antigua and Barbuda, ANUHCRAP2009/0015, 13 November 2013) the trial judge told the jury that 'A person is not under an obligation to retreat in the face of an attack', while also telling them they could weigh his failure to retreat or run away when the threat posed little danger. The Court of Appeal held that 'The trial judge properly directed the jury on the issue of reasonable force' and dismissed the self-defence complaint. So a court has directed, and the appeal court accepted, that there is no duty to retreat; retreat is a factor in judging whether force was reasonable. These passages were read through the court's own search engine, not the full PDF.

What the law says
Kevil Nelson v The Queen, ECSC Court of Appeal (Antigua and Barbuda), ANUHCRAP2009/0015, delivered 13 Nov 2013 — trial judge's direction quoted in the judgment
Even if you find as a fact that this threat and attack or actual attack pose little danger, his failure to sufficiently retreat, to run away or to otherwise prevent the deceased threat by any other means when he say he was being attacked, and again that’s if you believe the accused was being attacked at the time he shot the deceased…A person is not under an obligation to retreat in the face of an attack.
Kevil Nelson v The Queen (2013), Court of Appeal's finding
The trial judge properly directed the jury on the issue of reasonable force. I am not of the view that the appellant’s defence was undermined in any way.
Sherfield Bowen v The Queen, ECSC Court of Appeal (Antigua and Barbuda), Criminal Appeal No. 4 of 2005, delivered 20 Jun 2007, para. 33
[33] The matters which should be taken into account in directions on self-defence were conveniently adumbrated by Lord Morris in Palmer v R. ... Where an attack is minor, it may be only sensible to take some avoiding action. ... They must decide, on the evidence, whether the attack was such that self-defence was reasonably necessary and whether the act by the accused was reasonably proportionate in the circumstances.

  • Kevil Nelson v The Queen (ANUHCRAP2009/0015, 13 Nov 2013) (Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court)
  • Sherfield Bowen v The Queen (Criminal Appeal No. 4 of 2005, 20 Jun 2007) (Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court)
  • The King v Samuel Cox (ANUHCR 2022/0017, High Court, Smith J, 2023) — quotes Palmer's 'simple avoiding action' passage (Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court)

9fba43efacc8cad4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Luxembourg

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Article 416 of the Penal Code says there is no crime when a killing, wounding or blows were 'commanded by the present necessity of legitimate defence' of oneself or another. The Code says nothing about retreat, but the Court of Appeal (5th chamber, 8 July 2025) stated that the attack must be unjust, the response simultaneous and proportionate, 'and that no other way out be conceivable to escape the aggression', so courts in effect require avoiding the attack when possible. Another 2025 appeal ruling said judges weigh the real options open to the defendant at the moment, and that a blow struck against an attack that was only feared, not actual or imminent, is not self-defence. Once a defendant raises self-defence with a minimum of plausibility, the prosecution must disprove it. Force that does not qualify may still be partly excused: blows or killing 'immediately provoked by serious violence against persons' are 'excusable' (article 411), which cuts the sentence sharply (article 414, e.g. one to five years instead of life imprisonment).

At home

Article 417 counts as self-defence any killing or injury done while repelling, at night, someone climbing or breaking through the fences, walls or entrances of an inhabited house or flat (or its outbuildings), unless it is shown the defender could not have believed there was an attack on persons; it also covers defending against thieves or looters using violence against people. The same act done in daytime (article 412) is only an 'excuse', which reduces the penalty (article 414) instead of removing it.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 416
Il n'y a ni crime, ni délit, lorsque l'homicide, les blessures et les coups étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d'autrui.
Code pénal, art. 417
Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de la défense, les deux cas suivants: Si l'homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites, si les coups ont été portés en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d'une maison ou d'un appartement habités ou de leurs dépendances, à moins qu'il soit établi que l'agent n'a pas pu croire à un attentat contre les personnes, soit comme but direct de celui qui tente l'escalade ou l'effraction, soit comme conséquence de la résistance que rencontreraient les desseins de celui-ci; Si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vol ou de pillage, exécutés avec violence envers les personnes.
Code pénal, art. 411 and 414 (excuse)
Art. 411. Le meurtre, les blessures et les coups sont excusables, s'ils ont été immédiatement provoqués par des violences graves envers les personnes. [...] Art. 414. Lorsque le fait d'excuse sera prouvé: S'il s'agit d'un crime emportant la peine de la réclusion à vie, la peine sera réduite à un emprisonnement d'un an à cinq ans et à une amende de 500 euros à 5.000 euros;
Cour d'appel (5e chambre correctionnelle), arrêt du 8 juillet 2025, n° 299
Lorsqu'un prévenu invoque une cause de justification, il n'a pas à en rapporter la preuve ; il suffit que cette allégation soit dotée d'un minimum de vraisemblance pour que la charge de la preuve de son inexistence incombe au ministère public [...]. Encore faut-il que l'attaque soit injuste, que la riposte soit concomitante, proportionnée, et qu'aucune autre issue ne soit envisageable pour échapper à l'agression.
Cour d'appel (5e chambre correctionnelle), arrêt du 11 novembre 2025, n° 477
il faut que la riposte soit proportionnée à l'attaque. Pour apprécier la riposte, le juge devra tenir compte des possibilités réelles qui s'offraient au prévenu dans la situation où il se trouvait au moment des faits.

bede73a26c945a1a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Enugu

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.

Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

37ef75d84d58a8d8.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Morelos

Part of Mexico, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Código Penal para el Estado de Morelos, art. 23(IV) (reformed 2024 and 7 Oct 2026): a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack if the defence used is rationally necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. A sentence added in the 2024 reform requires the harm caused to be proportionate to the intensity and circumstances of the attack, considering context, especially gender violence. No avoidance or 'no other means' condition appears in the article, and it does not say the defender need not flee. National Supreme Court (SCJN) theses point both ways: a 1940 thesis (registro 814826) says flight should not be imposed as a condition, while a 1946 thesis (registro 806596) denied the defence where the accused 'could well have avoided the aggression by other means'. No state-specific thesis was found (web search budget ran out), so whether retreat is required is not settled. Excess (art. 25) is punished with one third of the penalty, still as intentional; it is not excess if the defender was in confusion, fear or terror.

At home

Art. 23(IV) presumes legítima defensa, unless proven otherwise, when harm, injury or even death is caused to someone who by violence or any means tries to enter or enters without right the place where the defender or their family lives, temporarily or permanently, its outbuildings, or a place with property they must protect; the same presumption covers harm to a person surprised in those places, or in offices or shops, in circumstances showing a possible attack.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Morelos, art. 23, fracción IV
IV. Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad racional de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte de la persona agredida o de quien lo defienda. Se presume que existe legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, en el caso de que se cause un daño, lesión o incluso privación de la vida, a quien a través de la violencia o por cualquier medio trate de penetrar o penetre sin derecho al lugar donde habiten, aunque sea en forma temporal o permanente, el que se defiende, a su familia o al de cualquier persona respecto de las que el agente tenga la obligación de defender, a sus dependencias de ese lugar o al sitio en el que se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que exista la misma obligación. Igual presunción favorecerá al que cause un daño a otra persona en el momento de sorprenderla en alguno de los lugares antes citados o en oficinas o comercios, en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión; El daño causado deberá guardar proporcionalidad con la intensidad y circunstancias de la agresión ilegítima que motive la legítima defensa. Al valorar dicha proporcionalidad, la autoridad deberá considerar el contexto del hecho, particularmente cuando se adviertan situaciones de violencia de género.
Código Penal para el Estado de Morelos, art. 25
ARTÍCULO *25. - En los casos de exceso de legítima defensa o exceso en cualquier otra causa de justificación se impondrá la tercera parte de la sanción correspondiente al delito de que se trate, quedando subsistente la imputación a título doloso. No se considerará exceso en la legítima defensa cuando concurran circunstancias en las que la persona que se defiende se encuentre en estado de confusión, miedo o terror que afecte su capacidad para determinar el límite adecuado de su respuesta o la racionalidad de los medios empleados.
Código Penal para el Estado de Morelos, art. 23, reform note (previous wording before Decreto 2345, 2024)
REFORMA VIGENTE.- Se reforma la fracción IV del artículo 23 del presente ordenamiento, por ARTÍCULO ÚNICO del Decreto No. 2345, publicado en el Periódico Oficial “Tierra y Libertad” número 6343, de fecha 2024/09/04. Vigencia: 2024/09/05. Antes decía: ... Se presume que existe legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, en el caso de que se cause un daño racionalmente necesario a quien por cualquier medio trate de penetrar o penetre sin derecho al lugar donde habiten, aunque sea en forma temporal, el que se defiende o su familia ...
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 814826 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA. EVITABILIDAD DEL PELIGRO), Informe 1940, p. 42
no debe imponerse como condición al injustamente agredido la posibilidad de la fuga, pues en esas condiciones el ejercicio de la legítima defensa se tornaría en imposible en la mayoría de los casos
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 806596 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA), S.J.F. Tomo LXXXVIII, p. 721 (1946)
no puede aceptarse la defensa legítima, si el procesado no estuvo en inminente peligro de perder la vida o en condiciones de suponer este peligro, y pudo muy bien evitar la agresión de que fue víctima por otros medios, o en último extremo, preverla.
What was tried

Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tlaxcala

Part of Mexico, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Tlaxcala, art. 28(IV) (reformed P.O. 26 Apr 2023): a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack if the defence is necessary, the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not provoke it. The current text has no wording requiring the person to avoid the attack or to have no other way out. No avoidance or 'no other means' condition appears in the article, and it does not say the defender need not flee. National Supreme Court (SCJN) theses point both ways: a 1940 thesis (registro 814826) says flight should not be imposed as a condition, while a 1946 thesis (registro 806596) denied the defence where the accused 'could well have avoided the aggression by other means'. No state-specific thesis was found (web search budget ran out), so whether retreat is required is not settled. Excess (art. 89) is punished with one quarter of the penalty; where the excess was in repelling physical, sexual or femicidal violence, the judge may order psychological treatment and protection of the family.

At home

Art. 28(IV) presumes the requirements are met for whoever causes harm, injury or death to someone who by violence, climbing or any means tries to enter or has entered without right their home or outbuildings (even if not their usual home), their family's, a place with property they must protect, the house where their family is, their workplace or their commercial, industrial or service business; or whom they find there in circumstances showing a possible imminent attack. It also presumes legítima defensa for a woman facing physical, sexual or femicidal violence, and for a person helping her.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Tlaxcala, art. 28, fracción IV (reformed P.O. 26 Apr 2023)
IV. Legítima defensa: Se repele una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa y racionalidad de los medios empleados y no medie provocación suficiente e inmediata por parte de la persona agredida o de quien la defienda de aquella agresión. Se presumirá que concurren los requisitos de la legítima defensa, respecto de quien cause un daño, lesión o privación de la vida, a quien, a través de la violencia, del escalamiento o por cualquier otro medio trate de ingresar o haya ingresado sin derecho, a su domicilio o sus dependencias, aunque no sea su domicilio habitual; al domicilio de su familia o el de cualquier persona que tenga el mismo deber de cuidar o defender; al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto a los que tenga la misma obligación; a la casa donde se encuentre su familia, su lugar de trabajo o su establecimiento comercial, industrial o de prestación de servicios; o bien, cuando encuentre, en alguno de esos lugares, a la persona que intente ingresar o haya ingresado, en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una inminente agresión. Se presumirá la legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, en los supuestos siguientes: a) Cuando quien ejerza la legitima defensa, sea una mujer, y al momento de desplegar la conducta, sea víctima o esté en peligro inminente de ser víctima, de violencia física, sexual o feminicida, ... y en esas circunstancias, repele la agresión, e b) Cuando una persona despliegue la conducta en auxilio de una mujer que, en el momento, sea víctima de violencia física, sexual o feminicida, ... a fin de repeler el acto violento de que se trate.
Código Penal para el Estado Libre y Soberano de Tlaxcala, art. 89
Artículo 89. Punibilidad en el caso de exceso. Al que incurra en exceso, en los casos previstos en las fracciones IV, V y VI del artículo 28 de este código, se le impondrá la cuarta parte de las penas o medidas de seguridad, correspondientes al delito de que se trate. (ADICIONADO, P.O. 26 DE ABRIL DE 2023) En caso de actualizarse exceso en la legítima defensa para repeler acciones de violencia física, sexual o feminicida, en términos de la Ley que Garantiza el Acceso a las Mujeres a una Vida Libre de Violencia para el Estado de Tlaxcala, la persona juzgadora podrá imponer tratamiento psicológico a la persona que haya incurrido en el mismo, así como la protección a su familia, en caso necesario.
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 814826 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA. EVITABILIDAD DEL PELIGRO), Informe 1940, p. 42
no debe imponerse como condición al injustamente agredido la posibilidad de la fuga, pues en esas condiciones el ejercicio de la legítima defensa se tornaría en imposible en la mayoría de los casos
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 806596 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA), S.J.F. Tomo LXXXVIII, p. 721 (1946)
no puede aceptarse la defensa legítima, si el procesado no estuvo en inminente peligro de perder la vida o en condiciones de suponer este peligro, y pudo muy bien evitar la agresión de que fue víctima por otros medios, o en último extremo, preverla.

c6a5d0bc53a844fd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Pennsylvania

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Pennsylvania's no-retreat rule is partial. The Crimes Code allows deadly force when a person believes it immediately necessary to protect against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or forcible sexual intercourse, but keeps the older rule that deadly force is not justified if the person knows they can avoid it with complete safety by retreating, except from their dwelling or place of work (18 Pa.C.S. § 505(b)(2)). Act 10 of 2011 (signed 28 June 2011) added that outside the home a person has no duty to retreat and may 'stand his ground' only if they are not engaged in criminal activity, are not illegally possessing a firearm, have a right to be where they were attacked, and the attacker displays or uses a firearm, replica firearm or other weapon capable of lethal use (§ 505(b)(2.3)); if the attacker is unarmed, the retreat duty still applies in public places and vehicles. The same law created a rebuttable presumption of reasonable belief when deadly force is used against someone unlawfully and forcefully entering a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle; it does not apply against a lawful resident, a parent taking their own child, a peace officer known to be one, or a defender engaged in criminal activity. Deadly force is not justified for someone who, intending to cause death or serious injury, provoked the use of force in the same encounter. A person who uses force justified under §§ 505 to 509 is immune from civil liability for the perpetrator's injuries, and a court must award fees and costs if a perpetrator's suit fails (42 Pa.C.S. § 8340.2, 2011). No statutory pretrial criminal immunity hearing was found.

At home

No duty to retreat from one's dwelling or place of work unless the person was the initial aggressor (or, at work, is attacked by a co-worker in their shared workplace) (18 Pa.C.S. § 505(b)(2)(ii)). Since 2011 a person is presumed to reasonably believe deadly force is necessary against someone unlawfully and forcefully entering, or present after forcibly entering, a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle, or trying to drag someone out (§ 505(b)(2.1)); the intruder is presumed to intend death, serious injury, kidnapping or rape (§ 505(b)(2.5)).

Category 'statute' reflects the 2011 stand-your-ground provision, but it applies only when the attacker displays or uses a firearm or other lethal weapon; otherwise a duty to retreat (outside home and workplace) remains.

What the law says
18 Pa.C.S. § 505(b)(2)(ii) (retreat)
the actor knows that he can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating, except the actor is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling or place of work, unless he was the initial aggressor or is assailed in his place of work by another person whose place of work the actor knows it to be.
18 Pa.C.S. § 505(b)(2.3) (Act 10 of 2011)

... an actor is presumed to have a reasonable belief that deadly force is immediately necessary to protect himself against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat if both of the following conditions exist: (i) The person against whom the force is used is in the process of unlawfully and forcefully entering, or has unlawfully and forcefully entered and is present within, a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle ...

... is justified in using such force and shall be immune from civil liability for personal injuries sustained by a perpetrator which were caused by the acts or omissions of the actor as a result of the use of force.

019f596245bff81a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Dakota

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

South Dakota rewrote its self-defence law in 2021 (SL 2021, ch 93), repealing the older justifiable-homicide sections (22-16-34 and 22-16-35) and replacing them with a new set of statutes; a 2006 amendment had already added no-retreat language to the defence-of-person section. A person may use or threaten deadly force if they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to themselves or another, or a forcible felony, and has no duty to retreat and may stand their ground if they are not engaged in criminal activity and are in a place where they have a right to be (SDCL 22-18-4.1). In a dwelling or residence there is no duty to retreat, and a presumption of reasonable fear applies against someone unlawfully entering or inside a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle (22-18-4.2, 4.3). Deadly force to protect property other than a dwelling is allowed only to prevent a forcible felony (22-18-4.7). The justification is not available to someone committing or escaping from a forcible felony, or to someone who provoked the force, unless they then faced deadly danger and had exhausted every reasonable means of escape, or withdrew in good faith and clearly said so (22-18-4.9). A person who used force as permitted is immune from criminal prosecution (which includes arrest, detention and charging) and from civil suits by the attacker or their heirs, and courts must award fees and lost income to a defendant found immune (22-18-4.8). Since a 2022 amendment, once the defendant raises a prima facie claim of immunity, the prosecution must overcome it by clear and convincing evidence.

At home

A person in a dwelling or residence where they have a right to be has no duty to retreat, may stand their ground, and may use deadly force if they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent imminent death, great bodily harm or a forcible felony (SDCL 22-18-4.2, 2021). They are presumed to have held reasonable fear when using deadly force against someone unlawfully entering or inside a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle, or dragging someone out (22-18-4.3).

What the law says
SDCL 22-18-4.1 (SL 2021, ch 93, § 3)
A person who uses or threatens to use deadly force in accordance with this section does not have a duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground, if the person using or threatening to use the deadly force is: (1) Not engaged in a criminal activity; and (2) In a place where the person has a right to be.
SDCL 22-18-4.2 (dwelling)
A person who is in a dwelling or residence, in which the person has a right to be: (1) Has no duty to retreat; (2) Has the right to stand his or her ground; and (3) Has the right to use or threaten to use: ... (b) Deadly force, if the person reasonably believes that using or threatening to use deadly force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to himself, herself, or another, or to prevent the imminent commission of a forcible felony.
SDCL 22-18-4.3 (presumption)
For purposes of § 22-18-4.2, a person is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or great bodily harm, to himself, herself, or another, when using or threatening to use defensive force that is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm if: (1) The person against whom the defensive force was used or threatened: (a) Was in the process of unlawfully entering a dwelling, residence, or occupied vehicle ...
SDCL 22-18-4.8 (immunity; amended 2022)
In a criminal prosecution, once a prima facie claim of self-defense immunity has been raised by the defendant, the burden of proof, by clear and convincing evidence, is on the party seeking to overcome the immunity from criminal prosecution ...
SDCL 22-18-4.9 (aggressor)
Any justification for the use or the threatened use of either force or deadly force is not available to a person who: (1) Is attempting to commit, committing, or escaping after the commission of a forcible felony; or (2) Initially provokes the use or threatened use of force against himself or herself, unless: ...

4932be71dac65fd5.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Gombe

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.
Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963), on ss. 59-65
When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Zamfara Shari'a Penal Code 2000, s. 204(c), as reproduced in Peters (2001), Appendix Five
204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
