Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Abia

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.

Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

7aaf8acb0f0ab1cb.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New Hampshire

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

New Hampshire's Criminal Code allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes another is about to use unlawful deadly force against them or a third person, or is likely to use unlawful force during a burglary, or is committing a kidnapping or forcible sex offence, or a felony inside the defender's dwelling or curtilage (RSA 627:4, II). The general rule still says deadly force is not justified if the person knows they and any third person can retreat with complete safety, but a 2011 amendment (SB 88, chapter 268) added that there is no duty to retreat within the dwelling, its curtilage, or anywhere the person has a right to be, provided they were not the initial aggressor. Deadly force is also not justified if the person could safely surrender property to someone asserting a claim to it, or could comply with a demand to refrain from an act they are not obliged to do. A person who provoked the use of deadly force with the purpose of causing death or serious bodily injury, or who was the initial aggressor, loses the justification (an initial aggressor can regain it only by withdrawing and clearly communicating that). Displaying a firearm or other means of self-defence to warn off a threat is not a criminal act (RSA 627:4, II-a). The 2011 law also gave civil immunity: a person who used force justified under the code is immune from civil liability for injuries to the perpetrator (RSA 627:1-a). New Hampshire has no statutory pretrial immunity hearing; justification is raised at trial. No statutory presumption of reasonable fear was found.

At home

Deadly force is allowed against a person likely to use any unlawful force in committing a felony against the defender within the defender's dwelling or its curtilage (RSA 627:4, II(d)); a 2026 act (2026, 323:1, effective 1 January 2027) extends this to a third person. There is no duty to retreat within the dwelling or curtilage. Deadly force is also allowed against someone likely to use unlawful force against a person present during a burglary (II(b)).

Official site was read through a summarising fetch tool that only returns short verbatim excerpts; quotes are assembled from those excerpts. Words in square brackets are paraphrase.

A person is justified in using deadly force upon another person when he reasonably believes that such other person:

...if he or she knows that he or she and the third person can, with complete safety: (a) Retreat from the encounter, except that he or she is not required to retreat if he or she is within his or her dwelling, its curtilage, or anywhere he or she has a right to be [and was not the initial aggressor]
RSA 627:4, II(d) (version in force until 1 Jan 2027)
Is likely to use any unlawful force in the commission of a felony against the actor within such actor's dwelling ...
RSA 627:1-a (civil immunity; 2011, 268:3)
...shall be immune from civil liability for personal injuries sustained by a perpetrator which were caused by the acts or omissions of the person as a result of the use of force.

879b4d3268cdcc0b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

British Virgin Islands

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

In the British Virgin Islands self-defence is a common-law defence applied by the Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal. In Shonovia Thomas v The Queen (Court of Appeal, BVI, HCRAP 2010/006, 27 August 2012) the court recorded that 'The judge explained to the jury that there was no duty to retreat' and that whether the accused retreated is one element in deciding whether the force used was reasonably necessary; the judgment also states that failure to retreat when it is possible and safe 'is not conclusive'. The Court of Appeal found no misdirection on self-defence. In Danny Benjamin v The Queen (Court of Appeal, BVI, 2016) the Crown relied on a textbook passage that retreating from danger should be given no more weight than a factor. The Thomas passages were read through the court's search engine, not the full PDF.

The judge explained to the jury that there was no duty to retreat and instructed that whether Shonovia retreated is an element to be considered in determining whether the force used was reasonably necessary.
Shonovia Thomas v The Queen (2012), separate passage
Failure to retreat when attacked and when it is possible and safe to do so, is not conclusive.
Shonovia Thomas v The Queen (2012), Court of Appeal's conclusion
I am not of the view that there was any misdirection by the trial judge. In the circumstances, the complaints made against the trial judge are not valid.

The paragraph makes the point that retreating from danger should not be over­explained or given more weight than a factor in self­defence. The learned trial judge’s directions to the jury were along these lines and cannot found to be a misdirection.

8a14f650e52986f1.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Anguilla

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Anguilla's courts treat self-defence as a common-law justification: in Petty v The Queen (Court of Appeal, 1994) the trial judge's direction that a killing in lawful self-defence is no offence was upheld, and in Regina v James Hodge (High Court) force that 'went above and beyond what was commensurate' was not self-defence. No Anguillan statute section on self-defence and no Anguillan source on retreat was found. The Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal, which also hears this place's appeals, has upheld 'no duty to retreat' directions in cases from the British Virgin Islands (Shonovia Thomas, 2012), Antigua and Barbuda (Kevil Nelson, 2013) and Saint Vincent (Marshall Phillips, 2024), but no decision from this place itself saying so was found, so the category stays unclear.

In any event, the defendant's conduct not amount to self defence but rather was retaliatory and went above and beyond what was commensurate with the actions of the virtual complainant.

0fcc65f0fe181737.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mauritius

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Mauritius's Criminal Code (of French origin) says there is neither crime nor misdemeanour when homicide, wounds or blows are 'commanded by an actual necessity of the lawful defence of oneself or of another person' (s. 246). The Constitution (s. 4(2)) says a death does not breach the right to life when it results from force that is reasonably justifiable, to an extent and in circumstances permitted by law, for the defence of any person from violence or for the defence of property. No text or court decision was found that says whether a person must retreat, so the retreat question is not settled by the sources found. No rule on defence of the home or on excessive self-defence was found in the sources opened. Mauritian courts read s. 246 through French doctrine: a 2026 District Court judgment (Police v Shiboo & anor, 2026 RDR 129) cites Teeluckdharry v The Queen 1957 MR 277, where the Supreme Court approved Encyclopédie Dalloz's three conditions (defence of oneself or another, current necessity of that defence, unjust aggression), and JurisClasseur's statement that the response must be necessary, measured and voluntary; neither addresses retreat.

What the law says
Criminal Code (Cap. 195), s. 246 – Homicide and wounds and blows in self defence
There is neither crime nor misdemeanour, where homicide, wounds or blows are commanded by an actual necessity of the lawful defence of oneself or of another person.
Constitution of Mauritius 1968, s. 4(2)
A person shall, not be regarded as having been deprived of his life in contravention of this section, if he dies as the result of the use, to such extent and in such circumstances as are permitted by law, of such force as is reasonably justifiable - (a) for the defence of any person from violence or for the defence of property;
Police v Shiboo & anor, 2026 RDR 129 (District Court, 4 June 2026), citing Teeluckdharry v The Queen 1957 MR 277 (Supreme Court) and Encyclopédie Dalloz
In TEELUCKDHARRY v THE QUEEN 1957 MR 277 the Supreme Court cited with approval the following excerpt from Encyclopédie Dalloz, Droit Criminel, Verbis “Légitime Défense”, note 6:- « Pour constituer l'état de légitime défense, il faut le concours de trois conditions: 1º. défense de soi-même ou d'autrui; 2º. nécessité actuelle de cette défense; 3º. agression injuste. » [English rendering of the French, mine: To constitute legitimate defence, three conditions must concur: 1. defence of oneself or another; 2. current necessity of that defence; 3. unjust aggression.]

eb672dcb7af043af.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Akwa Ibom

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.

52129c3e04ba6df0.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Rhode Island

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Rhode Island has no stand-your-ground law; its rules on deadly force come mainly from Supreme Court decisions. A person may use deadly force only when they reasonably believe it necessary to avoid death or great bodily harm, and outside the home they must retreat or attempt to retreat when they actually and reasonably believe a safe retreat is available (State v. Guillemet, State v. Fetzik, and more recently State v. Garrett, 2014, and State v. Guerrero, 2019, as cited by the Giffords Law Center). There is no exception for vehicles, workplaces or public places. In the home, a person attacked by a trespasser has no duty to retreat, including where the attacker first came in as a social guest (State v. Ordway; State v. Walton, 1992), but a person attacked by someone who lives in the same home must retreat if they know of a safe way out (State v. Quarles, 1986). By statute (§ 11-8-8), when a burglar or intruder is killed or hurt during a burglary or breaking and entering, the occupant is presumed in civil and criminal proceedings to have acted reasonably in self-defence and has no duty to retreat from them. Rhode Island has no official pattern criminal jury instructions; the instruction summarised here comes from an Attorney General series last updated around 2000. No civil immunity provision beyond the § 11-8-8 presumption, and no pretrial immunity hearing, was found.

At home

R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-8-8 (1976, amended 1977 and 1984): if a burglar or housebreaker is killed or injured while committing a burglary or breaking-and-entering offence (§§ 11-8-2 to 11-8-6), the owner, tenant or occupier is rebuttably presumed, in civil and criminal proceedings, to have acted by reasonable means in self-defence, and has no duty to retreat from that person. Case law (State v. Ordway; State v. Walton) also frees an occupant attacked by a trespasser in the home from retreating, but an occupant attacked by a co-occupant must retreat if aware of a safe avenue (State v. Quarles).

Case quotes were read through a summarising fetch tool limited to short excerpts; the cases themselves were not opened.

What the law says
R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-8-8 (P.L. 1976, ch. 216; 1977, ch. 17; 1984, ch. 212)
... it shall be rebuttably presumed as a matter of law in any civil or criminal proceeding that the owner, tenant, or occupier of the place where the offense was committed acted by reasonable means in self-defense and in the reasonable belief that the person engaged in the criminal offense was about to inflict great bodily harm or death upon that person or any other individual lawfully in the place where the criminal offense was committed. There shall be no duty on the part of an owner, tenant, or occupier to retreat from any person engaged in the commission of any criminal offense enumerated in §§ 11-8-2 — 11-8-6.
Rhode Island Attorney General model instruction X.L, Self-Defense (citing State v. Martinez, State v. Fetzik, State v. Guillemet)
The law requires a person to retreat or attempt to retreat when he or she actually and reasonably believes ...
Same instruction (citing State v. Quarles, 1986) – co-occupant
The person attacked is obligated to attempt retreat if he or she is aware of a safe available avenue of retreat

87dff9501cfca69d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Aguascalientes

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Aguascalientes's Penal Code (art. 27-II) allows a person to defend their own or another's legal interests by repelling an unforeseen, current or imminent unlawful attack, if the means used were reasonably necessary and the defender did not provoke it. The article says nothing about retreating or fleeing. A 2017 amendment added a separate justification for harm needed to stop intruders entering a home or business, or to stop attacks inside them, with no proportionality test other than 'sufficiency'. Excessive self-defence is still an intentional offence but is punished with one quarter of the normal penalty. Mexico's federal Penal Code (separate entry MEX) covers only federal offences; ordinary homicide and assault in Aguascalientes are tried under this state code.

At home

Since a 2017 amendment (P.O. 25 Dec 2017), art. 27 also justifies causing 'sufficient' harm to stop someone entering, or trying to enter, without right one's business, home or its outbuildings (or those of family or people one must protect), and to stop any real, current and imminent attack committed inside a business or a dwelling. Sufficiency is judged by the stealth and violence the intruder used to get in or to stay inside.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Estado de Aguascalientes, art. 27, fracc. II and final paragraphs
II. Cuando se actúa en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, repeliendo una agresión imprevista, actual o inminente, sin derecho, y siempre que exista la necesidad razonable del medio empleado para impedirla o rechazarla, y que no medie provocación suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de la persona a quien se defienda; [...] Se justificará igualmente la conducta típica y antijurídica, cuando se cause, a la persona o las personas, un daño suficiente para evitar la introducción o los actos idóneos tendientes a introducirse, sin derecho, a su negocio, su hogar o sus dependencias, a los de su familia, a los de cualquier persona que tenga el deber de defender, o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos sobre los que tenga la misma obligación. (ADICIONADO, P.O. 25 DE DICIEMBRE DE 2017) También se justificará la conducta típica y antijurídica, cuando se cause un daño suficiente para evitar cualquier agresión real, actual e inminente, que se cometa en el interior o en las dependencias de una negociación o de una casa habitación. [...] Para determinar la relación de suficiencia en los supuestos descritos en los dos párrafos anteriores, se tomará en cuenta la furtividad y la violencia que, sobre las personas o sobre las cosas, haya ejercido el agresor para introducirse al inmueble o que ejerza para mantenerse dentro de él. (ADICIONADO, P.O. 25 DE DICIEMBRE DE 2017) En los casos de exceso de legítima defensa se impondrá una cuarta parte de la sanción prevista para el delito de que se trate, quedando subsistente la imputación a título doloso.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal para el Estado de Aguascalientes (última actualización 13/07/2026) (H. Congreso del Estado de Aguascalientes)
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

b95e985aaf41ff75.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Anambra

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • Sunday Jackson v The State, SC/CR/1026/2022, Supreme Court of Nigeria, 7 March 2025 (certified true copy, 62 pp., scanned; text obtained by OCR) (CITY LAWYER Magazine (hosting the certified copy, watermarked TheNigeriaLawyer))
  • Sunday Jackson v The State (2025-03) Legalpedia 85898 (SC) - summary (Legalpedia)
  • Matthew Egheghe v The State, SC.304/2017, 23 January 2020, (2020) Legalpedia (SC) 11101 (summary) (Legalpedia)

  • Agbonmwanre Omoregie v The State, SC 301/2006, 19 December 2008, (2008-12) Legalpedia (SC) 18215 (summary) (Legalpedia)
  • Emmanuel Ogar Akong Edoko v The State, SC.315/2012, 27 February 2015 (summary; Cross River, Criminal Code s. 286) (Legalpedia)
  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

c4b8ca86ba4d163d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Akrotiri and Dhekelia (UK Sovereign Base Areas, Cyprus)

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

The Sovereign Base Areas have their own laws, separate from both Cyprus and the UK, and apply their own version of the 1959 colonial Criminal Code (Cap 154). Since 1 August 2020 (Ordinance 21/2020), sections 17A and 17B of that code give a defence where the force used was reasonable in the circumstances as the defender believed them to be, for self-defence, defence of others or property, preventing crime or making an arrest, and let defendants rely on the common-law defences 'as they apply in England and Wales'. There is no duty to retreat: s. 17B(7) says the possibility of retreat is only 'a factor to be taken into account, rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat'. Force that was disproportionate (or grossly disproportionate in a householder case) is not reasonable, and no partial 'excessive self-defence' verdict appears in these sections. The wording closely copies section 76 of England's Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008.

At home

Householder rule copied from England and Wales: in a 'householder case' (force used by a non-trespasser inside a dwelling, including Armed Forces live-in accommodation, against someone believed to be a trespasser), force is unreasonable only if it was 'grossly disproportionate' in the circumstances as the defender believed them to be (Criminal Code Cap 154, s. 17B(5), (10), inserted 2020).

What the law says
Criminal Code (Cap 154) as applied in the SBAs, s. 17A (inserted by Ordinance 21/2020, in force 1 August 2020)
17A.—(1) A person (“D”) has a defence to a charge of an offence involving the use of force, if the degree of force used by D is reasonable in the circumstances as D believes them to be for the purposes of— (a) self-defence; (b) defence of property; (c) the prevention of crime; or (d) effecting or assisting lawful arrest of an offender or suspected offender or person unlawfully at large. (2) A person may rely on the common law defences of self-defence or defence of property, as they apply in England and Wales.
Criminal Code (Cap 154, SBA), s. 17B(5)–(7)
(5) In a householder case, the degree of force used by D is not to be regarded as having been reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them to be if it was grossly disproportionate in those circumstances. (6) In a case other than a householder case, the degree of force used by D is not to be regarded as having been reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them to be if it was disproportionate in those circumstances. (7) In deciding the question mentioned in subsection (2), a possibility that D could have retreated is to be considered (so far as relevant) as a factor to be taken into account, rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat.

575317a92089e62c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Vermont

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Vermont has no stand-your-ground statute. 13 V.S.A. § 2305 makes a person 'guiltless' who kills or wounds in the just and necessary defence of their own life or another's, or who reasonably believed deadly force was necessary to repel someone attempting murder, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, burglary or robbery; it says nothing about retreat and preserves common-law defences (§ 2305(b)). The no-retreat rule is judicial: in State v. Hatcher, 167 Vt. 338, 348 (1997), the Vermont Supreme Court recited without disapproval the trial court's instruction that if the defendant honestly and reasonably believed deadly force was immediately necessary 'the law does not require him to retreat', and the Vermont Model Criminal Jury Instruction CR07-111 (Use of Deadly Force in Self Defense, 07/26/19) now tells juries the same thing, citing Hatcher. The committee's reporter's note says the instruction 'includes an instruction that under certain circumstances, the law does not require the defendant to retreat.' Force must still be only what is reasonably necessary, and an aggressor may not claim self-defence (CR07-091).

At home

13 V.S.A. § 2305(a)(2) covers deadly force to repel a person attempting burglary or robbery, among other crimes. No separate castle-doctrine statute or presumption of reasonable fear was found.

What the law says
13 V.S.A. § 2305(a)-(b) Justifiable homicide
(a) If a person kills or wounds another under any of the circumstances enumerated below, the person shall be guiltless: (1) in the just and necessary defense of the person's own life or the life of any other person; (2) if the person reasonably believed that the person, or any other person, was in imminent peril and that it was necessary to repel that peril with deadly force in the forceful or violent suppression of a person attempting to commit murder, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, burglary, or robbery; ... (b) This section shall not be construed to limit or infringe upon defenses granted at common law. (Amended 1983, No. 23, § 2; 2019, No. 165 (Adj. Sess.), § 2, eff. July 1, 2021; 2021, No. 27, § 4, eff. Oct. 1, 2021; 2021, No. 95 (Adj. Sess.), § 1, eff. Apr. 21, 2022.)
Vermont Model Criminal Jury Instructions, CR07-111 Self-Defense (Use of Deadly Force) (07/26/19)
Furthermore, if [he] [she] honestly and reasonably believed it was immediately necessary to use deadly force to protect himself from an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury, the law does not require [him] [her] to retreat.
State v. Hatcher, 167 Vt. 338, 348, 706 A.2d 429 (1997)
As for the duty to retreat, the court instructed that if defendant honestly and reasonably believed "it was immediately necessary to use deadly force to protect himself from an imminent threat of death or bodily injury, the law does not require him to retreat." Thus the jury could have acquitted on the basis of self-defense even if it found that defendant failed to exercise an opportunity to retreat.
Vermont Model Criminal Jury Instructions, Self Defense page, Reporter's Note
Use of Deadly Force. The instruction on the use of deadly force in self-defense, CR07-111, includes an instruction that under certain circumstances, the law does not require the defendant to retreat. See State v. Hatcher, 167 Vt. 338, 348 (1997).

4f97a510b6ddbc31.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Saint Vincent and the Grenadines

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Self-defence in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is applied by the Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal following Palmer v R. In Marshall Phillips v The King (Court of Appeal, SVGHCRAP2016/0005, VC 2024 CA 1, 29 February 2024) the trial judge told the jury 'there is no obligation on the accused to retreat or run away if he [is] attacked or if he feels he [is] under threat of an attack'. The Court of Appeal quoted this direction approvingly and held the judge 'did not err' in her self-defence direction, dismissing that ground. So a court direction, upheld on appeal, says there is no duty to retreat. The earlier McIntosh v The Queen (1970s) excerpt shows retreat was argued but not how it was decided. The Phillips passages were read through the court's search engine and a vLex summary, not the full PDF.

What the law says

[25] The learned trial judge went even further when she instructed: “Now bear in mind there is no obligation on the accused to retreat or run away if he [is] attacked or if he feels he [is] under threat of an attack
Marshall Phillips v The King (2024), Court of Appeal's conclusion
The trial judge therefore did not err in her direction on the issue of pre-emptive strike as it relates to self-defence and the first ground of appeal failed.
Edwin McIntosh v The Queen (Court of Appeal, Saint Vincent), ground of appeal (from previous entry)
he failed to direct them properly on the question of retreat and/or reasonable apprehension of danger.

b310a0bfde006d7a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

eSwatini

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

eSwatini applies Roman-Dutch common law to self-defence; there is no criminal code provision. In Motsa v King (Court of Appeal, case 25/2000, Beck JA with Leon JP and Steyn JA, delivered 13 June 2001 according to the judgment text; listed on eSwatiniLII as 13 December 2000) the court restated the conditions from Rex v Molife: the means of defence must be commensurate with the danger, and 'dangerous means of defence must not be adopted when the threatened injury can be avoided in some other reasonable way'. The court acquitted because the appellant had backed away until he could retreat no further, had tried to flee to his room and failed, and no less dangerous way of protecting himself had been shown to be open to him. The word 'retreat' appears in the facts; the rule is that deadly force is not excused where the injury could reasonably have been avoided another way, which is a form of avoidance requirement. The Constitution (2005), s. 15(4)(a), lists force used for the defence of any person from violence or for the defence of property among the cases where a resulting death does not breach the right to life.

What the law says
Motsa v King (25 of 2000) [2000] SZSC 21, Beck JA, quoting Rex v Molife
Homicide in self-defence is only excusable under certain strictly limited conditions - the means of defence must be commensurate with the danger and dangerous means of defence must not be adopted when the threatened injury can be avoided in some other reasonable way.
Motsa v King, application to the facts
Flight was unsuccessfully attempted, and no less dangerous way of protecting himself than the way be used has been shown to have been open to the appellant. Without other options available to him I do not consider that it can justifiably be found that he used excessive force to protect himself.
Constitution of the Kingdom of Swaziland 2005, s. 15(4)(a) (extract)
(a) for the defence of any person from violence or for the defence of property;

94da68b462b761d6.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

American Samoa

Part of United States, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

American Samoa has its own criminal code, enacted in 1979 (PL 16-43) and modelled on Missouri's criminal code (the annotation points to Missouri § 563.031). Under A.S.C.A. § 46.3305 a person may use physical force on another when and to the extent they reasonably believe it necessary to defend against what they reasonably believe is the use or imminent use of unlawful force. Deadly force is allowed only if the person reasonably believes it necessary to protect themselves or another against death, serious physical injury, rape, sodomy or kidnapping. An initial aggressor can claim self-defence only after withdrawing from the encounter and effectively communicating that withdrawal. The section, as read for this entry, says nothing about retreat, and no American Samoa court decision on retreat or any castle-doctrine, immunity or stand-your-ground provision was found. A case note says a finding of self-defence is a complete defence to third-degree assault (Galea'i v. Atofau, 16 A.S.R.2d 76 (1990)). Whether a person must retreat before using deadly force is therefore not settled by the sources found. Read through a summarising fetch tool limited to short verbatim excerpts; bracketed words join excerpts. The chapter index page (Chapter 33, Defense of Justification) failed to load, so other sections (e.g. defence of premises) were not checked. A.S.C.A. § 46.3303 (re-opened this pass) is 'Execution of public duty', not a retreat rule; § 46.3305 does not contain the word 'retreat' (its only related wording is the initial aggressor's withdrawal).

6b4505731975ad5d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Martinique

An overseas region of France, part of France itself. Shown with the entry for France, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 122-5 of the Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. The defence must be simultaneous with the attack; a blow struck after the attacker has left is treated as ordinary violence. Neither art. 122-5 nor art. 122-6 mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Judges decide whether the defence was disproportionate; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes that an excessive response may lead to mitigating circumstances or a conviction for a lesser offence rather than full exoneration.

At home

Art. 122-6 of the Penal Code presumes self-defence for a person who acts "to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place", and against perpetrators of violent theft or looting. The presumption is rebuttable and does not cover daytime intrusions, which fall under the general rule of art. 122-5.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

0caf64c948f51f5f.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Comoros

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

In the 1981 Penal Code of the Comoros (as amended, the version found), there is no crime when killing, wounding or blows were required by the 'present necessity of legitimate defence' of oneself or another. The article does not mention proportionality or retreat; its test is present necessity. Night-time defence against climbing or break-in into a home, and defence against violent theft or looting, are named as cases of such necessity. Whether a newer penal code has since replaced this text could not be confirmed.

At home

Article 316 counts as legitimate defence killing or wounding while repelling at night the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of a house, inhabited flat or their outbuildings, and defence against violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal (1981, as amended), arts. 315–316
ART.315.- Il n'y a ni crime ni délit lorsque l'homicide, les blessures et les coups étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense se soi même ou d'autrui. ART.316. - Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de défense, les deux cas suivants : 1°)- Si l'homicide a été commis et si des blessures ont été faites, ou si les coups ont été portés en repoussant pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction, des clôtures, murs ou entrées d'une maison , d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances, 2°)- Si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violences.

3679022b7abe7d51.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Saint Helena

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Saint Helena, a British Overseas Territory, has no criminal code of its own on self-defence found in its published laws; under the English Law (Application) Ordinance 2005 (in force 1 January 2006), the common law of England and the Acts of Parliament in force in England at that date apply in Saint Helena, so far as suitable to local circumstances. Self-defence there is therefore governed by English common law. Under that common law, as quoted from the practitioners' text Archbold by the Seychelles Court of Appeal in 2015, 'the old rule of law that a man attacked must retreat as far as he can has disappeared', and whether the person retreated is only one factor in judging whether the force was reasonable. The later English statute on this point (Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s. 76(6A), added in 2013) post-dates the 2006 cut-off and was not shown to apply in Saint Helena. No Saint Helena court decision on self-defence was found. Ascension and Tristan da Cunha have separate law lists and were not checked.

What the law says
English Law (Application) Ordinance 2005 (Ord. 10 of 2005), ss. 2–3
In this Ordinance, “Adopted English Law” means: the common law of England, including the rules of equity; and the Acts of Parliament which are in force in England at the time of commencement of this Ordinance. ... 3. (1) Subject to subsection (2) and other provisions of this Ordinance, the Adopted English Law applies in St Helena. ... (2) The Adopted English Law applies to St Helena only in so far as it is applicable and suitable to local circumstances, and subject to such modifications, adaptations, qualifications and exceptions as local circumstances render necessary.
English common law as stated in Archbold, quoted in Freminot v Republic (Seychelles Court of Appeal, 2015), para. 9
The old rule of law that a man attacked must retreat as far as he can has disappeared. ... Whether the accused did retreat is only one element for the jury to consider

8af202a0d59f58d9.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Samoa

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Samoa's Crimes Act 2013 (s 17) sets detailed self-defence rules in the style of older Commonwealth codes. A person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may repel force with force that is not meant to kill or cause grievous harm and is no more than necessary; deadly force is justified only under reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm, when the person believes on reasonable grounds that they cannot otherwise preserve themselves, and the force is no more than necessary. The Act does not require an innocent victim to retreat, but a person who started or provoked the fight can claim self-defence only if, before using force, they 'declined further conflict and quitted or retreated from it as far as was practicable' (s 17(3)(c)). Section 17(5) bars 'the wilful infliction of any hurt or mischief disproportionate to the assault'; no partial 'excessive self-defence' rule appears in the text.

At home

Crimes Act 2013, s 18: a person in peaceable possession of a dwellinghouse, and those lawfully assisting them, may use 'such reasonable force as is necessary' to prevent forcible breaking and entering if they believe on reasonable grounds that there is no lawful justification for it. Section 19 allows reasonable force against trespassers on land or buildings only if the defender does not strike or do bodily harm.

What the law says
Crimes Act 2013 (Samoa), s 17(1)–(2) Self-defence
(1) A person unlawfully assaulted, not having provoked the assault by any blows, words or gestures, is justified in repelling force, if the force the person uses: (a) is not meant to cause death or grievous bodily harm; and (b) is no more than is necessary for the purpose of self defence. (2) A person unlawfully assaulted, not having provoked the assault by any blows, words or gestures, is justified in repelling force by force although in so doing the person causes death or grievous bodily harm, if: (a) the person causes it under reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm from the violence with which the assault was originally made or with which the assailant pursues his or her purpose; and (b) the person believes, on reasonable grounds, that he or she cannot otherwise preserve himself or herself from death or grievous bodily harm; and (c) the force the person uses is no more than is necessary for the purpose of self defence.
Crimes Act 2013 (Samoa), s 17(3)(c) and (5)
(c) before the force was used, he or she declined further conflict and quitted or retreated from it as far as was practicable; ... (5) This section shall not justify the wilful infliction of any hurt or mischief disproportionate to the assault that it was intended to prevent.
Crimes Act 2013 (Samoa), s 18 Defence of dwellinghouse
A person in a peaceable possession of a dwellinghouse, and everyone lawfully assisting that person or acting by his or her authority, is justified in using such reasonable force as is necessary to prevent the forcible breaking and entering of the dwellinghouse by any person if the person believes, on reasonable grounds, that there is no lawful justification for the breaking and entering.

Part of France, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

French Penal Code art. 122-6 presumes self-defence for a person who acts to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, or to defend against violent theft or looting.

Code pénal (France), art. 122-5, al. 1
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte.

Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

37b76498b4b6c445.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bermuda

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Bermuda has its own Criminal Code Act 1907. A person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force causing death or grievous bodily harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous bodily harm and they believe on reasonable grounds "that he cannot otherwise preserve" the person defended (s. 257). The Code does not impose a general duty to retreat on an innocent victim, but the "cannot otherwise preserve" test means other ways of avoiding the danger are relevant. A person who started the fight or provoked the assault may use deadly force only if, before the need arose, they "declined and quitted conflict or retreated from conflict as far as was practicable" (s. 258). Anyone authorised to use force is criminally responsible for any excess (s. 269), and a killing caused by good-faith but excessive defensive force, without premeditation, is manslaughter rather than murder (s. 296).

At home

Section 253 makes it lawful for a person in peaceable possession of a dwelling-house, and anyone helping them, to use such force as they believe on reasonable grounds to be necessary to prevent the forcible breaking and entering of the house, by night or day, by someone they reasonably believe intends to commit an indictable offence inside.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act 1907, s. 257
(1) When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault, if the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous bodily harm. (2) If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable grounds, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous bodily harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous bodily harm.
Criminal Code Act 1907, s. 258 proviso (c)
Provided that the foregoing provisions of this section shall not have effect so as to excuse or justify— ... (c) the use by any person of force which causes death or grievous bodily harm where such person has not before the necessity to use such force arose declined and quitted conflict or retreated from conflict as far as was practicable.
Criminal Code Act 1907, s. 253
It is lawful for any person who is in peaceable possession of a dwelling-house, and for any person lawfully assisting him or acting by his authority, to use such force as he believes, on reasonable grounds, to be necessary in order to prevent the forcible breaking and entering of the dwelling-house, either by night or day, by any person whom he believes, on reasonable grounds, to be attempting to break and enter the dwelling-house with intent to commit any indictable offence therein.
Criminal Code Act 1907, s. 296
An unlawful killing by a person of another person is manslaughter and not murder if the offender while in the exercise in good faith of any right to use force against another person uses more force than that allowed to him by law in relation to the exercise of that right and causes the death of the person against whom the force is used without premeditation and without any intention of doing more bodily harm than he honestly believes is necessary for the purpose of exercising that right.

a2882f24bf35309f.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cayman Islands

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

The Cayman Islands Penal Code does not spell out self-defence itself: section 14 says that criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property 'shall be determined according to the principles of English common law'. Under those common-law principles, as summarised by the Crown Prosecution Service of England and Wales, a person who is attacked may do what is reasonably necessary to defend themselves (Palmer v R), and failing to retreat when it was possible and safe is not conclusive evidence against them but only a factor to weigh (R v Bird: the defendant need not show by walking away that he did not want to fight). So there is no strict duty to retreat; the force must be reasonable. The Code has a separate rule for force used in making an arrest (section 15), where the court considers how serious the offence being stopped was. No Cayman court decision on retreat was opened.

At home

The Cayman Penal Code has no separate rule on defending a home; section 14 sends the question to English common law. Whether Cayman courts follow England's 2013 'householder' rule (a statute that by its own terms covers England and Wales) was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code (2022 Revision), s. 14 (Defence of person or property)
Subject to any express provisions in this or any other law in operation in the Islands, criminal responsibility for the use of force in the defence of person or property shall be determined according to the principles of English common law.
English common law as summarised in CPS legal guidance (R v Bird; Palmer v R)
Failure to retreat when attacked and when it is possible and safe to do so, is not conclusive evidence ... It is simply a factor to be taken into account rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat ... [R v Bird:] It is not necessary that the defendant demonstrates by walking away that he does not want to engage in physical violence.

69d336c5cabe3772.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Australian Capital Territory

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The ACT Criminal Code 2002 (s 42) follows the Commonwealth model: conduct is self-defence if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or someone else (or for listed property and trespass purposes) and it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceive them. The section does not mention retreat and no duty to retreat is stated. Intentionally inflicting death or serious harm only to protect property or deal with a trespasser is excluded.

At home

No home-specific rule in s 42; force intended to cause death or serious harm may not be used only to protect property or to prevent or remove a criminal trespasser (s 42(3)).

What the law says
Criminal Code 2002 (ACT), s 42 Self-defence
(1) A person is not criminally responsible for an offence if the person carries out the conduct required for the offence in self-defence. (2) A person carries out conduct in self-defence only if— (a) the person believes the conduct is necessary— (i) to defend himself or herself or someone else; or (ii) to prevent or end the unlawful imprisonment of himself or herself or someone else; or (iii) to protect property from unlawful appropriation, destruction, damage or interference; or (iv) to prevent criminal trespass to land or premises; or (v) to remove from land or premises a person committing criminal trespass; and (b) the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them. (3) However, the person does not carry out conduct in self-defence if— (a) the person uses force that involves the intentional infliction of death or serious harm— (i) to protect property; or (ii) to prevent criminal trespass; or (iii) to remove a person committing criminal trespass; ...
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Code 2002 (ACT), republication R58 effective 23/02/26 (ACT Legislation Register, ACT Parliamentary Counsel)
Australia as a whole

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).

4e7da1136c5a7344.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

US Virgin Islands

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

The US Virgin Islands has its own criminal code (Title 14, V.I. Code). It allows 'the use of force to protect oneself, one's family, or one's property from a real or threatened attack' (14 V.I.C. § 43, as quoted by the V.I. Supreme Court), and lists violence used in self-defence against unlawful violence as lawful (§ 293(a)(6)). A killing is justified as self-defence if the defendant actually and reasonably believed they were in imminent danger of death or great bodily harm, and once self-defence is raised the prosecution must disprove it beyond a reasonable doubt (Viera v. People, 2019 VI 22). The right 'does not extend to the infliction of more harm than is necessary', and force greater than needed to stop the harm is unlawful (Marcelle v. People, 2011). No statute on retreat was found. In Gov't of the V.I. v. Fonseca (2001) the federal Third Circuit held that a trial instruction did not impose a duty to retreat; that instruction told jurors that a person who reasonably believed deadly force was needed was 'not required to retreat' and could stand their ground, but that a failure to retreat safely could be weighed in deciding whether the force went further than justified. In Viera the court relied partly on the fact that the defendant kept shooting after he had retreated to his car and was getting away. No castle-doctrine presumption, civil immunity or pretrial immunity hearing was found.

At home

The Virgin Islands Code lists as lawful violence used in self-defence or defence of another against unlawful violence offered to one's person or property (14 V.I.C. § 293(a)(6)), and a separate clause about preventing entry into a home was discussed in Gov't of the V.I. v. Fonseca (3d Cir. 2001), which held it did not apply where the other person never tried to get inside. The text of that home clause was not opened for this entry.

The V.I. Code text itself was not opened; statutory wording is as quoted in court opinions. Category is 'judicial' because the no-retreat rule appears only in an approved jury instruction; the instruction also lets jurors weigh a safe retreat, which overlaps with 'proportional'.

What the law says
Gov't of the V.I. v. Fonseca, Nos. 00-3628/3877/3878 (3d Cir. 2001) – trial instruction held not to impose a duty to retreat
If the defendants had a reasonable ground to believe and actually did believe that they were in imminent danger of death or serious bodily harm, and that deadly force was necessary to repel such danger, they were not required to retreat or to consider whether they could safely retreat. They were entitled to stand their grounds and use such force as was reasonable under the circumstances ... However, if the Defendant could have safely retreated but did not do so, their failure to retreat is circumstances under which you may consider, together with all the other circumstances, in determining whether they went further in repelling the danger, real or apparent, than they were justified in doing under the circumstances.
14 V.I.C. § 43, as quoted in Viera v. People, 2019 VI 22, ¶ 30
Virgin Islands law allows “the use of force to protect oneself, one’s family, or one’s property from a real or threatened attack.” See 14 V.I.C. § 43
Viera v. People, 2019 VI 22, ¶ 30 (excessive force)
Notably, “[t]he right of self-defense does not extend to the infliction of more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defense.” ... “The force used to deflect an aggressor’s threatened harm must be merely sufficient to stop the harm, and application of a greater force than that which is necessary is unlawful.” Marcelle v. People, 55 V.I. 536, 544-45 (V.I. 2011)
14 V.I.C. § 293(a)(6), as quoted in Fonseca
in self-defense or in defense of another against unlawful violence offered to his person or property

7ddb104cfffa969b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba)

Part of Netherlands, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are special municipalities of the Netherlands but have their own penal code, the Wetboek van Strafrecht BES. Its article 43 copies the Dutch rule: a person is not punishable for an act 'required by the necessary defence' of their own or another's body, sexual integrity or property against an immediate, unlawful attack. The courts apply the Dutch Supreme Court's approach that self-defence fails if the person not only could but also should have withdrawn from the attack, which requires a real chance to get away; in a 2025 Bonaire case the first-instance court accepted self-defence because there was no 'real possibility' for the accused to withdraw in a small fenced porch, 'if he was even obliged to do so in those circumstances', and found the single blow with an iron pipe not disproportionate. Exceeding the limits of necessary defence is not punishable if it was the immediate result of a violent emotion caused by the attack (art. 43(2), noodweerexces). No special rule for the home was found.

What the law says
Wetboek van Strafrecht BES, artikel 43 (version in force from 1 July 2025)
1 Niet strafbaar is hij die een feit begaat, geboden door de noodzakelijke verdediging van eigen of eens anders lijf, eerbaarheid of goed tegen oogenblikkelijke, wederrechtelijke aanranding. 2 Niet strafbaar is de overschrijding van de grenzen van noodzakelijke verdediging, indien zij het onmiddellijk gevolg is geweest van eene hevige gemoedsbeweging, door de aanranding veroorzaakt.
Gerecht in eerste aanleg van Bonaire, Sint Eustatius en Saba, 13 November 2025, ECLI:NL:OGEABES:2025:162
Het Gerecht oordeelt dat niet is gebleken dat er voor de verdachte op dat moment een reële mogelijkheid was zich te onttrekken aan de aanranding, als hij daartoe in die omstandigheden al gehouden was. [...] Van disproportionaliteit is geen sprake.
Hoge Raad 22 March 2016, ECLI:NL:HR:2016:456, r.o. 3.5.2 (as quoted in the Advocate-General's conclusion in a Caribbean case, ECLI:NL:PHR:2018:595)
Aan de subsidiariteitseis is niet voldaan indien de verdachte zich niet behoefde te verdedigen en er dus geen noodzaak tot verdediging bestond. Daarvan is bijvoorbeeld sprake indien de verdachte zich niet alleen aan de aanranding had kunnen, maar zich daaraan ook had moeten onttrekken. Bij de verwerping van een beroep op noodweer kan dus niet worden volstaan met het enkele argument dat de verdachte zich aan de aanranding had kunnen onttrekken. Het zich aan de aanranding kunnen onttrekken houdt in dat daartoe voor de verdachte een reële en redelijke mogelijkheid moet hebben bestaan.
