643bd886e5e17714.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Baykonur Cosmodrome

Part of Kazakhstan, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Baikonur is Kazakh territory leased to Russia until 2050; the basic instrument is the Agreement between the Russian Federation and the Republic of Kazakhstan on the status of the city of Baikonur and the formation and status of its executive bodies, signed in Moscow on 23 December 1995 (Bulletin of International Treaties 1999 No. 5, pp. 56-67), as cited by Zhukova (2024). Baizhanova and Botagarin (2020) state that Russian legislation applies on the territory of the city, that Russian law and Russian competent bodies apply to Russian civil and military personnel and their families on the complex, that a Russian garrison military court and city court sit there, and that citizens of Kazakhstan who commit crimes on the complex are to be held liable by Kazakh law-enforcement bodies under Kazakh law. Both legal systems settle the retreat question the same way, in statute: Russian Criminal Code art. 37(3) says the right of necessary defence applies 'regardless of the possibility of avoiding the socially dangerous attack or of seeking help from other persons or authorities', and the Plenum of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation, Resolution No. 19 of 27 September 2012 (as amended to 9 December 2025), para. 1, repeats that art. 37 applies to all persons 'regardless of the possibility of avoiding the socially dangerous attack or turning to other persons or authorities for help'. Kazakhstan's Criminal Code art. 32 has the same rule (see KAZ entry). Which country's courts try a given defender depends on the person's status under the 1995 Agreement, whose text was not opened; the article of the Agreement on criminal jurisdiction therefore cannot be cited.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, art. 37(3)
Положения настоящей статьи в равной мере распространяются на всех лиц независимо от их профессиональной или иной специальной подготовки и служебного положения, а также независимо от возможности избежать общественно опасного посягательства или обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или органам власти. [English rendering, mine: The provisions of this article apply equally to all persons regardless of their professional or other special training and official position, and regardless of the possibility of avoiding the socially dangerous attack or of seeking help from other persons or authorities.]
Plenum of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation, Resolution No. 19 of 27 September 2012 'On the application by courts of legislation on necessary defence and causing harm when detaining a person who has committed a crime' (as amended 31 May 2022 No. 11 and 9 December 2025 No. 33), para. 1
1. Обратить внимание судов на то, что положения статьи 37 УК РФ в равной мере распространяются на всех лиц, находящихся в пределах действия Уголовного кодекса Российской Федерации, независимо от профессиональной или иной специальной подготовки и служебного положения, от того, причинен ли лицом вред при защите своих прав или прав других лиц, охраняемых законом интересов общества или государства, а также независимо от возможности избежать общественно опасного посягательства или обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или органам власти. [English rendering, mine: 1. To draw the courts' attention to the fact that the provisions of article 37 of the Criminal Code apply equally to all persons within the reach of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, regardless of professional or other special training and official position, of whether the person caused harm in defending their own rights or the rights of others or legally protected interests of society or the state, and regardless of the possibility of avoiding the socially dangerous attack or turning to other persons or authorities for help.]
Baizhanova & Botagarin (2020), on which law applies in Baikonur (Kazakh text)
Қала аумағында Ресей заңнамасы қолданылады, бірақ Қазақстан азаматтарының құқықтары да сақталуы қажет. «Байқоңыр» кешенінің аумағында Ресей Федерациясының азаматтық жəне əскери қызметкерлеріне жəне олардың отбасы мүшелеріне Ресей заңнамасы қолданылады, сондай-ақ Ресейдің құзыретті органдары əрекет етеді. [English rendering, mine: Russian legislation applies on the territory of the city, but the rights of citizens of Kazakhstan must also be preserved. On the territory of the Baikonur complex, Russian legislation applies to civilian and military personnel of the Russian Federation and members of their families, and Russian competent bodies operate.]
Baizhanova & Botagarin (2020), on Kazakh citizens
«Байқоңыр» кешені аумағында қылмыс жасаған ҚР азаматы, ҚР аумағында тіркеуден өткен үшінші бір мемлекет азаматтары, азаматтығы жоқ адамдар ҚР құқық қорғау органдарымен ҚР заңнамасына сəйкес жауапкершілікке тартылуы тиісті. [English rendering, mine: A citizen of the Republic of Kazakhstan who commits a crime on the territory of the Baikonur complex, citizens of a third state registered in Kazakhstan, and stateless persons must be held liable by the law-enforcement bodies of Kazakhstan under Kazakh legislation.]
Zhukova (2024), identifying the basic agreement
Базисный документ, посвященный основным принципам и условиям использования комплекса «Байконур», — Соглашение между Российской Федерацией и Республикой Казахстан о статусе города Байконур, порядке формирования и статусе его органов исполнительной власти от 23.12.1995. [English rendering, mine: The basic document on the main principles and conditions of use of the Baikonur complex is the Agreement between the Russian Federation and the Republic of Kazakhstan on the status of the city of Baikonur and the procedure for forming and the status of its executive bodies of 23 December 1995.]

dd0c0380ed44e859.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Connecticut

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Connecticut General Statutes § 53a-19(a) allows reasonable force in defence of oneself or a third person, and deadly force only when the actor reasonably believes the other person is using or about to use deadly force or is inflicting or about to inflict great bodily harm. Section 53a-19(b) keeps a duty to retreat: a person is not justified in using deadly force 'if he or she knows that he or she can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety (1) by retreating', or by surrendering property to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to refrain from an act they need not perform. The retreat requirement does not apply to a person in their own dwelling or place of work who was not the initial aggressor, or to a peace officer or someone assisting one. Force is not justified for a person who provoked it intending injury, for an initial aggressor who has not withdrawn and communicated it, or in a combat by agreement (§ 53a-19(c)). The section dates from the 1969 Penal Code (1969, P.A. 828, § 19) and was last amended by P.A. 22-117, § 9, effective May 27, 2022.

At home

Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-19(b): 'the actor shall not be required to retreat if he or she is in his or her dwelling, as defined in section 53a-100, or place of work and was not the initial aggressor'. § 53a-20 separately allows deadly force to prevent or terminate an unlawful entry by force into a dwelling. No presumption of reasonable fear.

What the law says
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-19(b)
(b) Notwithstanding the provisions of subsection (a) of this section, a person is not justified in using deadly physical force upon another person if he or she knows that he or she can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety (1) by retreating, except that the actor shall not be required to retreat if he or she is in his or her dwelling, as defined in section 53a-100, or place of work and was not the initial aggressor, or if he or she is a peace officer or a private person assisting such peace officer at his or her direction, and acting pursuant to section 53a-22, or (2) by surrendering possession of property to a person asserting a claim of right thereto, or (3) by complying with a demand that he or she abstain from performing an act which he or she is not obliged to perform.
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-19(a) (deadly force limit)
except that deadly physical force may not be used unless the actor reasonably believes that such other person is (1) using or about to use deadly physical force, or (2) inflicting or about to inflict great bodily harm.
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-19 history (2025 General Statutes)
(1969, P.A. 828, S. 19; 1971, P.A. 871, S. 5; P.A. 92-260, S. 4; P.A. 05-180, S. 1; ... P.A. 22-117, S. 9

d5d8084bdbf4b3b2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Delaware

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Delaware allows deadly force when the defendant reasonably believes it is necessary to protect against death, serious physical injury, kidnapping or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat (11 Del. C. § 464(c)). Delaware keeps a duty to retreat for deadly force: it is not justified if the defendant knows the need can be avoided with complete safety by retreating, by handing over a thing to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to stop doing something they are not legally obliged to do (§ 464(e)(2)). There is no duty to retreat in or from one's own dwelling, nor from one's place of work unless the defendant was the initial aggressor; for non-deadly force there is no retreat requirement (§ 464(b)). Deadly force is also not justified if the defendant, intending to cause death or serious injury, provoked the use of force in the same encounter, and force may not be used to resist a known arrest by a police officer, lawful or not. In the home, § 469 (added by 63 Del. Laws c. 276) gives an occupant a specific defence for killing or injuring an unlawful intruder in a sudden encounter, on a reasonable belief the intruder would cause injury, or after the intruder refused to surrender. If the defendant's belief in the need for force was reckless or negligent, the justification is not available for offences that require only recklessness or negligence (such as manslaughter or criminally negligent homicide) (§ 470(a)). The sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit and no pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

11 Del. C. § 464(e)(2)(a)–(b): a defendant is not obliged to retreat in or from their own dwelling, and is not obliged to retreat in or from their place of work unless they were the initial aggressor. § 469 gives an occupant charged with killing or injuring an intruder unlawfully in the dwelling a defence if the encounter was sudden and unexpected and forced instant action, or the occupant reasonably believed the intruder would injure someone in the dwelling, or the intruder refused a demand to disarm or surrender.

What the law says
11 Del. C. § 464(e)(2)
The use of deadly force is not justifiable under this section if: ... (2) The defendant knows that the necessity of using deadly force can be avoided with complete safety by retreating, by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim of right thereto or by complying with a demand that the defendant abstain from performing an act which the defendant is not legally obligated to perform except that: a. The defendant is not obliged to retreat in or from the defendant’s dwelling; and b. The defendant is not obliged to retreat in or from the defendant’s place of work, unless the defendant was the initial aggressor ...
11 Del. C. § 464(c)
The use of deadly force is justifiable under this section if the defendant reasonably believes that such force is necessary to protect the defendant against death, serious physical injury, kidnapping or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat.
11 Del. C. § 469
In the prosecution of an occupant of a dwelling charged with killing or injuring an intruder who was unlawfully in said dwelling, it shall be a defense that the occupant was in the occupant’s own dwelling at the time of the offense, and: (1) The encounter between the occupant and intruder was sudden and unexpected, compelling the occupant to act instantly; or (2) The occupant reasonably believed that the intruder would inflict personal injury upon the occupant or others in the dwelling; or (3) The occupant demanded that the intruder disarm or surrender, and the intruder refused to do so.
11 Del. C. § 470(a)
but the defendant is reckless or negligent in having such belief ... the justification afforded by those sections is unavailable in a prosecution for an offense for which recklessness or negligence, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Delaware Code, Title 11, Chapter 4 – Defenses to Criminal Liability (§§ 464, 469, 470) (State of Delaware, Legislative Council)

768ddd92e0b87052.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nevada

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Nevada allows a killing in necessary self-defence or defence of another, or of an occupied home or occupied motor vehicle, against someone who manifestly intends to commit a violent felony (NRS 200.120). Since 2011 a person need not retreat before using deadly force if they are not the original aggressor, have a right to be at the place, and are not engaged in criminal activity; this applies anywhere the person lawfully is, not only at home. Bare fear is not enough: the circumstances must be enough to frighten a reasonable person and the person must have acted from that fear, not revenge (NRS 200.130(1)). A 2015 amendment added a rebuttable presumption of reasonable fear when the person killed was forcibly entering an occupied home or vehicle or committing a violent felony, as long as the defender did not provoke them (NRS 200.130(2)). The older NRS 200.200 still requires that the danger was urgent and that the person killed was the assailant or that the slayer had in good faith tried to decline further struggle, which limits initial aggressors. Civil suits against a person who used force against an armed burglar, home invader or car thief are barred unless the presumption of reasonable fear is overcome by clear and convincing evidence (NRS 41.095). Nevada has no statutory pretrial immunity hearing; a justified killing leads to acquittal at trial (NRS 200.190). Excessive force is not excused and can be prosecuted as manslaughter or murder.

At home

Killing is justifiable in defence of an occupied habitation or occupied motor vehicle against someone who violently or surreptitiously tries to enter to assault anyone inside (NRS 200.120(1)). Since 2015 a rebuttable presumption of reasonable fear applies when the person killed was unlawfully and forcibly entering an occupied home or vehicle (NRS 200.130(2)); civil presumption and immunity for force against armed burglars, home invaders or car thieves in a residence, transient lodging or vehicle (NRS 41.095).

What the law says
NRS 200.120(2) (no duty to retreat, added 2011, amended 2015)
A person is not required to retreat before using deadly force as provided in subsection 1 if the person: (a) Is not the original aggressor; (b) Has a right to be present at the location where deadly force is used; and (c) Is not actively engaged in conduct in furtherance of criminal activity at the time deadly force is used.
NRS 200.120(1)
Justifiable homicide is the killing of a human being in necessary self-defense, or in defense of an occupied habitation, an occupied motor vehicle or a person, against one who manifestly intends or endeavors to commit a crime of violence...
NRS 200.130 (presumption, added 2015)
There is a rebuttable presumption that the circumstances were sufficient to excite the fears of a reasonable person and that the person killing really acted under the influence of those fears and not in a spirit of revenge if the person killing: (a) Knew or reasonably believed that the person who was killed was entering unlawfully and with force, or attempting to enter unlawfully and with force, the occupied habitation or occupied motor vehicle, of another; (b) Knew or reasonably believed that the person who was killed was committing or attempting to commit a crime of violence; and (c) Did not provoke the person who was killed.
NRS 200.200
If a person kills another in self-defense, it must appear that: 1. The danger was so urgent and pressing that, in order to save the person’s own life, or to prevent the person from receiving great bodily harm, the killing of the other was absolutely necessary; and 2. The person killed was the assailant, or that the slayer had really, and in good faith, endeavored to decline any further struggle before the mortal blow was given.
NRS 41.095 (civil immunity)
An action to recover damages for personal injuries to or the wrongful death of the person who committed burglary, invasion of the home or grand larceny of the motor vehicle with the use or threatened use of a deadly weapon may not be maintained against the person who used such force unless the presumption is overcome by clear and convincing evidence to the contrary.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • NRS Chapter 41 - Actions and Proceedings in Particular Cases (Nevada Legislature)

5f1da660a790a05e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Federal Capital Territory

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The northern states and the FCT use the Penal Code (Penal Code Law 1959 of the Northern Region, continued as each state's Penal Code Law and, for the FCT, the Penal Code (Northern States) Federal Provisions Act; Kaduna re-enacted it in 2017, see NG-KD). Sections 59-67 give a right of private defence of body and property. Section 62 limits it to no more harm than necessary; section 63 says there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'; section 65 allows killing only against attacks causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, or abduction. The 1963 official annotation (Richardson) explains s. 63 as: no one may take the law into his own hands if there is reasonable opportunity to prevent the injury by recourse to the public authorities. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Sunday Jackson itself was a Penal Code case (s. 221(a), Penal Code Cap. 98, Laws of Adamawa State 1997), so the retreat condition is stated directly for the Penal Code states. In Tsammani JSC's concurring judgment the same four conditions are listed and s. 62 is quoted as a further limit. Twelve northern states also enacted Sharia Penal Codes from 2000; the Zamfara text (copied by Bauchi, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe) keeps 'the right of private defence of person or property' (s. 204(c), reducing a killing in excess of that right to diyyah), but its private-defence sections themselves were not opened, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code was not found.

What the law says
Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), ss. 59, 62, 63
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. [...] 62. The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. 63. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code Law, 1959, s. 65
65. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 62 and 63, to the voluntary causing of death only when the act to be repelled is of any of the following descriptions, namely- (a) an attack which causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt; or (b) rape or an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; or (c) abduction or kidnapping.
Richardson, Notes on the Penal Code Law (2nd ed. 1963), comment on s. 63
No person has the right to take the law into his own hands for the protection of his life and property if there is reasonable opportunity of preventing the injury by recourse to the public authorities.
Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963), on ss. 59-65
When the right of private defence arises under section 60, and there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (section 63), no more harm should be done than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (section 62).
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting earlier authority on necessity
In deciding whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 17, quoting Uwaekweghinya v State (2005)
For an accused to avail himself of the defence of self-defence, he must show by evidence that he took reasonable steps to disengage from the fight or make some physical withdrawal. But the issue of disengagement depends on the peculiar circumstances of each case. Sometimes it may be possible to run away from an unwarranted attack at times it may be impossible to physically withdraw.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Agim JSC concurring
Where a person successfully wrestles and disarms the other person that had come to stab him, took over the dagger, but did not escape or retreat after seizing the dagger and used same to stab the now unarmed assailant thrice on the throat killing him, the stabs on the assailant clearly amount to reprisal or revenge attacks and not acts of self defence or provocation.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4 (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Zamfara Shari'a Penal Code 2000, s. 204(c), as reproduced in Peters (2001), Appendix Five
204. When intentional homicide is not punishable with death Except in the circumstances mentioned in section 200, intentional homicide is punishable with the payment of diyyah and not with death in any of the following circumstances:- [...] (c) where the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Notes on the Penal Code Law, 1959 (Northern Region No. 18 of 1959), Second Edition 1963, annotated by S. S. Richardson (reproduces the code text with commentary) (anticor.world (scan of the 1963 Government Printer edition))
  • Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC 430/1962) [1963] NGSC 24 (25 March 1963) (NigeriaLII)
  • Sunday Jackson v The State, SC/CR/1026/2022, Supreme Court of Nigeria, 7 March 2025 (certified true copy, 62 pp., scanned; text obtained by OCR) (CITY LAWYER Magazine (hosting the certified copy, watermarked TheNigeriaLawyer))
  • Sunday Jackson v The State (2025-03) Legalpedia 85898 (SC) - summary (Legalpedia)
  • Laoye v The State, SC 200/1984, 25 October 1985, [1985] 2 N.S.C.C. 1251 (headnote) (vLex Nigeria)
  • Ruud Peters, The Reintroduction of Islamic Criminal Law in Northern Nigeria: A Study Conducted on Behalf of the European Commission (Lagos, September 2001), Appendix Five: Relevant provisions of the Shari'a Penal Codes (Zamfara text, Kano deviations noted) (ecoi.net (hosting the EC study))
  • Unreasonable Burdens and Archaic Expectations: A Discourse on the Unrealistic Nature of Self Defense Laws in Nigeria (Chidi Ezenwafor) (LawPavilion blog)
Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

854cae3b14c21184.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Pitcairn Islands

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Pitcairn has no criminal code of its own on self-defence: section 42 of its Constitution (2010) puts in force 'the common law, the rules of equity and the statutes of general application as in force in and for England for the time being', so far as local circumstances permit and subject to local Ordinances, and none of the Pitcairn ordinances checked contains a self-defence provision. Self-defence therefore follows English common law. Under that law, as clarified for England and Wales by section 76 of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, force is judged on the facts as the defender honestly believed them to be and must not be disproportionate, and the possibility of retreat is 'a factor to be taken into account, rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat'; section 76 says it is 'intended to clarify the operation of the existing defences'. No Pitcairn court decision was found saying whether section 76 itself, or the 2013 householder rule, counts as a statute of general application in Pitcairn, so the home rule is left blank. A Pitcairn Attorney-General's report of 2025 describes the 'UK statutory and common law framework' as applying in Pitcairn under s 42.

What the law says
Constitution of Pitcairn (Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010), s 42 Application of English law
42.—(1) Subject to subsection (2), the common law, the rules of equity and the statutes of general application as in force in and for England for the time being shall be in force in Pitcairn. (2) All the laws of England extended to Pitcairn by subsection (1) shall be in force in Pitcairn so far only as the local circumstances and the limits of local jurisdiction permit and subject to any existing or future Ordinance
Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 (UK), s 76(6A) and (9) (England and Wales)
(6A) In deciding the question mentioned in subsection (3), a possibility that D could have retreated is to be considered (so far as relevant) as a factor to be taken into account, rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat. ... (9) This section, except so far as making different provision for householder cases, is intended to clarify the operation of the existing defences mentioned in subsection (2).

bee553b61647799c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

North Dakota

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

North Dakota's Century Code allows deadly force in lawful self-defence or defence of others when necessary to protect against death, serious bodily injury or a violent felony, and never more force than is necessary and appropriate (NDCC 12.1-05-07). The code still contains the older Model Penal Code rule that deadly force is not justified if it can be avoided safely by retreat, but HB 1498, signed on 20 April 2021 and in force from 1 August 2021, added that a person who is not engaged in unlawful activity that gave rise to the need for force and did not provoke the attacker 'is not required to retreat within or from any place the individual otherwise is legally allowed to be'. In a dwelling, place of work, motor vehicle or occupied motor home or travel trailer, deadly force may be used to prevent arson, burglary, robbery or a violent felony there. A person who uses deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering (or dragging a person out of) a dwelling, workplace or occupied motor home is presumed to have had a reasonable fear of death or serious injury; the prosecution can rebut this only by proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and it does not apply against lawful residents, officers lawfully entering, and similar cases (12.1-05-07.1). Anyone who uses force as permitted by the chapter is immune from civil liability to the person they used it against, and a court must award lost income, attorney's fees and costs to a defendant found immune (12.1-05-07.2, amended 2021). A mistaken but honest belief in the need for force is an excuse, but if the belief was held negligently or recklessly it is no defence to crimes of negligence or recklessness (12.1-05-08). No statutory pretrial criminal immunity hearing was found.

At home

Deadly force is justified for a person in possession or control of (or licensed to be in) a dwelling, place of work, motor vehicle, or occupied motor home or travel trailer when needed to prevent arson, burglary, robbery or a violent felony there and lesser force would expose someone to substantial danger of serious injury (NDCC 12.1-05-07(2)(c)). A rebuttable presumption of reasonable fear applies against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering, or removing a person from, a dwelling, workplace or occupied motor home or travel trailer (12.1-05-07.1).

What the law says
NDCC 12.1-05-07(2)(b) (as amended by HB 1498, 2021)
However, the duty to retreat or avoid force does not apply under the following circumstances: ... (2) An individual who is not engaged in an unlawful activity that gives rise to the need for the use of deadly force and has not provoked the individual against whom the deadly force is used, unless the circumstances in subdivision b of subsection 2 of section 12.1-05-03 apply, is not required to retreat within or from any place the individual otherwise is legally allowed to be.
NDCC 12.1-05-07(1)
An individual is not justified in using more force than is necessary and appropriate under the circumstances.
NDCC 12.1-05-07.1 (presumption)
An individual is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or serious bodily injury to that individual or another when using deadly force if: a. The individual against whom the deadly force was used was in the process of unlawfully and forcibly entering, or had unlawfully and forcibly entered and remains within a dwelling, place of work, or occupied motor home or travel trailer ...
NDCC 12.1-05-07.2 (civil immunity)
An individual who uses force as permitted under this chapter is immune from civil liability for the use of the force to the individual against whom force was used or to that individual's estate ...
NDCC 12.1-05-08 (excuse)
However, if his belief is negligently or recklessly held, it is not an excuse in a prosecution for an offense for which negligence or recklessness, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.

1dc688596e1908ba.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Malta

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Article 223 of Malta's Criminal Code (Cap. 9) says no offence is committed when a homicide or bodily harm is 'imposed by actual necessity' in lawful defence of oneself or another, and Article 224 lists cases that count as such necessity (night-time break-in to a dwelling, violent theft, defence of chastity). The code does not use the word 'retreat'. A 1972 article in the University of Malta law students' journal Id-Dritt (A. Rutter Giappone, 'Legitimate defence', Id-Dritt vol. 2, pp. 14-17) states that Maltese case law reads 'actual necessity' to require that the danger 'could not be avoided by any other means', and that two decisions, Police vs. Carmelo Cassar (2 April 1927, Judge Camilleri) and Police vs. Saver Agius (7 November 1953, Judge Harding), 'agree with the English point of view and oblige the person assaulted to retreat'. In Cassar the court excluded legitimate defence 'for lack of actual necessity to repel the violence, the accused having been able to avoid the danger he claimed by taking shelter in a nearby shop and calling nearby people to protect him' (quoted in Italian; our rendering). The article also records the opposite view of continental writers and US courts and notes that excess from being taken by surprise and fear is not punished. This is a dated secondary source quoting old judgments; no recent Court of Criminal Appeal ruling on retreat was opened. A person who exceeds the limits commits an 'excusable' homicide (Articles 227-228), and the excess is unpunished if due to being taken unawares, fear or fright.

At home

Article 224 treats as 'actual necessity of lawful defence' homicide or bodily harm committed while repelling, at night, the scaling or breaking of enclosures, walls or entrance doors of a house or inhabited apartment (or connected appurtenances), and defence against theft or plunder with violence; by day the same act is only 'excusable' (reduced punishment) (Article 227(b)).

What the law says
Criminal Code (Cap. 9), articles 223-224
223. No offence is committed when a homicide or a bodily harm is ordered or permitted by law or by a lawful authority, or is imposed by actual necessity either in lawful self-defence or in the lawful defence of another person. 224. Cases of actual necessity of lawful defence shall include the following: (a) where the homicide or bodily harm is committed in the act of repelling, during the night-time, the scaling or breaking of enclosures, walls, or the entrance doors of any house or inhabited apartment, or of the appurtenances thereof having a direct or an indirect communication with such house or apartment; (b) where the homicide or bodily harm is committed in the act of defence against any person committing theft or plunder, with violence, or attempting to commit such theft or plunder; (c) where the homicide or bodily harm is imposed by the actual necessity of the defence of one's own chastity or of the chastity of another person.
A. Rutter Giappone, 'Legitimate defence', Id-Dritt vol. 2 (May 1972), pp. 15-16 (OCR text; spelling errors in the scan corrected where obvious)
The third disposition, is that the danger threatened must be absolute, that is, it could not be avoided by any other means. This brings us to a very controversial argument. Should the person assaulted try to retreat before inflicting any bodily harm or even killing the aggressor? The superior courts of the United States and continental writers hold that one is not obliged to do so because one cannot, in those circumstances, reason out what is best for his assailant. [...] Our courts also had occasion to give its own interpretation on this point in the cases Police vs. Saver Agius, the 7th November, 1953 and in the case Police vs. Carmelo Cassar on the 2nd April, 1927. Both these cases agree with the English point of view and oblige the person assaulted to retreat. In the case Police vs. Carmelo Cassar, Judge Camilleri said: 'Fu esclusa la legittima difesa ... fra altro sul motivo della mancanza della necessita attuale di respingere la violenza, avendo potuto il citato schivare il pericolo da lui preteso ricoverandosi in una vicina bottega e chiamando la gente vicina a proteggerlo.' [Our rendering of the Italian: Legitimate defence was excluded ... among other things because there was no actual necessity to repel the violence, the accused having been able to avoid the danger he claimed by taking shelter in a nearby shop and calling nearby people to protect him.]

16a8ddcbca7fb400.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

São Tomé and Principe

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

São Tomé and Príncipe's Penal Code (approved by Law 6/2012, on the Portuguese model) treats self-defence as a ground that removes unlawfulness (art. 31). Self-defence is an act carried out 'as a necessary means' to repel a current and unlawful aggression against any legally protected interests of the defender or a third party (art. 32). The code does not mention retreat or flight, and no court decisions from São Tomé on the point were found. If the means used in self-defence are excessive, the act is unlawful but the penalty may be specially reduced; if the excess came from disturbance, fear or fright that is not blameworthy, the person is not punished (art. 33).

What the law says
Código Penal (Lei n.º 6/2012), art. 32.º – Legítima defesa
Constitui legítima defesa o facto praticado, como meio necessário, para repelir a agressão actual e ilícita de quaisquer interesses juridicamente protegidos do agente ou de terceiro.
Código Penal, art. 33.º – Excesso de legítima defesa
1. Se houver excesso nos meios empregados em legítima defesa, o facto é ilícito, mas a pena pode ser especialmente atenuada. 2. Se o excesso resultar de perturbação, medo ou susto não censuráveis, o agente não é punido.

c217ce7b84ec6933.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kansas

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Kansas allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to themselves or a third person (Kan. Stat. § 21-5222(b)). Nothing requires a person to retreat when using force to protect themselves or another (§ 21-5222(c)), and a person who is not engaged in unlawful activity and is attacked in a place where they have a right to be 'has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand such person's ground' (§ 21-5230). These rules were carried over from former K.S.A. 21-3211 and 21-3218 into Kansas's recodified criminal code (L. 2010, ch. 136, effective July 2011). In a home, workplace or occupied vehicle the law presumes the defender reasonably believed deadly force was necessary when facing an unlawful or forceful intruder (§ 21-5224). The justification is not available to a person attempting, committing or escaping a forcible felony, a person who provoked force as an excuse to injure, or another initial provoker unless they reasonably faced imminent deadly danger and exhausted every reasonable means of escape, or withdrew in good faith and clearly said so (§ 21-5226). A person who used justified force is immune from criminal prosecution (which includes arrest, detention and charging) and from civil action, unless the person they used force against was an identified or recognisable on-duty law enforcement officer (§ 21-5231). Kansas courts decide immunity before trial at an evidentiary hearing like a preliminary examination, where the judge weighs all the evidence without deference to the state and the case continues only if the state shows probable cause that the force was not justified (State v. Hardy (2015); State v. Macomber, 309 Kan. 907 (2019)).

At home

Kan. Stat. § 21-5224: a person is presumed to reasonably believe deadly force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm when the other person is unlawfully or forcefully entering, or has entered and is present in, the defender's dwelling, place of work or occupied vehicle, or is removing someone from it against their will, and the defender knows or has reason to believe this. The presumption does not apply against a lawful resident not barred by a protective order, a parent or guardian taking their own child, a law enforcement officer lawfully entering whom the defender knows or should know is an officer, or if the defender is committing a crime or using the place to further one.

What the law says
Kan. Stat. § 21-5230
A person who is not engaged in an unlawful activity and who is attacked in a place where such person has a right to be has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand such person's ground and use any force which such person would be justified in using ...
Kan. Stat. § 21-5222(b)–(c)
A person is justified in the use of deadly force under circumstances described in subsection (a) if such person reasonably believes that such use of deadly force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to such person or a third person. (c) Nothing in this section shall require a person to retreat if such person is using force to protect such person or a third person.
Kan. Stat. § 21-5224(a)
a person is presumed to have a reasonable belief that deadly force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to such person or another person if: (1) The person against whom the force is used, at the time the force is used: (A) Is unlawfully or forcefully entering, or has unlawfully or forcefully entered, and is present within, the dwelling, place of work or occupied vehicle of the person using force ...
Kan. Stat. § 21-5226
is not available to a person who: (a) Is attempting to commit, committing or escaping from the commission of a forcible felony; (b) initially provokes the use of any force against such person or another, with intent to use such force as an excuse to inflict bodily harm upon the assailant; or (c) otherwise initially provokes the use of any force against such person or another, unless ...
Kan. Stat. § 21-5231(a)
A person who uses force which, subject to the provisions of K.S.A. 21-5226, and amendments thereto, is justified pursuant to K.S.A. 21-5222, 21-5223 or 21-5225, and amendments thereto, is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of such force ... As used in this subsection, "criminal prosecution" includes arrest, detention in custody and charging or prosecution of the defendant.

c92a00fb487678c3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Heard Island and McDonald Islands

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Heard Island and McDonald Islands is an uninhabited Australian external territory. Section 5 of the Heard Island and McDonald Islands Act 1953 is headed 'Laws of Australian Capital Territory to be in force' (its full wording could not be opened), so the self-defence rule is taken to be that of the ACT Criminal Code 2002, s. 42, and this entry follows the ACT entry. Under s. 42 conduct is self-defence if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or someone else (or for listed property and trespass purposes) and it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceive them; the section does not mention retreat. Intentionally causing death or serious harm only to protect property or deal with a trespasser is not self-defence.

(2) A person carries out conduct in self-defence only if— (a) the person believes the conduct is necessary— (i) to defend himself or herself or someone else; or ... and (b) the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them. (3) However, the person does not carry out conduct in self-defence if— (a) the person uses force that involves the intentional infliction of death or serious harm— (i) to protect property; or (ii) to prevent criminal trespass; or (iii) to remove a person committing criminal trespass;

cba76fc5571b75a7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Imo

Part of Nigeria, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Self-defence in the southern states follows the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, ss. 286-288, re-enacted as state law; Lagos has its own 2011 wording, see NG-LA). Section 286 allows a person who did not provoke the assault to use reasonably necessary force, and deadly force only where the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm and he believes on reasonable grounds that he 'cannot otherwise preserve' himself. Section 287 covers a person who provoked the fight and withholds protection unless he 'declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable' - the only place the code uses the word 'retreat'. What settles retreat is case law, not the code text. The Supreme Court's most recent full statement, Sunday Jackson v The State (SC/CR/1026/2022, 7 March 2025), lists four conditions that must all be met for self-defence, one of them being that 'there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat' (citing Ochani v State (2017) and Afosi v State (2013)), and it rejected the plea because 'there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat'. The same condition appears in Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), a Criminal Code s. 286 case. The older authority Laoye v The State (SC, 1985) said a person threatened need not 'take to his heels and run', but must show he does not want to fight and is prepared to disengage and make some physical withdrawal; Uwaekweghinya v State (2005), quoted in Jackson, says the same. Read together, the courts require avoidance where it is safely possible, so the category is 'retreat'; the earlier 'judicial' category rested on Laoye alone and did not take account of the 2013-2025 cases. Egheghe (2020) and Edoko v State (2015, Cross River) show these conditions being applied to Criminal Code s. 286 cases. Which state re-enacted which text: only Lagos (2011) was opened; the other southern states' criminal code laws were not opened, so this entry rests on the federal Criminal Code Act text and Supreme Court cases.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 286
286. Self-defence against unprovoked assault When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Criminal Code Act, Cap. C38, s. 287
287. Self-defence against provoked assault When a person has unlawfully assaulted another or has provoked an assault from another, and that other assaults him with such violence as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and to induce him to believe, on reasonable grounds, that it is necessary for his preservation from death or grievous harm to use force in self-defence, he is not criminally responsible for using any such force as is reasonably necessary for such preservation, although such force may cause death or grievous harm. This protection does not extend to a case in which the person using force, which causes death or grievous harm, first began the assault with intent to kill or to do grievous harm to some person; nor to a case in which the person using force which causes death or grievous harm endeavoured to kill or to do grievous harm to some person before the necessity of so preserving himself arose; nor, in either case, unless, before such necessity arose, the person using such force declined further conflict, and quitted it or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 7 March 2025), lead judgment of Idris JSC, pp. 17-18 - conditions
For a successful plea of self-defense, the following conditions must co-exist: (a) the accused must be free from fault in bringing about the encounter; (b) there must be present an impending peril to life or of great bodily harm, either real or apparent as to create the honest belief of an existing necessity; (c) there must be no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat; and (d) there must have been a necessity for taking life. See the case of OCHANI VS. STATE (2017) LPELR - 42352 (SC). In AFOSI VS. STATE (2013) LPELR - 20751 (SC), Ariwoola, JSC held that all the above ingredients must be established conjunctively.
Sunday Jackson v The State (SC, 2025), Idris JSC, p. 22 - application
Concerning conditions (c) and (d), it is clear from the statement of the Appellant that there was a reasonable mode of escape by retreat and there was no necessity to take the life of the deceased
Egheghe v The State (SC, 23 January 2020), conditions (c)-(e) as summarised by Legalpedia
(c)The accused person must have taken reasonable steps to disengage from the encounter, or make some physical withdrawal. (d)There must have been no safe or reasonable mode of escape by retreat. (e)There must have been a necessity for taking life.
Laoye v The State (SC, 1985), held 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval (headnote)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal
Omoregie v The State (SC, 2008), as summarised by Legalpedia
He must show that he did not want to fight and that he was at all material times prepared to withdraw.

Nigeria as a whole

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

976123f19b22f774.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Jan Mayen

A Norwegian island. Shown with the entry for Norway, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Under section 18 of the Norwegian Penal Code (2005), an otherwise punishable act is lawful when it is done to avert an unlawful attack, goes no further than necessary, and does not 'obviously' go beyond what is justifiable given how dangerous the attack is, what interest it violates and the attacker's guilt. The statute does not mention retreat, but because force must be 'necessary', a lawyer answering for the state youth-information service ung.no wrote in 2023 that if there were other ways to avert the attack, 'such as calling for help or running away', a killing cannot be claimed as self-defence; the Supreme Court's appeals committee has also upheld a conviction where the defendant had 'several alternative courses of action' and had partly provoked the fight (HR-2022-1377-U). Someone who goes too far can still be acquitted where 'special reasons' justify it, and the sentence can in any case be reduced (sections 80 and 81, as described by the national encyclopedia). Lawful self-defence is not just unpunished but lawful, so the Supreme Court held in 2018 (HR-2018-2427-A) that the defender cannot be ordered to pay damages when the attack was real.

At home

No separate home-defence rule was found; section 18 applies to attacks on persons and on property alike.

What the law says
Straffeloven (Penal Code 2005), § 18 første ledd (as quoted by the Supreme Court in HR-2022-1377-U)
En handling som ellers ville være straffbar, er lovlig når den a. blir foretatt for å avverge et ulovlig angrep, b. ikke går lenger enn nødvendig, og c. ikke går åpenbart ut over hva som er forsvarlig under hensyn til hvor farlig angrepet er, hva slags interesse som angrepet krenker, og angriperens skyld.

10192ec4d520bcd3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Andorra

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 27(1) of the Penal Code (Law 9/2005, consolidated text 2014) excludes criminal liability for acting in defence of oneself, one's rights or another person when four conditions are met: an unlawful aggression; rational necessity of the means used to prevent or repel it; harm that is not disproportionate to the seriousness of the aggression and the circumstances of the aggressor; and no sufficient provocation by the defender. The code does not mention retreat, and no Andorran court ruling on retreat was found. If not all the requirements are met (incomplete self-defence), the penalty is reduced in a 'qualified' way under articles 28 and 54.

At home

Article 27(1)(a): when defending one's home or domicile, unlawful entry ('l'entrada indeguda') counts as an unlawful aggression, so defence may begin from the intrusion itself; the other requirements (rational necessity of the means, no disproportionate harm, no provocation) still apply.

What the law says
Codi penal (Llei 9/2005, text refós 2014), art. 27(1)
Són circumstàncies que exclouen la responsabilitat criminal: 1. Actuar en defensa de la persona o de drets propis o d'altri, si hi concorren els requisits següents: a) Agressió il·legítima. En cas de defensa de béns, es considera agressió il·legítima l'acció constitutiva de delicte o contravenció penal que els posi en perill de deteriorament o pèrdua imminent. En cas de defensa de la llar o del domicili, es considera agressió il·legítima l'entrada indeguda. b) Necessitat racional del mitjà emprat per impedir-la o repel·lir-la. c) Que el mal causat per l'acció de defensa no sigui desproporcionat en relació amb la gravetat de l'agressió i amb les circumstàncies de l'agressor. d) No haver-hi hagut provocació suficient per part del defensor.
Codi penal, art. 28
Les circumstàncies expressades en l'article anterior, quan no hi concorrin tots els requisits necessaris per eximir de responsabilitat, atenuen de manera qualificada la pena d'acord amb el que disposa l'article 54.

aa18cbd621b7e086.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Grenada

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Grenada's Criminal Code s. 62 grades 'necessary force' by the crime resisted, allowing killing only 'in case of extreme necessity' against listed grave crimes. Grenadian Court of Appeal decisions on self-defence directions (Leroy Passee 1992, Peter Duncan 2005, Lennie Ross 2006, Roland Charles 2006) were found through the court's search engine, but none mentions retreat. The Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal, which also hears this place's appeals, has upheld 'no duty to retreat' directions in cases from the British Virgin Islands (Shonovia Thomas, 2012), Antigua and Barbuda (Kevil Nelson, 2013) and Saint Vincent (Marshall Phillips, 2024), but no decision from this place itself saying so was found, so the category stays unclear.

d3c08123554743cd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Saint Kitts and Nevis

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Self-defence in Saint Kitts and Nevis is governed by the common law as stated by the Privy Council in Palmer v R (1971), which the Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal applies. A person who reasonably believes their life is in danger, or that they face serious bodily harm, may use the force they believe on reasonable grounds is necessary, and is not guilty even if the killing was intentional. There is no fixed rule that one must retreat: the chance to retreat without danger is one of the circumstances the jury weighs in deciding whether the force was reasonably necessary. An older Court of Appeal case (Michaud v R, 1969) records a trial direction that a person facing a felonious attack has no duty to retreat and may stand their ground. No statute on retreat, home defence or excessive self-defence was found.

What the law says
Palmer v R [1971] AC 814 (PC), at p. 823, as quoted in Spencer v Director of Public Prosecutions (Court of Appeal, Saint Kitts and Nevis)
A man who is attacked in circumstances where he reasonably believes his life to be in danger or that he is in danger of serious bodily harm, may use such force as on reasonable grounds he believes is necessary to prevent and resist the attack. And if in using such force he kills his assailant he is not guilty of any crime even if the killing was intentional. And in deciding in a particular case whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as in fact was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything he is entitled to protect.
Michaud v R (West Indies Associated States Court of Appeal, Saint Kitts and Nevis), trial judge's direction quoted in the judgment
If the attack is a felonious one, the victim is under no duty to retreat but may stand his ground and repel

58e8a0da8c31f738.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ciudad de México (Mexico City)

Part of Mexico, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Mexico City's Penal Code (Código Penal para el Distrito Federal, still so named) lists legitimate defence as a justification in art. 29(B)(I): a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence used was necessary and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. The code does not mention retreating, fleeing or avoiding the attack. Intruders into a dwelling are presumed to be lawful targets of defence unless shown otherwise. Excess in self-defence is punished with one quarter of the penalty for the offence (art. 83). Mexico's federal Penal Code (entry MEX) applies only to federal offences.

At home

Art. 29(B)(I) presumes legitimate defence, unless proven otherwise, when harm is caused to someone who tries to enter or enters without right the place where the defender lives (temporarily or permanently), their family's home or that of anyone they must defend, its outbuildings, or a place holding property they must protect; the same applies to harm caused to an intruder surprised there in circumstances suggesting a possible attack.

What the law says
Código Penal para el Distrito Federal (Ciudad de México), art. 29, apartado B, fracc. I
I. (Legítima defensa).- Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente y sin derecho, en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa empleada y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de su defensor. Se presume que existe legítima defensa, salvo prueba en contrario, cuando se cause un daño a quien por cualquier medio trate de penetrar o penetre, sin derecho, al lugar en que habite de forma temporal o permanente el que se defiende, al de su familia o al de cualquier persona respecto de las que el agente tenga la obligación de defender, a sus dependencias o al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que exista la misma obligación. Igual presunción existirá cuando el daño se cause a un intruso al momento de sorprenderlo en alguno de los lugares antes citados en circunstancias tales que revelen la posibilidad de una agresión;
Código Penal para el Distrito Federal (Ciudad de México), art. 83, third paragraph
Al que incurra en exceso, en los casos previstos en las fracciones I, II, III y IV de la letra B del artículo 29 de este Código, se le impondrá la cuarta parte de las penas o medidas de seguridad, correspondientes al delito de que se trate, siempre y cuando con relación al exceso, no exista otra causa de exclusión del delito.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Código Penal para el Distrito Federal (última reforma publicada en la GOCDMX el 26 de agosto de 2026) (Congreso de la Ciudad de México)
  • Marco legal CDMX (listing) (Congreso de la Ciudad de México)
Mexico as a whole

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

c42b22d859fcf0d9.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New Mexico

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

New Mexico has no stand-your-ground statute; its no-retreat rule comes from the courts. The justifiable-homicide statute, unchanged in substance since 1963 (NMSA 30-2-7), allows a killing in the necessary defence of one's life, family or property, or in lawful defence of oneself or another when there are reasonable grounds to believe someone intends to commit a felony or great personal injury and the danger is imminent. In State v. Horton (1953) the Supreme Court held it was wrong to tell a jury that the defendant could not kill his assailant if he could yield without being killed, and the pattern instruction UJI 14-5190 now tells jurors that an attacked person 'need not retreat' and may stand their ground, at home or anywhere. The committee commentary adds that a person may still use no more force than is reasonably necessary, and that the person need not retreat even though they could do so safely. In State v. Anderson (2016-NMCA-007) the Court of Appeals held that leaving out UJI 14-5190 when the evidence supported it was fundamental error. The instruction was most recently amended by Supreme Court order effective 31 December 2025. A 2017 bill (HB 168) proposed a statutory presumption of reasonable belief, but the compiled statute contains no presumption and no 'deadly force' wording. No civil immunity statute or pretrial immunity hearing was found.

At home

NMSA 30-2-7(A) makes homicide justifiable in the necessary defence of one's life, family or property. The pattern instruction UJI 14-5190 says a person defending against an attack, defending another or defending property 'need not retreat' and may stand their ground and defend 'the person's habitation'. No separate castle statute or home-intruder presumption was found.

What the law says
NMSA 1978, § 30-2-7(A) (Laws 1963, ch. 303, § 2-8)
when committed in the necessary defense of his life, his family or his property, ...
UJI 14-5190 NMRA, Self defense; assailed person need not retreat (as amended eff. 31 Dec 2025)
A person who is [defending against an attack] [defending another from an attack] [or] [defending property] need not retreat. In the exercise of the right of [self defense] [defense of another] [or] [defense of property], [a person] may stand [the person’s] ground and defend [[herself] [himself]] [themselves] [another] [the person’s habitation] [or] [property].
State v. Horton, 1953-NMSC-044, 57 N.M. 257, 258 P.2d 371 (leading case)
Certainly the italicized sentence is erroneous in telling the jury the defendant could not kill his assailant if he could yield without being killed
UJI 14-5190 committee commentary
A person need not, however, retreat even though the person could do so safely.

be528a1c6440ff75.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Réunion

An overseas region of France, part of France itself. Shown with the entry for France, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 122-5 of the Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. The defence must be simultaneous with the attack; a blow struck after the attacker has left is treated as ordinary violence. Neither art. 122-5 nor art. 122-6 mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Judges decide whether the defence was disproportionate; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes that an excessive response may lead to mitigating circumstances or a conviction for a lesser offence rather than full exoneration.

At home

Art. 122-6 of the Penal Code presumes self-defence for a person who acts "to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place", and against perpetrators of violent theft or looting. The presumption is rebuttable and does not cover daytime intrusions, which fall under the general rule of art. 122-5.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

f18b84ac9be83924.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Guam

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Guam's Criminal and Correctional Code follows the Model Penal Code. Force is justified when immediately necessary to protect oneself against unlawful force on the present occasion (9 GCA § 7.84), and deadly force only when the person believes it necessary to prevent death, serious bodily harm, kidnapping, or compelled rape or sodomy (§ 7.86(b)). Guam keeps a duty to retreat: deadly force is not justified if the defendant knows they can avoid the need for it with complete safety by retreating, except that they need not retreat from their dwelling, place of work or vehicle unless they were the initial aggressor (§ 7.86(b)(2)). There is no exception for public places. The Castle Doctrine Act (P.L. 32-111, 2014) adds, for lawful occupants of business buildings, residences, vehicles and house boats (not yards or outdoor areas), an express no-retreat rule, a presumption of reasonable fear against someone unlawfully and forcefully entering, and immunity from criminal prosecution and civil action, with exceptions such as force against an identified on-duty police officer. A person defending another need not retreat before acting unless they know retreat would secure the other person's complete safety (§ 7.88(b)). No pretrial immunity hearing procedure was confirmed.

At home

No duty to retreat from one's dwelling, place of work or vehicle unless the defendant was the initial aggressor (9 GCA § 7.86(b)(2)(A)). Guam's Castle Doctrine Act (P.L. 32-111, 10 February 2014) adds that a lawful occupant of 'habitable property' (business buildings, residences, vehicles and house boats they have a legal right to occupy, but not yards or outdoor spaces) has no duty to retreat, is presumed to have reasonable fear of death or serious injury when using force against someone unlawfully and forcefully entering, and is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action (§§ 7.112-7.113).

The Guam code was read through a summarising fetch tool that returns only short verbatim excerpts; the ellipses and bracketed word join separate excerpts.

What the law says
9 GCA § 7.86(b)(2)
... knows that he can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating ... [except] the defendant is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling, place of work or vehicle, unless he was the initial aggressor
9 GCA § 7.84
immediately necessary for the purpose of protecting himself against the use of unlawful force
9 GCA § 7.112 (Castle Doctrine Act, P.L. 32-111, 2014)
A person is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or serious bodily injury ... a lawful occupant of habitable property has no duty or obligation to retreat
9 GCA § 7.113(b) (immunity)
is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of such force

11063ebf9928ea17.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cocos (Keeling) Islands (Australia)

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Cocos is an Australian external territory with no criminal code of its own: section 8A of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands Act 1955 (Cth), inserted by the Territories Law Reform Act 1992, makes the law of Western Australia 'as in force in Western Australia from time to time' the law of the Territory, so the Western Australian Criminal Code applies there (alongside Commonwealth offences). Under that Code (s 248, rewritten in 2008), a harmful act is self-defence if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or another from a harmful act, even one not imminent, it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they believe them to be, and there are reasonable grounds for those beliefs. The Code does not mention retreat, so no duty to retreat is written into the law; whether escape was possible would be weighed as part of whether the response was necessary and reasonable. If a killing would have been self-defence except that the response was not reasonable, the person is guilty of manslaughter instead of murder (s 248(3), excessive self-defence). A separate home-invasion rule (s 244) gives occupants wider room inside their home.

At home

Western Australia's home-invasion rule applies: under Criminal Code (WA) s 244 an occupant may use any force they believe on reasonable grounds is necessary to keep out or remove a home invader or defend against violence, but force intended or likely to cause death is lawful only if the occupant believes on reasonable grounds that violence is being or is likely to be used or threatened against a person (s 244(1A)).

What the law says
Cocos (Keeling) Islands Act 1955 (Cth), s 8A(1) (compilation of 11 December 2010)
Subject to this section, section 8G and Part IVAA, the provisions of the law of Western Australia (whether made before or after this section’s commencement) as in force in Western Australia from time to time are in force in the Territory.
Criminal Code (WA), s 248(3)–(4) Self-defence (applied in the Territory)
(3) If — (a) a person unlawfully kills another person in circumstances which, but for this section, would constitute murder; and (b) the person’s act that causes the other person’s death would be an act done in self‑defence under subsection (4) but for the fact that the act is not a reasonable response by the person in the circumstances as the person believes them to be, the person is guilty of manslaughter and not murder. (4) A person’s harmful act is done in self‑defence if — (a) the person believes the act is necessary to defend the person or another person from a harmful act, including a harmful act that is not imminent; and (b) the person’s harmful act is a reasonable response by the person in the circumstances as the person believes them to be; and (c) there are reasonable grounds for those beliefs.
Criminal Code (WA), s 244(1A) Home invasion (applied in the Territory)
Despite subsection (1), it is not lawful for the occupant to use force that is intended, or that is likely, to cause death to a home invader unless the occupant believes, on reasonable grounds, that violence is being or is likely to be used or is threatened in relation to a person by a home invader.

70802dcaff5ee8bf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Curaçao

Part of Kingdom of the Netherlands, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Curaçao has its own Criminal Code; self-defence (noodweer) is in article 1:114, as cited by the Court of First Instance of Curaçao. The court applies the same test as the Dutch Supreme Court: the act must be required by the necessary defence of one's own or another's body, honour or property against an immediate, unlawful attack, and must meet a subsidiarity and a proportionality requirement (ECLI:NL:OGEAC:2023:213). Under subsidiarity, self-defence fails if the defendant not only could have but also should have withdrawn from the attack; this requires a real and reasonable chance to escape and that escape could fairly be expected, which is not so when the situation is so threatening that withdrawing is no real alternative. In a 2021 shooting case the court held the defendant 'could and also should' have withdrawn (ECLI:NL:OGEAC:2021:275). Excessive self-defence caused by a violent emotion from the attack (noodweerexces) is also recognised, but was rejected in the cases opened.

At home

No separate home-defence rule was found in the decisions opened; the general test covers defence of body, honour and property.

What the law says
Gerecht in eerste aanleg van Curaçao, ECLI:NL:OGEAC:2023:213
Aan de subsidiariteitseis is niet voldaan indien de verdachte zich niet behoefde te verdedigen en er dus geen noodzaak tot verdediging bestond. Daarvan is bijvoorbeeld sprake indien de verdachte zich niet alleen aan de aanranding had kunnen, maar zich daaraan ook had moeten onttrekken. Het zich aan de aanranding kunnen onttrekken houdt in dat daartoe voor de verdachte een reële en redelijke mogelijkheid moet hebben bestaan. [...] Onttrekking aan de aanranding moet voorts van de verdachte kunnen worden gevergd. Dit behoeft bijvoorbeeld niet het geval te zijn wanneer de situatie zo bedreigend is dat zich onttrekken aan de aanranding geen reëel alternatief is.
Gerecht in eerste aanleg van Curaçao, ECLI:NL:OGEAC:2021:275 (citing art. 1:114 Wetboek van Strafrecht)
De gestelde aanranding moet in redelijkheid beschouwd zodanig bedreigend zijn voor de verdachte dat deze kan worden aangemerkt als een ogenblikkelijke aanranding in de zin van artikel 1:114 van het Wetboek van Strafrecht. [...] Als de verdachte op dat moment op grond van de uitlatingen en het gedrag van het slachtoffer vreesde door het slachtoffer neergeschoten te worden, had hij zich aan het slachtoffer kunnen - en ook moeten - onttrekken.
