af8899613142dedf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Wallis and Futuna

Part of France, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Wallis and Futuna shares France's Penal Code: article 711-1 makes Books I to V of the code applicable there, subject to local adaptations (for example, fines are set in local currency under article 711-3). Under article 122-5, a person is not criminally responsible for an act required by the need for self-defence of themselves or another, done at the same time as an unjustified attack, unless the means of defence were disproportionate to the seriousness of the attack; defence of property may not include intentional homicide. The code does not mention retreat, and no court ruling on retreat was checked here. Article 122-6 adds presumptions of self-defence for night-time break-ins into inhabited places and violent thefts or looting.

At home

Article 122-6 of the French Penal Code, which applies in Wallis and Futuna, presumes self-defence for a person who acts to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, or to defend against perpetrators of thefts or looting carried out with violence.

What the law says
Code pénal (France), art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal, art. 711-1 (as amended by loi n° 2026-813 du 24 août 2026)
Sous réserve des adaptations prévues au présent titre, les livres Ier à V du présent code sont applicables, dans leur rédaction résultant de la loi n° 2026-813 du 24 août 2026 visant à protéger les mineurs des risques auxquels les expose l'utilisation des réseaux sociaux, en Nouvelle-Calédonie, en Polynésie française et dans les îles Wallis et Futuna.

ee3e20ec497831f3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Brčko District

Part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Brčko District has its own Criminal Code (Krivični zakon Brčko distrikta BiH, consolidated 2020, amended 2024). Article 26 says an act done in necessary defence is not a crime, and defines it as defence that is absolutely necessary to repel a simultaneous or directly imminent unlawful attack on oneself or another and that is proportionate to the attack. The code does not mention retreat or the home, and no court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits may get a lighter sentence, or none if the excess came from strong irritation or fright caused by the attack.

What the law says
Krivični zakon Brčko distrikta BiH (Sl. glasnik BD 19/2020 – prečišćen tekst, 3/2024, 14/2024), član 26 – Nužna odbrana
(1) Nije krivično djelo ono djelo koje je učinjeno u nužnoj odbrani. (2) Nužna je ona odbrana koja je neophodno potrebna da učinilac od sebe ili od drugog odbije istovremeni ili direktno predstojeći protivpravni napad, a koja je srazmjerna napadu. (3) Učinilac koji prekorači granice nužne odbrane može se blaže kazniti, a ako je prekoračenje učinio zbog jake razdraženosti ili prepasti izazvane napadom, može se i osloboditi kazne.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Krivični zakon Brčko distrikta BiH (consolidated text) (Paragraf Lex BA)
  • Krivični zakon Brčko distrikta BiH (2003 text, PDF) (Tužilaštvo BiH)
Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole

Bosnia and Herzegovina has four criminal codes: one for the state level and one each for the Federation of BiH, Republika Srpska and Brčko District; ordinary crimes such as homicide are mostly tried under the entity codes, which were not checked here. The state-level Criminal Code (article 24) says an act committed in necessary defence is not a crime, and defines necessary defence as one that is absolutely necessary to repel a simultaneous or directly imminent unlawful attack on oneself or another and that is proportionate to the attack. The code does not mention retreat, and no court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits may receive a lighter sentence, and may be spared punishment entirely if the excess was caused by strong irritation or fright caused by the attack.

65e353f6ab3bb19a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Dominica

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Dominica's Offences Against the Person Act (Chapter 10:31, first enacted 1873) has an 'Excusable homicide' section, s. 11. It says no punishment applies to a person who kills another 'in his own defence'. The Act does not say what counts as self-defence, how much force is allowed, or whether a person must retreat first. Those questions are left to the common law, which this Act does not set out. No Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court judgment from a Dominica case on retreat could be opened, so nothing settles the retreat question here.

What the law says
Offences Against the Person Act, Chap. 10:31 (Revised Laws of Dominica 1990), s. 11 'Excusable homicide'
11. No punishment or forfeiture shall be incurred by any person who kills another by misfortune, or in his own defence, or in any other manner without felony.

da263e52bce96ad3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Liechtenstein

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Section 3 of Liechtenstein's Criminal Code (StGB 1987, modelled on Austria's § 3 StGB) says a person acts lawfully who uses only the defence necessary to fend off a present or imminent unlawful attack on life, health, bodily integrity, freedom or property, unless the attacked person obviously faced only minor harm and the defence was inappropriate. The code does not mention retreat. The Princely Supreme Court (Fürstlicher Oberster Gerichtshof, OGH), in its judgment of 10 February 2012 in 01 KG.2010.22 (a murder case), applying Austrian commentary (Lewisch, Wiener Kommentar zum StGB § 3), stated the test: the necessity of the defence depends on the kind and extent of the attack and the defender's concrete options; the attacked person must choose the mildest defence by kind and degree that works, but 'need take no risk as to the effectiveness' of the measure chosen, and 'no weighing of interests or proportionality test between the attacked and the impaired legal interest' takes place. The same judgment records the Court of Appeal's (Obergericht) reasoning, upheld by the OGH, that the attack having happened in a small cramped room did not change the finding of excess, adding that it did not appear from the findings 'that there were no chances of flight', as the room was unlocked — so the availability of escape was treated as one circumstance in judging whether kicks to the head were necessary, not as a freestanding duty to retreat. On that basis the entry is marked proportional (necessity test, with flight possibility only one factor); no source states in terms that retreat is or is not required. Exceeding the justified measure only from dismay, fear or fright is punishable only if negligent (§ 3(2)); the OGH held that excess driven also by anger ('sthenic affect') is not privileged.

What the law says
Strafgesetzbuch (StGB) vom 24. Juni 1987, LGBl. 1988 Nr. 37, § 3 Abs. 1
1) Nicht rechtswidrig handelt, wer sich nur der Verteidigung bedient, die notwendig ist, um einen gegenwärtigen oder unmittelbar drohenden rechtswidrigen Angriff auf Leben, Gesundheit, körperliche Unversehrtheit, Freiheit oder Vermögen von sich oder einem anderen abzuwehren. Die Handlung ist jedoch nicht gerechtfertigt, wenn es offensichtlich ist, dass dem Angegriffenen bloss ein geringer Nachteil droht und die Verteidigung, insbesondere wegen der Schwere der zur Abwehr nötigen Beeinträchtigung des Angreifers, unangemessen ist. [Our rendering: A person does not act unlawfully who uses only the defence necessary to repel a present or imminently threatening unlawful attack on the life, health, bodily integrity, freedom or property of himself or another. The act is however not justified if it is obvious that the person attacked faces only a minor harm and the defence, particularly because of the severity of the injury to the attacker needed to repel it, is inappropriate.]
Fürstlicher Oberster Gerichtshof (OGH), Urteil 10.02.2012, 01 KG.2010.22 – the OGH's own statement of the test
Bei der Notwendigkeit der Abwehr sind Art und Ausmass des Angriffs genauso bedeutsam wie die konkreten Verteidigungsmöglichkeiten und -fähigkeiten des Angegriffenen. Das Mass der Abwehr bestimmt sich regelmässig nach der Art, der Wucht und der Intensität des abzuwehrenden Angriffs, nach der Gefährlichkeit des Angreifers und nach den zur Abwehr zur Verfügung stehenden Mittel. Der Angegriffene hat dabei die nach Art und Mass gelindeste Abwehr zu wählen, wobei er allerdings kein Risiko bezüglich der Effektivität einer ergriffenen Verteidigungsmassnahme einzugehen hat (Lewisch, WK-StGB § 3 Rz 92 ff). [Our rendering: For the necessity of the defence, the kind and extent of the attack matter as much as the concrete defensive options and abilities of the person attacked. The measure of defence is determined as a rule by the kind, force and intensity of the attack to be repelled, the dangerousness of the attacker and the means available for defence. The person attacked must choose the mildest defence by kind and degree, but need take no risk as to the effectiveness of the defensive measure chosen.]
Same judgment – Obergericht reasoning recounted and upheld (flight chances; mildest effective defence; no weighing of interests)
An dieser Einschätzung vermag auch der Umstand nichts zu ändern, dass die gesamte Auseinandersetzung in einem kleinen beengten Raum stattgefunden hat. Dass Fluchtchancen nicht bestanden hätten, geht aus den erstgerichtlichen Feststellungen im Übrigen nicht hervor und ist auch aus den Ermittlungsergebnissen nicht abzuleiten, weil der Raum nach Einlass des GM*** offensichtlich unversperrt war. Kommen mehrere Möglichkeiten der Verteidigung in Betracht, so hat der Verteidiger die nach Art und Mass gelindeste Abwehr zu wählen. Der Verteidiger darf jene Abwehr wählen, die zur verlässlichen, sofortigen Gefahrenabwehr hinreichend wirksam ist, ihn also "gegenüber dem Angreifer unbedingt überlegen" macht (Lewisch aaO, Rz 95). [...] Bei der Abwehr finde weder eine Güterabwägung noch eine Prüfung der Verhältnismässigkeit von angegriffenem und beeinträchtigtem Rechtsgut statt. [Our rendering: Nor does the fact that the whole fight took place in a small cramped room change this assessment. That there were no chances of flight does not, moreover, follow from the first-instance findings and cannot be derived from the investigation results, since the room was evidently unlocked after GM*** was let in. Where several possibilities of defence are available, the defender must choose the mildest by kind and degree. The defender may choose the defence that is sufficiently effective for reliable, immediate repulsion of the danger, i.e. that makes him 'absolutely superior to the attacker'. ... In the defence there is neither a weighing of interests nor a proportionality test between the attacked and the impaired legal interest. (Note: the last sentence appears in the judgment's summary of the appellant's submissions.)]

3dc5f174787bccd1.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Macao S.A.R

Part of China, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Macao has its own Penal Code (1995), modelled on Portugal's. Art. 31 defines legítima defesa as an act carried out 'as the necessary means to repel a current and unlawful aggression' against legally protected interests of the defender or a third party; art. 32 makes excess of means unlawful but allows a specially reduced sentence, and excess from non-blameworthy disturbance, fear or fright is unpunished. The Court of Second Instance (TSI) has twice stated the requirements in a way that bears on avoidance: in case 126/2002 (19 June 2003) it held that 'necessity' means the defender 'has no alternative other than the means used', and quoted the former Tribunal Superior de Justiça (29 March 1995, case 293) that self-defence presupposes 'the impossibility of recourse to the public force'; in case 484/2006 (21 Feb 2008) it listed 'the impossibility of recourse to the public force' among the requirements, and the prosecution there argued this is 'an aspect of the necessity of the means'. The word 'retreat' or 'flight' does not appear; the rule is framed as the means being the only alternative and public help being unavailable, so this entry treats it as an avoidance requirement. No Court of Final Appeal decision on flight (the Portuguese 'commodus discessus' question) was opened.

At home

No home-defence rule in arts. 30-32 of the Macao Penal Code as quoted by the TSI; none of the decisions opened concerns a dwelling.

What the law says
Código Penal de Macau, art. 31 (Legítima defesa), as quoted in TSI case 126/2002 — original
Artigo 31.º (Legítima defesa) Constitui legítima defesa o facto praticado como meio necessário para repelir a agressão actual e ilícita de interesses juridicamente protegidos do agente ou de terceiro. Artigo 32.º (Excesso de Legítima defesa) 1. Se houver excesso dos meios empregados em legítima defesa, o facto é ilícito, mas a pena pode ser esepcialmente atenuada. 2. O agente não é punido se o excesso resultar de pertubação, medo ou susto não censuráveis.
Código Penal de Macau, arts. 31-32 — English rendering (not an official translation)
[Rendering by the researcher:] Art. 31 (Self-defence) Self-defence is an act carried out as the necessary means to repel a current and unlawful aggression against legally protected interests of the actor or of a third party. Art. 32 (Excess of self-defence) 1. If there is excess in the means used in self-defence, the act is unlawful, but the sentence may be specially reduced. 2. The actor is not punished if the excess results from non-blameworthy disturbance, fear or fright.
Tribunal de Segunda Instância, Recurso n.º 126/2002, 19 June 2003, pp. 11-12 — original
E a necessidade e racionalidade do meio da defesa são de ponderar em situação concreta em que o defendente se encontra. Diz-se necessidade que o defendente se encontra na situação em que, perante a agressão ilícita e actual, não há outra alternativa senão o meio utilizado, enquanto diz racionalidade que, perante a situação concreta, o meio seja suficiente para o seu fim de defesa, sem exigência de proporcionalidade. … O então Tribunal Superior de Justiça no Acórdão de 29/3/1995 do processo nº 293, na apreciação da questão idêntica, consignou que: “Pressupõem a legítima defesa a agressão ilegal e actual (por em execução ou iminente) não provocada pelo defendente, a impossibilidade de recurso à força pública e a racionalidade do meio utilizado, estando o elemento subjectivo, preenchido com o animus defendendi”.
TSI 126/2002 — English rendering (not an official translation)
[Rendering by the researcher:] The necessity and rationality of the means of defence are to be weighed in the concrete situation in which the defender finds himself. Necessity means that the defender is in a situation where, faced with the unlawful and current aggression, there is no alternative other than the means used, while rationality means that, in the concrete situation, the means is sufficient for its defensive purpose, without a requirement of proportionality. … The former Tribunal Superior de Justiça, in its judgment of 29 March 1995 in case no. 293, assessing an identical question, stated: 'Self-defence presupposes an unlawful and current aggression (in progress or imminent) not provoked by the defender, the impossibility of recourse to the public force and the rationality of the means used, the subjective element being satisfied by the animus defendendi.'
Tribunal de Segunda Instância, Processo n.º 484/2006, 21 February 2008, headnote 1 — original
Só se verifica uma situação de legítima defesa quando a agressão seja ilegal e actual (por em execução ou iminente), não provocada pelo defendente, ocorra a impossibilidade de recurso à força pública e a racionalidade do meio utilizado, estando o elemento subjectivo, preenchido com o animus defendendi. [Rendering: A situation of self-defence exists only when the aggression is unlawful and current (in progress or imminent), not provoked by the defender, there is the impossibility of recourse to the public force, and the means used is rational, the subjective element being satisfied by the animus defendendi.]
TSI 484/2006, prosecution response as recorded by the court, p. 4 — original
E aqui se inclui, como requisito de legítima defesa, a impossibilidade de recorrer à força pública, por se tratar de um aspecto da necessidade do meio. 3 - No entanto, o recorrente tinha condições para recorrer à força pública e a demais vias possíveis. [Rendering: And here is included, as a requirement of self-defence, the impossibility of resorting to the public force, since it is an aspect of the necessity of the means. 3 - However, the appellant was in a position to resort to the public force and to the other possible avenues.]
Tribunal de Segunda Instância, Processo n.º 164/2008, 24 April 2008, summary — original
A definição legal do art.o 31.o do Código Penal de Macau pressupõe sempre a actualidade do ataque do agressor para efeitos de verificação da legítima defesa. [Rendering: The legal definition in art. 31 of the Macao Penal Code always presupposes that the aggressor's attack is current for self-defence to be found.]
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

  • TSI Processo n.º 484/2006, acórdão de 21 de Fevereiro de 2008 (Retorsão — Legítima defesa) (Tribunais da RAEM (court.gov.mo))
  • TSI Processo n.º 164/2008, acórdão de 24 de Abril de 2008 (legítima defesa — art. 31 CP) (Tribunais da RAEM (court.gov.mo))

0b0380882b77db58.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tokelau

Part of New Zealand, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Tokelau, a New Zealand territory, has its own criminal law made by its General Fono: the Crimes, Procedure and Evidence Rules 2003. Rule 116(3) says everyone is justified in using, in their own defence or in defence of another, such force as is reasonable in the circumstances as the person believes them to be (the same wording as New Zealand's Crimes Act s 48). Rule 15(4)–(5) separately allows force reasonably necessary to prevent an offence likely to cause immediate and serious injury, but no more than is 'reasonably proportionate' to the harm feared. The Rules do not mention retreat, escape or the home in connection with force, and no Tokelau court decisions on retreat were found. No partial 'excessive self-defence' rule appears in the text.

What the law says
Crimes, Procedure and Evidence Rules 2003 (Tokelau), r 116(3) Insanity, necessity and self-defence
Everyone is justified in using in their defence or in the defence of another, such force as, in the circumstances as the person believes them to be, it is reasonable to use.
Crimes, Procedure and Evidence Rules 2003 (Tokelau), r 15(4)–(5)
A person is justified in using such force as may be reasonably necessary in order to prevent — ... the commission of an offence which would be likely to cause immediate and serious injury to any person ... Such force as may be reasonably necessary for the purposes of paragraph (4) means the use of no more force ... than is reasonably proportionate to the injury to the person or damage to property apprehended.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)

0861cd30718769c5.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Barbados

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Barbados's self-defence law comes from court decisions. In Jones v The Queen (Court of Appeal, Criminal Appeal No. 3 of 2002, 7 March 2003) the full judgment, now opened on the Barbados courts' website, sets out the trial judge's direction quoting Palmer v R, including that 'It may in some cases be only sensible and clearly possible to take some simple avoiding action'. That treats avoiding the attack as something that may be sensible in some cases, but neither Jones nor Edward Bailey v The Queen (Court of Appeal, 2019, also opened) says in words whether a person must retreat. The Caribbean Court of Justice (Troy Stanford, 2017) requires an honest belief in imminent attack. Retreat is therefore not settled by the sources found.

What the law says
Palmer v R (Privy Council, 1971), as quoted by the trial judge and set out in Jones v The Queen, Court of Appeal of Barbados, Criminal Appeal No. 3 of 2002, para. 12
“It is both good law andgood sense that a man who is attacked may defend himself. It is both good law and common sense that hemay do but may only do what is reasonably necessary. But everything will depend upon theparticular facts and circumstances. Ofthese a jury can decide. It may in some cases be only sensible and clearlypossible to take some simple avoiding action. Some attacks may be serious and dangerous, others may not be.”
Troy Stanford v The Queen, Caribbean Court of Justice (6 Apr 2017), media release (from previous entry)
the deliberate yet reasonable result of an accused's honest belief that he or another person was under imminent attack
What was tried

74bb36427cd42162.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Christmas Island (Australia)

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Christmas Island is an Australian external territory with no criminal code of its own: section 8A of the Christmas Island Act 1958 (Cth), inserted by the Territories Law Reform Act 1992, makes the law of Western Australia 'as in force in Western Australia from time to time' the law of the Territory, so the Western Australian Criminal Code applies there (alongside Commonwealth offences). Under that Code (s 248, rewritten in 2008), a harmful act is self-defence if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or another from a harmful act, even one not imminent, it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they believe them to be, and there are reasonable grounds for those beliefs. The Code does not mention retreat, so no duty to retreat is written into the law; whether escape was possible would be weighed as part of whether the response was necessary and reasonable. If a killing would have been self-defence except that the response was not reasonable, the person is guilty of manslaughter instead of murder (s 248(3), excessive self-defence). A separate home-invasion rule (s 244) gives occupants wider room inside their home.

At home

Western Australia's home-invasion rule applies: under Criminal Code (WA) s 244 an occupant may use any force they believe on reasonable grounds is necessary to keep out or remove a home invader or defend against violence, but force intended or likely to cause death is lawful only if the occupant believes on reasonable grounds that violence is being or is likely to be used or threatened against a person (s 244(1A)).

What the law says
Christmas Island Act 1958 (Cth), s 8A(1) (compilation of 11 December 2010)
Subject to this section, section 8G and Part IVA, the provisions of the law of Western Australia (whether made before or after this section’s commencement) as in force in Western Australia from time to time are in force in the Territory.
Criminal Code (WA), s 248(3)–(4) Self-defence (applied in the Territory)
(3) If — (a) a person unlawfully kills another person in circumstances which, but for this section, would constitute murder; and (b) the person’s act that causes the other person’s death would be an act done in self‑defence under subsection (4) but for the fact that the act is not a reasonable response by the person in the circumstances as the person believes them to be, the person is guilty of manslaughter and not murder. (4) A person’s harmful act is done in self‑defence if — (a) the person believes the act is necessary to defend the person or another person from a harmful act, including a harmful act that is not imminent; and (b) the person’s harmful act is a reasonable response by the person in the circumstances as the person believes them to be; and (c) there are reasonable grounds for those beliefs.
Criminal Code (WA), s 244(1A) Home invasion (applied in the Territory)
Despite subsection (1), it is not lawful for the occupant to use force that is intended, or that is likely, to cause death to a home invader unless the occupant believes, on reasonable grounds, that violence is being or is likely to be used or is threatened in relation to a person by a home invader.

b98063d59a649dd8.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Jersey

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Assault in Jersey is an offence 'contrary to customary law' (the indictment in Robertson v HM Attorney General [2023] JCA021 is in those words), and self-defence is likewise customary, not in a statute. The test the Royal Court puts to juries is set out in AG v Williams [2022] JRC103 (Royal Court, Deputy Bailiff MacRae, paras 32-35 quoting the summing-up) and repeated in Robertson [2023] JCA021 (Court of Appeal, para 14 quoting the same judge's summing-up): first, whether the defendant honestly believed force was necessary; second, whether the type and amount of force was reasonable, with force 'out of all proportion to the anticipated attack' or 'more force than is really necessary' being unreasonable; the Crown must disprove self-defence. Neither direction mentions retreat, and a search of all judgments on jerseylaw.je for 'retreat' with self-defence returned only a sentencing judgment using the word descriptively (AG v Porter [2024] JRC112). In Robertson the summing-up noted as a fact that the defendant 'accepted that before he kicked his brother in the head he could have walked off', but no court statement on whether retreat is required was found, so the retreat question is unsettled on the sources opened. Nothing was found on a separate rule for the home.

What the law says
AG v Williams [2022] JRC103 (Royal Court), paras 32-34, quoting the jury direction on self-defence
32. First, you must ask yourself whether the Defendant honestly believed that it was necessary to use force to defend himself at all. If you are sure that he did not honestly believe it was necessary to use force to defend himself, he cannot have been acting in self-defence and you must return a verdict of guilty. 33. But if you think the Defendant did honestly believe or may honestly have believed that it was necessary to use force to defend himself, you must move on to the second question which is to decide whether the type and amount of force the Defendant used was reasonable. Obviously a person who is under attack may react on the spur of the moment and he cannot be expected to work out exactly how much force he needs to use to defend himself. On the other hand, if he goes over the top and uses force out of all proportion to the anticipated attack on him, or more force than is really necessary to defend himself, the force used would not be reasonable. So you must take into account both the nature of any anticipated attack on the Defendant and what he in fact did. 34. If you are sure that the force the Defendant used was unreasonable, the Defendant cannot have been acting in lawful self-defence and you must return a verdict of guilty. If you think the force that the Defendant used was or may have been reasonable, then you must find him not guilty.
Robertson v HM Attorney General [2023] JCA021 (Court of Appeal), para 1 (the charge) and para 14 (summing-up quoted)
Statement of Offence Grave and criminal assault, contrary to customary law [...] As he has raised that defence, it is for the Crown to prove that he was not acting in self-defence. I will now direct you on the law in respect of self-defence. First you must ask yourselves whether the Defendant honestly believed that it was necessary to use force to defend himself (or to protect other persons and their property from attack) at all.
What was tried

jerseylaw.je loads fine by direct download; its search is a SharePoint REST endpoint (/_api/search/query) which was queried directly. Queries: '"self-defence"' over all judgments (106 hits; read Williams, Robertson, Withe); '"duty to retreat" OR retreat self-defence' (4 hits, all AG v Porter, where 'retreat' is a factual description of the victim); 'self-defence (householder OR "his own home" OR castle)' (2 sentencing hits); Jersey Law Reports index for 'self-defence' and 'retreat' (0 relevant hits). Web search for Jersey self-defence retreat returned only New Jersey (USA) results. BAILII /je/cases/ is behind an Anubis bot check from this shell. Not tried: the Jersey Law Commission, or JLR notes not indexed by the stub search.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

57a3fb9a615abc9b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Niue

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Niue's criminal offences used to be in Part 5 of the Niue Act 1966 (including a section 238 headed 'Common law defences'), but the New Zealand reprint shows that all of Part 5 was repealed in Niue on 20 September 2007 by the Niue Amendment Act 2007; the law that now sets out offences and defences in Niue was not opened here, so no statutory self-defence text is quoted. In Police v Tatui (High Court of Niue, 14 March 2019) Chief Judge Coxhead asked 'whether the force used in defending himself in the circumstances was reasonable', called reasonable force 'an objective test' judged on the threat as the defendant believed it to exist, and noted that a person must act on the instant without hindsight. He found 'the alternatives to defending himself were few, and in fact in my view were none', held that getting a gun to defend himself was reasonable, and acquitted the defendant. The decision weighs alternatives but does not state whether there is a duty to retreat, so the question is not settled by the sources opened.

What the law says
Police v Tatui [2019] NUHC 7 (High Court of Niue, Coxhead CJ) (excerpts)
whether the force used in defending himself in the circumstances was reasonable [...] Reasonable force is an objective test [...] the alternatives to defending himself were few, and in fact in my view were none
Niue Act 1966 (NZ), s. 238 'Common law defences' (repealed)
[Repealed] Section 238: repealed, on 20 September 2007, by section 5 of the Niue Amendment Act 2007 (2007 No 71).

e83d6644dfc7d685.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Gaza Strip

Part of Palestine, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Gaza applies the British Mandate Criminal Code Ordinance 1936, not the Jordanian code used in the West Bank. Its section 18 excuses an act done 'only in order to avoid consequences which could not otherwise be avoided' and which would have caused grievous harm to the person, honour or property of oneself or others one is bound to protect, provided the person did no more than was reasonably necessary and the harm caused was not disproportionate. The text does not use the word 'retreat', but the defence applies only where the harm could not otherwise be avoided. No Gaza court decisions on retreat were found. (Text taken from the Palestine file's sources; no new research was done for this split.)

At home

No home-defence rule was found in the Gaza code text.

What the law says
Criminal Code Ordinance 1936 (Gaza), s. 18
An act or omission which would otherwise be an offence may be excused if the person accused can show that it was done or omitted to be done only in order to avoid consequences which could not otherwise be avoided, and which if they had followed would have inflicted grievous harm or injury to his person or to his honour or his property or to the person or honour of others whom he was bound to protect or to property placed in his charge: Provided that in so acting he did no more than was reasonably necessary for that purpose, and that the harm inflicted by the act or omission was not disproportionate to the harm avoided.
Sources (read 2026-10-18)
  • Self-defence – national proceedings: Palestine (Cooperation and Judicial Assistance Database (CJAD), University of Nottingham)
Palestine as a whole

Palestinian territory has two different penal codes. In Gaza, the British Mandate Criminal Code Ordinance 1936 excuses an act done 'only in order to avoid consequences which could not otherwise be avoided' and which would have caused grievous harm to the person, honour or property of oneself or others one must protect, provided the person did no more than reasonably necessary and the harm caused was not disproportionate (s. 18). In the West Bank, the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960 applies; in the Jordanian text opened, killing or wounding in defence of oneself, one's honour or another person is legitimate only if done during the attack, the attack is unjust, and the person 'is unable to rid himself of this attack except by killing, wounding or the effective act' (art. 341(1)), and excess in defence may lead to exemption from punishment under the conditions of art. 89 (art. 60(3)). Both texts therefore make the defence depend on there being no other way out. The Jordanian copy opened is Jordan's own text amended to 2011; the West Bank applies the 1960 code without Jordan's post-1967 amendments, so the exact West Bank wording could not be confirmed. No court decisions on retreat were found for either territory.

73fa514276c773c0.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Singapore

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Under the Penal Code 1871, nothing done in the exercise of the right of private defence is an offence (s. 96). Deadly force is allowed against an assault the defender reasonably believes will otherwise cause death or grievous hurt, or is intended to commit rape, sexual penetration, kidnapping or abduction, or certain wrongful confinement (s. 102). Since 2020 (Act 15 of 2019), s. 98 says the right does not extend to more harm than is reasonably necessary and does not exist where there is a 'reasonable opportunity to have recourse to the protection of a public authority'. The Court of Appeal in Tan Chor Jin v PP [2008] SGCA 32 held (on the older s. 99(3)) that the defender must show there was no time to seek the protection of public authorities, that this test is objective and means 'reasonable opportunity of redress by recourse to the public authorities', and that the defender need not seek that protection if the time needed would let the harm be completed; it also said an aggressor, or a defender armed with a deadly weapon from the outset, is unlikely to have the right. Neither the code nor that decision says whether a safe chance to run away (as opposed to calling the authorities) defeats the defence, so the retreat question is left unsettled.

At home

No separate dwelling rule; s. 102-type limits apply. Killing while exceeding the right, without premeditation and without intending more harm than necessary, is culpable homicide not murder (s. 300, Exception 2).

What the law says
Penal Code 1871, s. 96
Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.
Penal Code 1871, s. 98 (as amended by Act 15 of 2019)
(1) The right of private defence does not extend to the inflicting of more harm than it is reasonably necessary in the circumstances. (2) There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is reasonable opportunity to have recourse to the protection of a public authority in the circumstances. Illustrations (a) Z ambushes A in a secluded area and attempts to kill A. A kills Z while fending off Z's attack. A is guilty of no offence because, in the circumstances, A had no reasonable opportunity to have recourse to the protection of a public authority. (b) Z ambushes A in a secluded area and attempts to kill A. A's right of private defence arises because, at that point of time, A had no reasonable opportunity to have recourse to the protection of a public authority. In the midst of the struggle between A and Z, a police patrol car arrives on the scene. A's right of private defence ceases the moment A had reasonable opportunity to have recourse to the protection of the police.
Penal Code 1871, s. 102 (extract)
The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in sections 98 and 106A, to the voluntary causing of death to the assailant, if the offence which gives rise to the exercise of the right is of any of the following descriptions: (a) an assault where the defender reasonably believes that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; (b) an assault where the defender reasonably believes that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; ...
Penal Code 1871, s. 300, Exception 2
Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, in the exercise of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law, and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence, without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
Court of Appeal, Tan Chor Jin v Public Prosecutor [2008] SGCA 32
(b) The defender must show that there was no time to seek the protection of public authorities. This is to conform to the second precondition stated at [39] above, viz, s 99(3) of the Penal Code. The test for whether the defender had time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities is an objective one. In this regard, it should be noted that the Indian cases appear, quite correctly, to equate the words “time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities” (see s 99(3) of the Penal Code) with “reasonable opportunity of redress by recourse to the public authorities” … Further, the defender should not be expected to seek the protection of the public authorities if the time needed to do so would result in the mischief being completed … (c) If the defender was the aggressor at the material time, it is prima facie less likely that he had a right of private defence … if, for instance the defender was armed with a deadly weapon from the outset, it is very unlikely that the right of private defence would ever arise.

951effb22a308594.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Utah

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Utah's Criminal Code allows deadly force only when a person reasonably believes it necessary to prevent death or serious bodily injury from imminent unlawful force, or to prevent a forcible felony such as aggravated assault, murder, kidnapping, rape, robbery, arson or burglary (Utah Code 76-2-402(2)). A person has no duty to retreat 'in a place where that individual has lawfully entered or remained', and failure to retreat is not a relevant factor in judging whether they acted reasonably (76-2-402(4)); this covers public places, vehicles and workplaces. The justification is lost by someone who provoked force as an excuse to injure, is committing or fleeing a felony (unless the force responds to unrelated factors), or was the aggressor or in an agreed fight unless they withdrew and said so; staying in an ongoing relationship or a place one has a right to be is not by itself 'combat by agreement'. Juries may consider the nature and immediacy of the danger, the other person's past violence and any pattern of abuse in the relationship (76-2-402(5)). For homes, vehicles and workplaces, 76-2-405 gives a presumption of reasonable fear in both civil and criminal cases. Since 2021 (Chapter 147, 2021 General Session) a defendant may ask for a pretrial justification hearing: once they make a prima facie claim, the state must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the force was not justified, or the charge is dismissed with prejudice (76-2-309); the hearing is not available for domestic-violence charges, minor offences, or force against an identified officer acting lawfully. No separate civil immunity statute was found in these sections.

At home

Utah Code 76-2-405 (version in force 1 May 2024) allows force to stop an unlawful entry into one's vehicle or an unlawful entry or attack on one's habitation or place of business or employment, and deadly force if the entry is violent, tumultuous or stealthy and aimed at personal violence, or is to commit a felony in the habitation. Anyone using force or deadly force against an unlawful forcible, violent, stealthy or felonious entry into their habitation is presumed, in both civil and criminal cases, to have acted reasonably and with reasonable fear of death or serious injury; a similar presumption covers occupied vehicles and places of business or employment.

What the law says
Utah Code 76-2-402(4) (as amended 2022)
Except as provided in Subsection (3)(a)(iii): (a) an individual does not have a duty to retreat from the force or threatened force described in Subsection (2) in a place where that individual has lawfully entered or remained; and (b) the failure of an individual to retreat under the provisions of Subsection (4)(a) is not a relevant factor in determining whether the individual who used or threatened force acted reasonably.
Utah Code 76-2-402(2)(b)
An individual is justified in using force intended or likely to cause death or serious bodily injury only if the individual reasonably believes that force is necessary to prevent death or serious bodily injury to the individual or another individual as a result of imminent use of unlawful force, or to prevent the commission of a forcible felony.
Utah Code 76-2-405(3)(a) (habitation presumption)
An actor who uses force or deadly force against an individual to defend the actor's habitation is presumed for the purpose of both civil and criminal cases to have acted reasonably and had a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or serious bodily injury if the entry or attempted entry is: (i) unlawful; and (ii) made or attempted: (A) by use of force; (B) in a violent and tumultuous manner; (C) surreptitiously or by stealth; or (D) for the purpose of committing a felony.
Utah Code 76-2-309(3)(b) (pretrial justification hearing, 2021)
At the pretrial justification hearing, after the defendant makes a prima facie claim of justification, the state has the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant's use or threatened use of force was not justified.

There are two different standards used when reviewing a claim of self-defense. When one is threatened with imminent serious bodily harm or death by another he may justifiably use deadly force if necessary to protect himself from great bodily harm or death.

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

San Marino

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

San Marino's Criminal Code (Law no. 17 of 25 February 1974) says, in article 41 ('Legittima difesa'), that a person is not punishable if forced by the need to defend their own or another's right against the present danger of an unjust attack, provided the threatened right is not of minimal importance compared with the right harmed and there is proportion between the means of defence used and those available. The code does not mention retreat or the home, and no San Marino court decisions on whether a person must avoid the attack were found. If the defender negligently exceeds the limits set by necessity, the penalties for negligent offences ('delitti') apply instead (art. 45, 'Eccesso colposo'). The text read is the code as originally published in 1974 on the Great and General Council's site; later amendments to these articles, if any, were not checked.

What the law says
Codice penale (Legge 25 febbraio 1974 n. 17), art. 41 Legittima difesa (original text)
Non è punibile chi ha commesso il fatto per essere stato costretto dalla necessità di difendere un diritto proprio od altrui contro il pericolo attuale di un'offesa ingiusta, sempre che il diritto minacciato non sia di minima importanza rispetto al diritto leso e vi sia proporzione fra i mezzi di difesa usati e quelli disponibili.
Codice penale 1974, art. 45 Eccesso colposo
Quando nel commettere il fatto si eccedono colposamente i limiti stabiliti dalla legge o dall'ordine dell'autorità ovvero imposti dalla necesità, si applicano le pene previste per i delitti.

f0406a9441f818e3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

District of Columbia

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

The District of Columbia has no self-defence statute; the rules come from D.C. Court of Appeals decisions and the standard 'Redbook' Criminal Jury Instructions. Deadly force is allowed when a person actually and reasonably believes they are in danger of death or serious bodily harm and that deadly force is necessary to repel it. D.C. takes what its highest court calls a 'middle ground' between 'the right to stand and kill, and the duty to retreat to the wall' (Gillis v. United States, 400 A.2d 311 (D.C. 1979)): there is no duty to retreat when the person actually and reasonably believes deadly force is necessary, but a person should take reasonable steps, such as stepping back or walking away, consistent with their own safety, and the jury may consider whether they could have done so when judging whether they acted reasonably (Redbook Instruction 9.503; Broadie v. United States, 925 A.2d 605 (D.C. 2007)). So retreat is not a strict legal requirement but is a factor the jury weighs. An aggressor, or a person who deliberately goes where their presence will provoke trouble, cannot claim self-defence unless they withdraw in good faith and communicate the withdrawal; words alone never justify force; and force may not be used against a police officer making a stop or arrest unless the officer uses excessive force. The sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit.

At home

No statute. According to the Metropolitan Police Department's self-defence training material based on D.C. case law, a person may use reasonable non-deadly force to protect their home or business from an imminent unlawful trespass or to eject a trespasser, and may use deadly force if they reasonably believe an intruder is entering the home or business intending to commit a felony (such as murder, rape, robbery or burglary) or to seriously harm an occupant. There is no statutory presumption of reasonable fear.

What the law says
Criminal Jury Instructions for the District of Columbia (Redbook), Instruction 9.503, Self-Defense—No Duty to Retreat Before Using Deadly Force
The law does not require a person to retreat or consider retreating when s/he actually and reasonably believes that s/he is in danger of death or serious bodily harm and that deadly force is necessary to repel that danger. But the law does say that a person should take reasonable steps, such as stepping back or walking away, to avoid the necessity of taking a human life, so long as those steps are consistent with the person’s own safety. In deciding whether [name of defendant] acted reasonably, you should therefore consider whether s/he could have taken those steps, consistent with his/her own safety.
Gillis v. United States, 400 A.2d 311, 313 (D.C. 1979), as quoted in the Redbook comment
This instruction represents the “middle ground” between “the right to stand and kill, and the duty to retreat to the wall before killing,”
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Instructions to Trainers Concerning Law of Self-Defense (District law pertaining to self-defense, with Redbook instructions 9.500–9.5xx) (Metropolitan Police Department, District of Columbia)

1d3ac66352fe4192.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Aruba

Part of Kingdom of the Netherlands, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Aruba has its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht van Aruba). The Court of First Instance of Aruba states the rule as: self-defence succeeds only if the act was 'required by the necessary defence' of one's own or another's body, honour or property against an immediate, unlawful attack (ECLI:NL:OGEAA:2020:100). In a 2017 homicide case (ECLI:NL:OGEAA:2017:310) the court rejected self-defence because getting away from the attacker (locking doors, calling for help, or fleeing the building) was 'really possible and could be required' of the defendant, so further defence was not necessary; it also found the stabbing far out of proportion. Courts also consider 'noodweerexces' (excessive self-defence caused by a violent emotion from the attack), which can remove punishment, but reject it where the response was grossly disproportionate or showed calm purpose. The exact article number of the Aruban code was not confirmed from a source opened here.

At home

No separate home-defence rule was found in the decisions opened; the general test covers defence of body, honour and property ('lijf, eerbaarheid of goed').

What the law says
Gerecht in eerste aanleg van Aruba, ECLI:NL:OGEAA:2020:100
Een beroep op noodweer kan slechts slagen indien het begane feit geboden is door de noodzakelijke verdediging van eigen of andermans lijf, eerbaarheid of goed tegen een ogenblikkelijke, wederrechtelijke aanranding.
Gerecht in eerste aanleg van Aruba, ECLI:NL:OGEAA:2017:310, r.o. 7.12
Het gerecht is dan ook van oordeel dat het zich onttrekken op de hiervoor genoemde wijzen reëel mogelijk was en ook van de verdachte kon worden gevergd, waardoor de door de verdachte gekozen verdere verdediging, zo dit al als verdediging kan worden gezien, niet noodzakelijk was.
Gerecht in eerste aanleg van Aruba, ECLI:NL:OGEAA:2017:310, r.o. 7.14 (noodweerexces)
is het gerecht van oordeel dat niet aannemelijk is geworden dat de overschrijding van de grenzen van een noodzakelijke verdediging het onmiddellijk gevolg is geweest van een hevige gemoedsbeweging die is veroorzaakt door de aanranding, waarbij het gerecht belang heeft toegekend aan de grote mate van disproportionaliteit van het door de verdachte toegepaste geweld.

5717ccfeb873b850.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Saint Barthelemy

Part of France, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Saint-Barthélemy is a French overseas collectivity. The French Senate notes that 'the State alone is competent in criminal law and criminal procedure' there, and IEDOM states that national laws apply directly outside the collectivity's own fields. French criminal law applies here because criminal law is reserved to the French State and national laws apply automatically ('identité législative'). Under art. 122-5 of the French Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. Art. 122-6 presumes self-defence against night-time break-ins into a home and against violent theft. Neither article mentions retreat, and no French source opened for this entry addresses whether flight is expected. See the France entry for more detail.

At home

French Penal Code art. 122-6 presumes self-defence for a person who acts to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, or to defend against violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal (France), art. 122-5, al. 1
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte.
Code pénal (France), art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

f82b1a27ecf273f2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Monaco

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 258 of Monaco's Penal Code says there is no crime or offence when homicide, wounds or blows were 'commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence' of oneself or another; Article 259 adds that this necessity covers repelling a night-time break-in into an inhabited home and defence against violent theft or pillage. Killing or wounding provoked by serious blows or violence is 'excusable' (art. 253), as is repelling a daytime break-in (art. 254). The code does not mention retreat. LégiMonaco's case-law explorer was opened but its full-text search runs through a script endpoint that returned HTTP 403 from the shell, so no Monegasque decision on whether a defender must retreat could be found. Nothing settles the retreat question.

At home

Article 259 counts as 'current necessity of defence' killing or wounding while repelling, at night, the scaling or breaking of the fences, walls or entrances of an inhabited house or apartment or its outbuildings; by day the same act is only 'excusable' (art. 254).

What the law says
Code pénal (Monaco), articles 258-259
Article 258: Il n'y a ni crime ni délit, lorsque l'homicide, les blessures et les coups étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d'autrui. Article 259: Entrent dans la nécessité actuelle de défense : 1° L'homicide commis, les blessures faites ou les coups portés en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d'une maison ou d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances ; 2° La défense opposée aux auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence. [Our rendering: Art. 258: There is neither crime nor offence when the homicide, wounds or blows were commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence of oneself or another. Art. 259: The current necessity of defence includes: 1. homicide, wounds or blows in repelling, at night, the scaling or breaking of the fences, walls or entrances of an inhabited house or apartment or their outbuildings; 2. defence against perpetrators of theft or pillage carried out with violence.]

Suggested next step: search 'légitime défense' 'nécessité actuelle' Monaco Cour de révision / Tribunal correctionnel on legimonaco.mc through a browser.

dd8e3235d03cf696.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Montserrat

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Montserrat's Penal Code (Cap. 4.02) s. 16 leaves force in defence of person or property to the common law, and s. 17 allows force 'reasonable in the circumstances' to prevent crime. A Montserrat appeal (Kenroy Hyman, 2012) confirms the prosecution must disprove self-defence. No Montserrat source on retreat was found. The Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal, which also hears this place's appeals, has upheld 'no duty to retreat' directions in cases from the British Virgin Islands (Shonovia Thomas, 2012), Antigua and Barbuda (Kevil Nelson, 2013) and Saint Vincent (Marshall Phillips, 2024), but no decision from this place itself saying so was found, so the category stays unclear.

What the law says
Kenroy Hyman v The Commissioner of Police (Montserrat), 2012
It is the prosecution which must negative self-defence.
What was tried

80768ad89389fcfd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Norfolk Island

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Norfolk Island, an Australian external territory, keeps its own Criminal Code 2007 (NI), a continued law administered on the Federal Register of Legislation; its self-defence rule (s 42) is the same model as the Commonwealth and ACT Codes. Conduct is self-defence only if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or someone else (or for listed property and trespass purposes) and it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceive them. The section does not mention retreat and no duty to retreat is stated; no court decision on retreat was opened. Intentionally inflicting death or serious harm solely to protect property or deal with trespassers is excluded.

At home

No home-specific rule; force intentionally inflicting death or serious harm may not be used only to protect property or to prevent or remove a criminal trespasser (s 42(3)).

What the law says
Criminal Code 2007 (NI), s 42 Self-defence
(1) A person is not criminally responsible for an offence if the person carries out the conduct required for the offence in self-defence. (2) A person carries out conduct in self-defence only if— (a) the person believes the conduct is necessary— (i) to defend himself or herself or someone else; ... and (b) the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them. (3) However, the person does not carry out conduct in self-defence if— (a) the person uses force that involves the intentional infliction of death or serious harm— (i) to protect property; or (ii) to prevent criminal trespass; or (iii) to remove a person committing criminal trespass; or (b) the person is responding to lawful conduct that the person knows is lawful.

9472e78509f1f6ba.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nauru

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Nauru's Crimes Act 2016 (s 51) says a person is not criminally responsible if they act in self-defence, which requires (among other things) that the conduct is 'a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them'. The Act does not mention retreat, but the Supreme Court weighs other options when deciding whether force was a reasonable response: in Republic v Andrews (2026) it quoted the English case R v Wang that there may be 'a number of alternative courses of action open, other than the use of force', and rejected self-defence for a second blow struck on the road more than 100 metres from the house against an unarmed, weakened man with his back turned, noting the accused 'could have stayed at home and called the police'. The prosecution must disprove self-defence beyond reasonable doubt; in that case the accused was convicted of intentionally causing serious harm. The sources opened did not cover a special home rule or a partial 'excessive self-defence' verdict.

What the law says
Crimes Act 2016 (Nauru), s 51(1) and (2)(b) (as set out in Republic v Andrews [2026] NRSC 12)
(1) A person is not criminally responsible for an offence if the person engages in the conduct constituting the offence in self-defence. ... The conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them.
Republic v Andrews [2026] NRSC 12 (Supreme Court, Keteca J, 23 February 2026)
There may well be a number of alternative courses of action open, other than the use of force, to a person subjected to a threat which cannot be carried out immediately. ... He could have stayed at home and called the police. He didn't.

e04347f2bbcd7e4b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Sint Maarten

Part of Kingdom of the Netherlands, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Sint Maarten, a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, has had its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht van Sint Maarten) since 1 June 2015, which carried over the old Netherlands Antilles rule 'in slightly different words but materially unchanged'. Article 1:114 makes conduct not punishable if it is 'required by the necessary defence' against an immediate unlawful attack on the body, sexual integrity or property of oneself or another. Cases from Sint Maarten go on final appeal to the Dutch Supreme Court, and its Advocate-General applied the Supreme Court's 2016 overview ruling in a Sint Maarten police shooting case: self-defence fails if the person not only could but also should have withdrawn from the attack, which requires a real and reasonable chance to get away. Exceeding the limits of necessary defence is not punishable if it was the immediate result of a violent emotion caused by the unlawful attack (art. 1:115(c), noodweerexces). No special rule for the home was found.

What the law says
Wetboek van Strafrecht van Sint Maarten, arts 1:114(1)(b) and 1:115(c) (as quoted in ECLI:NL:PHR:2018:595, para 7)
Artikel 1:114 “1. Niet strafbaar is een gedraging: […]; b. geboden door de noodzakelijke verdediging tegen de ogenblikkelijke wederrechtelijke aanranding van lijf, eerbaarheid of goed van de dader zelf of een ander; […].” Artikel 1:115 Niet strafbaar is hij die een gedraging pleegt: […] c. die door het onmiddellijk gevolg van een hevige gemoedsbeweging door een wederrechtelijke aanranding veroorzaakt, de grenzen van de noodzakelijke verdediging tegen de ogenblikkelijke wederrechtelijke aanranding van lijf, eerbaarheid of goed van hem of een ander overschrijdt; […].”
Conclusion of the Advocate-General, ECLI:NL:PHR:2018:595, para 7 (on the 2015 code)
Bij Landsverordening van 13 december 2012 is op 1 juni 2015 een nieuw Wetboek van Strafrecht van Sint Maarten (verder: SrStM) in werking getreden (AB Sint Maarten, 2013, no. 2). Het bepaalde van art. 43 SrNA (oud) is, in iets andere bewoordingen maar materieel onveranderd, overgeheveld naar de artikelen art. 1:114 en 1:115 SrStM
Hoge Raad 22 March 2016, ECLI:NL:HR:2016:456, r.o. 3.5.2 (as quoted in ECLI:NL:PHR:2018:595, para 8)
Aan de subsidiariteitseis is niet voldaan indien de verdachte zich niet behoefde te verdedigen en er dus geen noodzaak tot verdediging bestond. Daarvan is bijvoorbeeld sprake indien de verdachte zich niet alleen aan de aanranding had kunnen, maar zich daaraan ook had moeten onttrekken. Bij de verwerping van een beroep op noodweer kan dus niet worden volstaan met het enkele argument dat de verdachte zich aan de aanranding had kunnen onttrekken. Het zich aan de aanranding kunnen onttrekken houdt in dat daartoe voor de verdachte een reële en redelijke mogelijkheid moet hebben bestaan.

c5a494fbf211dc86.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Colorado

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Colorado's statute allows deadly force only if a person reasonably believes a lesser degree of force is inadequate and they have reasonable ground to believe, and do believe, that they or another person face imminent danger of death or great bodily injury, or the other person is committing burglary against an occupant of a dwelling or business, or kidnapping, robbery, sexual assault or certain assaults (Colo. Rev. Stat. § 18-1-704(2)). The statute does not mention retreat, but the Colorado Supreme Court has held that 'only initial aggressors must retreat before using force in self-defense' (Cassels v. People, 92 P.3d 951 (Colo. 2004)), and in People v. Monroe, 2020 CO 67, it held that prosecutors may not argue that a defendant acted unreasonably because they failed to retreat. The no-retreat rule therefore applies anywhere, by case law rather than statute. Force is not justified for someone who provoked the other intending to injure them, for an initial aggressor who has not withdrawn and clearly communicated it, in a fight by agreement, or (since SB 20-221 in 2020) when the force is based on discovering or disclosing the victim's gender, gender identity or sexual orientation (the 'panic defence' ban) (§ 18-1-704(3)). In the home, the 1985 'Make My Day' law gives occupants who use force against an unlawful intruder immunity from both criminal prosecution and civil liability (§ 18-1-704.5). Outside that home rule there is no statutory immunity from prosecution; self-defence is an affirmative defence that the prosecution must disprove, except for crimes of recklessness or negligence, where the jury is told it may consider the evidence but the prosecution does not bear that burden (§ 18-1-704(4), added 2003).

At home

Colo. Rev. Stat. § 18-1-704.5 (the 'Make My Day' law, added 1985, L. 85 p. 662): any occupant of a dwelling may use any degree of force, including deadly force, against a person who has made an unlawful entry, if the occupant reasonably believes the intruder has committed or intends to commit a crime in addition to the entry and might use any physical force, 'no matter how slight', against an occupant. An occupant who acts within the section is immune from criminal prosecution and from civil liability. Since 2016 'dwelling' excludes cells in detention facilities.

What the law says
Colo. Rev. Stat. § 18-1-704(2)
Deadly physical force may be used only if a person reasonably believes a lesser degree of force is inadequate and: (a) The actor has reasonable ground to believe, and does believe, that he or another person is in imminent danger of being killed or of receiving great bodily injury ...
Colo. Rev. Stat. § 18-1-704(3)
a person is not justified in using physical force if: (a) With intent to cause bodily injury or death to another person, he provokes the use of unlawful physical force by that other person; or (b) He or she is the initial aggressor; except that his or her use of physical force upon another person under the circumstances is justifiable if he or she withdraws from the encounter and effectively communicates to the other person his or her intent to do so ...; (c) The physical force involved is the product of a combat by agreement not specifically authorized by law ...
Colo. Rev. Stat. § 18-1-704.5(2)–(4)
any occupant of a dwelling is justified in using any degree of physical force, including deadly physical force, against another person when that other person has made an unlawful entry into the dwelling ... (3) Any occupant of a dwelling using physical force, including deadly physical force, in accordance with the provisions of subsection (2) of this section shall be immune from criminal prosecution for the use of such force. (4) ... shall be immune from any civil liability for injuries or death resulting from the use of such force.
People v. Monroe, 2020 CO 67, ¶19 (quoting Cassels v. People, 92 P.3d 951, 956 (Colo. 2004))
“In Colorado, only initial aggressors must retreat before using force in self- defense.” ... So, a non-aggressor may assert self-defense without (1) considering whether a reasonable person would retreat to safety rather than resorting to physical force, or (2) actually retreating from an attack even if she could safely do so.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • People v. Monroe, 2020 CO 67, No. 18SC708 (Colo. June 29, 2020) (Colorado Supreme Court)

9fbc54f06d017f9a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Wyoming

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Wyoming's self-defence statute (W.S. 6-2-602) says defensive force is reasonable when a reasonable person in like circumstances would judge it necessary to prevent injury or loss, 'and no more', including deadly force if necessary to prevent imminent death or serious bodily injury to oneself or another; necessity includes an honest belief that the danger exists, whether real or apparent. A person attacked in any place where they are lawfully present has no duty to retreat before using reasonable defensive force, as long as they are not the initial aggressor and are not engaged in illegal activity (6-2-602(e)); this covers public places, vehicles and workplaces. A presumption of reasonable fear applies to deadly force used against someone forcibly and unlawfully breaking into a home or habitation. A person who uses reasonable defensive force 'shall not be criminally prosecuted' for it (6-2-602(f)), which is a form of criminal immunity; no statutory procedure for a pretrial immunity hearing or civil immunity provision was found in this section. The common law governs any case the article does not cover (6-2-601). The year these provisions were enacted (commonly reported as 2018) was not confirmed from a primary source for this entry.

At home

A person using defensive force, including deadly force, is presumed to have reasonable fear of death or serious injury when the intruder was unlawfully and forcibly entering, or had forcibly entered, another's home or habitation (including trailers, campers and tents), or was dragging someone out; the intruder is presumed to intend violence (W.S. 6-2-602(b), (d)). The presumption does not apply against a lawful resident without a protection order, a parent or guardian taking their own child, or a peace officer or corrections employee entering on duty.

What the law says
W.S. 6-2-602(e)
A person who is attacked in any place where the person is lawfully present shall not have a duty to retreat before using reasonable defensive force pursuant to subsection (a) of this section provided that he is not the initial aggressor and is not engaged in illegal activity.
W.S. 6-2-602(a)
The use of defensive force whether actual or threatened, is reasonable when it is the defensive force that a reasonable person in like circumstances would judge necessary to prevent an injury or loss, and no more, including deadly force if necessary to prevent imminent death or serious bodily injury to the person employing the deadly force or to another person.
W.S. 6-2-602(b) (presumption)
A person is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or serious bodily injury to himself or another when using defensive force, including deadly force if: (i) The intruder against whom the defensive force was used was in the process of unlawfully and forcefully entering, or had unlawfully and forcibly entered, another's home or habitation ...
W.S. 6-2-602(f)
A person who uses reasonable defensive force as defined by subsection (a) of this section shall not be criminally prosecuted for that use of reasonable defensive force.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Wyoming Statutes Title 6 (Crimes and Offenses) (Wyoming Legislature)
  • Stand Your Ground in Wyoming (Giffords Law Center)

96f0e0aa9ad1f257.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bouvet Island

A dependency of Norway. Shown with the entry for Norway, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Under section 18 of the Norwegian Penal Code (2005), an otherwise punishable act is lawful when it is done to avert an unlawful attack, goes no further than necessary, and does not 'obviously' go beyond what is justifiable given how dangerous the attack is, what interest it violates and the attacker's guilt. The statute does not mention retreat, but because force must be 'necessary', a lawyer answering for the state youth-information service ung.no wrote in 2023 that if there were other ways to avert the attack, 'such as calling for help or running away', a killing cannot be claimed as self-defence; the Supreme Court's appeals committee has also upheld a conviction where the defendant had 'several alternative courses of action' and had partly provoked the fight (HR-2022-1377-U). Someone who goes too far can still be acquitted where 'special reasons' justify it, and the sentence can in any case be reduced (sections 80 and 81, as described by the national encyclopedia). Lawful self-defence is not just unpunished but lawful, so the Supreme Court held in 2018 (HR-2018-2427-A) that the defender cannot be ordered to pay damages when the attack was real.

At home

No separate home-defence rule was found; section 18 applies to attacks on persons and on property alike.

What the law says
Straffeloven (Penal Code 2005), § 18 første ledd (as quoted by the Supreme Court in HR-2022-1377-U)
En handling som ellers ville være straffbar, er lovlig når den a. blir foretatt for å avverge et ulovlig angrep, b. ikke går lenger enn nødvendig, og c. ikke går åpenbart ut over hva som er forsvarlig under hensyn til hvor farlig angrepet er, hva slags interesse som angrepet krenker, og angriperens skyld.

3af0a52ae017735a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ashmore and Cartier Islands

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Ashmore and Cartier Islands is an uninhabited Australian external territory. Under the Ashmore and Cartier Islands Acceptance Act 1933 (s. 6), the laws of the Northern Territory, including common-law rules, apply there so far as applicable, and Northern Territory courts have jurisdiction (s. 12). The Northern Territory Criminal Code allows 'defensive conduct' (s. 29) or 'self-defence' (s. 43BD) when the person believes the conduct is necessary to defend themselves or another and it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceive them. Neither section mentions retreat. See the Northern Territory entry for details.

At home

No home-specific rule: under the Northern Territory Criminal Code, which applies here, force intended to cause death or serious harm may not be used only to protect property, prevent trespass or remove a trespasser (s. 29(3); s. 43BD(3)).

What the law says
Ashmore and Cartier Islands Acceptance Act 1933 (Cth), s. 6
(1) Subject to this Act, a law of the Northern Territory as in force from time to time (including a law made before the commencement of this section) is, so far as applicable, in force in the Territory. (2) In subsection (1), law: (a) includes a principle or rule of common law or equity; and (b) does not include an Act.
Criminal Code Act 1983 (NT), s. 29(1)–(3) – Defensive conduct justified
(1) Defensive conduct is justified and a person who does, makes or causes an act, omission or event by engaging in defensive conduct is not criminally responsible for the act, omission or event. (2) A person engages in defensive conduct only if: (a) the person believes that the conduct is necessary: (i) to defend himself or herself or another person; [...] and (b) the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person reasonably perceives them. (3) A person does not engage in defensive conduct if the conduct involves the use of force intended to cause death or serious harm: (a) to protect property; or (b) to prevent trespass or remove a trespasser.
Criminal Code Act 1983 (NT), s. 43BD(1)–(2) – Self-defence (Schedule 1 and declared offences)
(1) A person is not criminally responsible for an offence if the person carries out the conduct constituting the offence in self-defence. (2) A person carries out conduct in self-defence only if: (a) the person believes the conduct is necessary: (i) to defend himself or herself or another person; [...] and (b) the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as he or she perceives them.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Criminal Code Act 1983 (NT) (Northern Territory Legislation)

220402b7daf75ac4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Brazilian Island

Part of Brazil, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

This entry is listed under Brazil, and Brazil's federal Penal Code is applied here; the island's territorial status was not checked against a source in this session. Under art. 25 of Brazil's Penal Code, self-defence covers a person who, "using the necessary means in moderation", repels an unjust current or imminent aggression; Brazilian legal teaching holds that flight is not required even when possible. The defender is liable for intentional or negligent excess (art. 23). See the Brazil entry for details.

At home

See Brazil: no separate home-defence rule in the Penal Code's general part.

What the law says
Código Penal (Brazil), art. 25
Art. 25 - Entende-se em legítima defesa quem, usando moderadamente dos meios necessários, repele injusta agressão, atual ou iminente, a direito seu ou de outrem.

bee1b48f44eabb2d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Gibraltar

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Gibraltar's Crimes Act 2011, s. 5, allows 'such force as is reasonable in the circumstances' to prevent crime or make an arrest; self-defence itself is left to the common law and the Act has no householder or retreat provision. In this run all 127 criminal judgments listed on the government's Gibraltar Law Reports site were downloaded and searched: three involve self-defence (Recio v R, 1988–90; Pannell v R, 1998; Lishman v R, 2019), and none mentions retreat. Retreat is not settled by a Gibraltar source.

What the law says
Crimes Act 2011 (Gibraltar), s. 5 (from previous entry)
5.(1) Subject to section 2 of the Constitution, a person may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances in the prevention of crime, or in effecting or assisting in the lawful arrest of offenders or suspected offenders or of persons unlawfully at large.
Lishman v R, Court of Appeal of Gibraltar, [2020 Gib LR 1] (6 Nov 2019), headnote
He pleaded not guilty on the basis of self-defence or loss of self-control under s.152 of the Crimes Act 2011.

gibraltarlaws.gov.gi judgment list (search box ignores query parameters, so every criminal case slug, 124, was fetched; 3 PDFs failed on malformed URLs).
